units.slavonic_diplomatic: CONCERNING THE CO-CELEBRANT When there are more than one priest co-celebrating, beginning with the evening, at Vespers, if an Entrance is to be performed, at least more than three priests must attend. They sing outside in the middle of the church in a semi-circle,¹ “O Gladsome Light” up to “and Holy Spirit, God.” They complete the rest of the hymn from inside the Holy Sanctuary. After that, the Prokimenon of the day is sung once from the Holy Sanctuary and twice from the outside. At the Liti, the clergyman first in order [rank or order of ordination] says “Hear us, O God” and “Peace be to all”; the second, “O Merciful Master,” and the third “Lord Jesus Christ our God”; then the first begins chanting “Theotokos Virgin” assisted by the others; but only he censes and circles around the Loaves with the Deacon.
units.english_cohort_translation: When more than one priest concelebrate, beginning in the evening at Vespers, if an Entrance is performed, at least three priests are required. Standing in the middle of the temple forming a semicircle,¹ they chant outside the Holy Sanctuary the Lucernarium hymn **“O Gladsome Light”** (*Φῶς ἱλαρὸν*) up to the phrase: **“and Holy Spirit, God”** (*καὶ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα θεόν*); and from within the Holy Sanctuary the remainder of the hymn is completed; and after it the Prokimenon of the day is chanted once from within the Holy Sanctuary and twice from outside. At the Litiya, the priest first in rank [by ecclesiastical dignity or order of ordination] intones the petition: **“Hear us, O God our Savior”** (*Ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν ὁ Θεός*), and the blessing: **“Peace be to all”** (*Εἰρήνη πᾶσι*); the second priest intones: **“O Merciful Master”** (*Δέσποτα πολυέλεε*); and the third priest intones: **“Lord Jesus Christ our God”** (*Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστὲ ὁ Θεός*); then the first priest begins the Artoklasia Troparion: **“O Theotokos Virgin, rejoice”** (*Θεοτόκε Παρθένε*), assisted by the others; but he alone censes and circles around the Loaves together with the Deacon.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the morning, the co-celebrating priests
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the morning, the co-celebrating priests sing nothing from the Holy Sanctuary except the usual and the one celebrating Priest, except “Come let us worship and bow down to Christ” at the Entrance. Then is sung the Apolytikion (during which the first in seniority of ordination censes the Holy Table and the Icons). Then follows the Kontakion, and “Holy God” the third time.² The Exclamations are recited by them in order, alternately one after the other. The clergyman first in order [rank or order of ordination] blesses the Holy Gifts and the people. The clergymen receive the Holy Gifts in order of seniority of ordination, and the last one in seniority gives communion to the Deacon.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the morning at the Divine Liturgy, the concelebrating priests chant nothing from within the Holy Sanctuary beyond what is customary for a priest celebrating alone, except the Entrance Hymn: **“O come, let us worship and fall down before Christ”** (*Δεῦτε προσκυνήσωμεν καὶ προσπέσωμεν Χριστῷ*) at the Small Entrance. Then is chanted the Dismissal Troparion (during which the priest first in seniority of ordination censes the Holy Table and the sacred Icons); then follows the Kontakion, and the Trisagion **“Holy God”** (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*) for the third time.² The priestly Exclamations are recited by them in order, alternately one after the other. The priest first in rank blesses the Precious Gifts as well as the people, whenever required; and they receive the Pure Mysteries each according to his rank, with the last priest in seniority imparting communion also to the Deacon.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: 2. units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on Priestly Concelebration and Order of Seniority:* Although all presbyters share equally in the sacerdotal grace of the priesthood and owe mutual honor and respect to one another, they nevertheless precede each other strictly according to their ecclesiastical offices (*offikia*) or according to seniority of ordination. Note the solemn patriarchal caution against liturgical accretions born of clerical ambition: presbyters must never chant the episcopal acclamation *“Lord, save the pious”* (*Κύριε σῶσον τοὺς εὐσεβεῖς*), nor may they introduce individual spoken commemorations of the living and the dead while holding the Holy Gifts after the Great Entrance, adhering strictly to the summary and established traditional formula: *“May the Lord God remember us all in His kingdom.”*

units.slavonic_incipit: κεκανονισμένης ὥρας· Εἶτα εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸ
units.slavonic_diplomatic: κεκανονισμένης ὥρας· Εἶτα εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸ Ἱερὸν δίδωσι καὶ λαμβάνει³ συγχώρησιν παρὰ τῶν μελλόντων συλλειτουργῆσαι καὶ οὕτως ἐνδύονται πάντες. Κατὰ τὴν Δοξολογίαν ἐξέρχονται, προηγουμένων τῶν Ἱερέων, καὶ τελευταῖος ἔρχεται ὁ προεξάρχων φέρων καὶ Μίτραν ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς καὶ τὴν Ποιμαντορικὴν ῥάβδον ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ χειρί. Κατὰ τὴν Εἴσοδον ψάλλων ἐν συνοδείᾳ καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν Ἀρχιερέων καὶ Ἱερέων τὸ Εἰσοδικὸν εὐλογεῖ μετὰ τῶν δικηροτρικήρων, εἰσέρχεται εἰς τὸ Βῆμα πρῶτος, ἑπομένων τῶν ἄλλων Ἀρχιερέων καὶ Ἱερέων, καὶ θυμιᾷ περὶ τὴν ἁγίαν Τράπεζαν καὶ τὴν Πρόθεσιν, τάς τε ἱερὰς Εἰκόνας ἐκ τῶν Βημοθύρων καὶ τὸν λαὸν ψάλλων τὸ Ἀπολυτίκιον⁴ καὶ τελευταῖον τὸ Κοντάκιον. Τὸ Ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς ἀφοῦ ψαλῇ δὶς ἔξωθεν, τὸ τρίτον λέγεται ἀπὸ τοῦ Βήματος, τὸ τέταρτον ἔξωθεν καὶ αὖθις τὸ πέμπτον ἔσωθεν. Εἶτα, Δόξα, Καὶ νῦν, ἔξωθεν, ὡς καὶ τὸ Ἅγιος ἀθάνατος, καὶ μετ’ αὐτὸ ψάλλεται πάλιν ἐκ τοῦ Βήματος ἀργότερον τὸ Ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς κατὰ Στάσεις τέσσαρας ἐναλλὰξ ὑπὸ τῶν δύο δεξιᾷ καὶ ἀριστερᾷ ἱσταμένων Ἀρχιερέων καὶ Ἱερέων καὶ εὐλογεῖ ὁ προεξάρχων διὰ τῶν δικηροτρικήρων λέγων τὸ Κύριε, Κύριε, ἐπίβλεψον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. Μετὰ τὸ Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς, ψάλλεται αὖθις ἔξωθεν ὑπὸ τοῦ δεξιοῦ Χοροῦ τὸ Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός, ἀφοῦ ὁ Διάκονος εἴπῃ τὴν Ἐκφώνησιν Δύναμις. Τότε ψάλλεται ἔσωθεν τὸ Κύριε σῶσον τοὺς εὐσεβεῖς καὶ ἔξωθεν ἐπαναλαμβάνεται δὶς ὑπὸ τῶν Χορῶν· αὖθις ἔσωθεν ψάλλεται τὸ Καὶ ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν. Εἶτα λέγεται ἡ φήμη τοῦ Πατριάρχου ἅπαξ ἔσωθεν καὶ δὶς ἔξωθεν, καὶ ἂν μὲν ὁ προεξάρχων ᾖ Μητροπολίτης καὶ οἱ συλλειτουργοὶ Ἐπίσκοποι, ψάλλεται καὶ ἡ τοῦ Μητροπολίτου φήμη, ἔσωθέν τε καὶ ἔξωθεν· ἂν δὲ πάντες ὦσι Μητροπολῖται ἢ πάντες Ἐπίσκοποι, παραλείπεται ἡ φήμη τοῦ πρώτου τῇ τάξει. Ἐν ἑκάστῃ εὐλογίας περιπτώσει εὐλογεῖ ὁ πρῶτος τῇ τάξει, καὶ οὗτος λαμβάνει τὰ Ἅγια ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ Διακόνου καὶ τοῦ Ἱερέως κατὰ τὴν δευτέραν Εἴσοδον καὶ μνημονεύει ζώντων τε καὶ τεθνεώτων· ἀλλ’ αἱ Ἐκφωνήσεις διανέμονται κατὰ σειρὰν εἰς τρόπον μέχρι καὶ τῶν συλλειτουργούντων Ἱερέων. Τὰ Ἅγια εὐλογεῖ μόνον ὁ προεξάρχων, ἀλλ’ οἱ Ἀρχιερεῖς κοινωνοῦσι τῶν Ἀχράντων Μυστηρίων ἰδίᾳ χειρί, οἱ δὲ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ Διάκονοι μετέχουσι τούτων παρὰ τοῦ τελευταίου τῇ τάξει Ἀρχιερέως.

Κατὰ τὴν Εἴσοδον ψάλλων ἐν συνοδείᾳ καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν Ἀρχιερέων καὶ Ἱερέων τὸ Εἰσοδικὸν εὐλογεῖ μετὰ τῶν δικηροτρικήρων, εἰσέρχεται εἰς τὸ Βῆμα πρῶτος, ἑπομένων τῶν ἄλλων Ἀρχιερέων καὶ Ἱερέων, καὶ θυμιᾷ περὶ τὴν ἁγίαν Τράπεζαν καὶ τὴν Πρόθεσιν, τάς τε ἱερὰς Εἰκόνας ἐκ τῶν Βημοθύρων καὶ τὸν λαὸν ψάλλων τὸ Ἀπολυτίκιον⁴ καὶ τελευταῖον τὸ Κοντάκιον.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: 4. Ἐὰν ᾖ Μνημόσυνον, ψάλλεται ἐκ τοῦ Βήματος μετὰ τὸ τοῦ Ἁγίου τῆς ἡμέρας Ἀπολυτίκιον καὶ τὸ τῶν Κεκοιμημένων Μνήσθητι Κύριε ὡς ἀγαθὸς τῶν δούλων σου.
units.english_cohort_translation: Εἶτα λέγεται ἡ φήμη τοῦ Πατριάρχου ἅπαξ ἔσωθεν καὶ δὶς ἔξωθεν, καὶ ἂν μὲν ὁ προεξάρχων ᾖ Μητροπολίτης καὶ οἱ συλλειτουργοὶ Ἐπίσκοποι, ψάλλεται καὶ ἡ τοῦ Μητροπολίτου φήμη, ἔσωθέν τε καὶ ἔξωθεν· ἂν δὲ πάντες ὦσι Μητροπολῖται ἢ πάντες Ἐπίσκοποι, παραλείπεται ἡ φήμη τοῦ πρώτου τῇ τάξει. Ἐν ἑκάστῃ εὐλογίας περιπτώσει εὐλογεῖ ὁ πρῶτος τῇ τάξει, καὶ οὗτος λαμβάνει τὰ Ἅγια ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ Διακόνου καὶ τοῦ Ἱερέως κατὰ τὴν δευτέραν Εἴσοδον καὶ μνημονεύει ζώντων τε καὶ τεθνεώτων· ἀλλ’ αἱ Ἐκφωνήσεις διανέμονται κατὰ σειρὰν εἰς τρόπον μέχρι καὶ τῶν συλλειτουργούντων Ἱερέων. Τὰ Ἅγια εὐλογεῖ μόνον ὁ προεξάρχων, ἀλλ’ οἱ Ἀρχιερεῖς κοινωνοῦσι τῶν Ἀχράντων Μυστηρίων ἰδίᾳ χειρί, οἱ δὲ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ Διάκονοι μετέχουσι τούτων παρὰ τοῦ τελευταίου τῇ τάξει Ἀρχιερέως.

units.slavonic_incipit: entering the Holy Sanctuary, he gives
units.slavonic_diplomatic: entering the Holy Sanctuary, he gives and receives³ forgiveness from his future co-celebrants, and thus they all vest. During the Doxology they exit the Holy Sanctuary preceded by the Priests, the last one to exit being the Chief Celebrant bearing the Miter on his head and the Pastoral Staff in his right hand. At the Entrance, singing with the rest of the Hierarchs and the Priests the Entrance Hymn, he blesses with the Dikirotrikira, enters the Holy Sanctuary first followed by the other Hierarchs and Priests, and censes around the Holy Table and the Prothesis*, the Icons and the people from the gates of the Holy Sanctuary, chanting the Apolytikion⁴ and lastly the Kontakion. The “Holy God,” after it is sung twice outside, the third is sung from the Holy Sanctuary, the fourth outside, and immediately the fifth inside. Then “Glory, Now and ever” outside, as well as “Holy Immortal”; and after that, again from the Holy Sanctuary “Holy God” is sung in a slower tempo in four segments alternately by the two ranks of Hierarchs and Priests standing on the right side and on the left. The Chief Celebrant blesses with the Dikirotrikira, chanting “Lord, Lord, look down from heaven.” After “Have mercy on us,” the right Choir sings “Holy God [the entire Trisagios Hymn]” as soon as the Deacon proclaims “Dynamis! [with Strength!]” Then, inside the Holy Sanctuary is sung “Lord, save the faithful”; it is repeated twice outside by the Choirs; then, inside is sung “And hear us.” Then the Fimi [Acclamation] of the Patriarch is sung once inside and twice outside. If the presiding Hierarch is a Metropolitan and the co-celebrants are Bishops, then the Fimi [Acclamation] of the Metropolitan is also sung, inside and outside; if they are all Metropolitans or all Bishops, the Fimi of the clergyman first in rank is omitted. In every situation of a blessing, the first in rank blesses, and he is the one who receives the Holy Gifts from the hands of the Deacon and the Priest during the Second Entrance and he commemorates the living and the dead; but the exclamations are divided in order and manner even down to the co-celebrating Priests. The Holy Gifts are blessed only by the Chief Celebrant, but the Hierarchs take communion by their own hand; the Priests and Deacons receive the Gifts from the Hierarch last in seniority of ordination.
units.english_cohort_translation: ...entering the Holy Sanctuary, he gives and receives³ forgiveness from his future concelebrants, and thus all vest. During the Great Doxology they process out of the Holy Sanctuary preceded by the priests, and the presiding hierarch comes out last, wearing the miter upon his head and holding the pastoral staff in his right hand. At the Small Entrance, chanting the Entrance Hymn together with the rest of the hierarchs and priests, he blesses with the dikerotrikera; he enters the Holy Sanctuary first, followed by the other hierarchs and priests, and censes around the Holy Table and the Table of Oblation [Prothesis], the holy icons from the Holy Doors, and the people, while chanting the Dismissal Troparion⁴ and finally the Kontakion.

Then “Glory, Now and ever” outside, as well as “Holy Immortal”; and after that, again from the Holy Sanctuary “Holy God” is sung in a slower tempo in four segments alternately by the two ranks of Hierarchs and Priests standing on the right side and on the left. The Chief Celebrant blesses with the Dikirotrikira, chanting “Lord, Lord, look down from heaven.” After “Have mercy on us,” the right Choir sings “Holy God [the entire Trisagios Hymn]” as soon as the Deacon proclaims “Dynamis! [with Strength!]” Then, inside the Holy Sanctuary is sung “Lord, save the faithful”; it is repeated twice outside by the Choirs; then, inside is sung “And hear us.” Then the Fimi [Acclamation] of the Patriarch is sung once inside and twice outside. If the presiding Hierarch is a Metropolitan and the co-celebrants are Bishops, then the Fimi [Acclamation] of the Metropolitan is also sung, inside and outside; if they are all Metropolitans or all Bishops, the Fimi of the clergyman first in rank is omitted. In every situation of a blessing, the first in rank blesses, and he is the one who receives the Holy Gifts from the hands of the Deacon and the Priest during the Second Entrance and he commemorates the living and the dead; but the exclamations are divided in order and manner even down to the co-celebrating Priests. The Holy Gifts are blessed only by the Chief Celebrant, but the Hierarchs take communion by their own hand; the Priests and Deacons receive the Gifts from the Hierarch last in seniority of ordination.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: * [The table inside the Holy Sanctuary on which the Holy Gifts are prepared for the Holy Eucharist.]
units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on Hierarchical Concelebration:* When bishops concelebrate with their presiding Metropolitan, or Metropolitans with their presiding Patriarch, the junior hierarchs kiss the right hand of the Primate upon exchanging the liturgical kiss of peace and mutual forgiveness before vesting. If a Memorial Service (*Mnemosynon*) coincides with the Liturgy, after the Dismissal Troparion of the saint of the day, the Dismissal Troparion of the Departed is chanted from within the Holy Sanctuary: *“Remember, O Lord, as Thou art good, Thy servants, and forgive whatever sins they have committed in this life; for none is sinless except Thee Who art able to grant rest unto the departed”* (*Μνήσθητι Κύριε ὡς ἀγαθὸς τῶν δούλων σου*). Notice the intricate four-stasis distribution of the slow hierarchical Trisagion between the right and left stations of the clergy framing the episcopal blessing with the dikirion and trikirion (*dikerotrikera*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Τελευτήσαντός τινος τῶν εὐσεβῶν, προσκαλεῖται παρὰ τῶν Συγγενῶν αὐτοῦ ὁ ἱερὸς Κλῆρος· ἐλθόντες δὲ εἰς τὸν οἶκον, ἐν ᾧ τὸ λείψανον κεῖται, ἐὰν ᾖ καὶ Ἀρχιερεύς, λαμβάνουσι καιρὸν οἱ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ Διάκονοι· καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἱερεῖς βάλλουσιν Ἐπιτραχήλια, οἱ δὲ Διάκονοι ἐνδύονται Στιχάρια καὶ Ὠράρια κρατοῦντες θυμιατὰ καὶ δικηροτρίκηρα, τότε εἷς Ἱερεὺς μετὰ Διακόνου εἰσέρχονται ὅπου ὁ νεκρὸς κεῖται, καὶ ὁ μὲν Διάκονος ἐκφωνεῖ Εὐλόγησον Δέσποτα, ὁ Ἱερεὺς Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ Διάκονος τὸ Τρισάγιον(2), ὁ Ἱερεὺς Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν, καὶ ψάλλουσιν εἰς ἦχον δ΄ τὰ Τροπάρια Μετὰ πνευμάτων δικαίων τετελειωμένων· Εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν σου Κύριε, ὅπου πάντες οἱ Ἅγιοί σου ἀναπαύονται· Δόξα, Σὺ εἶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, Καὶ νῦν, Ἡ μόνη Ἁγνὴ καὶ Ἄχραντος Παρθένος. Εἶτα ὁ Διάκονος Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου . . . ἔτι δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ ἀναπαύσεως (καὶ συγχωρήσεως(3)) τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦ κεκοιμημένου δούλου [τοῦ Θεοῦ] σου (δεῖνα)(4), καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῷ πᾶν πλημμέλημα ἑκούσιόν τε καὶ ἀκούσιον, ὅπως Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τάξῃ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ, ἔνθα οἱ δίκαιοι ἀναπαύονται κλπ. Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, ὁ Ἱερεὺς τὴν Εὐχὴν Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν Πνευμάτων, καὶ τὴν νεκρώσιμον Ἀπόλυσιν. Εἶτα ἄραντες τὸ λείψανον προπορευομένων τῶν Ἱερέων μετὰ λαμπάδων καὶ τῶν (1) (Ἡ Ἀγγλικὴ μετάφρασις τῆς Νεκρωσίμου Ἀκολουθίας εἶναι τοῦ Sacramental Services, vol. 3, Narthex Press, Northridge, CA., 1995.) (2) (Ἡ λέξις Τρισάγιον ἐδῶ ἐννοεῖ τὸ Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός, Παναγία Τριάς, καὶ τὴν Κυριακὴν Προσευχήν.) (3) (Αὐτὴ ἡ φράσις παραλείπεται εἰς πολλὰ σύγχρονα τεύχη, πιθανὸν ὡς περιττή.) (4) (Τὸ τεῦχος τοῦ Βιολάκη ἔχει μόνον «τοῦ δούλου σου»)

units.english_cohort_translation: Upon the death of one of the faithful, the clergy are summoned by the relatives of the deceased; and coming to the house wherein the body lies, if a hierarch is present, the priests and the deacons receive the liturgical blessing (*kairos*) from him. The priests put on their epitrachilia, and the deacons vest in sticharia and oraria, carrying censers and the dikerotrikera. Then one priest together with a deacon enter where the deceased lies, and the deacon exclaims: **“Master, give the blessing”** (*Εὐλόγησον Δέσποτα*). The priest: **“Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages”** (*Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός...*); the deacon chants the Trisagion Prayers; the priest intones the exclamation: **“For Thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** (*Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν...*).

units.english_cohort_translation:
- **“With the spirits of the righteous made perfect, give rest to the soul of Thy servant, O Savior, keeping him in the blessed life which is with Thee, O Lover of mankind.”** (*Μετὰ πνευμάτων δικαίων τετελειωμένων...*)
- **“In Thy place of rest, O Lord, where all Thy saints repose, give rest also to the soul of Thy servant, for Thou alone art immortal.”** (*Εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν σου Κύριε, ὅπου πάντες οἱ Ἅγιοί σου ἀναπαύονται...*)
- **Glory:** **“Thou art our God, Who didst descend into Hades and loose the bonds of the captives; do Thou Thyself give rest to the soul of Thy servant.”** (*Δόξα: Σὺ εἶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν...*)
- **Both now and ever:** **“O Virgin, alone pure and undefiled, who without seed didst bring forth God, intercede that his soul may be saved.”** (*Καὶ νῦν: Ἡ μόνη Ἁγνὴ καὶ Ἄχραντος Παρθένος...*)

units.english_cohort_translation: **“Have mercy on us, O God, according to Thy great mercy, we pray Thee: hear and have mercy... Again we pray for the repose [and forgiveness] of the soul of the servant of God (Name), departed this life, and that every transgression, deliberate or unintended, may be forgiven him; that the Lord God may establish his soul where the righteous repose. The mercies of God, the kingdom of heaven, and the remission of his sins, let us ask of Christ our immortal King and our God... Let us pray to the Lord.”**

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Order of the House Trisagion and Funeral Rubrics:* In historical codices and canonical euchologia, the initial panikhida or funeral litany conducted at the home of the deceased initiates the rites of Christian burial. The designation *Trisagion* in this liturgical rubric encompasses the entire opening hexapsalmic or initial prayer cycle: the Thrice-Holy Hymn (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), the All-Holy Trinity prayer (*Παναγία Τριάς*), the Lord's Prayer (*Πάτερ ἡμῶν*), and the priestly doxological exclamation (*Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν*), preceding the four classical mortuary troparia in Tone 4 (*Hymns for the Departed (Поко́инъ) Troparia*). Textual variations between the 1888 editio princeps and modern Athenian and Venetian euchologia are notable: the petitionary phrase *“and forgiveness”* (*καὶ συγχωρήσεως*) is frequently omitted as redundant in modern editions, and Violakis preserves the archaic vocative *“of Thy servant”* (*τοῦ δούλου σου*) rather than the expanded modern recension *“of the servant of God”* (*τοῦ δούλου τοῦ Θεοῦ*).

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: Upon the death of one of the faithful, the Clergy are summoned by the family; coming to the home where the remains of the deceased are, if a Hierarch is present, the Priests and Deacons receive keron [his blessing] from him. The Priests wear Epitrachilia and the Deacons wear Sticharia and Oraria, carrying censers and Dikirotrikira. Then one of the Priests with a Deacon enter where the deceased is laying, and the Deacon exclaims “Father, give the blessing.” The Priest: “Blessed is our God”; the Deacon: the Trisagion(2); the Priest: “For Yours is.” Then they sing in Mode IV the Hymns “Among the spirits of the righteous made perfect . . . In Your place of rest, O Lord, where all Your Saints repose. Glory . . . You are our God . . . Now and ever . . . units.slavonic_incipit: Διακόνων ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως φέροντος Μανδύαν
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Διακόνων ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως φέροντος Μανδύαν καὶ Ράβδον, καὶ τῶν Ψαλτῶν ψαλλόντων τὸ Ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς [*] ἀπερχόμεθα εἰς τὸν ναόν, ἀφ’ οὗ δὲ εἰσέλθωμεν τὸ μὲν λείψανον ἀποτίθεται ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τοῦ Ναοῦ, ὁ δὲ Ἀρχιερεὺς εὐλογήσας διὰ τρικηρίου ἀνέρχεται εἰς τὸν θρόνον, ὁ Διάκονος ἐκφωνεῖ Εὐλόγησον Δέσποτα, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων καὶ εὐθὺς οἱ Χοροὶ ἄρχονται ψάλλειν εἰς ἦχον πλάγιον τοῦ β΄.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: [*] (In later times, the distances between the home of the deceased, the church, and the burial ground have generally become considerably greater than those at the time of the publication of the Typikon (1888). As a result of these increased distances from point to point, the hymns accompanying the route of the casket are now chanted at different locations. For example, the initial Trisagios Hymn (Holy God, etc.) begins to be sung when the casket enters the Narthex from the outside and continues to be sung up to the point when the casket arrives at the Soleas and up to the beginning of the Funeral Service proper.)
units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funerary Procession and the Seventeenth Kathisma:* In later eras, urban distances between family residences, parish temples, and cemeteries expanded considerably beyond the compact parochial layout of nineteenth-century Constantinople. Consequently, the funeral processional chant of the Asmatic Trisagion (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), traditionally chanted continuously through the streets, is commonly begun when the casket enters the narthex from outside and maintained until placed before the solea and tetrapod in the nave. The funeral office itself centers upon the sublime funeral psalmody of the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 LXX), structured into three distinct stases divided by funeral litanies and tone modulations: the First Stasis is chanted in Tone 6 with the refrain *Alleluia*; the Second Stasis shifts to Tone 5 with the penitential refrain *“Have mercy on me, O Lord”*; and the Third Stasis modulates into Tone 8 with the resurrectional refrain *Alleluia*.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: [5] (Violakis' version “O palami” (“With the palm of Your hand”) is found in various sources, such as the Musikos Pandektis, Athens, 1936, vol 3, p. 376, and Nikos Karitsiotis, Musikon Agiasmatarion, Athens, 1951, p. 33. More numerous sources, including the more authoritative Mega Efchologion as well as the Mikron Efchologion have “O pale men” (“of old”). See the Mega Efchologion, Venice, 1862 (reprinted in Athens, 1986), p. 407, and Mikron Efchologion, Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, 1956, p. 201.)
units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Textual Variants in the Second Evlogitarion:* The opening phrase of the second Troparion of the Funeral Evlogitaria exhibits a celebrated textual variant between the 1888 Constantinopolitan recension of George Violakis and older euchological witnesses. Violakis prints the poetic anthropomorphic reading *“O palame”* (*Ὁ παλάμῃ* — *“With the palm of Thy hand Thou didst fashion me”*), a textual tradition documented in the Athenian musical collections including the *Musikos Pandektis* (Athens, 1936, vol. 3, p. 376) and Nikos Karitsiotis, *Musikon Agiasmatarion* (Athens, 1951, p. 33). Conversely, the venerable Venetian and Roman liturgical monument editions, represented by the *Mega Euchologion* (Venice, 1862/1867, p. 407) and the *Mikron Euchologion* of the Apostolike Diakonia (Athens, 1956, p. 201), preserve the temporal adverbial incipit *“O palai men”* (*Ὁ πάλαι μέν* — *“Thou Who of old didst fashion me out of nothing”*). Both liturgical traditions preserve the identical theological confession: humanity fashioned *ex nihilo* by the divine hand according to the divine image, fallen through transgression, and restored to paradise through Christ's redemption.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: salvation gave birth to God in the flesh. — Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia, glory to You, O God {and give rest to your servant.} {6} If there are many Priests, after each of these Evlogitaria, the Deacon says “Let us pray to the Lord.” And from all the Priests present, each Priest, in order of seniority of ordination, says “For You are the Resurrection.” (See the Orologion for the text of the Evlogitaria for the Reposed.)
units.english_cohort_translation: If there are many priests concelebrating, after each of these Evlogitaria they commemorate the deceased, with the deacon reciting at each: **“Let us pray to the Lord”** (*Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*). And from all the priests present, each priest in order of seniority of ordination exclaims: **“For Thou art the Resurrection, and the Life, and the Repose of Thy servant...”** (*Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις...*). *(See the Horologion for the complete text of the Funeral Evlogitaria).*

units.english_cohort_translation: **“What pleasure in life abides without sorrow? What glory stands upon earth unchanging? All things are feebler than shadows, all things more deceptive than dreams: in a single moment death takes them all away. But in the light of Thy countenance, O Christ, and in the sweetness of Thy beauty, give rest unto him whom Thou hast chosen, for Thou art the Lover of mankind.”** (*Ποία τοῦ βίου τρυφὴ διαμένει λύπης ἀμέτοχος...*)

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funeral Evlogitaria and the Damascene Idiomela:* The Funeral Evlogitaria (*Νεκρώσιμα Εὐλογητάρια*) in Tone 5, punctuated by the refrain *“Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes”* (Psalm 118:12 LXX), bridge the seventeenth kathisma of the Psalter to the Eight Idiomela (*Ἰδιόμελα*) composed by Saint John of Damascus. In ancient Studite and Constantinopolitan euchologies, when multiple presbyters concelebrate, the Little Ektenia for the Departed is intoned by the deacon after each strophe, and the concelebrating presbyters pronounce the resurrectional exclamation (*Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις*) in descending order of ordination seniority. Note the editorial annotation regarding the refrain *“and give rest to Thy servant”* (*καὶ ἀνάπαυσον τὸν δοῦλόν σου*), documented by Karitsiotis in his *Musikon Agiasmatarion* (p. 36) as an established musical and rubrical tradition in modern Byzantine chant editions.

units.slavonic_incipit: Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι ὅταν ἐννοήσω τὸν
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι ὅταν ἐννοήσω τὸν θάνατον καὶ ἴδω ἐν τοῖς τάφοις κειμένην τὴν κατ’ εἰκόνα θεοῦ πλασθεῖσαν ἡμῖν ὡραιότητα ἄμορφον, ἄδοξον, μὴ ἔχουσαν εἶδος. Ὢ τοῦ θαύματος! τί τὸ περὶ ἡμᾶς τοῦτο γέγονε μυστήριον; πῶς παρεδόθημεν τῇ φθορᾷ; πῶς συνεζεύχθημεν τῷ θανάτῳ; ὄντως θεοῦ προστάξει, ὡς γέγραπται, τοῦ παρέχοντος τοῖς μεταστᾶσι τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν.

units.slavonic_incipit: I called to mind the prophet,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: I called to mind the prophet, crying, “I am but dust and ashes.” In addition, I studied the tombs once more, considered the naked bones, and asked myself: Now which of these was king, and which the common soldier? Which was the rich man, which the indigent? Which man was upright and which a sinner? Nevertheless, Lord, in Your compassion, to Your servant give rest, among the righteous.
units.english_cohort_translation: **“I remembered the Prophet crying aloud: I am but dust and ashes; and again I looked into the tombs, and saw the bare bones, and said: Who then is king or soldier? Who is rich or poor? Who is righteous or a sinner? But grant rest unto Thy servant with the righteous, O Lord, as Thou art the Lover of mankind.”** (*Ἐμνήσθην τοῦ Προφήτου βοῶντος, ἐγώ εἰμι γῆ καὶ σποδός...*)

units.slavonic_incipit: Your creating command became my beginning
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Your creating command became my beginning and my being. For it was Your will to bring together visible and invisible nature to fashion me a living creature. You shaped my body from the earth then gave me a spirit by Your divine and quickening breath. Wherefore, O Savior, give rest to Your servant in the land of the living, where the righteous dwell.
units.english_cohort_translation: **“Thy creating command was my beginning and my substance; for desiring to fashion me a living creature out of invisible and visible nature, Thou didst mould my body from the earth and didst give me a soul by Thy divine and life-creating breath. Therefore, O Christ, number Thy servant in the land of the living, in the tents of the righteous.”** (*Ἀρχή μοι καὶ ὑπόστασις, τὸ πλαστουργόν σου γέγονε πρόσταγμα...*)

units.slavonic_incipit: O Savior, giver of life, grant
units.slavonic_diplomatic: O Savior, giver of life, grant rest to our brother whom You called away from temporal things, crying to You, “Glory to You, O Lord!” Mode IV Plagal I weep and I lament when I ponder death, when I see our beauty, formed in God’s image, lying in the tombs bereft of form, disfigured, without glory. O, the wonder of it! How did this mystery befall us? How were we given over to decay? How were we paired with death? Surely, as it is written, by the command of God, who gives rest to the departed.

Truly by the command of God, as it is written, Who grants repose unto the departed.”** (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι ὅταν ἐννοήσω τὸν θάνατον...*)

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Theological Anthropology of the Damascene Idiomela:* The funeral idiomela of Saint John of Damascus constitute a profound Byzantine patristic treatise on Christian anthropology and eschatology. In Tone 6 (*Ἀρχή μοι καὶ ὑπόστασις*), the hymnographer articulates the composite nature of humanity as a microcosm uniting the spiritual (*ἀόρατος φύσις*) and the corporeal (*ὁρατὴ φύσις*) created through the divine inbreathing (Genesis 2:7 LXX). In Tone 8 (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι*), the tragedy of bodily dissolution is confronted not through Stoic resignation but through Christological hope: corruption (*φθορά*) and physical mortality are acknowledged as an unnatural intrusion into the divine image (*κατ’ εἰκόνα θεοῦ*), overturned conclusively by Christ's own descent into the tomb and His life-bearing Resurrection.

units.slavonic_incipit: Καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Ἀπόστολος, Οὐ θέλω
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Ἀπόστολος, Οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν περὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, Εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος πρὸς τοὺς ἐληλυθότας πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἰουδαίους, ὁ Διάκονος, Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός, καὶ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς τὰς δύο συγχωρητικὰς Εὐχάς, καὶ εἰς τὸ τέλος, Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης σαρκός, ὁ Διάκονος, Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, καὶ μνημονεύουσιν αὖθις ἅπαντες οἱ παρευρισκόμενοι Ἱερεῖς, καὶ ἀκολούθως ἡ παρὰ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως νεκρώσιμος Ἀπόλυσις. Εἰς δὲ τὸν τελευταῖον τοῦ λειψάνου ἀσπασμὸν ψάλλεται ὑπὸ τοῦ β΄ χοροῦ τὸ Προσόμοιον, Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν δῶμεν ἀδελφοὶ τῷ θανόντι, εὐχαριστοῦντες Θεῷ, καὶ συνοδεύομεν τὸ λείψανον μέχρι τοῦ τάφου ψάλλοντες τὸ Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι.

units.slavonic_incipit: Ἐὰν ᾖ Διακαινήσιμος ἑβδομάς, ψάλλομεν μέχρι
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Ἐὰν ᾖ Διακαινήσιμος ἑβδομάς, ψάλλομεν μέχρι τοῦ Ναοῦ τὸ Χριστὸς ἀνέστη (τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ μέχρι τῆς Ἀποδόσεως τοῦ Πάσχα). Μετὰ τὸ Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς ψάλλει τὸ Χριστὸς ἀνέστη ἅπαξ καὶ οἱ δύο Χοροὶ ἀνὰ μίαν, εἶτα ψάλλονται αἱ Καταβασίαι τοῦ Κανόνος τοῦ Πάσχα· εἰς τὸ τέλος δὲ ἑκάστης Καταβασίας τὸ Χριστὸς ἀνέστη τρίς, τὸ Ἀναστὰς ὁ Ἰησοῦς, καὶ ὁ Διάκονος Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις· καὶ ἐν ταῖς λοιπαῖς οἱ Ἱερεῖς, ἀπ’ θ΄ ψάλλεται τὸ Σαρκὶ ὑπνώσας δίς, καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Ἀπόστολος καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον. Εἰς τὸ τέλος ὁ Διάκονος τὸ Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός, καὶ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς ἀναγινώσκει τὰς δύο συγχωρητικὰς Εὐχάς· εἰς τὸ τέλος Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων κτλ. ὡς ἀνωτέρω καὶ ἡ Ἀπόλυσις, ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν ψάλλομεν τὸ Ἀναστάσεως ἡμέρα, τὸ αὐτὸ ψάλλομεν καὶ μέχρι τοῦ τάφου. Μετὰ τὴν Διακαινήσιμον ἑβδομάδα, ἀφοῦ εἰσέλθωμεν ἐν τῷ Ναῷ μετὰ τοῦ λειψάνου, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, εἶτα τὸ Χριστὸς ἀνέστη ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως ἅπαξ, καὶ δὶς ὑπὸ τῶν Χορῶν· καὶ ἀκολούθως ἡ νεκρώσιμος συνήθης Ἀκολουθία, ὡς προδιετυπώθη.

units.slavonic_incipit: Ἰστέον δέ, ὅτι ἡ αὐτὴ τάξις
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Ἰστέον δέ, ὅτι ἡ αὐτὴ τάξις τῆς νεκρωσίμου Ἀκολουθίας ψάλλεται εἰς ἅπαντας τοὺς κοιμηθέντας, καὶ εἰς Βασιλεῖς, Πατριάρχας, Ἀρχιερεῖς, Ἱερεῖς, καὶ εἰς ἄνδρας καὶ γυναῖκας, μικρούς τε καὶ μεγάλους, καὶ εἰς αὐτὰ ἔτι τὰ βρέφη, εἰς ὧν τὴν Ἀκολουθίαν ἀφαιροῦνται τὰ κατ’ ἦχον Ἰδιόμελα, λέγεται δὲ καὶ ἡ διὰ τὰ βρέφη ἐν τῷ Εὐχολογίῳ σημειουμένη Εὐχή, ὡς καὶ ἴδιος Ἀπόστολος καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: And immediately the Apostolos “I would not have you ignorant concerning those who are asleep,” and the Gospel “The Lord said to the Jews who came to him.” The Deacon: “Have mercy on us, O God” and the Hierarch recites the two Prayers of forgiveness, and at the end, “God of spirits and all flesh.” The Deacon intones “Let us pray to the Lord” and all the Priests present commemorate [the departed]; then follows the Dismissal Prayer for the Reposed by the Hierarch. During the final respects and kissing of the departed, the Second Choir chants the Prosomion “Come, brethren, let us give one final kiss to the departed, thanking God”; and we accompany the corpse to the tomb chanting the “I weep and I lament.” If we are in Bright [Renewal] Week, as we go into the Church, we chant “Christ is risen” (we chant this hymn until the Leave-taking of Easter).
units.english_cohort_translation: And immediately follows the Epistle (*Apostolos*): **“Brethren, I would not have you ignorant concerning those who are asleep”** (*Οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν περὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων* — 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17); and the Gospel: **“The Lord said to the Jews who came unto Him: Amen, amen, I say unto you, he that hears My word...”** (*Εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος πρὸς τοὺς ἐληλυθότας πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἰουδαίους* — John 5:24–30). The deacon intones the litany: **“Have mercy on us, O God, according to Thy great mercy...”** (*Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός*); and the hierarch recites the two prayers of absolution, and at the end the prayer: **“O God of spirits and of all flesh...”** (*Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης σαρκός*). The deacon intones: **“Let us pray to the Lord”** (*Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*); and all the presbyters present commemorate the departed once more; and subsequently the hierarch pronounces the Funeral Dismissal. During the final kissing of the body, the second choir chants the automelon: **“Come, brethren, let us give the last kiss unto the departed, giving thanks unto God”** (*Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν δῶμεν ἀδελφοὶ τῷ θανόντι, εὐχαριστοῦντες Θεῷ*); and we accompany the body to the tomb while chanting: **“I weep and I lament”** (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: After the “Blessed is God,” the Archbishop chants the “Christ is risen” once and each of the two Choirs chant it also once. Then are sung the Katavasie of the Canon of Easter. At the end of each Katavasia, we chant “Christ is risen” three times and the “Jesus, having risen.” The Deacon: “Let us pray to the Lord,” and the Archbishop “For You are the Resurrection” [after the First Katavasia]. After the remaining Katavasie, the Priests [each at a time] intone this same Exclamation. After the 9th Katavasia, we chant “Having slept in the flesh as a mortal” twice, and immediately follow the Apostolos and the Gospel. units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Paschal Funeral Rite and the Egalitarian Order of Burial:* Violakis establishes the fundamental liturgical principle that the funeral office of the Great Church of Christ maintains an essential structural identity across all ranks of human life—from emperors and patriarchs down to ordinary laymen and infants—witnessing to the Pauline proclamation cited on the facing page: *“For ye are all one in Christ Jesus”* (Galatians 3:28). For infants who depart before reaching the age of reason and personal sin, the mournful Damascene idiomela are omitted, replaced by prayers celebrating innocence and eternal union with Christ. Furthermore, when a funeral coincides with Bright Week (Renewal Week), grief is transformed into Paschal triumph: the entire funeral office is replaced by the Paschal Canon of Saint John Damascene, the singing of *“Christ is risen”*, and the joyful Paschal Stichera, reflecting the ancient Christian conviction that death during the feast of the Resurrection constitutes immediate entry into the radiant joy of the empty tomb.

units.slavonic_incipit: Τὰ εἰς τοὺς κεκοιμημένους ἀδελφοὺς γινόμενα
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Τὰ εἰς τοὺς κεκοιμημένους ἀδελφοὺς γινόμενα Τρίτα δηλοῦσι, κατὰ τὸν Ἱερὸν Συμεὼν Θεσσαλονίκης, ὅτι ὁ κοιμηθεὶς ἀδελφὸς ὑπὸ τῆς Ἁγίας Τριάδος ἐξ ἀρχῆς συνετέθη. Τὰ δὲ Ἔνατα τῶν κεκοιμημένων σημαίνουσιν ὅτι ὁ διαλυθεὶς εἰς τὰ ἐξ ὧν συνετέθη, ἔχει νὰ συγκαταριθμηθῇ μετὰ τῶν ἐννέα αὔλων ταγμάτων τῶν Ἀγγέλων, ὡς ἄϋλος καὶ αὐτός. Τὰ δὲ τεσσαρακοστὰ δηλοῦσιν ὅτι, ἐν τῇ μελλούσῃ Ἀναστάσει συντεθεὶς πάλιν, κατὰ τρόπον ὑψηλότερον, ἔχει καὶ αὐτὸς νὰ ἀναληφθῇ ὡς ὁ Κύριος καὶ ἁρπαγεὶς ἐν νεφέλαις νὰ ὑπαντήσῃ τῷ Κριτῇ. Ταύτας τὰς τρεῖς καταστάσεις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σημαίνουσι τὰ Τρίμηνα καὶ Ἑξάμηνα καὶ Ἐννεάμηνα. Καὶ ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν, ταῦτα τελοῦνται ὑπὲρ καθαρισμοῦ τοῦ ἀποθανόντος.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CONCERNING MEMORIAL SERVICES The Trita [three-day memorial service] performed for the departed brethren declare [signify], according to the Sacred Symeon of Thessalonika, that the brother fallen asleep was put together from the beginning by the Holy Trinity. The Enata [nine-day memorial service] performed for those fallen asleep declare [signify] that he who was dissolved back to the elements from which he was composed will be numbered among the nine incorporeal ranks of the Angels, being now incorporeal himself. The Tessarakonta [forty-day memorial service] declare that, if in the future Resurrection the departed person has been recomposed but in a higher manner, and he will ascend to Heaven like the Lord, taken up in the clouds to meet the Judge. The three-month, six-month, and nine-month memorial services signify the three different states of being of Man. And, simply speaking, these memorial services are performed for the spiritual purification of the dead person.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Third-Day Memorial Service (*Trita*) performed for our fallen-asleep brethren signifies, according to the Holy Symeon of Thessalonica, that the departed brother was composed from the beginning by the Holy Trinity. The Ninth-Day Memorial Service (*Enata*) for the reposed signifies that he who has been dissolved into the elements from which he was composed is to be numbered together with the nine bodiless ranks of the Angels, being now bodiless himself. The Fortieth-Day Memorial Service (*Tessarakonta*) signifies that, having been recomposed in a more exalted manner in the future Resurrection, he also is to be taken up like the Lord and caught up in the clouds to meet the Judge. units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Mystagogical Theology of Memorial Services according to Saint Symeon of Thessalonica:* This final chapter of the Violakis Typikon codifies the mystagogy of commemorative services for the departed (*Mnemosyna* / *Panakhyda*), drawing upon the liturgical commentary of Saint Symeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica (†1429, *De fine nostro et de ordine sepulturae*, PG 155:669–698). The traditional intervals of commemorative prayer are invested with deep trinitarian, angelological, and eschatological symbolism: the third day honors the Holy Trinity as the Creator of man; the ninth day commemorates the nine angelic choirs with whom the disembodied soul now shares communion; the fortieth day prefigures the General Resurrection when the glorified body shall be caught up into the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:17) to encounter Christ the Judge; while the annual cycles (three, six, nine months, and annual memorials) perpetuate the prayer of the Church for the soul's continuous purification. The inscription *“ΤΕΛΟΣ ΚΑΙ Τῼ ΘΕῼ ΔΟΞΑ”* marks the formal conclusion of the authoritative typikon text promulgated by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1888.

units.slavonic_incipit: Ὁ παρὼν Πίναξ τοῦ Ἑορτοδρομίου ἐγράφη
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Ὁ παρὼν Πίναξ τοῦ Ἑορτοδρομίου ἐγράφη ἀρχικῶς ἐπὶ τῇ βάσει τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ Ἡμερολογίου. Εἰς τὸ ἔτος 1921, ἡ Ἑλληνορθόδοξος Ἐκκλησία υἱοθέτησε τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον. Ἐφ’ ὅσον τὸ παρὸν Τυπικὸν ἐξεδόθη τὸ ἔτος 1888, ἦτο φύσει ἀδύνατον διὰ τὸν Γεώργιον Βιολάκην ἵνα ἦτο ἐνήμερος αὐτῆς τῆς ἀλλαγῆς πρὸς τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον.

units.slavonic_incipit: The present Chart of the Feasts
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The present Chart of the Feasts was originally written on the basis of the Julian Calendar. In the year 1921, the Greek Orthodox Church adopted the Gregorian Calendar. Since the present Typikon was published in 1888, it naturally was impossible for George Violakis to have been aware of this change to the Gregorian Calendar.
units.english_cohort_translation: The present Chart of the Feasts was originally compiled upon the basis of the Julian Calendar. In the year 1921 [and 1924], the Greek Orthodox Church adopted the Revised Julian / Gregorian Calendar. Inasmuch as this Typikon was published in the year 1888, it was naturally impossible for George Violakis to have foreseen this calendar transition.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In order to make this chart more useful in our time, the editors of the present work (Demos and Bogdanos) present the dates of the Julian Calendar (JC) together with the exactly corresponding dates in the Gregorian Calendar (GC) with the pertinent guidelines.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Calendar Reform and the Paschalion Table of George Violakis:* The *Pinax tou Eortodromiou* (*Πίναξ τοῦ Ἑορτοδρομίου*) represents the perpetual Paschalion table appended to the 1888 editio princeps of George Violakis, calculating moveable feast cycles, Paschal dates, Triodion intervals, and the duration of the Apostles' Fast. Following the Meletian Congress of Constantinople in 1923 and the subsequent adoption of the Revised Julian Calendar (in civil and liturgical synchrony with the Gregorian reckoning for fixed feasts) by the Church of Greece and the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1924, twentieth-century editors added comparative concordance columns to reconcile the 1888 tables with both the Old Calendar (Julian, observed across Mount Athos, Jerusalem, and traditional Slavic jurisdictions) and the New Calendar (Revised Julian/Gregorian, observed across Constantinople, Greece, and diaspora communities).

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Comparative Paschal and Triodion Cycles (Julian and Gregorian Reckonings):* The comparative tables framed on physical leaves p941 and p942 (printed pages 926 and 927) establish the mathematical parameters of the liturgical year under the Julian Calendar (Old Calendar, JC) and the Revised Julian / Gregorian Calendar (New Calendar, GC). The 13-day solar disparity shifts the entire 127-day moveable liturgical cycle: under the Julian Calendar, Holy Pascha oscillates between March 22 and April 25 JC (a 35-day inclusive span), whereas in the civil Gregorian reckoning it falls between April 4 and May 8 GC. This chronological shift profoundly affects the coincidence matrix: immovable commemorations of mid-January (such as St. Theodosios the Cenobiarch on Jan 11 and St. Anthony the Great on Jan 17) can never coincide with the Triodion under the Gregorian reckoning, whereas late-June commemorations (the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist on June 24 and the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul on June 29) are brought within the movable post-Paschal cycle whenever Pascha occurs late.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ΠΕΡΙΛΑΜΒΑΝΟΜΕΝΩΝ ΙΗ΄ ΚΙΝΗΤΩΝ ΕΟΡΤΩΝ ΤΩΝ ΑΠΑΝΤΩΣΩΝ ΕΝΤΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΤΡΙΩΔΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥ ΠΕΝΤΗΚΟΣΤΑΡΙΟΥ Ἑρμηνευτικοὶ τούτου κανόνες Σπουδαῖον ἐκρίθη καὶ ἐπάναγκες τοῖς τε Ἱερεῦσι καὶ τοῖς ψάλταις τὸ γινώσκειν, εἰ δὲ μή γε, τὸ εὑρίσκειν εὐχερέστερον τὴν λύσιν ἀποριῶν καὶ δυσχερειῶν, ὅσας συνεπάγεται ἡ τῶν ἀκινήτων λεγομένων ἑορτῶν, ἤτοι τοῦ Μηνολογίου, σύμπτωσις μετὰ τῶν κινητῶν τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ Πεντηκοσταρίου. Καὶ ποιεῖται μὲν καθ’ ἑκάστην σύμπτωσιν ἐπαρκῆ λόγον περὶ τούτων τὸ Τυπικόν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲν ἧττον εἷς Πίναξ, οἷος ὁ ἑπόμενος, παρέχει μείζονα τὴν εὐχέρειαν καὶ ἱκανοποιεῖ τὴν περιέργειαν τοῦ φιλομαθοῦς· ἐπειδὴ δὲ αἱ κινηταὶ ἑορταὶ τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ Πεντηκοσταρίου οὔτε πέραν τῆς ΙΑ΄ Ἰανουαρίου τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ Ἡμερολογίου (ἥτις ἐστὶ τὸ πρωϊμώτερον ὅριον τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου) κατέρχονται [24 Ἰανουαρίου εἰς τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον], οὔτε δύνανται προχωρῆσαι ἐπέκεινα τῆς ΚΕ΄ Μαΐου-ΙΗ [Ἰουλίου 3-ΓΗ], ἥτις ἐστὶ τὸ ἔσχατον ὅριον μέχρι τοῦ ὁποίου ἐκτείνεται τὸ τέλος τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, ἤτοι ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἁγίων Πάντων, διὰ τοῦτο ὁ Πίναξ ταῦτα ἔχει ἀρχῆς καὶ τέλους ὅρια, καὶ μόνον τὰς ἐν τῷ χρονικῷ τούτῳ διαστήματι ἑορτὰς τοῦ Μηνολογίου περιλαμβάνει, παρέχων ὡς ἐν κατόπτρῳ τὰς δυνατὰς εὐκολίας, ὥστε νὰ δύνανται οὕτω πως οἱ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ ψάλται συμβιβάζειν ἀκόπως τὴν τυπικὴν τῶν ἱερῶν Ἀκολουθιῶν διάταξιν, καὶ διαλύειν πάντα δισταγμόν, καὶ διασκεδάζειν πᾶσαν ἐνδεχομένην ἀπορίαν. Ὅπως δὲ κατανοηθῇ καὶ ἀποβῇ εὐχερεστέρα ἡ τοῦ Πίνακος χρῆσις, ἀναγκαῖαι ἐθεωρήθησαν αἱ ἑξῆς σημειώσεις:

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source:
CONTAINING THE 18 IMMOVABLE FEASTS
OCCURRING WITHIN
THE TRIODION AND PENTIKOSTARION PERIODS

Interpretive Rules

    It was deemed important and necessary for the Priests and Chanters to know, if not also to find it easier to solve, the perplexities and difficulties that arise when the so-called immovable feasts, that is, those of the Minologion, coincide with the movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentikostarion periods. However, while the Typikon has written a great deal about each of these coincidences, they were never presented in a Chart; therefore, the following was developed, to help the curious find their answers. Since the movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentikostarion periods do not begin earlier than January 11 on the Julian Calendar-JC (the earliest date for the beginning of the Triodion period) [January 24 on the Gregorian Calendar-GC] nor do they extend beyond May 25-JC [July 3-GC,] the latest date that the Pentikostarion period may end, that is, the Feast of All Saints, for this reason the Chart has these beginning and ending boundaries, and only refers to those feasts of the Minologion that occur within this time span in order to facilitate the use of the Typikon

In order to make the use of the Chart easier, we deemed it important to make the following observations:
units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Canon of Coincidences between the Menologion, Triodion, and Pentecostarion:* The preamble to the *Pinax tou Eortodromiou* introduces the theoretical framework governing the occurrence of immovable commemorations within the variable seasons of the movable paschal cycle. In historical Byzantine liturgical typika (such as the 1545 editio princeps of the Sabaite Typikon and the successive Constantinopolitan editions of the *Tserkovne Oko* and the Violakis synthesis), rubricists faced intricate problems of concurrence (*syndromē* / *synempitōsis*) when festal commemorations intersected with the pre-Lenten, Lenten, Holy Week, and Paschal cycles. George Violakis designed this perpetual chart as a rapid rubrical reference engine, circumscribing the liturgical domain between the earliest possible opening of the Triodion (January 11 JC / January 24 GC) and the latest possible termination of the Pentecostarion cycle on the Sunday of All Saints (May 25 JC / July 3 GC).

units.slavonic_incipit: Α΄. Τὸ Ἅγιον Πάσχα ταλαντεύεται ἐντὸς
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Α΄. Τὸ Ἅγιον Πάσχα ταλαντεύεται ἐντὸς τοῦ μεταξὺ τῆς ΚΒ΄ Μαρτίου-ΙΗ καὶ ΚΕ΄ Ἀπριλίου-ΙΗ [Ἀπριλίου 4-ΓΗ— Μαΐου 8-ΓΗ] ἐκ τριάκοντα τεσσάρων ἡμερῶν διαστήματος· ἑπομένως καὶ ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἔναρξις κινεῖται ἐντὸς τοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ΙΑ΄ Ἰανουαρίου-ΙΗ μέχρι τῆς ΙΓ΄ Φεβρουαρίου-ΙΗ [Ἰανουαρίου 24-ΓΗ — Φεβρουαρίου 28-ΓΗ] χρονικοῦ χώρου· τῶν δ’ ἐν ταῖς δυσὶ πρώταις στήλαις τοῦ Πίνακος ἑκάστης ἑορτῆς κειμένων ἀριθμῶν, οἱ πρῶτοι μὲν δεικνύουσι τὰς ἡμερομηνίας ἀφ’ ὧν, ὅταν ἄρχηται τὸ Τριῴδιον, συμπίπτει τὸ Πάσχα εἰς τὴν ὑπὸ τῆς δευτέρας στήλης δεικνυομένην ἡμερομηνίαν, ἀπέναντι δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τούτων σημειοῦνται αἱ ἡμέραι καὶ ἑβδομάδες τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἢ τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, καθ’ ἃς συμπίπτει ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἔτει ἡ ζητουμένη ἑορτή· καὶ ἐν τῇ τελευταίᾳ στήλῃ σημειοῦνται οἱ ἐν τῷ Τυπικῷ ἀριθμοὶ τῶν παραγράφων τῆς Τυπικῆς Διατάξεως, ἐν αἷς διασαφηνίζονται τὰ τῆς ἱερᾶς Ἀκολουθίας κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην. Παραδείγματος χάριν, ἐπιθυμοῦμεν ἵνα γνωρίζωμεν κατὰ τὸ ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) ἔτος ἡ ἑορτὴ τῆς Ὑπαπαντῆς ἐν τίνι ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἐν τίνι ἑβδομάδι τοῦ Τριῳδίου συμπίπτει· εὑρίσκομεν τὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τοῦ Πάσχα τοῦ ἔτους ἐκείνου, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ Θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, εἶτα βλέπομεν ἐν ταῖς δυσὶ στήλαις τῆς ἑορτῆς ταύτης, καὶ εὑρίσκομεν ἐν μὲν τῇ α΄ στήλῃ τὸν ἀριθμὸν κθ΄, ὅς ἐστιν ἡ ἡμερομηνία τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου κατὰ τὸ ἔτος ἐκεῖνο, ἐν δὲ τῇ β΄ στήλῃ τὸ ἀριθμὸν θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, ὅς ἐστιν ἡ ἡμερομηνία τοῦ Πάσχα τοῦ ἔτους ἐκείνου, ἀπέναντι δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τούτων σημειοῦνται καὶ ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἑβδομάς, ὡς καὶ ἡ ἡμέρα ἐν ᾗ συμπίπτει ἡ ἑορτή, ἔστι δὲ ἡ πέμπτη τῆς τοῦ Τελώνου καὶ Φαρισαίου ἑβδομάδος.

units.slavonic_incipit: Β΄. Αἱ ἐν τῷ Τριῳδίῳ καὶ
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Β΄. Αἱ ἐν τῷ Τριῳδίῳ καὶ τῷ Πεντηκοσταρίῳ συμπίπτουσαι ἀκίνητοι τοῦ Μηνολογίου ἑορταί εἰσι τὸν ἀριθμὸν ιη΄, ἀπὸ τῆς ἑορτῆς τοῦ ὁσίου Θεοδοσίου (Ἰανουαρίου ΙΑ΄), καθ’ ἣν δυνατὸν νὰ ἄρχηται τὸ Τριῴδιον, μέχρι τῆς ἑορτῆς τῆς Γ΄ εὑρέσεως τῆς τιμίας Κεφαλῆς τοῦ Προδρόμου (Μαΐου ΚΕ΄), ἥτις δυνατὸν νὰ τελῇ ἐντὸς τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου. Ἐξ αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν ἑορτῶν αἱ μὲν ιβ΄ ἀνήκουσι τῷ Τριῳδίῳ, αἱ δὲ ς΄ τῷ Πεντηκοσταρίῳ, ὡς δείκνυσιν ὁ Πίναξ.

units.slavonic_incipit: Γ΄. Ἐκ τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ΙΑ΄
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Γ΄. Ἐκ τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ΙΑ΄ Ἰανουαρίου-ΙΗ μέχρι τῆς ΙΓ΄ Φεβρουαρίου-ΙΗ [Ἰανουαρίου 24-ΓΗ — Φεβρουαρίου 26-ΓΗ] περιλαμβανομένων ἑορτῶν, ὡς καὶ τῶν δύο τελευταίων τοῦ Μαΐου, ἤτοι τῆς τοῦ ἁγίου Κωνσταντίνου καὶ τῆς τοῦ Προδρόμου, αἱ μὲν δυνατὸν νὰ τελῶσιν ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ ἐκτὸς αἱ δὲ ἐντὸς τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου καὶ ἐκτός, ἀναλόγως τῆς ἐποχῆς τοῦ Πάσχα. Ὡς ἐκ τούτου, ὅταν αἱ στῆλαι τῶν διαφορουμένων τούτων ἑορτῶν μὴ προβαίνωσιν ἐπέκεινα τοῦ σημειουμένου ὁρίου τῶν ἀριθμῶν, εὔδηλον ὅτι αἱ ἑορταὶ αὗται τελοῦσιν ἐν ἐκείνοις τοῖς ἔτεσιν αἱ μὲν ἔξω τοῦ Τριῳδίου, αἱ δὲ ἔξω τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου.

units.english_cohort_translation: 1. Holy Pascha [Easter] may occur between March 22-JC and April 25-JC [between April 4-GC and May 8-GC], a thirty-four day period [comprising 35 calendar dates inclusively]. Therefore, the beginning of the Triodion period may occur between January 11-JC and February 13-JC [between January 24-GC and February 28-GC]. The first column of the Chart indicates the beginning date of the Triodion period; the second column indicates the date of Holy Pascha [Easter]. The third column shows the date and name of each of the 18 immovable feasts and, below it, the days of the movable feasts with which each immovable feast may coincide; and the fourth column displays the paragraph and page numbers in the present work where the rubrical order of service for each concurrence is set forth in detail. We provide the following concrete example: if we desire to know in the year 1889 on which day and in which week of the Triodion period the Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante* / *Presentation*) occurs, we first determine the date of Pascha for that year—which in this case is April 9. We then examine the first two columns under this feast, where we find in the first column the number 29 [i.e., January 29], which represents the date of the beginning of the Triodion period in that year; in the second column we find April 9, which represents the date of Holy Pascha for that year. In the third column, directly across from those dates, the table designates the precise week and day of the Triodion period upon which this immovable feast falls—which in this case is the Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Boundaries of the Paschal Oscillation (Rules 1–3):* Rules 1 through 3 codify the mathematical architecture of the Byzantine computus as articulated in the Violakis Typikon. The 35-day inclusive oscillation of Holy Pascha (from the vernal equinox terminus of March 22 JC to the latest possible Pascha on April 25 JC) directly regulates the opening of the pre-Lenten Triodion 70 days earlier (January 11 to February 13 JC). The table identifies 18 critical intersection points with the fixed Menologion. In Rule 1, Violakis selects the year 1889—the very year following the publication of the 1888 editio princeps—as a pedagogical model: with Pascha falling on April 9, the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee occurred on January 29, causing the Great Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*, February 2) to fall on the Thursday of the pre-Lenten Week of the Publican and the Pharisee. Rule 3 clarifies the status of boundary feasts (such as St. Constantine and Helen on May 21 and the Third Finding of the Head of the Forerunner on May 25), which are celebrated as ordinary Menologion offices outside the Pentecostarion cycle whenever Pascha occurs early.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: [Σημειωτέον ὅτι ἡ σχέσις ἀκινήτων καὶ κινητῶν ἑορτῶν διαφέρει μεταξὺ τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ καὶ τοῦ Γρηγοριανοῦ Ἡμερολογίου (ὅρα Comparative Outline of Movable Feasts between the Julian and Gregorian Calendar, (σελ. 926). Κατὰ τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον, ἐν ᾧ τὸ Τριῴδιον ἄρχεται 24 Ἰανουαρίου (13 ἡμέρας ἀργότερον τῆς ἡμερομηνίας ἐνάρξεως εἰς τὸ Ἰουλιανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον) αἱ πρῶται τέσσαρες ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ εἰς τὸν Πίνακα—11, 17, 18 καὶ 20 Ἰανουαρίου—δὲν πρόκειται πλέον νὰ συμβοῦν ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου. Ἡ πρώτη πιθανὸν ἐνωρίτερη ἀκίνητος ἑορτὴ ἡ ὁποία δύναται νὰ συμβῇ ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου εἶναι 25 Ἰανουαρίου, Γρηγορίου τοῦ Θεολόγου. units.slavonic_incipit: Δ΄. Ἐν τῷ Πίνακι δὲν ἐλήφθη
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Δ΄. Ἐν τῷ Πίνακι δὲν ἐλήφθη ὑπ’ ὄψει ἡ προκύπτουσα, ὡς ἐκ τῶν Βισέκτων ἐτῶν, φαινομενικὴ μεταξὺ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ τοῦ Πάσχα ἀνωμαλία, καθότι τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀδύνατον καθορισθῆναι ἐν Πίνακι. Διὸ καὶ ὀφείλομεν διασαφηνίσαι ἐνταῦθα ὅτι, ὅταν ἔχωμεν ἐν νῷ δύο ἔτη μὴ Βίσεκτα καὶ τὰ δύο ὄντα, ἅτινα ἔχουσι τὸ Πάσχα κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν, εἶναι βέβαιον ὅτι ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἔναρξις, ὡς καὶ αἱ τοῦ Μηνολογίου ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ μετὰ τῶν κινητῶν τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, συμβαίνει κατ’ αὐτὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν ἀπαρεγκλίτως. Ἀλλ’ ὅταν λάβωμεν ἐν νῷ δύο ἔτη, ὧν τὸ μὲν Βίσεκτον, τὸ δὲ μή, ἔχοντα ὅμως τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τοῦ Πάσχα, προκύπτει δυσχέρειά τις περὶ τὰς ἀκινήτους ἑορτὰς τὰς συμπιπτούσας πρὸ τῆς ἐμβολίμου ἡμέρας τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, διότι τὰ τοιαῦτα ἔτη ἔχουσι τὰς ἡμερομηνίας τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Τριῳδίου διαφόρους, ἑπομένως καὶ πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς τὰς πρὸ τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου. Οὕτω, λόγου χάριν, ἔχομεν τὸ μὴ Βίσεκτον ἔτος ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) καὶ τὸ Βίσεκτον ͵αϡ΄ (1900), ἅτινα ἔχουσι τὸ Πάσχα αὐτὴν τὴν Θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, τοῦ πρώτου ἡ ἀρχὴ τοῦ Τριῳδίου συμπίπτει τῇ ΚΘ΄ Ἰανουαρίου, τοῦ δευτέρου δὲ τῇ Λ΄ διὰ τοὺς προῤῥηθέντας λόγους. Κατὰ συνέπειαν, μετὰ τὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τῆς κατὰ τὸ Βίσεκτον ἔτος ἀρχῆς τοῦ Τριῳδίου μέχρι τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, ὅτε καὶ γίνεται ἡ προσθήκη τῆς ἐμβολίμου ταύτης ἡμέρας, πρέπει διὰ τὰς ἐπιλαχούσας ἐν τῷ διαστήματι τούτῳ ἑορτὰς νὰ λαμβάνωμεν οὐχὶ τὴν ἀπέναντι τοῦ Πασχαλίου ἀριθμοῦ ἐν τῷ Πίνακι σημειουμένην ἡμέραν τῆς ἑβδομάδος, ὡς ἡμέραν τῆς ἐπιγραφομένης ἑορτῆς, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὑπὸ ταύτην κειμένην, ἤτοι τὴν ἀπέναντι τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῆς κατὰ τὸ Βίσεκτον ἐκεῖνο ἔτος ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἡμερομηνίαν, ὡς μήπω ἐλθούσης τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου· μετὰ τὴν ΚΘ΄ ὅμως αἱ ἡμέραι τῶν ἐπιλαχουσῶν ἑορτῶν

units.english_cohort_translation: [It should be noted, however, that the relationship between immovable and movable feasts in the Gregorian Calendar differs from that in the Julian Calendar (see the Comparative Outline of Movable Feasts, p. 926). In accordance with the Gregorian Calendar, where the Triodion period begins on 24 January (13 days later than the date of beginning in the Julian Calendar) the first four immovable feasts listed in the Chart — 11, 17, 18 and 20 January — will no longer fall within the Triodion period. The earliest possible immovable feast to fall within the Triodion period will now be 25 January, St. Gregory the Theologian. Similarly, since the end of the movable feasts (Sunday of All Saints) will now be delayed until 3 July, three more immovable feasts may possibly fall within the Pentikostarion period: 24 June, the Nativity of John the Baptist; 29 June, Peter and Paul the Apostles; and 30 June, the 12 Apostles.]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: When we have in mind two consecutive regular (i.e. non-Leap) years that have Pascha [Easter] on the same date, it is certain that the date of the beginning of the Triodion period, as well as the dates of the immovable feasts of the Minologion with the coinciding movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentikostarion periods, occur in these two years on the same dates without any change. When, on the other hand, we have in mind two years, one of which is a Leap Year and the other is not, both of these years having the same date for Pascha [Easter], we confront a difficulty in the coinciding patterns between the immovable feasts that occur before February 29 and the movable feasts within that time frame.
units.english_cohort_translation: When we consider two regular, common (non-leap) years that celebrate Holy Pascha on the same calendar date, it is certain that the date of the beginning of the Triodion period, as well as the dates of the immovable feasts of the Menologion concurring with the movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentecostarion periods, occur in both years upon the identical dates without any variation. When, on the other hand, we compare two years of which one is a Leap Year and the other is common, both years having the identical date for Holy Pascha, we encounter a discrepancy in the concurrence patterns between the immovable feasts that occur before February 29 and the movable cycle within that interval. This discrepancy arises because these two years have different dates for the opening of the Triodion period and, consequently, different dates for the concurrence between all immovable feasts occurring before February 29 and the movable feasts. For example, consider the common year 1889 and the leap year 1900: both celebrate Holy Pascha on April 9. In the year 1889, however, the beginning of the Triodion occurs on January 29, whereas in the leap year 1900 the beginning of the Triodion occurs one day later—namely, on January 30. units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Bissextile Leap-Year Triodion Discrepancy (Rule 4):* Rule 4 addresses the computistic shift introduced by bissextile intercalation (*dísekton étos* / leap year). In the Julian computus, the interval between Septuagesima (the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee) and Pascha Sunday is invariant at 10 weeks (70 days). However, whenever February receives an intercalary 29th day (*embolimos hēmera*), the calendar date of the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee must advance by one day relative to a common year sharing the same Paschal date (e.g., January 30 instead of January 29 for an April 9 Pascha). For all immovable commemorations falling before February 29 (such as St. Anthony, St. Euthymius, the Three Hierarchs, the Meeting of the Lord, and St. Charalampus), this intercalation shifts the weekday of concurrence one row lower in the table. Once the intercalary leap day of February 29 has passed, the normal 70-day cadence resumes, and all subsequent commemorations (beginning with the 40 Martyrs of Sebaste and the Annunciation) coincide upon identical liturgical days. Note that 1900 was a leap year under the Julian Calendar (which maintains an uncorrected four-year leap rule), though a common century year under the Gregorian Calendar.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: μέχρι τέλους, ἔρχονται ἀπέναντι τοῦ Πασχαλίου ἀριθμοῦ. Ἐκ τοῦ παραλληλισμοῦ δύο ἑορτῶν, μιᾶς μὲν συμπιπτούσης πρὸ τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, ἑτέρας δὲ συμπιπτούσης μετὰ τὴν ΚΘ΄, ἀποδεικνύονται σαφῶς τὰ προειρημένα. Παραδείγματος χάριν, ἡ ἑορτὴ τῆς Ὑπαπαντῆς, ἥτις ἐστὶ μία τῶν πρὸ τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου ἑορτῶν, ἐν μὲν τῷ μὴ Βισέκτῳ ἔτει ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) συμπίπτει τῇ Πέμπτῃ τῆς τοῦ Τελώνου καὶ Φαρισαίου ἑβδομάδος (ὡς προείρηται ἐν § Α΄), ἐν δὲ τῷ Βισέκτῳ ͵αϡ΄ (1900) τῇ Τετάρτῃ τῆς αὐτῆς ἑβδομάδος. Ἡ ἑορτὴ ὅμως τοῦ Εὐαγγελισμοῦ, ἥτις ἐστὶ μετὰ τὴν ἐμβόλιμον τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, συμπίπτει κατ’ ἀμφότερα τὰ ἔτη ἐν μιᾷ καὶ τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἤτοι τῷ Σαββάτῳ τῆς Ε΄ Ἑβδομάδος· τοιουτοτρόπως σκεπτέον καὶ περὶ πάσης ἄλλης ζητουμένης ἑορτῆς πρὸς ἄρσιν τῆς φαινομενικῆς ἀνωμαλίας τῶν ἡμερῶν τοῦ Πίνακος ἐπὶ τῇ συμπτώσει Βισέκτου ἔτους.

Παραδείγματος χάριν, ἡ ἑορτὴ τῆς Ὑπαπαντῆς, ἥτις ἐστὶ μία τῶν πρὸ τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου ἑορτῶν, ἐν μὲν τῷ μὴ Βισέκτῳ ἔτει ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) συμπίπτει τῇ Πέμπτῃ τῆς τοῦ Τελώνου καὶ Φαρισαίου ἑβδομάδος (ὡς προείρηται ἐν § Α΄), ἐν δὲ τῷ Βισέκτῳ ͵αϡ΄ (1900) τῇ Τετάρτῃ τῆς αὐτῆς ἑβδομάδος. Ἡ ἑορτὴ ὅμως τοῦ Εὐαγγελισμοῦ, ἥτις ἐστὶ μετὰ τὴν ἐμβόλιμον τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, συμπίπτει κατ’ ἀμφότερα τὰ ἔτη ἐν μιᾷ καὶ τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἤτοι τῷ Σαββάτῳ τῆς Ε΄ Ἑβδομάδος· τοιουτοτρόπως σκεπτέον καὶ περὶ πάσης ἄλλης ζητουμένης ἑορτῆς πρὸς ἄρσιν τῆς φαινομενικῆς ἀνωμαλίας τῶν ἡμερῶν τοῦ Πίνακος ἐπὶ τῇ συμπτώσει Βισέκτου ἔτους.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: addition of one more day (i.e. February 29), we delay the beginning of the Triodion period by one date. Similarly, we delay the coinciding movable feasts by one date as well. As another example for clarification, we have two immovable feasts occurring one before February 29 and the other after. The first, namely the Feast of the Presentation of our Lord, which is one of the feasts prior to February 29, in a non-Leap Year (1889), occurs on Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee (as indicated in column 3), but in the Leap Year (1900) on Wednesday of that week. The Feast of the Annunciation, however, since it occurs after February 29, will fall in both those years on one and the same day, that is, the Saturday of the Fifth Week. It is in this manner that all other feasts of the Chart can be determined.
units.english_cohort_translation: **Conclusion of Rule 4 and Rule 5 (*Κανὼν Δ΄, Τέλος καὶ Κανὼν Ε΄*)** addition of one more day (i.e., February 29), we delay the opening date of the Triodion period by one day. In like manner, we delay the concurring movable feasts by one date as well. As another illustrative example for clarification, consider two immovable feasts occurring respectively before and after February 29: the first, namely the Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante* / *Presentation*), being one of the feasts prior to February 29, in a common year (1889) occurs on Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee (as indicated in column 3); in the leap year (1900), however, it occurs on Wednesday of that same week. The Feast of the Annunciation, on the other hand, since it occurs after February 29, falls in both years upon one and the same day—that is, the Saturday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent. In this identical manner all other feasts of the Chart can be determined.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Pre- and Post-Leap Day Coincidence and Extreme Paschal Limit (Rule 5):* The concluding section of Rule 4 and Rule 5 delineates the contrasting behavior of liturgical concurrences before and after the intercalary pivot of February 29. By contrasting the Meeting of the Lord (February 2, which shifts from Thursday to Wednesday between 1889 and 1900) with the Annunciation of the Mother of God (March 25, which remains fixed on the Saturday of the Akathist / Fifth Week of Great Lent in both years), Violakis provides an infallible operational diagnostic for typikaris. Rule 5 addresses the extreme terminal boundary of the Paschal computus: when Pascha falls on April 24 JC (May 7 GC) in a leap year, the Triodion begins on February 14 JC (February 27 GC) rather than February 13 JC. This constitutes the absolute latest possible opening of the Triodion in the history of the Orthodox Church, compressing the post-Paschal season and minimizing the Apostles' Fast to its shortest possible statutory duration.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Perpetual Concurrence Matrix:* Physical leaf p952 introduces the structural legend for the tabular Paschalion and Menologion concordance of George Violakis. The dual-dating rubric reflects the pastoral reality of the Eastern Christian diaspora, correlating the classical Julian computus (*Paskhalia*) with the civil Revised Julian and Gregorian calendars. The 13-day delta shifts the liturgical window of immovable commemorations relative to the variable 70-day pre-Paschal and 50-day post-Paschal cycles.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Early Pre-Lenten Concurrences (January 11–18):* Physical leaf p954 tabulates the earliest possible concurrences between the immovable Menologion and the pre-Lenten Triodion cycle. The solitary entry for Saint Theodosios the Cenobiarch (January 11) marks the theoretical frontier: only when Holy Pascha falls upon its earliest possible terminus of March 22 JC does the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee open on January 11, displacing the saint's full festive office. For Saint Anthony the Great (January 17), the commemoration sweeps across every day of the pre-Lenten opening week until Pascha reaches March 28 JC, where Anthony coincides directly with the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee itself.

units.english_cohort_translation: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Liturgical Concurrences of Saint Charalambos (10 February):* Physical leaf p964 documents the migration of the feast of the Holy Hieromartyr Charalambos across the opening weeks of the Great Fast and Cheesefare. When Pascha falls early (March 22 JC), the commemoration lands on Tuesday of the Second Week of Lent (§ 28, p. 190), governed by the rubrics for weekday commemorations occurring with the Presanctified Liturgy. When Pascha falls on March 24 JC, Charalambos coincides with the Sunday of Orthodoxy (§§ 23–25, pp. 188–189), requiring the full festal synthesis with the Sunday of the Triumph of Orthodoxy and the commemoration of the Holy Icons.

units.english_cohort_translation: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 956–957):* In the Greek text of leaf p971 (p. 956), Column 4 exhibits a vertical displacement: the typesetter omitted the citation for Friday of the Third Week (§ 6, pp. 197–198), printing § 4–5 opposite Friday and shifting all subsequent rubric references upward by one row throughout the page, leaving Wednesday of Clean Week without a section number. The facing English page (p. 957) rectified this displacement by restoring the rubrical references to their proper liturgical days. For Pascha Sunday on March 25 (Kyrio-Pascha), the Greek archetype notes § 69 (Easter Eve) alongside §§ 70–72, which is supplied in this critical edition.

units.english_cohort_translation: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 966–967):* On physical leaf p981 (Greek text), Column 4 assigns §§ 5–6 (p. 253) to Monday after Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers (row January 30), leaving Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers blank, whereas facing leaf p982 (English text) assigns §§ 7–8 (pp. 253–254) to Monday and restores §§ 5–6 (p. 253) to Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers. For Bright Monday (February 13), leaf p981 leaves Column 4 unprinted; the rubric citation (§§ 1–2, pp. 251–252) is restored from the facing English page. For the Translation of the Relics of Saint Athanasius (May 2), the non-canonical phrasing in the 1888 English column for Wednesday of the Apodosis of Pascha is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1. In the Greek archetype (p. 966), Column 4 entries exhibit vertical typographic shifting relative to Ascension Thursday and the Apodosis of Pascha, harmonized herein in accordance with the liturgical rubrics of the Typikon.

units.english_cohort_translation: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 968–969):* On physical leaf p984 (English text), Column 4 for February 1–5 displays a major typesetting corruption, printing "7 (257)" across five consecutive rows (Saturday through Tuesday of the Week of the Myrrh-Bearers) and "7–8 (257)" on Monday, whereas the Greek archetype on leaf p983 properly directs the reader to §§ 7–8 (pp. 253–254) for the Week of the Myrrh-Bearers and § 4 (p. 256) on Monday. units.english_cohort_translation: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 972–973):* On physical leaf p988 (English text), Column 4 for February 4–5 provides generic section references §§ 4–6 (pp. 259–260), whereas the Greek archetype on leaf p987 provides more specific cross-references to § 3 (p. 259) & § 26 (p. 248) on Tuesday and § 3 (p. 259) & § 25 (p. 248) on Monday. For Sunday of the Samaritan Woman and the preceding Monday (rows January 29–30), the Greek and English compositors swapped the rubric citations §§ 1–3 and §§ 4–6; both readings are recorded parenthetically. For the feast of Saints Constantine and Helen (May 21), the Greek archetype notes § 24 (p. 273, Eve of All Saints) alongside §§ 25–27, restored in this critical edition. Furthermore, non-canonical phrasing for Wednesday of the Apodosis of Mid-Pentecost in the 1888 English column is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1.

units.english_cohort_translation: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 974–975):* On physical leaf p990 (English text), the non-canonical phrasing for Saturday of the Apodosis of Pentecost, Friday of the Apodosis of the Ascension, and Wednesday of the Apodosis of Pascha is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1. In the Greek archetype on leaf p989, the Column 4 citation for Saturday of the Apodosis of Pentecost is printed as "23 (273)" opposite Friday with the Saturday row left blank, whereas the facing English edition on leaf p990 properly attributes § 24 (p. 273) to Saturday and § 23 (p. 273) to Friday through Tuesday; this is adopted in the critical edition. On Friday (row February 7), the Greek archetype records an additional reference "3–5 (266–267)" which corresponds to the rubrics for the preceding days that carry over onto leaf p991.

units.slavonic_incipit: As mentioned, this present list of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: As mentioned, this present list of definitions was compiled from numerous sources including internet searches. Some of the terms were also presented in the Glossary of The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by Theodore Bogdanos. In the present list, the definitions taken from or modified from the Bogdanos book are marked by an asterisk. The Bogdanos list was later expanded to include many additional citations for terms used in the Violakis Typikon itself or related to them. The terms were selected for inclusion because we felt they might be generally unfamiliar to the average reader (or in our case, the average church musician) or in need of further elucidation on other grounds. Also, because of the complexity of some subjects, the definitions have occasionally been expanded into small essays by the perceived necessity for greater clarity.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *ACOLYTE (ἀκόλουθος, ὁ) 'follower': One who follows or assists the priest during services, ceremonies or processions. In today's church, an acolyte's duties may be performed by male children (altar boys). In the early Church, however, the acolytes were adults.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ACROSTIC (ἀκροστιχίς, ἡ): The term is derived from two Greek words: Akros, meaning the end or tip [of a verse], and STICHOS meaning a line [of verse]. A stichos is similar to a STANZA, although not as long. An acrostic poem, then, is a poem or verse of several lines in which the initial letters of all the lines read in exact sequence spell a word which may be the name of the author or other appellation/dedication. An acrostic may also begin with a successive letter of the Greek alphabet beginning with alpha. The earliest example of an acrostic was a Hebrew poem in which the consecutive lines or verses began with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. This kind of poem is also known as an 'abecedarian poem'; the a-b-c-d can be perceived in this title. The most famous Scriptural acrostic is PSALM 119, where, each of the 22 stanzas of 8 verses begins with a successive Hebrew letter.

units.slavonic_incipit: It is upon this table that
units.slavonic_diplomatic: It is upon this table that the Word of God rests in the text of the book called the Holy Gospel and it is upon this table that our Lord is sacrificed offering His gifts "on behalf of all and for all." units.slavonic_incipit: The practice of the ancient church
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The practice of the ancient church was simply to celebrate the "breaking of bread" in homes, on a simple wooden table not unlike that used in the Last Supper. In time though, the place on which the bread was broken changed from common wooden tables to the tombs of those men and women of the faith who were persecuted and martyred in the name of the Lord. This practice evolved into the use of marble altar tables (reminiscent of tombs) in which the sacred relics of saints and martyrs of the Church are placed at the time of its Consecration.

units.slavonic_incipit: Today, the Altar Table is covered
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Today, the Altar Table is covered with two cloths. The first cover on the bare surface of the table, the KATASARKION, is reminiscent of the shroud placed on our Lord in the tomb at His burial. It is placed on the table by the bishop during the service of the consecration of the church and remains there permanently as the very Body of our Lord has sanctified it. The second and often richly ornate cloth, placed over the Katasarkion, stems from a gesture of respect and love by the builders of the Great Church (St. Sophia) in Constantinople. This beautiful cloth "gold-threaded and adorned with precious stones" covered the table which housed the relics of the martyrs and upon which were placed the precious gifts of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today, the faithful as members of the body of Christ, may offer beautiful altar covers in like manner.

units.slavonic_incipit: In a legend recorded by Eusebius
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In a legend recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea, King Abgarus of Edessa had written to Jesus, asking Him to come and cure him of an illness. Instead, the apostle Thaddaeus is said to have come, bearing a cloth featuring Jesus' facial features, by which the king was miraculously healed. Since Jesus was still living at the time, this image would not seem to have a connection with His alleged burial shroud, today known as the shroud of Turin. The vicissitudes of the Edessa image between the first century and his own time are not reported by Eusebius.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The image is next said to have surfaced in 525 A.D. during a flood of the Daisan, a tributary stream of the Euphrates. In the course of the reconstruction work, a cloth bearing the facial features of a man was discovered hidden in a wall above one of the gates of Edessa.

units.slavonic_incipit: There is no record explaining why
units.slavonic_diplomatic: There is no record explaining why or when the image was hidden in this manner, although some have suggested that it was to extend the assumed protection provided by the cloth to the whole city, or to hide it from persecutors of the Christian faith, persecutions being recorded in the area from the late first century until the time of the Emperor Constantine the Great. If the image was truly brought to Edessa in the first century, it might well have been hidden during the reign of Abgarus' son Ma'nu VI, who is thought to have reverted to paganism.

units.slavonic_incipit: Evagrius Scholasticus in his Ecclesiastical History
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Evagrius Scholasticus in his Ecclesiastical History mentions the image of Edessa as being discovered in 544, that it was "created by God, and not produced by the hands of man." This idea of an icon that was Acheiropoietos (Ἀχειροποίητος) Lit. "not made by human hand" is a separate enrichment of the original legend. Similar legends of supernatural origins have also accrued to other Orthodox icons.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: St. John of Damascus († 749) mentions the image in his anti-iconoclastic work On Holy Images, quoting an instance when King Abgarus had requested an image of Jesus and Jesus himself put a cloth to his face to produce the image. units.slavonic_incipit: The Mandylion disappeared again after the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Mandylion disappeared again after the Persians conquered Edessa in 609. An Arab legend, related to historian Andrew Palmer when he visited Urfa (Edessa) in 1999, relates that the towel (mendil) of Jesus was thrown into a well in what is today the city's Great Mosque. The Christian tradition is at variance with this, recounting that, in 944, it was exchanged for a group of Muslim prisoners— at that time the Image of Edessa was taken to Constantinople where it was received amidst great celebration by emperor Romanos I, who deposited it in the Palatine Chapel. It remained there until the Crusaders sacked the city in 1204 and carried off many of its treasures to western Europe – though the "Image of Edessa" is not mentioned in this context in any contemporary document.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Other documents from the 6th century— it is said— in the Vatican Library and the University of Leiden, Netherlands, seem to suggest another image at Edessa. A 10th-century codex, Codex Vossianus Latinus Q 69 found by Gino Zaninotto in the Vatican Library contains an 8th-century account saying that an imprint of Christ's whole body was left on a canvas kept in a church in Edessa: it quotes a man called Smera in Constantinople saying “King Abgar received a cloth on which one can see not only a face but the whole body” (in Latin: “Faciei figuram sed totius corporis figuram cernere poteris.”) This image is apparently not the same as the mandylion whose widely-disseminated and familiar iconic image is of a face alone.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Some modern scholars have suggested that by folding the Shroud of Turin in a certain way, it is possible to display a rectangle of fabric showing only the face, suggesting that the Shroud and the Mandylion may in fact be one and the same relic. This interpretation is also a means of explaining the provenance of the Shroud – of which no record exists before the thirteenth century.
