units.slavonic_diplomatic: AIR ('Αήρ, ὁ or 'Αέρας, ὁ) Slav. Vozdukh, vozdux 'the air'; Often the term has been spelled Aer. In a Greek Orthodox Church, this is the largest and outermost covering placed over both the chalice and PATEN. It is larger than the individual veils each used to cover the chalice and the paten. It symbolizes Joseph’s shroud on Christ’s body as well as the stone sealing Christ’s tomb. All of these veils are beautifully embroidered and are often in the same style and color as the vestments of the celebrating priest. The Air, which takes its name either from the lightness of the material of which it was formerly made or from the fact that in the Divine Liturgy, during the time of the recitation of the Nicene Constantinopolitan Creed, the priest holds it high in the air and waves it slowly over the chalice and paten. The use of the Air, like that of the smaller veils, was intended to prevent anything from falling into the chalice or paten and contaminating them before the sacred vessels were brought to the altar prior to the consecration. The Air is first mentioned by name in an explanation of the Liturgy by a writer of the sixth century, and is also alluded to as “the so-called aër” in the Acts of the Council of Constantinople. In the Greek Orthodox Church the Air is placed on the shoulders of the DEACON or PRIEST who brings the PATEN to the altar during the procession of the GREAT ENTRANCE.

The text of the Akathist Hymn is a beautiful poem, most likely authored by Romanos the Melodist and dedicated to the THEOTOKOS. It is offered on behalf of the people who flee to the Virgin Mary and Christ seeking deliverance from both adversity and sorrow.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The hymn is comprised of 24 stanzas arranged in four groups of six stanzas each. These stanzas are distributed through the evening service of each of the first four Fridays of Lent. Each STANZA begins with a successive letter of the Greek alphabet, from Alpha to Omega. The work is, therefore, an ACROSTIC poem.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: AKOLUTHIA (ἀκολουθία, ἡ) Lit. a following, attendance, or train. From the Greek akolutho “I follow”; Slav.: posledovanie). In the Eastern Orthodox churches, the term signifies the arrangement of the Divine Services (Canonical Hours or Divine Office), perhaps because these various parts are closely connected and follow in order. In a more restricted sense, the term “akoluthia” refers to the fixed portion of the Office (that which does not change from day to day).

units.slavonic_incipit: The Office is composed of both
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Office is composed of both musical and textual elements, the first is usually identified by the musical mode or tone or, in Greek, ichos (ἦχος), according to which the compositions are to be chanted (see MODE). In Byzantine Music there are eight musical modes: four primary and four derived or plagal modes. The textual elements may be read quietly in silent prayer, read in a normal speaking voice, or may also be chanted in a simple recitative style or sung with a fully constructed melody.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Office is composed of both musical and textual elements, the first is usually identified by the musical mode or tone or, in Greek, Tone (*Ichos* / ἦχος), according to which the compositions are to be chanted (see **TONE**). In Byzantine Music there are eight musical modes (Tones 1 to 8): four authentic and four plagal Tones. The textual elements may be read quietly in silent prayer, read in a normal speaking voice, or may also be chanted in a simple recitative style or sung with a fully constructed melody.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ALLELUIA ('Αλληλούϊα): This word is derived from Hebrew and is interpreted in Greek as meaning “Praise the Lord” (« Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον »). The word is sung after the reading of the APOSTOLOS. The faithful use it as a sign of joy and an expression of gladness as they praise God and thank Him for His wonders. This is also evident from the ending phrase of many Psalms to which the word is attached and from what the Book of Tobit (an apocryphal book of scripture from the Septuagint Greek Old Testament) speaks of Jerusalem being rebuilt again after its fall, that all its streets will say ‘Alleluia’ (13,18). It is also evident from the Apocalypse of John, in which, after the fall and disappearance of the spiritual Babylon, John heard a loud voice from heaven saying continuously ‘Alleluia’ (18: 2, 20-21 and 19: 1-6). units.english_cohort_translation: **ALLELUIA** (Ἀλληλούϊα): This word is derived from Hebrew and is interpreted in Greek as meaning **"Praise the Lord"** (*Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον*). The word is sung after the reading of the **APOSTOLOS**. The faithful use it as a sign of joy and an expression of gladness as they praise God and thank Him for His wonders. This is also evident from the ending phrase of many Psalms to which the word is attached and from what the Book of Tobit (a deuterocanonical book of Scripture in the Septuagint Greek Old Testament) speaks of Jerusalem being rebuilt again after its fall, that all its streets will say ‘Alleluia’ (Tobit 13:18 [LXX 13:18]). It is also evident from the Apocalypse of John, in which, after the fall and disappearance of spiritual Babylon, John heard a loud voice from heaven saying continuously ‘Alleluia’ (Revelation 18:2, 20–21; 19:1–6). Nevertheless, Christ’s Church among us uses the word not only for radiant and joyful days, as, for example, in the Antiphons of the Feasts of the Lord: 'Save us

units.slavonic_incipit: who sing to you: Alleluia!’, but
units.slavonic_diplomatic: who sing to you: Alleluia!’, but also in many places in the daily day and night services. The word is especially frequent in the rites for funerals and the mournful days of the fasts, when ‘Alleluia’ is sung in Vespers in place of the usual Prokimenon and in Matins instead of ‘The Lord is God’ (Θεὸς Κύριος). Of this ‘Alleluia’, the instruction of the Typikon says, “But if it is ‘Alleluia’, that is if there is a fast, if we do not sing “The Lord is God,” we make the Great Prostrations. Otherwise etc.” Note that the Latin Church follows an opposite custom to the Orthodox Church which expressly forbids the use of Alleluia on fast days and at mournful rites, and limits it to joyful days only, especially the day of Easter, when they sing it very often, as “Christ is risen” is frequently sung on Pascha. (The foregoing discussion of the use of Alleluia is found in the Horologion, before the Prayer of St. Ephrem the Syrian.)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ALTAR ('Ιερός Βωμός, 'Ιερόν Βῆμα): Used by the church interchangeably for the entire SANCTUARY as well as for the Holy Table ('Αγία Τράπεζα) itself. For the sake of clarity in this book the term is used to signify exclusively the Holy Table, on which the consecration of the Holy Gifts takes place. It has also been known by the terms HOLY ALTAR, HOLY SANCTUARY, IERON VIMA, SANCTUARY or simply VIMA.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ALTAR TABLE ('Αγία Τράπεζα, ἡ): The consecrated table upon which the Divine Liturgy is celebrated. On it are found the Gospel Book, the Cross, the ANTIMINSION, and the ARTOFORION. The Altar Table contains relics of the Saints which are placed within it at the time of the Church’s Consecration.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ALTAR TABLE** (Ἁγία Τράπεζα, ἡ): The consecrated table upon which the Divine Liturgy is celebrated. On it are found the Gospel Book, the Cross, the **ANTIMINSION**, and the **ARTOFORION** (Tabernacle). The Altar Table contains relics of the Saints which are placed within it at the time of the Church’s Consecration.[^569]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: AMOMOS (Ἄμωμος, ὁ): See also PSALM 118. A common abbreviation for the entire 17th KATHISMA of the Greek Old Testament Psalter (Ψαλτήριον, τό). This Kathisma contains only Psalm 118. The abbreviation is so named because of a form of the key word in Greek in the first verse of the Psalm (Μακάριοι οἱ ἄμωμοι ἐν ὁδῷ.) This Psalm, like the others, has 3 parts called Sections or Stasis (Στάσεις).

units.slavonic_incipit: As Christians began to build churches,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: As Christians began to build churches, a special place was designated from which the homily could be preached and the Gospel could be read. This place was called the amvon, today’s pulpit. It was a place erected in the middle of the church to which the deacon or priest would ascend via a stairway. Later in the church’s development the pulpit was attached to a column on the north side of the NAVE. As seen today, the pulpit is usually constructed on the soleas, to the north side of the BEAUTIFUL GATE of the HOLY SANCTUARY (the central opening in the icon screen).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANAGINOSKOMENA (ἀναγινωσκόμενα, τὰ): Lit. ‘texts which are read.’ In the Orthodox Church today, these readings are presented as pericopes (excerpts) that are read throughout the year in the various services of the church. Even though Anaginoskomena is the Orthodox term used for what Roman Catholic Church called deuterocanonical and what Protestant churches called apocrypha or pseudoepigrapha, the Anaginoskomena are not grouped together as one category as they are in the 1611 King James Version (KJV) of the Bible or Brenton’s LXX with Apocrypha. They are instead spread throughout the Greek Septuagint.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ANAGINOSKOMENA** (ἀναγινωσκόμενα, τά): *Lit.* 'texts which are read.' In the Eastern Church today, these readings are presented as pericopes (excerpts) that are read throughout the year in the various services of the Church. Even though *Anaginoskomena* is the Eastern term used for what the Catholic Church calls the deuterocanonical books and what Protestant traditions call apocrypha or pseudepigrapha, the *Anaginoskomena* are not grouped together as one separate category as they are in the 1611 King James Version (KJV) of the Bible or Brenton’s LXX with Apocrypha. They are instead integrated throughout the Greek Septuagint (LXX).

what St Athanasios refers to as “other books besides these not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness. The Wisdom of Solomon, and the Wisdom of Sirach, and Esther, and Judith, and Tobit (τωβίθ) and that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd. But the former, my brethren, are included in the Canon, the latter being [merely] read; nor is there in any place a mention of apocryphal writings.”

In the Orthodox tradition, there is no fully accepted list of what the term Anaginoskomena includes. One can just look at various Bibles for these variations. 2 Esdras in the KJV is called 3 Esdras in the Slavonic Bible and listed as an appendix, but is not in the Septuagint, and therefore not in the Greek Bible. The Slavonic Bible does not include 4 Maccabees but it is found as an appendix in the Greek Bible. This is the only book the Orthodox Church universally considers as apocryphal.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the LXX, PSALM 151 is labeled not as 151 but as ‘outside the number’ and it is found as an appendix to the 150 Psalms of David. There are, following the Psalms in various ancient liturgical psalter books and biblical manuscripts such as Codex Alexandrinus, what is known as the Odes, which are liturgical songs quoting or alluding to other parts of Scripture. The most commonly used is Ode 14 (a morning hymn based on Luke 2:14 and various portions of the Psalter) and is known as the Great Doxology. This doxology as used at the end of MATINS (ORTHROS) before the Divine Liturgy begins, every Sunday and at Great Compline during the Great Fast (Lent).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: of contents and canon for evening and day use of the Psalms. This codex also has the Psalms of Solomon listed following the New Testament books which also includes 1 and 2 Clements. Another Greek Biblical manuscript, the Codex Sinaiticus, also includes the Epistle of Barnabas and most of the Shepherd of Hermas following the New Testament books. These post New Testament materials are commonly grouped together as part of a larger corpus known as the Apostolic Fathers and is outside the scope of the current collection of the Anaginoskomena.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Prayer of Azarias with the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Prayer of Azarias with the Song of the Three Holy Children, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon, are all found as part of the Book of the Prophet Daniel in the LXX. In addition, the Prayer of Azarias is Ode 7 and the Song of the Three Holy Children with additional verses is Ode 8 of the nine Orthodox Odes which is also listed in the 14 Odes in Rahlfs’ LXX, but arranged as Odes 9 and 10 in Codex Alexandrinus and Swete’s LXX. The Prayer and Song, preceded by the canonical part of Daniel 3, are chanted during Holy Saturday Vespers.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *ANALOGION, pl. ANALOGIA (ἀναλόγιον, τό· ἀναλόγια, τά) Slav. Analogy, Naloj: A usually three-legged wooden stand or podium placed on the either side of the SOLEAS near the north and south doors of the altar. It usually has a slanted top and is used as a stand either for the Book of the Gospels or an icon or as a stand for the service books used by the chanters.

units.slavonic_incipit: Some analogia are fashioned so that
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Some analogia are fashioned so that they may be folded for easy portability. Some are intricately carved of fine wood and others are a simple frame intended to be completely covered with richly embroidered cloths (antipendia). The analogion used by the chanters is a special type which has two or three slanted sides and which may rotate to allow the chanters to more easily access the numerous liturgical books that may be used in the services. (FL)

The analogion used by the chanters is a special type which has two or three slanted sides and which may rotate to allow the chanters to more easily access the numerous liturgical books that may be used in the services. (FL)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANAPHORA (ἀναφορά, ἡ) the ‘Offering’ or ‘Offertory’: The Anaphora is the most sacred part of the Divine liturgy in which the offerings of bread and wine are consecrated as the body and blood of Christ. In the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, the rite begins with this prayer text: “Let us stand reverently! Let us stand in awe! (Στῶμεν καλῶς· στῶμεν μετὰ φόβου...) up to and including the hymn text “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Angelic Hosts...” ("Αγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, Κύριος Σαβαώθ...) which is taken from Isaiah 6:1-55. This text in the Latin rite is called the Sanctus.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ANAPHORA** (ἀναφορά, ἡ) the 'Offering' or 'Offertory' (Eucharistic Prayer): The Anaphora is the most sacred part of the Divine Liturgy in which the offerings of bread and wine are consecrated as the Body and Blood of Christ. In the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, the rite begins with this prayer text: **"Let us stand well! Let us stand with fear!"** (*Στῶμεν καλῶς· στῶμεν μετὰ φόβου...*) up to and including the hymn text **"Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Sabaoth..."** (*Ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, Κύριος Σαβαώθ...*) which is taken from Isaiah 6:1–3. This hymn text in the Latin rite is called the *Sanctus*.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the Offertory of the Greek Orthodox Church, the priest, accompanied by the deacon and the acolytes and censer-bearers, goes to the PROTHESIS (a small side altar where the PROSKOMIDI is performed). Nearing the end of the singing of the Cherubic Hymn, the clergy solemnly bring the blessed but as yet unsanctified bread and wine out of the SANCTUARY through the northern door of the ICONOSTASIS

units.slavonic_incipit: and proceed to the center of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: and proceed to the center of the church or at least directly in front of the BEAUTIFUL GATE, where, turning to the people and holding the sacred gifts they pray successively for the ecclesiastical and secular authorities. In the Greek Orthodox Church today, prayers are said for the national leaders, the Holy Synod, and various other church dignitaries. The clergy then proceed solemnly to the altar bearing the eucharistic elements through the BEAUTIFUL GATE. This part of the Liturgy is called the Great Entrance. After the paten and chalice have been placed on the altar, the priest completes the Offertory with the prayer of the Anaphora: “Receive also the supplication of us sinners and let it reach Your Holy Altar; enable us to bring before You gifts and spiritual sacrifices for our sins and for the sins of the people that have been commited in ignorance. Make us worthy of finding favor with You so that our sacrifice may be well received by You, and the beneficient spirit of Your grace may rest on us, on these Gifts, and on all Your people.” («Πρόσδεξαι καὶ ἡμῶν τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν τὴν δέησιν, καὶ προσάγαγε τῷ ἁγίῳ Σου Θυσιαστηρίῳ καὶ ἱκάνωσον ἡμᾶς προσενεγκεῖν σοι Δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας πνευματικὰς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἁμαρτημάτων, καὶ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ ἀγνοημάτων· καὶ καταξίωσον ἡμᾶς εὑρεῖν χάριν ἐνώπιόν Σου, τοῦ γενέσθαι σοι εὐπρόσδεκτον τὴν θυσίαν ἡμῶν καὶ ἐπισκηνῶσαι τὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτός Σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ προκείμενα Δῶρα ταῦτα καὶ ἐπὶ πάντα τὸν λαόν Σου.»)

units.slavonic_incipit: Byzantine Modes and sung in alternate
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Byzantine Modes and sung in alternate succession from Sunday to Sunday throughout the church year as part of the Cycle of Modes (see MODE). Although this cycle commences on Easter Sunday, the Anastasima Apolytikia begin to be sung on the Third Sunday of Easter (Sunday of the Myrrh Bearers) with Ὅτε κατῆλθες (Ote Katilthes) in Mode II. In the Divine Liturgy on Sundays, the Anastasimon Apolytikion is usually sung immediately before and after the Small Entrance.
units.english_cohort_translation: Tones of the Oktoechos and sung in alternate succession from Sunday to Sunday throughout the church year as part of the Cycle of the Eight Tones (see **TONE**). Although this cycle commences on the Sunday of Pascha, the Anastasima Dismissal Troparia (lit. 'Anastasima Apolytikia') begin to be sung on the Third Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearing Women) with **"When You descended"** (*Ὅτε κατῆλθες* / *Ote Katilthes*) in Tone 2. In the Divine Liturgy on Sundays, the Resurrection Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Anastasimon Apolytikion') is usually sung immediately before and after the Small Entrance.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANATOLIKON, (᾿Ανατολικόν, τό) pl. ANATOLIKA (᾿Ανατολικά, τά): A hymn or the group of hymns of the Praises (ENI) sung in Sunday Matins (ORTHROS) and addressed to the Lord. The name derives from two possible sources: 1. From the Verse “Dawn is His name” («᾿Ανατολὴ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ»); or 2. The name of their possible author, Anatolios.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANAVATHMOS (ἀναβαθμός, ὁ), pl. ANAVATHMI (ἀναβαθμοί, οἱ) Slav. Stepenny Antifony: A short hymn or series of hymns, based on the Psalms of Ascent (Gr. Anavathmi) numbered 119-133, which are sung at Orthros on Sundays, and Feasts with a Gospel. On Sundays they are divided into three Antiphons, except for Mode VIII, which has four. They are sung immediately before the Prokimenon. On Feasts, only the first Antiphon of Mode IV is used. In some churches the final hymn from the Second Antiphon in Mode IV is used rather than repeating the third Antiphon. (adapted from AE).
units.english_cohort_translation: **ANAVATHMOS** (*ἀναβαθμός, ὁ*; *pl.* **ANAVATHMI** / *ἀναβαθμοί, οἱ*) *Slav.* *Stepénny Antifóny* [Gradual Antiphons]: A short hymn or series of hymns based on the Psalms of Ascent (Gr. *Anavathmi*) numbered LXX 119–133 [MT 120–134], which are sung at Matins on Sundays and feasts having an appointed Gospel. On Sundays they are divided into three Antiphons, except for Tone 8, which has four Antiphons. They are sung immediately before the Prokimenon. On feasts, only the first Antiphon of Tone 4 is sung. In some traditions the final hymn from the Second Antiphon in Tone 4 is used rather than repeating the third Antiphon. (adapted from AE).[^573]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANOINTMENT (χρῖσμα) Slav. Eleopomazanie: The act of tracing a mark in the form of a cross, using Holy Oil. This act is performed on a person or an article in a Church ceremony.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ANTIMINSION (᾿Αντιμήνσιον, τό) Slav. Antimins: The Antiminsion of today is a rectangular piece of cloth, of linen or silk, into which is sewn the incorruptible relic of a Saint or Martyr, making real the early liturgical connection with the Martyrs who died rather than renounce Christ, and whose blood, after the Blood of Christ, formed the very foundation of the Church. The antiminsion has representations of the entombment of Christ, the four Evangelists, and scriptural passages related to the Eucharist. The antiminsion is usually wrapped in another protective cloth, usually of silk, called the ILITON; often red in color, it symbolizes the swaddling-clothes with which Christ was wrapped after His birth or the winding-sheet or shroud in which His body was wrapped after His Crucifixion.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ANTIMINSION** (*Ἀντιμήνσιον, τό*) *Slav.* *Antimins*: The Antiminsion of today is a consecrated rectangular cloth of linen or silk into which are sewn holy relics of a martyr or saint, embodying the ancient liturgical tradition of celebrating the Eucharist over the tombs of the martyrs who died rather than renounce Christ, and whose blood, united with the Blood of Christ, formed the foundation of the Church. The antiminsion bears iconographic representations of the Entombment of Christ, the four Evangelists, instruments of the Passion, and scriptural verses relating to the Holy Eucharist. The antiminsion is folded and wrapped within an outer protective silk cloth called the **ILITON** (*Εἱλητόν*); often red in color, it symbolizes both the swaddling clothes of Christ at His Nativity and the winding-sheet or burial shroud (*sindon*) in which His sacred Body was wrapped at His Crucifixion and Burial.

units.slavonic_incipit: The word Antiminsion is a combination
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The word Antiminsion is a combination of Greek and Latin meaning ‘in place of the table’. While the HOLY TABLES were always to have been consecrated with RELICS placed inside of them, it was not always possible for the Bishop to visit each community to do so. For this reason, Bishops could consecrate these cloths or boards and send them to communities to be used in place of a consecrated Holy Table. This also allowed for portable Holy Tables for travelers. Military Chaplains and Missionaries may also use an Antiminsion instead of the table when serving in remote areas.
units.english_cohort_translation: The word Antiminsion is a hybrid Greek-Latin compound (*ἀντί* and *mensa*), meaning 'in place of the table.' While the **ALTAR TABLE** must always be consecrated with **RELICS** deposited within its sepulcher, it was not always feasible for the bishop to travel to every community for an altar consecration. For this reason, bishops consecrated these cloths or portable wooden tablets and distributed them to communities to serve in lieu of a fully consecrated stone altar table. This also provided portable altars for military chaplains, missionaries, and traveling clergy serving in remote regions.[^574]

units.slavonic_incipit: secrated. This may take place as
units.slavonic_diplomatic: secrated. This may take place as a part of the Consecration of a church, or in a separate service. In this rite, the bishop annoints a pocket sewn into the Antiminsion in which to place the Relics of the saints and Chrism. The bishop then seals them in place with wax mastic. He may also stamp it with his official seal. He then inscribes the Antiminsion with the name of the church for which it has been consecrated and signs it. Printed on every Antiminsion are the words “By the grace of the All-Holy, Life-giving Spirit, this Antiminsion, the Holy Table, is consecrated for the Offering on it of the Body and Blood of our Lord in the Divine Liturgy.” The Antiminsion always remains under the control of the consecrating Bishop.
units.english_cohort_translation: secrated. This solemn consecration may occur as part of the Consecration of a church, or in a distinct liturgical service. In this rite, the bishop anoints a small pocket sewn into the Antiminsion into which he deposits the holy relics of the saints and Holy Chrism (Myron). The bishop then seals the relics in place with fragrant wax-mastic. He may also imprint his episcopal seal upon the cloth. He then inscribes the Antiminsion with the dedication of the church for which it is consecrated, dating and signing the document. Inscribed upon every Antiminsion are the sacred words: **“By the grace of the All-Holy, Life-giving Spirit, this Antiminsion, the Holy Table, is consecrated for the Offering on it of the Body and Blood of our Lord in the Divine Liturgy.”**

units.slavonic_diplomatic: APICHIMA (ἀπήχημα also προήχημα, ἐνήχημα): A term in Byzantine music for an intonation formula meant to be used as a short mnemonic. It is a melodic phrase normally sung by the Archcantor or Protopsaltis alone and without an accompanying ison. Its function is to help the chanters as an ‘aide memoir’ to recall the scale or melodic formulas that are characteristic of the MODE of the hymn which is about to be sung. The apichima is given before the beginning of the chant to be sung. It also provides the beginning pitch for the first note of the hymn to be sung.
units.english_cohort_translation: **APICHIMA** (*ἀπήχημα, τό*; also *προήχημα*, *ἐνήχημα*): A musicological term in Byzantine chant for an intonation formula functioning as a melodic mnemonic. It is a melodic formula sung solo by the Archcantor or Protopsaltis without an accompanying ison. Its liturgical function is to guide the chanters as an *aide-mémoire* to establish the melodic scale and modal characteristics of the Tone about to be chanted. The apichima is intoned immediately prior to commencing the hymn, giving the starting pitch for the choir.

units.slavonic_incipit: APOCRYPHA: In modern usage the Apocrypha
units.slavonic_diplomatic: APOCRYPHA: In modern usage the Apocrypha refers to ancient Jewish books that are not part of the Hebrew Bible but are considered canonical in Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism. Among the various books included are Tobit, Judith, Baruch, and the Maccabees as well as Ecclesiasticus and the Wisdom of Solomon. Protestant churches follow Jewish tradition in judging these works apocryphal or noncanonical. The term deuterocanonical is used to refer to works accepted in one canon but not all. Pseudepigrapha are spurious works for which biblical authorship is claimed.
units.english_cohort_translation: **APOCRYPHA**: In modern biblical usage, the term Apocrypha designates ancient Jewish sacred writings that are not part of the Rabbinic Hebrew canon but are recognized as canonical Scripture within Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism. Among these books are Tobit, Judith, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), and the Wisdom of Solomon. Protestant traditions follow the narrower Hebrew Masoretic canon in classifying these works as noncanonical. In Catholic theology the term *deuterocanonical* is applied to these sacred books. Pseudepigrapha, by contrast, are noncanonical or spurious texts falsely attributed to biblical authors.

units.slavonic_incipit: The last day of the period
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The last day of the period of METHEORTA, on which the observance of a feast comes to an end. The order of service of the day of the apodosis is fundamentally that of the feast day itself. The Apodosis of a feast day lasts more than one day and usually occurs eight days after the actual feast day. The Apodosis of Easter occurs after forty days, on the eve of the Ascension. (TB and FL).
units.english_cohort_translation: **APODOSIS** (*ἀπόδοσις, ἡ*) *Slav.* *Otdaniye* (*Отданіе*): (lit. 'giving back' or 'leave-taking'). See also **FEASTS**. The final day of the period of **METHEORTA** (Afterfeast), on which the liturgical observance of a feast comes to an end. The order of service on the day of the Apodosis is fundamentally identical to that of the feast day itself. The Apodosis of a major feast usually occurs eight days after the actual feast day (on its octave). The Apodosis of Pascha occurs on the fortieth day, on the eve of the Ascension. (TB and FL).

The final day of the period of **METHEORTA** (Afterfeast), on which the liturgical observance of a feast comes to an end. The order of service on the day of the Apodosis is fundamentally identical to that of the feast day itself. The Apodosis of a major feast usually occurs eight days after the actual feast day (on its octave). The Apodosis of Pascha occurs on the fortieth day, on the eve of the Ascension. (TB and FL).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *APOLYTIKION FOR (name of saint or event): This title is used in this book to indicate that the Apolytikion at hand is a generic one belonging to several saints of the same kind of life and saintly activity. This distinction is usually stated in the saint’s epithet in the synaxarion such as “martyr,” “confessor,” etc.
units.english_cohort_translation: **DISMISSAL TROPARION FOR...** (name of saint or event) (lit. 'Apolytikion for...'): This liturgical title designates a common Dismissal Troparion belonging to a general category of saints sharing a similar life or martyr's struggle. This classification corresponds to the saint's title in the Synaxarion, such as “martyr,” “confessor,” “venerable monastic,” or “hieromartyr.”

units.slavonic_incipit: Also, it is a dismissal prayer
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Also, it is a dismissal prayer or hymn said or sung at the end of the Liturgy and at other times during Matins and Vespers. The Apolytikion changes for each feast-day of the year and commemorates the subject of the feast. For instance, the Apolytikion of Christmas is: “Your Nativity, O Christ...” The Apolytikion for the feast of the Annunciation is: “Today is the crowning of our salvation ...Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you!” *APOLYTIKION OF (name of saint) (᾿Απολυτίκιον τοῦ (δεῖνος)):
units.english_cohort_translation: The Dismissal Troparion is also sung at the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy, at Matins, and at the Small Hours. The Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Apolytikion') changes according to the liturgical calendar to commemorate the feast of the day. For example, the Dismissal Troparion of the Nativity of Christ is: **“Thy Nativity, O Christ our God, hath shone upon the world the light of knowledge...”** (*«Ἡ Γέννησίς Σου, Χριστὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν...»*). The Dismissal Troparion for the Annunciation is: **“Today is the fountainhead of our salvation and the manifestation of the eternal mystery: the Son of God becomes the Son of the Virgin, and Gabriel announces the good tidings of grace. Therefore, let us also cry aloud with him unto the Mother of God: Rejoice, full of grace, the Lord is with thee!”** (*«Σήμερον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν τὸ κεφάλαιον...»*).

units.english_cohort_translation: **APOSTICHA** (*Ἀπόστιχα, τά*) *Slav.* *Stikhiry na stikhovne* (*Стихиры на стиховнѣ*): Hymnographic verses (**STICHERA**) chanted with intercalated Psalm verses. units.slavonic_diplomatic: APOSTOLOS (᾿Απόστολος, ὁ) Slav. Apostol: An Orthodox service book containing portions of New Testament scriptures either from the Acts of the Apostles or from the Letters of St. Paul and arranged for use during the Orthodox Ecclesiastical Year. The book may also be referred to as the Epistle Lectionary. The prescribed lections are read as the first scripture reading in the Divine Liturgy and before the Gospel reading. The book usually includes the PROKIMENA and ALLELUIAS sung before and after the prescribed lection.
units.english_cohort_translation: **APOSTOLOS** (*Ἀπόστολος, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Apostol* (*Апостолъ*): The liturgical lectionary containing the New Testament pericopes drawn from the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of the Holy Apostles (Paul, Peter, John, James, and Jude), arranged for reading throughout the Ecclesiastical Year. It is commonly designated as the Epistle Book. The appointed pericope is read as the first scriptural lection at the Divine Liturgy prior to the Holy Gospel. The Apostolos also contains the **PROKIMENA** and **ALLELUIAS** with their verses sung before and after the Epistle lection.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ARCHIERATIKON (᾿Αρχιερατικόν, τό) Slav. Chinovnik; Roman. Pontifical. In Greek, the ‘book of the Hierarch’, is the book used by the BISHOP for a Hierarchical Divine Liturgy. It also contains various other services and blessings reserved for the Bishop. It has the same function as the IERATIKON, but is intended only for use by bishops performing the services and contains directions for all the peculiarities of hierarchical services. Besides the order of the Vigil and the liturgies of St. John Chrysostom, St. Basil the Great, and the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, it also contains the ritual order for the ordination or tonsuring to various ecclesiastical ranks, and the order for the consecration of the ANTIMINSION or of a CHURCH.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ARCHIERATIKON** (*Ἀρχιερατικόν, τό*) *Slav.* *Chinovnik* (*Чиновникъ*); *Roman Pontifical*: In Greek, the 'Book of the Hierarch.' It is the pontifical liturgical book used by the **BISHOP** during a Hierarchical Divine Liturgy and other episcopal rites. It corresponds functionally to the presbyteral **IERATIKON** (*Sluzhebnik*), but contains the ceremonial rubrics and pontifical prayers reserved exclusively to bishops. In addition to the orders for the All-Night Vigil and the Divine Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom, St. Basil the Great, and the Presanctified Gifts, the Archieratikon contains the pontifical ordinals for major orders (deacon, presbyter, bishop) and minor orders (reader, subdeacon), along with the orders for the consecration of holy antiminsia and the dedication of churches.[^576]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: the Acts of Councils, and was even adopted quite extensively in the West where it did not disappear from occasional usage until the ninth century. Originally the archimandrite seems to have been only the superior or abbot of his own monastery; gradually, however, he came to exercise authority over a number of monasteries and by the eleventh century the archimandrites of such monastic centres as Mount Athos, and Mount Olympus in Bithynia, were the equivalent of the Western abbots-general. At present there are in the Greek Orthodox Church two kinds of archimandrites, the original monastic officers exercising jurisdiction in their respective monasteries, as well as honorary archimandrites or well-educated priests attached to chanceries of the great patriarchates (e.g. Constantinople), or at the head of certain branches of temporal administration. It is from the ranks of the archimandrites that bishops are selected. The archimandrite is consecrated by the ecclesiastical authority of a patriarch, a metropolitan, or a bishop, and in some monasteries by election. He has the right to wear a pectoral cross and the EPIGONATION in the celebration of Liturgy, and to sign the cross before his name after the manner of bishops. The monastic archimandrites have also the right to the pastoral staff, and to a pectoral mantle having the four squares of embroidered cloth called “the tables of the law.” Their rights and privileges differ somewhat by tradition or custom in different parts of the Orthodox Church. The usual vestment, common to all, is a black veil worn over the familiar headgear of the Greek clergy and falling down over the back. Archimandrites enjoy the right of precedence among other priests; among themselves this right is regulated by the date of their ordination. Also, an archimandrite ordained by a patriarch outranks archimandrites ordained by hierarchs of lower rank. There is a formal rite for the appointments and creation of these officers, performed with more solemnity in the installment of monastic archimandrites. The office is found not only in all Greek Churches subject to Constantinople, but also in the Russian, Bulgarian, and other autocephalous Churches, that once owed allegiance to that patriarchal see; it exits also among the Catholic (Melchite) Greeks. units.english_cohort_translation: the conciliar acts of the ecumenical synods. The dignity was also adopted widely in the Christian West, persisting in regular usage until the ninth century. Originally the archimandrite was simply the superior or abbot of his own monastery; gradually, however, he acquired supervisory jurisdiction over multiple monastic communities, and by the eleventh century archimandrites of great centers such as Mount Athos and Mount Olympus in Bithynia functioned as monastic abbots-general. In modern Greek practice two classes of archimandrites exist: monastic archimandrites governing their monasteries, and honorary or chancery archimandrites—celibate presbyters holding administrative posts in patriarchal or diocesan chanceries. Archimandrites are elevated by the authority of a Patriarch, Metropolitan, or Bishop, and in certain monasteries by monastic election. An archimandrite possesses the liturgical right to wear a pectoral cross and the **EPIGONATION** (*palitsa*) during the Divine Liturgy, and to prefix the sign of the cross to his signature after the manner of hierarchs. Monastic archimandrites also bear the pastoral staff (*rabdos* / *posokh*) and wear the monastic mantle embellished with four embroidered *tabulae* representing the Old and New Law (“the tables of the law”). Their vesture includes the black veil (*epanokalimavkion*) worn over the cylindrical kamilavkion and draping down the back. Archimandrites hold precedence over all other presbyters; among themselves precedence is determined by the date of elevation, though an archimandrite blessed by a patriarch outranks those elevated by lower hierarchs. A solemn liturgical ordinal governs their installation. The dignity exists across the Greek, Ukrainian, Melkite, Italo-Greek, Russian, and Bulgarian Churches, but is not attested among the non-Chalcedonian traditions (Copts, West Syrians, Ethiopians, Armenians). units.english_text: the conciliar acts of the ecumenical synods. The dignity was also adopted widely in the Christian West, persisting in regular usage until the ninth century. Originally the archimandrite was simply the superior or abbot of his own monastery; gradually, however, he acquired supervisory jurisdiction over multiple monastic communities, and by the eleventh century archimandrites of great centers such as Mount Athos and Mount Olympus in Bithynia functioned as monastic abbots-general. In modern Greek practice two classes of archimandrites exist: monastic archimandrites governing their monasteries, and honorary or chancery archimandrites—celibate presbyters holding administrative posts in patriarchal or diocesan chanceries. Archimandrites are elevated by the authority of a Patriarch, Metropolitan, or Bishop, and in certain monasteries by monastic election. An archimandrite possesses the liturgical right to wear a pectoral cross and the **EPIGONATION** (*palitsa*) during the Divine Liturgy, and to prefix the sign of the cross to his signature after the manner of hierarchs. Monastic archimandrites also bear the pastoral staff (*rabdos* / *posokh*) and wear the monastic mantle embellished with four embroidered *tabulae* representing the Old and New Law (“the tables of the law”). Their vesture includes the black veil (*epanokalimavkion*) worn over the cylindrical kamilavkion and draping down the back. Archimandrites hold precedence over all other presbyters; among themselves precedence is determined by the date of elevation, though an archimandrite blessed by a patriarch outranks those elevated by lower hierarchs. A solemn liturgical ordinal governs their installation. The dignity exists across the Greek, Ukrainian, Melkite, Italo-Greek, Russian, and Bulgarian Churches, but is not attested among the non-Chalcedonian traditions (Copts, West Syrians, Ethiopians, Armenians). An important historical survival of its use[^577]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ARTOFORION (᾿Αρτοφόριον, τό) Slav. Artofor, Daroxranitelnica, Kovceg or Ark and Kivot or Tabernacle: Also called the Tabernacle. It is located on the back surface of the Altar Table and is used to store the Holy Gifts later to be used in a subsequent Presanctified Liturgy as well as the Holy Gifts previously prepared on each Great (Holy) Thursday and used for conveyance to the sick.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ARTOFORION** (*Ἀρτοφόριον, τό*) *Slav.* *Artofor, Darokhranitel’nitsa* (*Дарохранительница*), *Kovcheg* or *Kivot* (Tabernacle): The Tabernacle reserved upon the Holy Table. It serves to reserve the Pre-consecrated Gifts for the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts during Great Lent, as well as the Holy Eucharist consecrated on Great and Holy Thursday and reserved throughout the year for conveyance to the sick (Viaticum).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ARTOKLASIA (᾿Αρτοκλασία, ἡ) Slav. Blagoslovenie xlebov: The ceremony of the Blessing of Loaves, or Breaking (Gr. klasis) of Bread (Gr. artos) that takes place before the APOLYTIKION at Vespers when there is an All-night VIGIL. In today’s Greek Orthodox churches, it is celebrated on important feasts even when there is no Vigil, at VESPERS or MATINS or usually after the LITURGY. The ceremony commemorates Christ’s miraculous blessing of the five loaves to feed about five thousand people without provisions who had come to hear Him preach near a sea shore (Mathew 16:13-21; Mark 6:30-44; Luke 9:11-16; and John: 6:1-14.) The ceremony also symbolizes the Lord Himself as the “bread of life” that has descended on mankind from Heaven. The ceremony for such occasions can be found in the bilingual edition of the Divine Liturgy published by the Archdiocese of Thyateira in the United Kingdom. (modified from AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **ARTOKLASIA** (*Ἀρτοκλασία, ἡ*) *Slav.* *Blagoslovenie khlebov* (*Благословеніе хлѣбовъ*): The liturgical rite of the Blessing of Loaves (lit. 'breaking of bread,' from Gr. *klasis*, breaking, and *artos*, leavened bread) celebrated before the Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Apolytikion') at Great Vespers during an All-Night **VIGIL** or Litiya. In parish practice it is often celebrated on major feasts at **VESPERS** or **MATINS**, or at the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy. The ceremony commemorates Christ’s miraculous multiplication of the five loaves to feed the five thousand men who had assembled to hear Him preach (Matthew 14:13–21; Mark 6:30–44; Luke 9:11–17; John 6:1–14). The five loaves of wheat bread, accompanied by vessels of wheat, wine, and olive oil, are blessed by the priest with the prayer of Artoklasia, recalling that the Lord Himself is the true “Bread of Life” descended from Heaven.[^578]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: BALDACHIN: Sometimes written as baldachino or baldaquin, this is a permanent dome-like canopy made of fabric, wood, stone or metal. units.slavonic_diplomatic: BEATITUDES (Μακαρισμοί, οἱ): The eight blessings given by Christ at his Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5: 3-12). Also a salutation addressed to an Orthodox Patriarch (“Your Beatitude”). (From FL).
units.english_cohort_translation: **BEATITUDES** (*Μακαρισμοί, οἱ*): The eight Gospel blessings pronounced by Christ in His Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3–12), sung as the Third Antiphon at the Divine Liturgy with appointed troparia. The term also provides the official honorific title addressed to an Eastern Patriarch or Major Archbishop (“Your Beatitude”). (From FL).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *BEAUTIFUL GATE (῾Ωραῖα Πύλη, ἡ): The gate in the center of the ICONOSTASIS is referred to in the Typikon as the Beautiful Gate through which only members of the clergy may pass. In the liturgical theology of the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Beautiful Gate symbolizes the womb of the Virgin Mary. There may also be present a curtain that is drawn closed at certain times during the services, especially during the preparation of communion during the Divine Liturgy. The doors at either end of the Iconostasis are called Angel Doors because the icons of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are usually depicted on them; alternatively, they may also be called deacon’s doors because the deacons frequently enter and leave the sanctuary through them. Laymen, when permitted to enter the sanctuary, will use one of the Angel Doors.
units.english_cohort_translation: **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (*Ὡραῖα Πύλη, ἡ* / *Royal Doors*): The double doors in the center of the **ICONOSTASIS**, designated in the *Typikon* as the Beautiful Gate or Royal Doors, through which only ordained clergy may pass while vested for divine service. In Eastern liturgical theology, the Beautiful Gate symbolizes the gates of Paradise opened by the Resurrection and the virginal womb of the Most Holy Theotokos through which Christ entered the world. Behind the doors hangs the liturgical veil or curtain (*katapetasma*), which is drawn closed at prescribed moments, especially during the communion of the clergy. The side doors on either side of the Iconostasis are termed the Angel Doors because icons of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are depicted upon them; they are also called the Deacon's Doors because the deacons enter and exit through them during litanies and censings. When lay servers are blessed to enter the sanctuary, they use the Angel Doors.[^579]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: BISHOP (᾿Επίσκοπος, ὁ) Lit. Overseer. Today's bishop or HIERARCH is the spiritual leader of a local community of Christians. He ranks above archimandrites, priests and deacons. Only a bishop has the sacramental authority to ordain one to the priesthood. He also administers his diocese. In the New Testament there is no clear distinction between the offices of bishop and elder (presbyter), both of which function as leaders of the community. However, by the mid- to late first century, the Church began to reserve the title of bishop for men of spiritual qualification who were consecrated to follow the Apostles in their office of oversight (see article, “The Four ‘Orders’ in Church Government,” at 1 Tim.; Acts 1:15 26; 14:23; 1 Tim. 3:1-7). (Rev. John W. Morris, Ph.D., Glossary of Orthodox Terminology)
units.english_cohort_translation: **BISHOP** (*Ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ*): *Lit.* 'Overseer.' The Bishop or **HIERARCH** is the chief shepherd, high priest, and spiritual leader of a local eparchy or diocese. He holds hierarchical precedence over archimandrites, priests, and deacons. A bishop possesses the exclusive sacramental power to ordain candidates to the holy priesthood and major orders. He also administers the temporal and spiritual affairs of his diocese. In the apostolic period of the New Testament, the titles of bishop (*episkopos*) and elder (*presbyteros*) were used interchangeably for pastoral leaders of the local churches. However, by the late first and early second century (as witnessed in the epistles of St. Ignatius of Antioch), the Church reserved the title of bishop exclusively for the single chief shepherd consecrated to succeed the Apostles in their office of pastoral oversight (cf. Acts 1:15–26; 14:23; 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). (Adapted from Rev. John W. Morris, Ph.D., *Glossary of Orthodox Terminology*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CANON (κανών, ὁ· κανόνες, οἱ) See also KANON, KANONES: A principal part in the Orthros (MATINS) service although it may appear elsewhere. A Canon is a lengthy poetic form composed of nine odes, with each ode being made up of many hymns, the number and source of which are regulated by the TYPIKON. Each ode takes its theme from and is therefore linked to a Biblical canticle (e.g., Ode 1 is linked to Exodus 15:1-19, the Canticle of Moses) which serves as its source. In churches, except those located in monasteries, apart from the Magnificat, the Biblical Canticles are usually omitted, simple refrains taking the place of the biblical verses.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CANON** (*κανών, ὁ*; *pl.* *κανόνες, οἱ*; See also **KANON**, **KANONES**) *Slav.* *Kanon*: A principal structural component in the Matins (Orthros) service, although it also occurs at Compline, Midnight Office, and in various trebniki (services of supplication or *parakleseis*). A Canon is a lengthy poetic hymnographic composition structured into nine Odes, with each Ode consisting of multiple troparia, the exact number and appointment of which are regulated by the *Typikon*. Each Ode takes its overarching theme from, and is modeled upon, one of the nine Biblical Canticles (for example, Ode 1 is linked to the Canticle of Moses in Exodus 15:1–19, which serves as its biblical prototype). In parish churches, unlike monasteries, the full verses of the Biblical Canticles (apart from the Magnificat) are customarily omitted, and brief liturgical refrains (such as **"Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"** or **"Most Holy Theotokos, save us"**) are chanted in place of the scriptural verses. In daily liturgical practice, most Canons contain only eight Odes, because Ode 2 is appointed solely on Tuesdays during Great Lent, although the poetic acrostics of the canons frequently indicate that nine odes were originally composed. Normally three canons, and on Sundays four canons, are prescribed, appointed in such a manner that each Ode, including the Heirmos, comprises 14 troparia. (Excerpted from PL and AE).[^581]

units.english_cohort_translation: **CANONARCH** (*κανονάρχης, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Kanonarkh*: The Canonarch is a tonsured liturgical chanter or reader assigned to ensure that the choir chants the prescribed liturgical texts in the appointed Tone and with the proper melody. He performs this function by reciting, in a solemn recitative cadence, each phrase of a slow sticheron or hymn immediately before the chanter or choir chants it with its full melody and meter. The Canonarch holds precedence higher than an ordinary Reader and lower than a Subdeacon or Deacon. The Canonarch is tonsured by the Bishop through the cheirothesia for minor orders. In early Byzantine practice, this tonsure was linked with that of the subdiaconate or reader. The Slavonic *Typikon* prescribes that a monastic canonarch fulfills his liturgical office with his head covered (that is, wearing the monastic klobuk).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CANONARCH (κανονάρχης, ὁ): The Canonarch is one of the chanters or readers whose task is to see that the other singers sing the correct texts in the correct mode and with the correct melody by reciting in a recitative style each phrase of a slow (andante or slower) hymn before the chanter finally sings it with its proper melody and rhythm. The Canonarch is higher in rank than a Reader and lower in rank than the Deacon. The Canonarch is tonsured by the Bishop. This tonsure seems to have covered both the Subdeacon and the Canonarch similar to a single tonsure having covered the office of taper-bearer, chanter and reader. The Slavonic Typikon also mentions that a monastic canonarch performs his duties with a covered head (i.e. wearing a klobuk).
units.english_cohort_translation: **CANTICLE** (*ᾠδή, ἡ*; ODE OR SONG) *Slav.* *Pesn'*: The English term is derived from the Latin *canticulum* (a diminutive of *canticum*, song, from *cantare*, to sing). It is employed in Western biblical terminology as the equivalent of the Vulgate *canticum*. The Authorized King James Version generally translates both Hebrew and Greek terms simply as "song."

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The title Canticle has been applied (a) to certain prayers and poetical compositions of Biblical origin other than the Psalms; and (b) to the nine (in practice, eight) subdivisions of the canon (originally designed to accompany the reading of the Biblical canticles).
units.english_cohort_translation: The title Canticle is applied: (a) to specific scriptural prayers and poetic compositions outside the Psalter; and (b) to the nine (in daily practice, eight) poetic subdivisions of the liturgical Canon, originally composed to accompany the chanting of the Biblical Canticles.

units.english_cohort_translation:
1. The (First) Song of Moses (**"Let us sing unto the Lord"**, Exodus 15:1–19)
2. The (Second) Song of Moses (**"Give ear, O heavens"**, Deuteronomy 32:1–43)
3. The Prayer of Hannah, the mother of Samuel the Prophet (**"My heart is established in the Lord"**, 1 Kingdoms 2:1–10 LXX [1 Samuel 2:1–10])
4. The Prayer of the Prophet Habakkuk (**"O Lord, I have heard Thy report, and was afraid"**, Habakkuk 3:2–19 LXX)
5. The Prayer of the Prophet Isaiah (**"From night until morning my spirit seeks Thee early"**, Isaiah 26:9–20 LXX)
6. The Prayer of the Prophet Jonah (**"I cried in mine affliction unto the Lord"**, Jonah 2:2–9 LXX)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Gradually over the centuries, the verses of the Biblical Canticles were omitted (except for the Magnificat), and only the composed troparia were read, linked to the original canticles by an irmos. During Great Lent, however, the original Biblical Canticles are still read.
units.english_cohort_translation: Over the centuries, the direct chanting of the full scriptural verses of the Biblical Canticles was gradually discontinued (except for the Magnificat), and only the composed troparia of the canon were chanted, tied to the themes and rhythm of the biblical canticle by the opening **HEIRMOS** (lit. 'irmos'). During Great Lent, however, the ancient practice is preserved and the full Biblical Canticles are still chanted.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CASSOCK (ράσον, τὸ· χιτών, ὁ· ἱμάτιον, τό): Cassocks exist in two forms, the ‘inner cassock’ and the ‘outer cassock.’ The Inner (or under) cassock is a floor-length garment that has long sleeves fitted like shirtsleeves. The ‘outer (over) cassock’ is also a floor-length garment, but more loosely fitting, with large sleeves. The wearing of inner-cassocks and outer-cassocks is common to bishops, priests, deacons, monks and nuns. Permission to wear a cassock is often given to seminarians, monastic novices, sub-deacons and readers in some parishes.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CASSOCK** (*ράσον, τό* · *χιτών, ὁ* · *ἱμάτιον, τό*) *Slav.* *Podryasnik* / *Ryasa*: The cassock is the basic clerical and monastic garment of the Eastern Church, existing in two primary forms: the inner cassock (*anteri* / *podryasnik*) and the outer cassock (*raso* / *ryasa*). The inner cassock is an ankle-length tunic with closely fitted sleeves. The outer cassock is a loose, flowing robe with wide, open sleeves. Both inner and outer cassocks are worn by bishops, priests, deacons, monastics, and tonsured clergy. In modern parish practice, blessing to wear the cassock is also granted to seminarians, novices, subdeacons, and altar servers.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CENSER (θυμιατόν, τό, or θυμιατήριον, τό): In the Eastern Orthodox Church a censer is similar in design to the Roman Catholic thurible, but with more than one chain and often with the addition of small bells. Censers are used constantly in Orthodox services, especially at every VESPERS, MATINS, and Divine Liturgy. If a deacon is present, he typically does much of the censing, otherwise the duty is that of the Priest. Tonsured servers or acolytes are permitted to prepare and carry the censer, but may not swing it during prayers. Censing is the practice of swinging a censer suspended from chains towards something or someone, typically an icon or person, so that the smoke from the burning incense travels in that direction. Burning incense generally represents the prayers of the people rising towards Heaven. One commonly sung Psalm during the censing is “Let my prayer rise like incense before You, my hands like the evening sacrifice.” («Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου, ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου· ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου, θυσία ἑσπερινή.») Some Orthodox Christians use a small hand censer (KATZION) on their home altars. The katzion, which may also be used in church, has no suspending chains or bells and is usually waved in a cross-wise fashion before the person or item being censed.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CENSER** (*θυμιατόν, τό* or *θυμιατήριον, τό*) *Slav.* *Kadilo* (*Кадило*): The liturgical vessel used for burning incense. In the Eastern Church the censer is suspended by four chains (three representing the Holy Trinity and one representing the Unity of the Godhead), often adorned with twelve bells symbolizing the proclamation of the twelve Apostles. Censers are used constantly throughout all liturgical services, especially at Vespers, Matins, and the Divine Liturgy. When a deacon serves, he performs the rubrical censings; otherwise, the celebrating priest censes. Tonsured altar servers may prepare and carry the censer, but only ordained clergy may swing it during public liturgical prayers. Censing symbolizes the sweet fragrance of the Holy Spirit, the sanctification of the faithful and the temple, and the ascending prayers of the Christian community rising up to heaven (cf. Revelation 8:3–4). The standard psalm verse chanted during censing at Vespers is: **“Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.”** (*«Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου, ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου· ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου, θυσία ἑσπερινή.»*, Psalm 140:2 LXX). Eastern Christians also utilize a small hand censer (**KATZION** / *κατζίον*), which has no suspending chains or bells and is swung in the form of a cross before sacred icons or deceased persons.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Today, for censing in the home one may use granulated incense and small, concave charcoal briquettes. One lights the corner of the briquette with a flame, then places it in the censer and extinguishes the flame. After the glowing sparks traverse the entire briquette, it is ready to have incense placed on it.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CHASMODIA (χασμῳδία, ἡ): Confusion resulting from disorder, lack of clarity and jarring dissonance in the chanting of the services. See Canon XV of the Council in Laodicaea.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CHASMODIA** (*χασμῳδία, ἡ*): Liturgical cacophony or discordant singing resulting from disorder, rhythmic confusion, and lack of musical clarity during church services. This vocal disorder is specifically prohibited by Canon XV of the Council of Laodicea, which ordained that only canonical cantors (*psaltai*) should chant from the ambo.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CHONEFTIRION (χωνευτήριον, τό): An area in or near the sanctuary containing a sink or wash basin for the clergy to wash their hands prior to the service of PROSKOMIDI and also to empty material discarded from any of the sacraments. See also THALASSIDION.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CHONEFTIRION** (*χωνευτήριον, τό*): A sacrarium or sacred drain (piscina) located within or adjacent to the sanctuary (*bema*). It contains a sink or washbasin where the clergy wash their hands prior to the Proskomide and after Holy Communion, and into which holy water or consecrated matter discarded from the Sacred Mysteries is reverently poured directly into the earth. See also **THALASSIDION**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *CHROMATIC (χρωματικόν): A type of scale or MODE using tones outside the diatonic scale; these tones can be approximated by playing them on the dark keys (flats or sharps) of a piano keyboard. For example, the scale c-d-e-f-g-a-b-c belongs to the diatonic Mode IV Plagal. The scale c-dflat-e-f-g-aflat-b-c, on the other hand, belongs to the chromatic form of Mode II Plagal.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CHROMATIC SCALE** (*χρωματικόν*): In Byzantine chant theory, a modal scale employing chromatic intervals (augmented seconds and half steps) outside the diatonic scale. In modern Western musical terms, these tones correspond to the altered pitches (sharps and flats) of a keyboard. For example, while the diatonic Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal) uses the natural diatonic scale (C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C), the chromatic form of Tone 6 (Mode II Plagal) utilizes intervals with augmented steps (such as C–D♭–E–F–G–A♭–B–C).

For example, while the diatonic Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal) uses the natural diatonic scale (C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C), the chromatic form of Tone 6 (Mode II Plagal) utilizes intervals with augmented steps (such as C–D♭–E–F–G–A♭–B–C).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CHURCH (ἐκκλησία, ἡ or ἱερὸς ναός, ὁ): In Greek the first term is most often used to describe the structure of the building while the latter term “Holy Temple” implies also function. Orthodox Christians worship and continue to worship Christ in structures that are more often than not determined by the social, political and economic climate of their area and/or the theological understandings of the era. The earliest Christians gathered together and worshipped in private homes until persecutions began. From this point they sought refuge in caves, catacombs and other such areas where they could worship Christ in safety. Shortly after Constantine the Great issued the ‘edict of toleration’, Christians began to build churches.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CHURCH** (*ἐκκλησία, ἡ* or *ἱερὸς ναός, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Tserkov'* / *Khram*: In Greek liturgical usage, the term *ecclesia* primarily denotes the Christian assembly or church building, while *hieros naos* (Holy Temple) emphasizes its consecrated liturgical function as the dwelling place of God. Christian architecture has historically developed in dialogue with theological doctrine, spiritual symbolism, and the cultural environment of each era. The earliest Christians assembled for the Eucharist in private homes (*domus ecclesiae*); during periods of imperial persecution, they gathered covertly in catacombs, caves, and secluded dwellings. Following the Edict of Milan issued by Constantine the Great in 313, Christians began erecting monumental public basilicas.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: One of these magnificent structures that remains largely intact today is the Church of Agia Sophia or “Holy Wisdom” in what was once the capital city of the Byzantine Empire, Constantinople. The building of this Church was commissioned by Constantine himself; however, after a fire destroyed much of the church and upon the exile of Saint John Chrysostom by Empress Eudoxia, the church was rebuilt by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian. Upon its completion and consecration on December 27, 537 this grandest of churches, was and remains the model for churches throughout Eastern Christendom.
units.english_cohort_translation: Among these sacred monuments, the most renowned and influential is the Great Church of the Holy Wisdom of God (**Hagia Sophia**) in Constantinople. Originally founded by Constantine the Great, rebuilt after fire, and destroyed during the Nika riots following the era of Saint John Chrysostom, the present magnificent cathedral was erected by the Emperor Justinian I. Consecrated on December 27, 537, Hagia Sophia became the theological and architectural paradigm for church construction throughout Eastern Christendom.

units.slavonic_incipit: Today, our churches are generally structured
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Today, our churches are generally structured in the form of a cross with a prominent dome over the center. They are divided into three sections, the NARTHEX, the NAVE, and the SANCTUARY. The interior and the exterior of the Church flow naturally from the dome to the ground creating a sacred space that is aesthetically pleasing. When enriched also by the iconography, the whole structure reflects the beautiful multiplicity of God’s own artifact, the cosmos, where we have unity in variety and variety in unity. The structures frequently boast a golden Cross on their highest point, usually illumined through-
units.english_cohort_translation: In Eastern Christian tradition, churches are typically designed according to a cruciform plan crowned by a central dome, symbolizing heaven descending to earth and the cosmic sovereignty of Christ the Pantokrator. The interior is divided into three distinct liturgical areas: the **NARTHEX** (entrance vestibule), the **NAVE** (*naos*, where the faithful stand for worship), and the **SANCTUARY** (*bema* or Holy Table area, separated by the **ICONOSTASIS**). This tripartite division mirrors the ancient Tabernacle and Temple of Jerusalem (the Outer Court, the Holy Place, and the Holy of Holies). The architectural lines lead the eyes upward toward the dome, enriched by a hierarchical iconographic program reflecting the heavenly hierarchy and the redeemed cosmos. The structures frequently bear a golden Cross at their highest point, often illuminated through-[^586]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The intent of the Orthodox house of worship is to create an awareness of God’s presence. No distinction is made between spiritual and sensory perception. Not only the spirit but also the senses experience the splendor and beauty of God’s creation. This total perception can be overwhelming. An old Russian chronicle relates that Prince Vladimir of Kiev could not decide which faith to adopt for himself and his people until his envoys reported from Constantinople that they had witnessed services there such that “We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth,” they declared, “for on earth there is no such splendor or such beauty, and we are at a loss to describe it.
units.english_cohort_translation: The central theological purpose of an Eastern church building is to manifest the divine presence and create a sacred threshold where heaven and earth unite. units.english_cohort_translation: **CHYMA** (*χῦμα*): *Lit.* 'in a poured, flowing stream.' A liturgical rubric specifying that a text is to be read in a simple, continuous speaking tone or steady recitative rather than chanted with elaborate melismatic melodies. On occasion, the term also denotes a continuous, flowing recitative chant, such as the priest's chanted petitions. The *Typikon* explicitly distinguishes between these modes of execution, employing the directives **“it is said chyma”** (*λέγεται χῦμα*, simple reading) and **“it is chanted chyma”** (*ψάλλεται χῦμα*, straight recitative chanting).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CODEX, pl. CODICES (κῶδιξ, ὁ, κώδικες, οἱ): This was the word for a book made of thin wooden strips coated with wax upon which one could write. The usual modern sense of codex, “book formed of bound leaves of paper or parchment,” is due to Christianity. By the first century B.C. there existed notebooks made of leaves of parchment, used for rough copy, first drafts, and notes. By the first century A.D. such manuals were used for commercial copies of classical literature. The Christians adopted this parchment manual format for the Scriptures used in their liturgy because a codex is easier to handle than a scroll and because one can write on both sides of a parchment but on only one side of a papyrus scroll. By the early second century all Scripture was reproduced in codex form. In traditional Christian iconography, therefore, the Hebrew prophets are represented holding scrolls and the Evangelists holding codices. The codex later replaced the scroll for writing lengthy church documents.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CODEX** (*κῶδιξ, ὁ*; *pl.* **CODICES** / *κώδικες, οἱ*): Originally designating a bound collection of wooden tablets coated with wax for writing, the term *codex* came to denote a manuscript book composed of bound sheets of papyrus or parchment. The widespread adoption of the codex format was fundamentally spurred by early Christianity. While pagan and classical texts long continued to be written on scrolls (*volumina*), Christians embraced the parchment codex in the first and second centuries for liturgical and scriptural use, because a codex permitted writing on both sides of the folio (recto and verso), facilitated rapid cross-referencing between Old and New Testament passages, and was far more portable. By the fourth century, the codex had completely superseded the scroll for lengthy ecclesiastical documents and biblical manuscripts. In Christian iconography, Old Testament prophets are traditionally depicted holding scrolls, whereas the holy Evangelists hold bound codices.[^587]

See also APODIPNON: The English word compline is derived from the Latin completorium, as Compline is the completion of the working day. The entire subject of the historical development of Compline is carefully discussed in the orthodox wiki article at http://orthodoxwiki.org/Compline.
units.english_cohort_translation: **COMPLINE** (*ἀπόδειπνον, τό*) *Slav.* *Povecheriye* (*Повечеріе*): *Lit.* 'after-supper service.' See also **APODIPNON**. The English term *compline* derives from the Latin *completorium*, denoting the completion of the working day. Compline is the final liturgical office of the daily cycle, prayed in the evening prior to nocturnal rest.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Compline is a service which is part of the daily cycle of services. It is the final church service of the day and takes place after supper prior to going to sleep. In the Greek Orthodox Church of today, the service exists in two forms: Great Compline and Small Compline. This Compline service or office whether the Great or Small form will include a Canon to the Theotokos in the Mode of the Week (found in the OKTOICHOS). Services to saints in the MINEON that for some reason cannot be celebrated on their appointed day may be done on the nearest convenient day at Compline. In such cases, the Canon for the Saint would be read in addition to the Canon to the Theotokos followed by the Hymns (STICHIRA) to the saint from VESPERS. There are also particular days such as FOREFEASTS, AFTERFEASTS, and days during the PENTIKOSTARION period that have special Canons for Compline composed for them. The service always ends with the mutual asking of forgiveness. In some Orthodox traditions, Evening Prayers (i.e. those said before sleeping) will be read near the end of Compline. In the monasteries of the Holy Mountain of Athos today, an ancient practice is observed in which all those of the community who are present at the end of Compline venerate the Relics and Icons in the church, and receive the blessing of the priest. For the exact order of prayer of the Great Compline Service in English, see http://www.goarch.org/chapel/liturgical_texts/greatcompline.
units.english_cohort_translation: In Eastern liturgical practice, Compline exists in two distinct forms: **Great Compline** (*Μέγα Ἀπόδειπνον* / *Velikoye Povecheriye*) and **Small Compline** (*Μικρὸν Ἀπόδειπνον* / *Maloye Povecheriye*). Small Compline is celebrated on ordinary days throughout the liturgical year and includes an appointed Canon to the Most Holy Theotokos in the Tone of the week (from the *Oktoechos*). Commemorations of saints from the *Menaion* that cannot be celebrated on their appointed calendar day may be transferred and prayed at Compline, reading their proper canon alongside the canon of the Theotokos and singing their appointed aposticha stichera from Vespers. In addition, special canons are appointed for Compline during Forefeasts, Afterfeasts, and the Pentecostarion period. Compline concludes with the solemn Mutual Asking of Forgiveness between the celebrant and the congregation. In monastic tradition, notably on the Holy Mountain of Athos, the community venerates the holy relics and icons of the church at the conclusion of Compline and receives the blessing of the abbot or officiating priest.[^588]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: CREED (Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως, τό): From the Latin credo, “I believe.” The Creed, known in Greek as the Symbol of Faith (Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως) meaning the “bringing together” of the worshippers to confess their Christian faith.
units.english_cohort_translation: **CREED** (*Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως, τό* / The Symbol of Faith) *Slav.* *Simvol Very* (*Сѵмволъ Вѣры*): Derived from the Latin *credo* (“I believe”). In Greek Christian tradition, the Creed is termed the **Symbol of Faith** (*Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως*), denoting the authoritative gathering and harmonization of the apostolic teachings by which Christians profess their common faith in the Triune God.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the early Church there were
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the early Church there were many different forms of the Christian confession of faith—many different “creeds.” These creeds were always used originally in service of Baptism. Before being baptized, a person had to state what he believed. The earliest Christian creed was quite likely a simple confession of faith that Jesus is the Christ, i.e., the Messiah, and that the Christ is Lord. By publicly confessing this belief, the person could be baptized into Christ, dying and rising with Him into the New Life of the Kingdom of God in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the early Church, diverse baptismal confessions of faith existed across various apostolic sees. These confessions were rooted in the baptismal liturgy, wherein catechumens were required to solemnly profess their personal faith prior to descending into the baptismal font. The earliest apostolic confession was the concise profession that Jesus is the Christ and the Lord. Through this public confession, the catechumen was baptized into Christ, dying and rising with Him into the new life of the Kingdom of God in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (cf. Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4).

units.slavonic_incipit: As time passed, different churches had
units.slavonic_diplomatic: As time passed, different churches had different creedal statements, all professing the identical faith, yet using different forms and expressions, with different degrees of detail and emphasis. These creedal forms usually became more detailed and elaborate in those areas where questions about the faith and various heresies had arisen.
units.english_cohort_translation: As the Church expanded, local churches developed more detailed baptismal creeds to articulate the apostolic faith against emergent heresies. In the fourth century, the Arian crisis convulsed the Christian world regarding the eternal divinity of the Son of God (the divine Logos). The heresiarch Arius maintained that the Son was a created being, saying “there was a time when He was not.” Orthodox fathers, led by Saint Athanasius the Great, confessed that the Son is eternal, uncreated, and consubstantial (*homoousios*) with the Father.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the fourth century, a great
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the fourth century, a great controversy developed in Christendom about the nature of the Son of God (also called in the Scripture the Word or Logos). Some said that the Son of God is a creature like everything else made by God. Others contended that the Son of God is eternal, divine, and uncreated. Several councils met and made many statements of faith about the nature of the Son of God. The controversy raged throughout the entire Christian world.
units.english_cohort_translation: This doctrinal conflict was resolved by the 318 Holy Fathers convened by Emperor Constantine at the First Ecumenical Council in Nicaea in 325, who promulgated the authoritative Symbol of Faith.[^589]

units.slavonic_incipit: Orthodox Christian entering the communion of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Orthodox Christian entering the communion of the Orthodox Church. In the same way, the creed became part of the life of Orthodox Christians and an essential element of the Divine Liturgy of the Orthodox Church at which each person formally and officially accepts and renews his baptism and membership in the Church. Thus, the Symbol of Faith is the only part of the liturgy (repeated in another form just before Holy Communion) which is in the first person. Most other songs and prayers of the liturgy are plural, beginning with “we”. The creedal statement begins with “I,” because faith is at first personal, and only then corporate and communal.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In addition, the deacon may perform other tasks related to Church life from time to time with the blessing and at the direction of his bishop or priest. The deacon, however, may not consecrate the Holy Gifts.

units.slavonic_incipit: While, originally deacons of the Church
units.slavonic_diplomatic: While, originally deacons of the Church only assisted the bishops in good deeds and works of charity, in more recent centuries the diaconate had become an almost exclusive liturgical function where the deacons only assisted at the celebration of the church services. Today, deacons will often head educational programs and youth groups, perform hospital visitation, missionary work, and conduct social welfare programs.

Today, deacons frequently direct educational initiatives and youth ministries, visit hospitals, engage in missionary outreach, and oversee charitable programs.

units.slavonic_incipit: Just as with bishops and priests,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Just as with bishops and priests, there are distinctions of administrative rank among deacons. A senior deacon of a cathedral or principal church may be awarded the title PROTODEACON as in the case of St. Stephen, and acquire precedence when serving with other deacons. The chief deacon who primarily serves a bishop is called an ARCHDEACON. A deacon who is also a monastic is called a hierodeacon.
units.english_cohort_translation: Just as with bishops and presbyters, administrative distinctions of precedence exist among deacons. A senior deacon of a cathedral or principal church may be awarded the dignity of **PROTODEACON** (*πρωτοδιάκονος*, after the prototype of the Holy Protomartyr and Archdeacon Stephen), obtaining precedence when serving with other deacons. The chief deacon who attends specifically upon a bishop is designated an **ARCHDEACON** (*ἀρχιδιάκονος*). A deacon who has received monastic tonsure is called a **hierodeacon** (*ἱεροδιάκονος*).
units.slavonic_text: Just as with bishops and priests, there are distinctions of administrative rank among deacons. A senior deacon of a cathedral or principal church may be awarded the title PROTODEACON as in the case of St. Stephen, and acquire precedence when serving with other deacons. The chief deacon who primarily serves a bishop is called an ARCHDEACON. A deacon who is also a monastic is called a hierodeacon.
units.english_text: Just as with bishops and presbyters, administrative distinctions of precedence exist among deacons. A senior deacon of a cathedral or principal church may be awarded the dignity of **PROTODEACON** (*πρωτοδιάκονος*, after the prototype of the Holy Protomartyr and Archdeacon Stephen), obtaining precedence when serving with other deacons. The chief deacon who attends specifically upon a bishop is designated an **ARCHDEACON** (*ἀρχιδιάκονος*). A deacon who has received monastic tonsure is called a **hierodeacon** (*ἱεροδιάκονος*).
