units.slavonic_diplomatic: DEUTEROCANON (ἀναγινωσκώμενα, τά): The Roman Catholic term for the deuterocanonical books of the Bible. These are books considered by the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches to be canonical parts of the Christian Old Testament but are not present in the Hebrew Bible. The word deuterocanonical comes from the Greek meaning “belonging to the second canon.” The etymology of the word is misleading, but it does suggest the hesitation with which these books were accepted into the canon by some theological scholars. Note that the term does not mean non-canonical; despite this it has sometimes been used as a euphemism for the Apocrypha.
units.english_cohort_translation: **DEUTEROCANON** (*ἀναγινωσκώμενα, τά* / *Anaginoskomena*, "books read"): The ecclesiastical designation for the deuterocanonical books of the Sacred Scriptures. These comprise the holy books recognized by the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches as inspired, canonical components of the Christian Old Testament, which are absent from the rabbinic Hebrew Masoretic canon. The term *deuterocanonical* derives from the Greek meaning “pertaining to the second canon.” Although the etymology might suggest a secondary status, reflecting the historical deliberations before their universal conciliar ratification, the term in Catholic and Orthodox theology does not imply inferior authority or non-canonicity, despite occasional conflation by outside commentators with the Apocrypha.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Protestant Christians usually do not classify any texts as deuterocanonical; they either omit them from the Bible, or include them in a section designated Apocrypha. The similarity between these different terms contributes to the confusion between the Roman Catholic and Orthodox deuterocanon and the texts considered noncanonical by other groups of Christians.
units.english_cohort_translation: Protestant communions do not classify these sacred books as canonical Scripture; they generally omit them from published editions or segregate them under the heading of Apocrypha. The divergence in nomenclature often generates confusion between Catholic and Orthodox canonical corpora and non-canonical pseudepigrapha.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: If one were to peer through the central BEAUTIFUL GATE into the Sanctuary, one would find a small marble shelf or table on either side of the back wall. This area on the left is known as the PROTHESIS while that on the right is known as the DIAKONIKON. The unique purpose of these areas in the Sanctuary can best be understood by the differing items that rest upon them and the differing icons that are found immediately behind them.
units.english_cohort_translation: Looking through the central **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (*Ὡραία Πύλη* / Royal Doors) into the Sanctuary, one observes a recessed marble table or niche on either side of the eastern wall. The table situated on the north (liturgical left) is the **PROTHESIS** (Table of Oblation / *Proskomide*), while that on the south (liturgical right) is the **DIAKONIKON**. The distinctive functions of these two sanctuary chambers are defined by the sacred vessels resting upon them and the sacred iconography adorning their respective walls.

units.slavonic_incipit: The PROTHESIS is the place where
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The PROTHESIS is the place where the Eucharistic Gifts are prepared during the Morning MATINS Service (ORTHROS), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Additionally, it is the place where the Eucharistic items, i.e. the Holy Chalice, the Holy PATEN, the communion cloths, the spoon that dispenses the gifts etc., are stored.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **PROTHESIS** is the sacred table upon which the Eucharistic Gifts of bread and wine are prepared during the Proskomide office, performed during the morning Matins (*Ὄρθρος* / Orthros) prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. In addition, the holy vessels and implements—the Holy Chalice, the Holy Paten (*Diskos*), the liturgical veils and Aer, the Asterisk, the Spear, and the Communion Spoon—are vested and preserved upon it. Upon the wall behind the Prothesis is customarily depicted the icon of the Nativity of Christ, commemorating that Christ is the sacrificial Lamb offered “on behalf of all and for all.”

units.slavonic_incipit: Early in the Church’s history, these
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Early in the Church’s history, these shelves or tables were not found in the Sanctuary. Instead the Holy Gifts were prepared and the liturgical items of the Church were kept in a separate building called the SKEVOPHYLAKION. It was from this place that the Gospel and the Offerings were brought into the Church at the appropriate time in the service by the clergy (our processions today with the Gospel during the Small Entrance and the Offering during the Great Entrance are reminiscent of this practice). The SKEVOPHYLAKION or place for guarding the vessels,” with time, fell into disuse being replaced by the Prothesis and the Diakonikon, now located in the Sanctuary.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the early centuries of the Church, these subsidiary tables were not located within the sanctuary proper. Instead, the Eucharistic Gifts were prepared and the liturgical treasures preserved in an adjacent, independent structure designated the **SKEVOPHYLAKION** (*σκευοφυλάκιον*, vessel-guardhouse). From this external treasury the Holy Gospel and the Eucharistic Offerings were solemnly carried into the temple at the appointed liturgical moments by the clergy—a ceremonial movement preserved today in the processions of the Small Entrance with the Gospel and the Great Entrance with the Gifts. Over time, as liturgical architecture evolved, the separate *skevophylakion* fell into disuse, replaced by the integrated Prothesis and Diakonikon niches within the sanctuary itself.

It was from this place that the Gospel and the Offerings were brought into the Church at the appropriate time in the service by the clergy (our processions today with the Gospel during the Small Entrance and the Offering during the Great Entrance are reminiscent of this practice). units.slavonic_diplomatic: “One of the most important extant Patriarchal Diataxes is attributed to a leading figure of the chancery in the second half of the 14th century. The Protonotary (Πρωτονοτάριος), Kyr. Deacon Gemistos (ca. 1397), [later called the MEGA SAKELLARIOS] of the Great and most-holy Church of God. An important note found in the upper margin of f. 3r in Athos Vatopedi 135 (AD 1390), the principle manuscript of the Diataxis, gives a precise date for its composition, August 1386. If indeed Dimitrios Gemistos wrote this Diataxis, this does not mean Gemistos created something entirely new out of nothing. A comparison of his Diataxis with other sources reveals that he composed it utilizing both local and foreign traditions: the traditions of the patriarchal rite in Constantinople and the Athonite Diataxis for the Divine Liturgy by Philotheos Kokkinos (ca. 1300-1377/78), twice patriarch of Constantinople (1353-54, 1364-1376).

An important scribal annotation recorded in the upper margin of folio 3r in manuscript Athos Vatopedi 135 (AD 1390), the principal codex of the Diataxis, provides a precise date for its composition: August 1386. units.slavonic_incipit: Implicit in Anton Baumstark’s famous assertion
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Implicit in Anton Baumstark’s famous assertion that it is the nature of liturgy “to relate itself to the concrete situations of times and places,”[1] is the possibility that the historical situation which gave rise to a liturgical document can be deduced from a study of that document. Thus, in the case of Gemistos’ Diataxis, historical currents also emerge through close reading of the text of the Diataxis and a reconstruction of the rites contained therein. Gemistos’ choice of the Philothean Diataxis speaks volumes about the powerful influence of Athonite, hesychast monasticism on the Constantinopolitan
units.english_cohort_translation: > Implicit in Anton Baumstark’s celebrated maxim that it is the nature of liturgy “to relate itself to the concrete situations of times and places,”[1] is the premise that the historical situation which gave rise to a liturgical monument can be deduced through rigorous analysis of that document. Thus, in the case of Gemistos’ Diataxis, historical currents emerge through close exegesis of the text and the liturgical reconstruction of the rites therein contained. Gemistos’ adoption of the Philothean Diataxis speaks volumes about the profound influence of Athonite hesychast monasticism upon the Constantinopolitan[^595]

This is a transformation that will have at its core a strong central patriarchate with a powerful administrative bureaucracy utilizing all the ancient imperial and sacred symbols to convey its authority.

units.slavonic_incipit: patriarchal throne. Looking beyond the historical
units.slavonic_diplomatic: patriarchal throne. Looking beyond the historical situation in which Gemistos’ Diataxis was created, one can already see developing the rough outline of the transformation the Byzantine Church will undergo, one that will allow it to survive through the long centuries of Turkish domination. This is a transformation that will have at its core a strong central patriarchate with a powerful bureaucracy using all the ancient imperial and religious symbols to convey its power.
units.english_cohort_translation: > In order to discern these currents at work, the distinct strata of sources embedded within Gemistos’ Diataxis must be differentiated and identified. Subsequently, the manner in which he deployed his sources requires critical examination. Only at this juncture can we begin to comprehend why he selected the sources he employed. In other words, to ascertain precisely what Gemistos himself authored, what he adapted, and what he interpolated into his Diataxis, those sections displaying literary dependence must be compared systematically with their demonstrable exemplars (the Philothean Diataxis and the official Euchologion for ordination rites). An explanation must be formulated to account for their textual concordance as well as their variations. The findings of this analytical deconstruction illuminate the historical origins of the Diataxis.

units.slavonic_incipit: In order to see these currents
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In order to see these currents at work, the different layers of sources in Gemistos’ Diataxis need to be peeled apart and identified. Then, how he used his sources needs to be examined. Only at this point can we begin to understand why he used the sources he used. In other words, in order to understand what exactly Gemistos himself wrote, what he adapted, and what he inserted into his Diataxis, these sections in Gemistos’ Diataxis which show literary dependence must be further compared with their obvious sources (the Philothean Diataxis, the Euchologion for the ordination rites). An explanation must be found, or at least attempted, to account for their agreement, but also for their differences. The results of this fascinating deconstructing process cast light on the origins of the Diataxis.

units.slavonic_incipit: The first step in the process
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The first step in the process of thoroughly analyzing Gemistos’ Diataxis is to untangle the text of the Philothean Diataxis from it and place Gemistos in comparison with this direct ancestor in the Byzantine liturgical Diataxis tradition. Nowhere is Gemistos’ dependency on the Philothean Diataxis more apparent than in the prothesis rite: nearly seventy-five percent of the prothesis rite in Gemistos’ text is taken directly from the Philothean Diataxis either word-for-word or with only superficial modifications. Throughout the rest of his Diataxis, Gemistos used Philotheos’ Diataxis much less, and most of this other material is either original or from another, unknown source. Plainly, one of Gemistos’ reasons for composing his patriarchal Diataxis was to combine the Philothean Diataxis, and especially the prothesis rite from Philotheos’ Diataxis, with the patriarchal rite and Constantinopolitan traditions. So while Gemistos’ desire to incorporate the Philothean Diataxis is clear by his extensive use of the Philothean Diataxis, his motives for doing so are not. Philotheos, after all, was a recently deposed patriarch, someone whose legacy
units.english_cohort_translation: > The initial phase in analyzing Gemistos’ Diataxis requires disentangling the Philothean Diataxis from his text and establishing Gemistos’ relationship to this direct precursor in the Byzantine Diataxis tradition. Nowhere is Gemistos’ dependence upon the Philothean Diataxis more pronounced than in the Prothesis rite: approximately seventy-five percent of the Prothesis rite in Gemistos’ text is adopted directly from the Philothean Diataxis, either verbatim or with merely stylistic modifications. Throughout the remainder of his Diataxis, Gemistos utilizes Philotheos’ text far more sparingly, drawing primarily upon original compositions or unidentified sources. Evidently, one of Gemistos’ principal objectives in compiling his Patriarchal Diataxis was to synthesize the Philothean Diataxis—most notably its monastic Prothesis rite—with the patriarchal cathedral ceremonial and Constantinopolitan traditions. Yet while Gemistos’ intent to incorporate the Philothean Diataxis is manifest, his underlying motives remain complex. Philotheos, after all, was a deposed patriarch whose ecclesiastical legacy[^596]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: was so controversial that his commemoration was forbidden by his immediate successor, Patriarch Makarios. What is more, Philotheos’ Diataxis represents the tradition of Athonite monasticism. Its incorporation within the patriarchal/cathedral liturgical tradition marks its ascendancy, and with it the ascendancy of the monastic tradition, within the larger Byzantine liturgical tradition. But perhaps it is equally a sign that the patriarchal chancery accepted not only Philotheos’ Diataxis as a new liturgical rule, but also marks a rehabilitation of Philotheos by the patriarchate.
units.english_cohort_translation: > A distinct portrait of Dimitrios Gemistos emerges from the critical examination of his Diataxis and the differentiation of its sources. He was preeminently a Byzantine churchman, conservative in disposition and staunchly loyal to the Constantinopolitan patriarchate. Gemistos was likewise a career administrator, commencing his thirty-year tenure in the patriarchal chancery as a notary under Philotheos in the 1360s. By the close of his career he attained the high dignity of Mega Sakellarios (*Μέγας Σακελλάριος*), demonstrating distinguished administrative competence. As an experienced official, he possessed complete mastery of patriarchal chancery terminology and an intimate understanding of the bureaucratic hierarchy and traditions of the Great Church. The precision of his knowledge is corroborated by comparative analysis of surviving chancery records. Having served in the patriarchal administration for two decades prior to drafting his Diataxis, his administrative expertise was comprehensive. Gemistos’ institutional loyalty extended personally to the occupants of the patriarchal throne; his incorporation of the non-Constantinopolitan Philothean Diataxis was motivated not by an impulse toward innovation, but by institutional conservatism and reverence for Philotheos Kokkinos.

units.slavonic_incipit: A discernible image of Dimitrios Gemistos
units.slavonic_diplomatic: A discernible image of Dimitrios Gemistos emerges when the text of his Diataxis is studied and its various sources disentangled and investigated. He was first and foremost a Byzantine Churchman, conservative in nature and fiercely loyal to the Constantinopolitan patriarchate. Gemistos was also a career bureaucrat and began his thirty year career in the patriarchal chancery as a notary under Philotheos sometime in the 1360’s. By the end of his life he had become the Mega Sakellarios, thus proving himself to have been capable and successful. Characteristic of any successful bureaucrat, he was fully conversant with the official terminology of the patriarchate. Equally characteristic is Gemistos’ detailed understanding of the inner workings of the patriarchal bureaucracy, which had its own hierarchy and traditions. The accuracy of his understanding is readily corroborated by a comparison of other extant chancery documents. His mastery of the chancery is not the least bit surprising when we consider that Gemistos worked and flourished in the chancery for twenty years before he wrote his Diataxis. Gemistos’ loyalty to the patriarchate equally extended to individuals who sat on the patriarchal throne. For, as we have seen, even though Gemistos introduced a non-Constantinopolitan source, the Philothean Diataxis, into the Constantinopolitan rite, this was motivated not by a desire to innovate, but by conservatism and loyalty: it was done to settle liturgical questions but also because of his high regard for Philotheos Kokkinos.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Constantinopolitan Patriarchate. For example, he shows himself more than fluent in the technical vocabulary needed to describe the liturgical rites at the Hagia Sophia. In addition, Gemistos regularly offers in marginal notes alternate formulas which further demonstrate a vast knowledge of liturgical traditions. At times, these asides concern the patriarchal rite and Constantinopolitan traditions, but at other times he notes alternate rubrics for when the patriarch would not be celebrating the liturgy, or if the liturgy would not be celebrated in the “Great Church.” An examination of Gemistos’ other major source embedded within the Diataxis, the Euchologion, further confirms his fidelity to Constantinopolitan traditions. When the Euchology texts in Gemistos are compared with sources both anterior and contemporary to him, what emerges is that Gemistos indeed remained faithful to the Constantinopolitan Euchology tradition, but, at the same time, he tailored his Euchology sources to the specific liturgical needs of the Hagia Sophia and the elaborate patriarchal rite. Gemistos’ changes, however, demonstrate not an intent to innovate, but rather a conservative inclination that sought to clarify and codify more precisely the liturgical order. At one point he even insists in a curious marginal note that when prevailing customs “seem superfluous” and even “redundant,” it still is far “safer that the prevailing customs be said and maintained,” than the implied threat of their abrogation.
units.english_cohort_translation: > An examination of Gemistos’ other primary source embedded within the Diataxis, the Euchologion (*Εὐχολόγιον*), further demonstrates his fidelity to Constantinopolitan tradition. When Gemistos’ Euchology texts are compared with anterior and contemporary witnesses, it is evident that he remained faithful to received Constantinopolitan Euchology, while adapting his material to the specific liturgical requirements of Hagia Sophia and the patriarchal office. Gemistos’ revisions reflect a conservative effort to clarify and systematize liturgical order rather than introduce novelty. In one remarkable marginal note, he observes that even when customary rites appear superfluous or redundant, it remains far safer that received customs be observed and preserved than threatened with abrogation. Here Gemistos defends the ancient practice of subdeacons intoning the proclamation **"All who are faithful!"** (*Ὅσοι πιστοί*) twice during the Anaphora—a ceremonial action whose original historical rationale had become obscured by his era.

units.slavonic_incipit: A careful examination of the Diataxis
units.slavonic_diplomatic: A careful examination of the Diataxis of Dimitrios Gemistos reveals his purposes in composing his Diataxis. Clearly, he wanted to write a patriarchal Diataxis that carefully set forth the role of the patriarch and the members of the patriarchal chancery in the celebration of the Divine Liturgy and the various rites of ordination. A comparison with another Constantinopolitan documents, Euchologia, chancery texts such as the Ekthesis Nea, other Diataxeis, locates Gemistos squarely within the liturgical traditions of Constantinople and the world view of the patriarchate. This is not at all surprising, given Gemistos’ prominence within the Constantinopolitan patriar-
units.english_cohort_translation: > Thorough analysis of Dimitrios Gemistos’ Diataxis reveals his programmatic intent: to establish an authoritative patriarchal Diataxis codifying the ceremonial roles of the Patriarch and chancery officials during the Divine Liturgy and ordination rites. Comparative analysis with contemporary Constantinopolitan documents—Euchologia, chancery formularies such as the *Ekthesis Nea*, and related Diataxeis—locates Gemistos firmly within the liturgical ethos of Constantinople. This coherence is natural, given Gemistos’ prominent standing within the patriarchal[^598]

units.english_cohort_translation: > Gemistos’ Diataxis is preserved in nineteen extant manuscripts, spanning from Athos Vatopedi MS 135 (copied in November 1390, shortly after the text’s original composition in August 1386) to Athos Panteleimon MS 677 (AD 1890). These witnesses transmit four primary recensions: (1) the comprehensive archetype, representing the longer Patriarchal recension; (2) an abbreviated archival recension; (3) a subsequent archieratical (episcopal) redaction; and (4) an abbreviated Eucharistic redaction focused exclusively upon the celebration of the Divine Liturgy.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: chal chancery, and thus in the Orthodox Church in the Byzantine Empire. If we refuse to view this Diataxis simply as a liturgical document, it then becomes easy and even necessary for us to read between its lines in order to understand its liturgical and historical context.
units.english_cohort_translation: > The original Patriarchal recension delineates the Prothesis rite, the ceremonial vesting of the Patriarch, the preliminary rite of metropolitan election and ordination, the ordination of readers and subdeacons, and the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, interspersed with ordination rites for metropolitans, presbyters, and deacons. units.slavonic_incipit: Gemistos’ Diataxis exists in nineteen known
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Gemistos’ Diataxis exists in nineteen known manuscripts. The manuscripts date from Athos Vatopedi 135, copied in November 1390 shortly after the composition of the Diataxis in August 1386, to Athos Panteleimon 677 (AD 1890). Contained in these manuscripts are four basic recensions of the Diataxis: the longer and original “patriarchal” form of the Diataxis; an abbreviated archival form; a later, “archieratical” redaction; and another abbreviated form that concentrates solely on the rites of the Divine Liturgy. The original patriarchal recension describes the PROTHESIS rites, the vesting of the patriarch, the preliminary rite for metropolitan ordination, the ordination of readers and subdeacons, and then the Divine Liturgy of John Chrysostom. Interspersed within the Liturgy are the rites of metropolitan ordination, priests, and deacons. For all of these rites, the original text contains all the necessary Euchology and diakonika texts. Equally characteristic of the original text of the Diataxis is the presence of detailed instructions for the members of the patriarchal chancery and specific references to the architecture of the Hagia Sophia. The editor of the archival recension has removed all the Euchology and diakonika texts seemingly to conserve paper and space. The patriarchal and archieratical forms of the Diataxis are closely related in form and content. The distinguishing characteristics of the archieratical form are that the celebrant of the Divine Liturgy has been changed from patriarch to archiereus, and that most references to the architecture of the Hagia Sophia have been removed. It would seem that these changes were done so that the Diataxis could be used by other bishops in their own dioceses. The shorter, patriarchal recension of the Diataxis is more radical. Present are references to the patriarch, the Hagia Sophia, and various members of the patriarchal chancery; gone, however, are the rubrics for the prothesis rite along with all the euchology texts. Also present are some elements of the liturgical formulary not yet common to the strictly Constantinopolitan
units.english_cohort_translation: > The editor of the archival recension excised the Euchology prayers and diaconal petitions to economize parchment. The patriarchal and archieratical recensions are closely related in structure and substance; however, the archieratical redaction substitutes the general title *archiereus* (bishop) for *patriarch* and eliminates most topographical references to Hagia Sophia, adapting the Diataxis for diocesan episcopal use. The shorter patriarchal recension is more radical: while retaining references to the Patriarch, Hagia Sophia, and chancery personnel, it omits the Prothesis rubrics and Euchology prayers, incorporating certain liturgical elements not yet standard in pure Constantinopolitan[^599]

units.english_cohort_translation: > Textual evaluation of Gemistos’ manuscript tradition demonstrates that subsequent recensions arose in response to specific elements of the archetype. The original title explicitly announces that the Diataxis sets forth the order of the Patriarchal Divine Liturgy celebrated in the Great Church (Hagia Sophia) and “both how and when the order of ordinations takes place.” Consequently, authentic rubrics for the patriarchal liturgy and ordination offices constitute indispensable components of Gemistos’ original work. Because these core elements are missing in the Archieratical and Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recensions, both must be classified as secondary redactions.

units.slavonic_incipit: At first glance, the textual issues
units.slavonic_diplomatic: At first glance, the textual issues surrounding the Diataxis of Dimitrios Gemistos seem difficult to resolve. But a curious feature of the textual history of Gemistos’ Diataxis is that subsequent recensions were created in reaction to one or more characteristic element of the original Diataxis. A basic taxonomy of the manuscripts comes quickly into focus through a careful analysis of the various recensions. The very title of the Diataxis states that the Diataxis sets forth the details of the patriarchal Divine Liturgy celebrated in the Great Church (i.e., the Hagia Sophia) and “both how and when the order of ordinations take place.” Therefore, the content of the original text of the Diataxis must contain rubrics specifically for the patriarchal liturgy and the various ordination rites. This content presumed in the title, however, is missing in two recensions, the Archieratical and the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic.” Accordingly these two recensions can be described as later and not representative of the original text of the Diataxis. The editor of the Archieratical recension refashioned the Original Patriarchal recension of the Diataxis by changing the main celebrant from patriarch to archiereus and omitting any references to the concelebrating hierarchs, architectural features of the Hagia Sophia, and the members of the patriarchal chancery. By doing this, the redactor of this recension created a Diataxis appropriate to any hierarch and not just the patriarch of Constantinople during the Byzantine Empire. The redactor of the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recension was no less active. This editor removed the Euchology texts and the diakonika of CHR as well as the texts for the ordination rites, leaving only the rubrics for the celebration of the patriarchal liturgy and mere indications and incipits where these texts once stood.
units.slavonic_text: At first glance, the textual issues surrounding the Diataxis of Dimitrios Gemistos seem difficult to resolve. But a curious feature of the textual history of Gemistos’ Diataxis is that subsequent recensions were created in reaction to one or more characteristic element of the original Diataxis. A basic taxonomy of the manuscripts comes quickly into focus through a careful analysis of the various recensions. The very title of the Diataxis states that the Diataxis sets forth the details of the patriarchal Divine Liturgy celebrated in the Great Church (i.e., the Hagia Sophia) and “both how and when the order of ordinations take place.” Therefore, the content of the original text of the Diataxis must contain rubrics specifically for the patriarchal liturgy and the various ordination rites. This content presumed in the title, however, is missing in two recensions, the Archieratical and the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic.” Accordingly these two recensions can be described as later and not representative of the original text of the Diataxis. The editor of the Archieratical recension refashioned the Original Patriarchal recension of the Diataxis by changing the main celebrant from patriarch to archiereus and omitting any references to the concelebrating hierarchs, architectural features of the Hagia Sophia, and the members of the patriarchal chancery. By doing this, the redactor of this recension created a Diataxis appropriate to any hierarch and not just the patriarch of Constantinople during the Byzantine Empire. The redactor of the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recension was no less active. This editor removed the Euchology texts and the diakonika of CHR as well as the texts for the ordination rites, leaving only the rubrics for the celebration of the patriarchal liturgy and mere indications and incipits where these texts once stood.

units.slavonic_incipit: The guiding editorial principle of the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The guiding editorial principle of the present edition has been to establish as near as possible the text that Gemistos originally wrote and not to create a hypothetical text that never existed. Additionally, no component part of the Diataxis should be seen as anything other than the original text of Gemistos’ Diataxis. In other words, this edition of the Diataxis is not a critical edition of the ordination rites
units.english_cohort_translation: > The guiding editorial principle of the critical edition is to reconstruct, as faithfully as the witnesses permit, the authentic archetype composed by Dimitrios Gemistos in 1386, eschewing hypothetical composite readings. Every constituent element must be evaluated as an integral part of Gemistos’ coherent patriarchal synthesis, distinguishing this edition from a generic critical edition of Byzantine ordination rites.[^600]

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: The first level of the critical apparatus contains the variant readings that serve to reconstruct the original text of the Diataxis. The second level of apparatus contains the variant readings from the archieratical recension of Gemistos' Diataxis when these readings do not bear witness to the original text. The third level of apparatus is exclusively reserved for those instances where Habert deviated from the text of his exemplar, Paris Greek 1362. This level also includes the various titles he gave to different sections of the Diataxis. I have attempted to include all of Habert's variations — all orthographical, all prayer variants etc., in order to give an accurate report of the nature of his text.

units.slavonic_incipit: probably saw himself as someone merely
units.slavonic_diplomatic: probably saw himself as someone merely codifying existing traditions and liturgical practices. His view on this would be perfectly akin to another contemporary Byzantine liturgist, Archbishop Symeon of Thessalonika ( 1429), who also reformed the liturgy. But Alexander Lingas, who has evaluated the content of Symeon' reforms, concludes that far from being “revolutionary,” the reforms “represented the harmonization and systematization of existing precedents for the inclusion of texts and music from outside the Byzantine cathedral tradition.”[2] Only when the liturgical rites are viewed as things static or unchangeable can these developments — or any developments — be considered as mere innovation and not simply the natural continuous evolution of the rites which is the stuff of liturgical history.”

units.slavonic_incipit: The natural scale is a scale
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The natural scale is a scale consisting of five whole tones and two semitones as it is produced on the white keys of a keyboard instrument. There is, of course, a corresponding scale in each key. Music is called “diatonic” if it is confined to the notes of this scale, to the exclusion of chromatic tones. For instance, in the key of C major, the melodic progression c-d-e and the chord d-a-c represent diatonic harmony. “Diatonicism” means music whose tonality is predominantly diatonic, i.e., nonchromatic. See Powers, Harold S. and Jeffery, Peter in the bibliography.

units.slavonic_incipit: While the hymn Axion Esti is
units.slavonic_diplomatic: While the hymn Axion Esti is chanted in the liturgy, the priest (or deacon) commemorates inaudibly names of the departed and then names of the living. In the early church, these names were kept in special books or on wooden planks wired together so that they could be opened or folded like separate pages. These books were called diptycha. units.slavonic_diplomatic: The “diptychs of the living” contained the names of the patriarchs, the bishops, illustrious persons, lay and ecclesiastical, and benefactors. From them came the first ecclesiastical calendars and martyrologies. The “diptychs of the dead” contained the names of those who, when living, were qualified for inscription on the “diptychs of the living.” Thus originated the later necrologies. Exclusion from these lists invoked a grave ecclesiastical penalty. The contents of the diptychs were read aloud from the ambo or altar, and traces of the fixed usage of the Roman Church in the 5th century may still be found in the Canon of the Mass.
units.english_cohort_translation: The “diptychs of the living” contained the names of patriarchs, bishops, illustrious persons, both clerical and lay, and ecclesiastical benefactors. From them originated the earliest ecclesiastical calendars and martyrologies. The “diptychs of the dead” contained the names of those who, while living, had been inscribed upon the diptychs of the living; from these arose later necrologies. Removal of a name from these lists constituted a grave ecclesiastical penalty (excommunication). The contents of the diptychs were read aloud from the ambo or altar, and traces of this fifth-century Roman practice survive in the *Memento* of the Canon of the Mass.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: DOGMATIKON (Δογματικόν, τό) pl. DOGMATIKA (Δογματικά, τά): These are THEOTOKIA that conclude the STICHIRA at “Lord, I cry out” at Great Vespers on Saturdays. Their title comes from the fact that they are usually succinct presentations of the dogma of the Incarnation, with particular emphasis on the virginity and motherhood of Mary.
units.english_cohort_translation: **DOGMATIKON** (*Δογματικόν, τό*, pl. *Δογματικά, τά* / Dogmatika): These are the festal *Theotokia* chanted in the Eight Tones that conclude the stichira at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*) at Great Vespers on Saturday evenings. Their designation derives from the fact that they present concise, theological expositions of the dogma of the Incarnation, with special emphasis upon the perpetual virginity and divine maternity of the Most Holy Theotokos.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: DOMESTIKOS (Δομέστικος, ὁ) pl. DOMESTIKI (Δομέστικοι, οἱ): Today, as in the past, there are two ranks of Domestiki serving in the Patriarchal Church of St. George. The lowest rank is that of the Second Domestikos which is the first step in the order of the Domestiki. The next rank in ascending order is that of the First Domestikos which is followed by the two higher orders of the LAMBADARIOS or lead chanter serving at the ANALOGION near the left end of the SOLEAS and the PROTOPSALTIS or head chanter serving at the ANALOGION near the right end of the soleas. The Second Domestikos position is usually taken by younger men known for their high vocal quality and their endurance.
units.english_cohort_translation: **DOMESTIKOS** (*Δομέστικος, ὁ*, pl. *Δομέστικοι, οἱ* / Domestikoi): In contemporary practice, as in antiquity, two ranks of Domestikoi minister in the Patriarchal Church of Saint George at the Phanar. The junior rank is that of Second Domestikos, which constitutes the initial grade within the order of cantors. The next rank in ascending order is First Domestikos, which is followed by the two principal choir leaders: the **Lambadarios** (*Λαμπαδάριος*, lead chanter directing the left choir at the analogion near the left end of the soleas) and the **Protopsaltis** (*Πρωτοψάλτης*, archcantor directing the right choir at the analogion near the right end of the soleas). The office of Second Domestikos is customarily assigned to younger singers noted for superior vocal agility and stamina.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *DORMITION (κοίμησις, ἡ): Lit. ‘Sleep,’ used figuratively for death as in the death of a sacred personage such as the Dormition of the Theotokos (15 August). Both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches believe that, after her death, the Virgin Mary was bodily taken up, or ‘assumed’, into heaven. By the proclamation of Pope Pius XII in 1950, the belief in Mary’s bodily assumption to heavem was made an official, inviolate dogma in the Roman Catholic Church. In Orthodoxy, because of the lack of any scriptural support, this belief has remained a part of the age-old tradition of revering and honoring Mary without deifying her in any sense. However fervent and common, this belief has remained essentially optional in the Eastern Church. Thus, in referring to Mary’s death, the Western Church uses the term assumption instead of
units.english_cohort_translation: **DORMITION** (*Κοίμησις, ἡ*; lit. "falling asleep"): Used figuratively for death, specifically designating the repose of a sacred personage, preeminently the **Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos** (August 15). Both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches profess that, following her sacred death, the Virgin Mary was assumed bodily into heaven. By the apostolic constitution *Munificentissimus Deus* of Pope Pius XII in 1950, the dogma of the bodily Assumption of the Virgin Mary was defined for the Catholic Church. In the Eastern tradition, preserved throughout patristic hymnography and the liturgical Typikon, the feast celebrates the bodily translation of the Mother of God to heaven after her death, with the Western Church customarily employing the title *Assumption* rather than[^605]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: DOXA (Δόξα) KE NYN (Καὶ νῦν): These are abbreviations each for a line of text beginning with them. These texts usually precede prayers and hymns commonly found in all service books of the church. The first word is the abbreviation in Greek for “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit” («Δόξα πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι» and the second (2 words) are an abbreviation for “And now and ever and unto the ages of ages.” («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). See also DOXASTIKON, below.
units.english_cohort_translation: **DOXA** (*Δόξα*) **KAI NYN** (*Καὶ νῦν*): Standard liturgical abbreviations indicating the chanting of the minor doxology preceding appointed prayers and hymns in all ecclesiastical liturgical books (Sluzhebnyky and Horologia). The first formula abbreviates: **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"** («Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι»); the second formula abbreviates: **"Now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). See also **DOXASTIKON** below.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *DOXASTIKON, -A (Δοξαστικόν, τό, pl. Δοξαστικά, τά): A hymn (STICHIRON) sung after the short doxology “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit’ (Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι) at the end of a cycle of stichira at Vespers or Matins. It sings in an extended and melodically elaborate manner of the sacred event or person celebrated in each occasion. After the Doxastikon, another hymn is sometimes sung with the verse “And now, and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). Doxastika are mainly chanted at the end of the Esperia and APOSTICHA in Vespers and after the Praises (Eni) in Matins (Orthros).
units.english_cohort_translation: **DOXASTIKON** (*Δοξαστικόν, τό*, pl. *Δοξαστικά, τά*; Slav. *Slavnik*): A stichiron hymn sung after the verse **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"** (*Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι*) at the conclusion of a series of stichira at Vespers or Matins. It expounds in an extended, melismatic melody the sacred feast or saint commemorated on that day. Following the Doxastikon, a matching Theotokion is appointed with the verse: **"Now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). Doxastika are chanted principally at the conclusion of the Lamplighting Sticheron verses (*Esperia*) and the Aposticha at Vespers, and following the Praises (*Ainoi*) at Matins (*Orthros*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: This ancient hymn of praise is common to both East and West. In the East it has two forms, the Greater and Lesser Doxology. The former is used at Matins on Sundays and Feasts, the latter at Matins on ordinary days and at Compline. Like the Latin Te Deum, the hymn itself is followed by a series of verses from the Psalter. The Great Doxology ends with the solemn singing of the Trisagion. The Lesser Doxology ends with the prayer “Grant, Lord, this day,” which, at both Vespers and non-festal Matins, precedes the bowing of heads by the priests. The word ‘doxology’ is also used for other short ascriptions of praise to the Holy Trinity. See DOXASTIKON and EKPHONISIS. (AE).
units.english_cohort_translation: This ancient hymn of praise is common to both East and West. In the Byzantine rite, it possesses two forms: the Great Doxology and the Lesser Doxology. The Great Doxology is sung solemnly at Matins on Sundays and Feasts; the Lesser Doxology is read at daily Matins and at Compline. Like the Latin *Te Deum*, the hymn concludes with a series of versicles drawn from the Psalter. The Great Doxology terminates with the singing of the Trisagion (*"Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us"*). The Lesser Doxology concludes with the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day without sin"**, which, at both daily Vespers and non-festal Matins, precedes the prayer of the bowing of heads by the presbyter. The designation *doxology* also applies to shorter ascriptions of glory to the Holy Trinity. See **DOXASTIKON** and **EKPHONISIS**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EFCHOLOGION TO MEGA (Εὐχολόγιον τὸ Μέγα) Slav. Trebnik. Lit. The Great Book of Prayers or Great Efchologion. The Slavonic word Trebnic literally means ‘Book of Needs.’ It contains the prayers of the priest, deacon, and reader for Vespers, Orthros, and the Divine Liturgy as well as the other sacraments and services of blessings (often referred to in the Western Church as “sacramentals.” There is also an abbreviated edition called the Small Efchologion (Μικρὸν Εὐχολόγιον).
units.english_cohort_translation: **EFCHOLOGION TO MEGA** (*Εὐχολόγιον τὸ Μέγα* / Great Euchologion; Slav. *Trebnik* and *Sluzhebnik*; lit. "Great Book of Prayers"): The Slavonic term *Trebnik* signifies "Book of Needs" (*Treby*). The comprehensive Euchologion contains the sacerdotal prayers for the priest and deacon, and petitions for the reader at Vespers, Matins (*Orthros*), and the Divine Liturgies (the rites comprising the *Sluzhebnik* or *Liturgikon*), as well as the Holy Mysteries (Sacraments) and sacramental blessings for various pastoral occasions. An abbreviated sacerdotal edition containing the daily offices and Liturgies is termed the *Small Euchologion* (*Μικρὸν Εὐχολόγιον*) or *Sluzhebnik*.

The comprehensive Euchologion contains the sacerdotal prayers for the priest and deacon, and petitions for the reader at Vespers, Matins (*Orthros*), and the Divine Liturgies (the rites comprising the *Sluzhebnik* or *Liturgikon*), as well as the Holy Mysteries (Sacraments) and sacramental blessings for various pastoral occasions. An abbreviated sacerdotal edition containing the daily offices and Liturgies is termed the *Small Euchologion* (*Μικρὸν Εὐχολόγιον*) or *Sluzhebnik*.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EKPHONISIS (ἐκφώνησις, ἡ) Slav. vovzglas: Singing or reading in a loud declamatory style. See also EXCLAMATION. Used chiefly with the final doxology that ends every prayer, it is often, but not always, sung aloud, even when the prayer itself is directed to be read ‘in a low voice’ (Greek μυστικῶς). (Modified from AE).
units.english_cohort_translation: **EKPHONISIS** (*᾿Εκφώνησις, ἡ*; Slav. *Vozglas*): A liturgical exclamation intoned aloud in a solemn, declamatory chant style. See also **EXCLAMATION**. Applied preeminently to the concluding trinitarian doxology that terminates silent priestly prayers, it is intoned aloud by the priest even when the preceding prayer is directed to be read secretly (*mystikos* / *μυστικῶς*).[^607]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In terms of the character of a melody, ekphonisis stands between Psalmody, in which deviations from the main reciting tone (the ISON or vasis) occur only at the beginnings and endings of phrases, and singing proper, which has a well defined melodic and rhythmic form. In the Liturgy, ekphonisis is used primarily for the rendering of the Epistle, the Gospel, and Old Testament, as well as for the prayers exclaimed by the priest or deacon.
units.english_cohort_translation: In melodic contour, *ekphonisis* occupies an intermediate position between simple psalmody—wherein inflections from the reciting tone (*ison* or *basis*) occur only at the beginnings and cadences of phrases—and ornate hymnody, which possesses defined melodic and rhythmic forms. In the Divine Liturgy, *ekphonisis* is utilized for the chanting of the Holy Gospel, Epistle, and Old Testament readings, as well as for the sacerdotal exclamations intoned by the celebrating priest or deacon.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ENGOLPION (᾿Εγκόλπιον, τό) Lit. ‘an item worn on the chest’. In the Western Churches, originally the term also included pectoral crosses. In the Orthodox Church today, however, the term is used for a medallion with an icon in its center which is worn, suspended from the neck by a decorative chain where it hangs over the mid-chest. It is part of the vesture of an Orthodox or Eastern Catholic HIERARCH and is worn over his OMOPHORION. As the Bishop vests with the Engolpion, he prays: “Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου.») See also VESTMENTS. The term Engolpion is also used for a liturgical book such as the one used by the READER (᾿Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου).
units.english_cohort_translation: **ENGOLPION** (*᾿Εγκόλπιον, τό*; lit. "that which is worn on the breast"; Slav. *Panagia*): In early Western usage, the designation encompassed pectoral crosses; in the contemporary Eastern Church, it denotes an oval medallion bearing the sacred icon of the Theotokos (hence *Panagia*) or Christ the Savior, suspended around the neck by a decorative chain over the chest. It constitutes part of the pontifical vesture of an Eastern hierarch and is worn over the omophorion. When vesting with the Engolpion, the Bishop prays: **"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me"** («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου»—Psalm 50:12 [LXX 50:12 / MT 51:10]). See also **VESTMENTS**. The term *Engolpion* also designates a handy liturgical manual, such as the Reader's Handbook (*᾿Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*).

When vesting with the Engolpion, the Bishop prays: **"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me"** («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου»—Psalm 50:12 [LXX 50:12 / MT 51:10]). See also **VESTMENTS**. The term *Engolpion* also designates a handy liturgical manual, such as the Reader's Handbook (*᾿Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EOTHINON (῾Εωθινόν, τό): Meaning ‘of the dawn’ in Greek. The word is used to refer either to (a) one of the eleven Gospels (Eothina Evangelia), read each Sunday at Matins, or to (b) the eleven Idiomela Doxastika by the Emperor Leo the Wise [866-912] that are sung in the Orthros on Sunday at the end of the Praises or Lauds (Αἶνοι.) There is one such idiomelon to correspond to each of the eleven Gospels, of which they are poetic summaries. In the old ‘Sung’, or ‘Cathedral’ office, as described by St Symeon of Thessaloniki [† 1429], they were sung immediately before the Resurrection Gospel in the ORTHROS. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **EOTHINON** (*῾Εωθινόν, τό*, pl. *῾Εωθινά, τά*; lit. "pertaining to the dawn"): Derived from the Greek *heos* ("dawn"). The term designates either: (a) one of the eleven Resurrectional Matins Gospels (*Eothina Evangelia*) read in cyclical order on Sundays at Matins; or (b) the eleven Idiomela Doxastika composed by Emperor Leo VI the Wise (reigned 866–912), chanted on Sundays at the conclusion of the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Lauds*) at the verse **"Glory to the Father..."**. Each idiomelon corresponds poetically to one of the eleven Matins Gospels, providing a poetic synthesis of the Resurrection appearance. In the ancient Constantinopolitan cathedral ("Asmatic" or "Sung") office described by Saint Symeon of Thessalonika († 1429), these hymns were chanted immediately preceding the reading of the Resurrection Gospel at Matins.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EPANOKALYMAFCHON (᾿Επανωκαλύμαυχον, τό): A black veil worn by bishops and archimandrite monks. The veil is attached to the top of the traditional black ‘stove-pipe’ hat or KALIMAFCHION. The latter without a veil may be worn by other clergy.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EPANOKALYMAFCHON** (*᾿Επανωκαλύμαυχον, τό*; Slav. *Klobuk* or *Namitka*): A flowing black veil worn over the kamilavka (*Kalimafchion*) by bishops, archimandrites, and monastics. The veil attaches to the crown of the cylindrical black headdress. Secular priests and lower clergy wear the kamilavka without a veil.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EPIGONATION (᾿Επιγονάτιον, τό) Slav. Nabedrennik: The epigonation (Greek: “upon the knee” or Russian palitsa is a vestment used by clergy in the Orthodox Church as a special honor. It is a stiff, rhomboid-shaped cloth that hangs over the knee on the right side of the body below the waist. It is suspended by one corner from a strap drawn over the left shoulder. In the Greek tradition it is usually a sign that the priest has an advanced academic degree and a blessing to hear confessions. In the Russian tradition it is an award for service. If a Russian priest has been awarded both the nabedrennik and the palitsa, he shifts the former to the left side. It is considered to symbolize the weapon of the Holy Word or a sword of Christ.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EPIGONATION** (*᾿Επιγονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *Palitsa*; cf. *Nabedrennik*): A liturgical vestment awarded as an ecclesiastical distinction. The term derives from the Greek *epi gonatos* ("upon the knee"). It consists of a stiff, diamond-shaped (rhomboid) fabric suspended from one corner by a ribbon worn over the left shoulder, hanging at the right knee below the waist. In the Greek tradition, it signifies that a presbyter holds advanced theological degrees and possesses the episcopal blessing to serve as a spiritual father (*Pnevmatikos*) and hear confessions. In the Slavic tradition, it is awarded as a liturgical honor for distinguished service; when a presbyter is awarded both the oblong *nabedrennik* (thigh-shield) and the rhomboid *palitsa* (*epigonation*), he wears the *palitsa* on the right hip and shifts the *nabedrennik* to the left. Liturgically, the Epigonation symbolizes the spiritual sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (cf. Ephesians 6:17).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: When vesting with the Epigonation, the Priest prays: “Gird your sword at your thigh, mighty one, in your splendor and beauty. Stretch out your bowstrings, go forth and prevail in the cause of truth, gentleness and justice, and may your right hand lead you to wondrous deeds (Psalm 44 (45):3-4); now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Περίζωσαι τὴν ῥομφαίαν Σου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν Σου, δυνατέ, τῇ ὡραιότητί Σου καὶ τῷ κάλλει Σου· καὶ ἔντεινε, καὶ κατευοδοῦ, καὶ βασίλευε, ἕνεκεν ἀληθείας, καὶ πραότητος, καὶ δικαιοσύνης· καὶ ὁδηγήσει Σε θαυμαστῶς ἡ δεξιά Σου (Ψαλμ. 44 (45):3-4. Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: When vesting with the Epigonation, the Priest prays: **"Gird Thy sword upon Thy thigh, O Mighty One, in Thy splendor and in Thy beauty. units.slavonic_diplomatic: EPIKLISIS (᾿Επίκλησις, ἡ): The “invocation” or “calling down from above” is that section of the ANAPHORA or Eucharistic Prayer by which the priest invokes the Holy Spirit (or the power of His blessing) upon the Eucharistic bread and wine.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EPIKLISIS** (*᾿Επίκλησις, ἡ*; lit. "invocation" or "calling down from above"): The solemn section of the Anaphora (Eucharistic Prayer) in which the celebrating bishop or priest invokes the Holy Spirit upon the gifts of bread and wine, that He may change them into the precious Body and Blood of Christ. In the Byzantine rite, the Epiklesis follows the Words of Institution and the Anamnesis (*remembrance*) of the Savior’s saving passion, cross, tomb, and resurrection.

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: EPIKLISIS (᾿Επίκλησις, ἡ): The “invocation” or “calling down from above” is that section of the ANAPHORA or Eucharistic Prayer by which the priest invokes the Holy Spirit (or the power of His blessing) upon the Eucharistic bread and wine. In the Greek Orthodox Church, the Epiklisis comes after the ANAMNISIS or remembrance of Jesus’ words and deeds at the Last Supper.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EPILYCHNII PSALMI: See LAMPLIGHTING PSALMS EPIMANIKIA (᾿Επιμανίκια, τά) Slav. Poruchi: The laced cuffs worn about the wrist and distal forearm by the deacon and clergymen of higher rank. The deacon wears them under the STICHARION, while the other clergy wear them over it. They represent strength, patience and good will and are symbolic of the bonds placed around the hands of our Lord during His passion.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EPIMANIKIA** (*᾿Επιμανίκια, τά*; Slav. *Poruchi* or *Narukavnytsi*): Sacerdotal cuffs laced securely around the wrists and forearms of deacons, presbyters, and hierarchs. The deacon wears them over the sleeves of his inner cassock, beneath the wide sleeves of the *sticharion*; priests and bishops wear them over the cuffs of the *sticharion* / *podryasnik*. Mystically, they signify spiritual strength, patience, and divine power, recalling the cords that bound the sacred hands of our Savior Jesus Christ during His holy Passion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EPITRACHILION (᾿Επιτραχήλιον, τό) Slav. Epitraxil, Obvyjnik: An Orthodox liturgical vestment derived from the two Greek words for the neck (trachos) and upon (epi) and in that sense is the equivalent of the Western STOLE, the chief difference being that the Epitrachilion is always joined down the middle, normally by a series of ornamental studs. It is also broader then the Western Stole. It is the characteristic priestly vestment, worn only by bishops and priests. A priest should not celebrate any service unless he is wearing it. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **EPITRACHILION** (*᾿Επιτραχήλιον, τό*; Slav. *Epitrakhil*, *Obvyjnik*): An Eastern liturgical vestment derived from the two Greek words for upon (*epi*) and neck (*trachilos*); functionally equivalent to the Western stole. The principal morphological distinction is that the Epitrachilion is joined together down the front seam, either sewn continuously or fastened by a series of ornamental buttons. It is also broader than the Western stole. It is the indispensable sacerdotal vestment, worn by bishops and priests; a presbyter does not celebrate any divine service or sacred mystery without donning the epitrachilion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: When vesting with the Epitrachilion, the Priest prays: “Blessed is God Who pours His grace upon His Priests, as ointment upon the head, which runs down over the beard, the beard of Aaron, runs down to the hem of his garment (Psalm 132 (133):2); now and ever and to the ages of ages. units.slavonic_incipit: It could be considered as essentially
units.slavonic_diplomatic: It could be considered as essentially the ORARION of the DEACON, adapted for use by priests and bishops. It is worn around the neck with the two ends hanging down equally in front (more or less to the ankle) and with the two adjacent sides sewn or buttoned up together in the center, leaving enough space at the top through which to place the head. In practice it is never unfastened. It is usually made of brocade with seven embroidered or appliquéd crosses, one at the back of the neck and three down each side. (modified from wikipedia free encylopedia http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epitrachelion)
units.english_cohort_translation: The Epitrachilion may be understood historically as the deacon's **Orarion** (*᾿Ωράριον*), looped around the neck and adapted for priestly and episcopal ministry. It is draped around the neck with both ends hanging down equally in front to the lower hem of the sticharion, the two adjoining inner edges being sewn or buttoned together down the midline, leaving an aperture at the upper loop through which the head passes. In established liturgical practice it remains permanently joined. It is customarily fashioned of rich brocade or damask and adorned with seven embroidered crosses: one situated behind the neck, and three descending down each side.

units.slavonic_incipit: The priest wears the epitrachilion whenever
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The priest wears the epitrachilion whenever he is serving as a priest (as opposed to simply attending a service). For some services, e.g. Vespers or Matins, he wears the epitrachilion by itself. When he is fully vested for the Divine Liturgy, he wears the epitrachilion over the STICHARION and under the ZONI and the FELONION.
units.english_cohort_translation: The priest wears the epitrachilion whenever performing any sacerdotal function (as distinguished from merely being present in choir). For lesser offices and treby (e.g., Vespers, Matins, or molebens without full vesting), he dons the epitrachilion over his cassock. When fully vested for the Divine Liturgy, he wears the epitrachilion over the **Sticharion** (*Στιχάριον*) and beneath the **Zone** (*Ζώνη*) and **Felonion** (*Φελόνιον*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EVLOGITOS (Εὐλογητός): Used as an abbreviation for the complete opening prayer of many services. This prayer text line is as follows: “Blessed is our God always, now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen.” («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε, νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») This prayer is used at the beginning of VESPERS, the MESONYKTIKON of Sunday and, without any concurring feast, during the period of the MOVABLE FEASTS of the Triodion and Pentikostarion if the feast coincides with a Feast of the Mother of God or a celebrated Saint. In small Vespers after the prayer of the 9th Hour a dismissal prayer is not done because at this point the VESPERS begins without the Evlogitos. The prayer is also done at Sunday MATINS and every other service except for a) The Divine Liturgy b) The Service of Holy Baptism and c) The Service of Holy Matrimony. In the latter three cases, the opening prayer is “Blessed is the kingdom of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Εὐλογημένη ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ῾Αγίου Πνεύματος, νῦν καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») At VESPERS and MATINS during bright or renewal week, as well as the APODOSIS or LEAVE-TAKING (᾿Απόδοσις) of Pascha (Easter) and also prior to each daily read EXAPSALMOS the opening prayer is “Glory to the holy, consubstantial, life-giving and undivided Trinity, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Δόξα τῇ ῾Αγίᾳ καὶ ῾Ομοουσίῳ καὶ ζωοποιῷ καὶ ἀδιαιρέτῳ Τριάδι· πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν») [See our translation of the Protheoria pgs. 4-5 and the Typikon pg. 4; also the Synekdimos pg. 246.] Note that the service of the morning prayer or ORTHROS begins immediately following the dismissal of the MIDNIGHT SERVICE or MESONYKTIKON (Μεσονυκτικόν).
units.english_cohort_translation: **EVLOGITOS** (*Εὐλογητός*): An abbreviation designating the initial blessing and sacerdotal exclamation that opens the majority of liturgical services: **“Blessed is our God always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») This exclamation commences Vespers, the Midnight Office (*Mesonyktikon*) on Sundays, and, in the absence of a concurring feast, the services during the seasons of the Triodion and Pentecostarion when coinciding with a Feast of the Mother of God or a ranked Saint. At Small Vespers following the prayer of the Ninth Hour, no dismissal is made, and Vespers at that point begins without the *Evlogitos*. The exclamation is likewise intoned at Sunday Matins (*Orthros*) and at every other divine service, with three principal statutory exceptions: (a) the Divine Liturgy, (b) the Mystery of Holy Baptism, and (c) the Mystery of Holy Crowning (Matrimony). In these three mysteries, the opening exclamation is: **“Blessed is the kingdom of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Εὐλογημένη ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ῾Αγίου Πνεύματος, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») Furthermore, at Vespers and Matins during Bright Week (Renewal Week), as well as on the **Apodosis** (lit. units.slavonic_diplomatic: *EXAPOSTILARION, pl. EXAPOSTILARIA (ἐξαποστειλάριον, τό· ἐξαποστειλάρια, τά) Slav. Svetilen. Lit. Hymn of Light: In Greek the word means “to send out”. These are one or two hymns chanted before the ENI (Hymns of Praise) toward the end of the Orthros (Morning Prayer). On regular Sundays, there are eleven Exapostilaria written by the son of Leo the Wise, Constantine Porphyrogenitos [912-959]. Each of these Esapostilaria corresponds to one of the eleven Resurrection Gospels whose general theme is the Resurrection and the events surrounding it. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **EXAPOSTILARION, pl. EXAPOSTILARIA** (*᾿Εξαποστειλάριον, τό· ἐξαποστειλάρια, τά*; Slav. lit. *Svetilen*; lit. "Hymn of Light"): In Greek the term signifies "that which is sent forth". These are one or two proper hymns chanted before the **Praises** (*Αἶνοι* / Eni) toward the conclusion of Matins (*Orthros*). On ordinary Sundays, there are eleven Resurrectional Exapostilaria composed by the son of Emperor Leo the Wise, Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (reigned 912–959). Each of these Exapostilaria corresponds poetically to one of the eleven Resurrection Gospels, the overarching theme of which is the radiant Resurrection of Christ and the events surrounding it.

units.slavonic_incipit: In summary, there are three types
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In summary, there are three types of Exapostilaria: (1) Resurrectional, which follow the cycle of 11 resurrectional Gospel readings and Gospel stichira; (2) Festal, which pertain to the feast being celebrated; and (3) Trinitarian, which are sung at certain Lenten services in honor of the Holy Trinity.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EXAPTERYGA (῾Εξαπτέρυγα, τά): The so-called ‘fans’ representing an order of angels and in Greek meaning literally ‘six-winged.’ These ‘fans’ are metallic disks carried on poles by acolytes during liturgical processions. These poles normally stand in a containing box behind the altar table on either side of a central pole holding the cross. The fan in Greek, has also been called a RIPIDION (ριπίδιον, τό) and in Latin, a flabellum.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EXAPTERYGA** (*῾Εξαπτέρυγα, τά*): The liturgical processional fans representing the celestial choir of Seraphim, derived from the Greek meaning literally "six-winged". These fans are metallic disks embossed with images of the six-winged Seraphim, mounted on shafts and carried by acolytes during solemn liturgical processions. When not carried in procession, these shafts stand in sockets behind the Holy Table on either side of the central processional Cross. In Greek, the fan is also designated a **Ripidion** (*ῥιπίδιον, τό*), and in Latin, a *flabellum*.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: EXERETOS (᾿Εξαιρέτως): ‘Especially’ or ‘above all.’ This is a common abbreviation for a longer prayer in the Divine Liturgy which is as follows: “Especially our most holy, blessed and glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary.” («᾿Εξαιρέτως τῆς παναγίας, ἀχράντου, ὑπερευλογημένης, ἐνδόξου, Δεσποίνης ἡμῶν Θεοτόκου, καὶ ἀειπαρθένου Μαρίας.») In the Divine Liturgy, it is immediately followed by the singing of a hymn type called the Magnificat (Μεγαλυνάριον.) The most commonly used Megalynarion is the “It is truly fitting to call you blessed...” («῎Αξιόν ἐστιν ὡς ἀληθῶς...») This hymn may be replaced by another magnificat proper to the feast or Saint of the day as instructed in the Pretheory of the Typikon. These hymns are also listed in a collection located at the end of the Handbook of the Church Reader or Holy Services of Vespers, Matins and Divine Liturgy, Thirteenth edition, 1992, Athens, Greece published by the Apostoliki Diaconia of the Church of Greece.
units.english_cohort_translation: **EXERETOS** (*᾿Εξαιρέτως*; lit. "especially" or "above all"): The initial word of the great sacerdotal exclamation commemorating the Mother of God during the Anaphora of the Divine Liturgy: **“Especially our most holy, spotless, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary.”** («᾿Εξαιρέτως τῆς παναγίας, ἀχράντου, ὑπερευλογημένης, ἐνδόξου, Δεσποίνης ἡμῶν Θεοτόκου, καὶ ἀειπαρθένου Μαρίας.») In the Divine Liturgy, it is immediately followed by the singing of the hymn designated the **Megalynarion** (*Μεγαλυνάριον* / Slav. *Zadostoinyk*). The customary hymn sung at this point is **“It Is Truly Right”** (*῎Αξιόν ἐστιν ὡς ἀληθῶς...* / *Axion Estin*). This hymn is replaced on Great Feasts by the proper festal Megalynarion (the Heirmos of the Ninth Ode with its refrain) appointed for the feast or Saint of the day, as instructed in the *Protheoria* of the *Typikon*. These festal hymns are also compiled in a collection at the conclusion of the *Handbook of the Church Reader* (*῾Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*) or *Holy Services of Vespers, Matins, and Divine Liturgy* (Thirteenth edition, 1992, Athens, Greece, published by Apostoliki Diakonia of the Church of Greece).

"especially" or "above all"): The initial word of the great sacerdotal exclamation commemorating the Mother of God during the Anaphora of the Divine Liturgy: **“Especially our most holy, spotless, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary.”** («᾿Εξαιρέτως τῆς παναγίας, ἀχράντου, ὑπερευλογημένης, ἐνδόξου, Δεσποίνης ἡμῶν Θεοτόκου, καὶ ἀειπαρθένου Μαρίας.») In the Divine Liturgy, it is immediately followed by the singing of the hymn designated the **Megalynarion** (*Μεγαλυνάριον* / Slav. *Zadostoinyk*). The customary hymn sung at this point is **“It Is Truly Right”** (*῎Αξιόν ἐστιν ὡς ἀληθῶς...* / *Axion Estin*). This hymn is replaced on Great Feasts by the proper festal Megalynarion (the Heirmos of the Ninth Ode with its refrain) appointed for the feast or Saint of the day, as instructed in the *Protheoria* of the *Typikon*. These festal hymns are also compiled in a collection at the conclusion of the *Handbook of the Church Reader* (*῾Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*) or *Holy Services of Vespers, Matins, and Divine Liturgy* (Thirteenth edition, 1992, Athens, Greece, published by Apostoliki Diakonia of the Church of Greece).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: FELONION, -A (Φελόνιον, τό· pl. Φελόνια, τά): See also VESTMENTS. Today the Felonion is a liturgical vestment worn by a priest in the Orthodox Church. It is worn over the priest’s other vestments and is similar to the chasuble used in the Roman Catholic Church. The Felonion is an ornate circular garment with a opening in the center for the wearer’s head. When worn, it reaches to the wearer’s wrists in front, so that if the wearer holds both arms straight out, the Felonion forms a semi-circle when viewed from the front or the back. In its present form, the front is largely cut away (from about the waist down) to facilitate the movement of the priest’s hands. The rubrics may direct that the priest is to ‘lower the Felonion’, that is to let it fall over his hands at the moment of the Dismissal, indicating that the service is finished. Russian felonia often have a row of buttons across the chest so that the front of the vestment can be raised or lowered. The Felonion is a descendant of a first-century paenula (a garment worn as a coat by both sexes.) (Modification of AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **FELONION, pl. FELONIA** (*Φελόνιον, τό· pl. Φελόνια, τά*; Slav. *Phelon*, *Ryza*): See also **VESTMENTS**. In contemporary practice, the Felonion is the principal sacerdotal vestment worn by a priest in the Eastern Church. It is worn over the priest’s other vestments (*sticharion*, *epitrachilion*, and *zone*) and corresponds functionally to the Western chasuble. The Felonion is an ample, conical or circular vestment with an opening in the center for the celebrant’s head. When donned, it reaches to the wearer’s wrists in front, so that when the celebrant holds both arms extended, the vestment forms a semicircle when viewed from front or back. In its developed Byzantine form, the front is deeply cut away (from approximately the waist downward) to facilitate the unimpeded movement of the priest’s hands during liturgical ministrations. Rubrics occasionally direct the priest to “lower the Felonion”, that is, to let it fall over his hands at the Dismissal (*Apolysis*), indicating that the divine service is completed. Slavic *felonia* frequently feature a stiffened collar rising behind the neck, and occasionally a row of small buttons across the chest so that the front of the vestment can be raised or lowered. The Felonion descends historically from the Greco-Roman *paenula*, an outer protective garment worn as a cloak in the early centuries.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: There are two main styles of Felonion. Greek Felonia are tailored to fit over the shoulders, while Russian Felonia have a high, stiffened collar that covers the back of the head.
units.english_cohort_translation: Two principal stylistic varieties of Felonion predominate in the Christian East: Greek *felonia*, which are tailored to fit softly over the shoulders without a raised collar; and Slavic *felonia*, which feature a high, stiffened collar that rises behind the back of the head.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *FESTAL PRECEDENCE: When two feasts are celebrated together, one takes precedence over the other because of its higher rank (e.g., a Lord’s Feast takes precedence over a Saint’s Feast). This precedence is reflected in the ordering of the hymnology of these services. The hymns of the service of the dominant feast precede the hymns of the less dominant feast within each liturgical section (e.g. the Praises or the Apolytikia at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy).
units.english_cohort_translation: **FESTAL PRECEDENCE**: When two feasts coincide on the same day, one takes precedence over the other by reason of its higher liturgical rank (e.g., a Feast of the Lord takes precedence over a Saint’s Feast). This precedence determines the hierarchical order of hymnody: the hymns of the dominant feast precede the hymns of the lesser feast within each liturgical section (e.g., at the **Praises** [*Αἶνοι*] or among the **Dismissal Troparia** [*᾿Απολυτίκια* / lit. *Apolytikia*] chanted at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: FOTAGOGIKON (Φωταγωγικόν, τό, pl. Φωταγωγικά, τά): Lit. illuminating. A hymn or group of hymns sung in place of the exapostilaria in the Matins (Orthros) of the fasting days of Great Lent. They are located at the end of the PARAKLITIKI.
units.english_cohort_translation: **FOTAGOGIKON** (*Φωταγωγικόν, τό, pl. Φωταγωγικά, τά*; lit. "illuminating hymn"): A hymn or cycle of hymns chanted in place of the Exapostilaria at Matins (*Orthros*) on the fasting weekdays of Great Lent. These hymns are arranged according to the Eight Tones and printed at the conclusion of the *Paraklitiki* (*Octoechos*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: A long series of petitions recited by the priest or deacon at the beginning of the Divine Liturgy and in other services. The choir or chanter responds to each petition with “Lord, have mercy” («Κύριε, ἐλέησον.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: **GREAT EKTENIS** (*Μεγάλη ᾿Εκτενής, ἡ*; lit. from *ἐκτείνω*, "to stretch out" or "extend"): A long series of liturgical petitions recited by the deacon or priest at the beginning of the Divine Liturgy and other services. The choir or chanter responds to each petition with **“Lord, have mercy”** («Κύριε, ἐλέησον»).

units.english_cohort_translation: (*δισκάριον*, lit. "small tray") and in the chalice—both covered with veils and united under the Great Veil (**Aer**)—from the table of the **Prothesis** (*Πρόθεσις*). They exit the **Sanctuary** through the north door, moving to the center of the **Soleas**, where they pause to recite commemorative prayers. They re-enter the Sanctuary through the central Holy Doors (the Beautiful Gate), and lay the paten and the chalice upon the **Holy Table** (*῾Αγία Τράπεζα*) or **Altar**. This procession takes place during the chanting of the Cherubic Hymn (*Χερουβικόν*) in the Divine Liturgy. When a bishop is officiating, the ritual movements and prayers of the procession expand in length and solemnity.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *GREAT SYNAPTI (Μεγάλη Συναπτή, ἡ): Lit. from the Greek verb ‘sinapto’ (συνάπτω), ‘I gather together’ or ‘I touch’: Essentially the same as the GREAT EKTENIS, The Great Synapti, however, may appear within a Special Service (e.g., the Kneeling Service in Appendix A of Bogdanos’ The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order) with some of its petitions referring to that particular Special Service and its liturgical function and aim.
units.english_cohort_translation: **GREAT SYNAPTI** (*Μεγάλη Συναπτή, ἡ*; lit. from the Greek verb *συνάπτω*, "to gather together" or "to bind"): Essentially identical to the **Great Ektenis**. units.slavonic_diplomatic: HADES (῞Αδης, ὁ) Slav. Ad): The underworld below or hell. Lit. The term was used in ancient Greece for the underworld where souls reside after death.
units.english_cohort_translation: **HADES** (*῞Αδης, ὁ*; Slav. *Ad*): The netherworld, the realm of the dead, or hell; historically used in ancient Greece for the abode where souls reside after death, and in Christian theology for the realm despoiled by Christ in His Resurrection.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *HOLY EUCHARIST (Θεία Εὐχαριστία, ἡ): Instituted by Christ Himself at the Last Supper, the Holy Eucharist is the central and most important sacramental act in the life of the Church. It is celebrated in the Divine Liturgy as its central event and is synonymous with it. During the Holy Eucharist, the bread and wine are changed by the power of the Holy Spirit into the Body and Blood of Christ. The faithful receive the consecrated elements through communion and thus become one with Christ. As sacrament, the Holy Eucharist effects the most perfect union between God and man. At the same time, it unites the communicants with one another as members of Christ’s Body, the Church. The faithful offer thanks (eucharist or ‘thanksgiving’) to God for His many blessings and for the salvation that He has wrought for them, especially through His ministry on earth, His death and resurrection.
units.english_cohort_translation: **HOLY EUCHARIST** (*Θεία Εὐχαριστία, ἡ*): Instituted by Christ Himself at the Mystical Supper, the Holy Eucharist is the central and most exalted sacramental Mystery in the life of the Church. It is celebrated in the Divine Liturgy as its culminating sacrifice and is synonymous with it. During the Holy Eucharist, the bread and wine are changed by the power and descent of the Holy Spirit into the Body and Blood of Christ. The faithful receive the consecrated Holy Gifts in Holy Communion and thereby become one with Christ. As Mystery, the Holy Eucharist accomplishes the most perfect communion between God and man. At the same time, it unites the communicants with one another as members of Christ’s Body, the Church. The faithful offer thanksgiving (*Eucharistia*) to God for His many blessings and for the salvation that He hath wrought for them, especially through His earthly ministry, His death upon the Cross, and His third-day Resurrection.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: HOURS (῞Ωρα, ἡ, pl. ῏Ωραι, αἱ) Slav. Chasy: Though predominantly done in Holy Monasteries, the Hours are services regularly celebrated in parish churches in cities and towns. The 1st, 3rd, and 6th Hours are done before the Matins (Orthros) service, and the 9th Hour before Vespers. The text of these Hours is found in the book The Mega Orologion, before the Service of Matins (Orthros). A special distinct group called the Great (or Royal) Hours is performed on the Eve of Christmas, the Eve of Epiphany, and on Friday of Holy Week. Their texts can be found in the services of these feasts.
units.english_cohort_translation: **HOURS** (*῞Ωρα, ἡ, pl. ῏Ωραι, αἱ*; Slav. *Chasy*): Though predominantly celebrated in holy monasteries, the Hours are services regularly celebrated in parish churches in cities and towns. The First, Third, and Sixth Hours are chanted before Matins (*Orthros*), and the Ninth Hour before Vespers. The text of these Hours is found in the liturgical book *The Great Horologion* (*῾Ωρολόγιον τὸ Μέγα* / *Chasoslov*), preceding the Service of Matins (*Orthros*). A distinct solemn cycle called the Great (or Royal) Hours is celebrated on the Eve of the Nativity of Christ, the Eve of Theophany, and on Great and Holy Friday. Their texts are contained in the festal propers of those days.
