units.slavonic_diplomatic: HYMN OF KASSIANI (Τροπάριον τῆς Κασσιανῆς, τό): St. Kassiani is also known by the names Kassia, Casia, Ikasia, Cassia, Cassiane, Kassiana,or Eikasia. She was a Hymnographer (9th c.) born in Constantinople to a noble family, who later matured as an unusually beautiful and learned woman— so much so that she was chosen to participate in a 'bridal show', at which the Emperor Theophilos was to choose a wife. Struck by Kassiani's beauty, the Emperor approached her and said 'Through a woman came forth the baser things,' referring to Eve's transgression. Kassiani responded, 'Through a woman came forth the better things', referring to the redemptive Incarnation of Christ through His Most Pure and human Mother. Stung by her too intelligent reply, the Emperor rejected her and instead chose Theodora as his wife. Following this, Kassiani entered monastic life and founded a women's monastery in Constantinople, closely allied with the famous Stoudion Monastery. Serving as abbess of the monastery, she wrote many liturgical hymns, at least twenty of which are included in the services of the Church. Of these hymns, the best-known (or at least most closely associated with her) is the Hymn of Kassiani, sung at the Matins Service of Holy Wednesday, usually sung on Holy Tuesday Evening. Her feast day is celebrated on 7 September.
units.english_cohort_translation: **HYMN OF KASSIANI** (*Τροπάριον τῆς Κασσιανῆς, τό*): Saint Kassiani is also known by the names Kassia, Casia, Ikasia, Cassia, Cassiane, Kassiana, or Eikasia. She was a Byzantine hymnographer (9th c.) born in Constantinople to a noble family, who later matured as an extraordinarily gifted, beautiful, and learned woman—so much so that she was chosen to participate in a "bridal show" (bride-show), at which the Emperor Theophilos was to select an empress. Struck by Kassiani's radiant beauty, the Emperor approached her and remarked: "Through a woman came forth the baser things," referring to Eve's transgression. Kassiani readily replied: "Through a woman came forth the better things," referring to the redemptive Incarnation of Christ through His Most Pure and Virgin Mother. Stung by her sharp and intelligent reply, the Emperor rejected her and instead chose Theodora as his wife. Following this, Kassiani embraced the monastic life and founded a women's monastery in Constantinople, closely affiliated with the renowned Monastery of the Stoudion. Serving as abbess (hegumenia) of the monastery, she composed numerous liturgical hymns, at least twenty of which are preserved in the liturgical books of the Church. Of these compositions, the most famous is the renowned Doxastikon of Holy Wednesday Matins (customarily chanted on the evening of Great and Holy Tuesday), known universally as the **Hymn of Kassiani** (**"Lord, the woman fallen into many sins"** / *Κύριε, ἡ ἐν πολλαῖς ἁμαρτίαις περιπεσοῦσα γυνή*). Her feast is commemorated on September 7.

units.english_cohort_translation: **IERATIKON** (*῾Ιερατικόν, τό*; Slav. *Sluzhebnik*): Also designated the *Ierotelestikon* or *Liturgikon*. The official sacerdotal Sluzhebnik containing the fixed rubrics and prayers chanted and recited by the priest and deacon for Great and Daily Vespers, Matins (*Orthros*), the Divine Liturgies of Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Basil the Great, and the Presanctified Gifts, as well as supplementary prayers and dismissals.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *IKONOSTASION (εἰκονοστάσιον, τό): Also spelled Iconostasion this is the screen of icons separating the SANCTUARY from the SOLEAS. Also known as the TEMPLON, it has three doors: 1) On the north, depicting the Archangel Michael; 2) On the south, depicting the Archangel Gabriel; and 3) The central door, called the BEAUTIFUL GATE, through which only clergy may pass. While in some jurisdictions, the term 'Royal Door' has been used to describe the Beautiful Gate, it should be used only for the central door leading from the Narthex into the Nave through which Byzantine Royalty entered the church in antiquity.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: IKOS, pl. IKI (Οἶκος, οἱ): Each of the 24 Stanzas of the Akathist Hymn to the Theotokos is called an Ikos; also an Ikos is a specially constructed stanza, in honor of a particular feast, which is sung, together with the Kontakion, between the 6th and 7th Odes of the Canon.
units.english_cohort_translation: **IKOS, pl. IKOI** (*Οἶκος, ὁ· pl. Οἶκοι, οἱ*): Stanza or "house" (Slav. *Ikos*). Each of the twenty-four poetic stanzas of the Akathist Hymn to the Most Holy Theotokos is designated an Ikos. Furthermore, in the structure of the liturgical Canon at Matins, the Ikos is the poetic stanza chanted immediately following the Kontakion between the Sixth and Seventh Odes. The Ikos amplifies and unpacks the theological mystery articulated in the Kontakion and, as a rule, terminates with the same refrain as the Kontakion.

units.slavonic_incipit: Only a bishop may consecrate an
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Only a bishop may consecrate an Antiminsion. This may take place as a part of the consecration of a church, or in a separate rite. In this rite, the bishop will anoint a pocket sewn into the Antiminsion in which to place the Relics of the saints and Chrism sealing them in place with wax mastic. He then inscribes the Antiminsion with the name of the church for which it has been consecrated and signs it. He may also stamp it with his official seal.
units.english_cohort_translation: Only a bishop possesses the authority to consecrate an Antiminsion. This consecration occurs either during the solemn dedication and consecration of a church, or through an independent episcopal rite. In this rite, the bishop anoints a small sewn relic-pocket within the Antiminsion with Holy Chrism (*Agion Myron*), deposits therein the sacred relics of holy martyrs, and seals them securely with fragrant wax-mastic. He subsequently inscribes the Antiminsion with the dedication of the church for which it is consecrated, subscribes his episcopal signature, and imprints his official diocesan seal upon it.

units.slavonic_incipit: The use of an Antiminsion always
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The use of an Antiminsion always remains under the jurisdiction of the Bishop. He bestows an Antiminsion and CHRISM on a priest as a sign that the priest has his authorization to celebrate the Sacred Mysteries. If a bishop withdraws this authorization from the priest, he also removes the ANTIMINSION.
units.english_cohort_translation: The canonical custody and use of an Antiminsion remains under the statutory jurisdiction of the ruling Bishop. He bestows the Antiminsion and Holy Chrism upon the priest as the tangible sign and mandate of canonical faculty to celebrate the Sacred Mysteries. If the bishop revokes or suspends this pastoral faculty from the priest, he reclaims and removes the Antiminsion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: IMEROLOGION (῾Ημερολόγιον, τό): For use in the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America this is a book published yearly by the Patriarchate of Constantinople containing the order of service for all services for a given ecclesiastical year. The book is derived annually using the directives contained in the TYPIKON.
units.english_cohort_translation: **IMEROLOGION** (*῾Ημερολόγιον, τό*): Liturgical calendar or ordo book. In current ecclesiastical practice, this is the annual directorium published under the authority of the Church containing the day-to-day order of services and rubrical assignments for each liturgical year. The volume is compiled annually in strict conformity with the directives of the canonical **Typikon**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: IRMOS (εἱρμός, ὁ): A word meaning “link” in Greek. The Irmos is the first hymn of each ode of a Canon. It has a double function: it “links” the ode thematically with the Biblical canticle which serves as its prototype, and, by establishing the meter and melody for all the other hymns (TROPARIA) of the ode, it is the first “link” in their chain. (From APL)
units.english_cohort_translation: **HEIRMOS** (*Εἱρμός, ὁ*; Slav. *Irmos*; lit. "link" or "drawing together"): The initial thematic stanza or model hymn opening each Ode of a liturgical Canon. The Heirmos fulfills a twofold structural function: it links the Ode thematically to the scriptural Biblical Canticle upon which it is founded, and, by establishing the melodic pattern, rhythm, meter, and acrostic framework for all subsequent troparia in the Ode, it serves as the primary architectural link in the hymnographic chain.

The title is bestowed as a recognition of these saints' outstanding service in the spreading and assertion of Christianity, comparable to that of the original apostles. units.english_cohort_translation: **ISODIKON** (*Εἰσοδικόν, τό*; Slav. *Vkhodnoye*): The Introit or Entrance Hymn chanted by the sacred ministers and chanters at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy after the procession moves from the Sanctuary onto the Soleas before the Holy Doors. The general Sunday and weekday Isodikon is the scriptural verse: **“Come, let us worship and bow down before Christ. O Son of God, Who art risen from the dead, save us who sing to Thee: Alleluia!”** (*Δεῦτε προσκυνήσωμεν καὶ προσπέσωμεν Χριστῷ· σῶσον ἡμᾶς Υἱὲ Θεοῦ, ὁ ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν, ψάλλοντάς σοι, ᾿Αλληλούϊα*). On Great Feasts of the Lord, proper festal Eisodika replace the ordinary refrain. Following the intonation of the Isodikon, the clergy enter the Sanctuary through the Beautiful Gate.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Entrance Hymn chanted by the clergy at the Small Entrance in the Divine Liturgy after they have exited the Sanctuary and stood at the center of the Soleas, facing the ALTAR TABLE. The most common Isodikon is “Come, let us worship and bow down” (Δεῦτε προσκυνήσωμεν καὶ προσπέσωμεν...) After chanting the Isodikon, the clergy re-enter the Sanctuary through the BEAUTIFUL GATE.
units.english_cohort_translation: **ISODOS** (*Εἴσοδος, ἡ*; Slav. *Vkhod*): Entrance; a solemn liturgical procession in which the celebrating clergy, preceded by taper-bearers holding processional candles (and deacons bearing ripida and censers), process out of the Sanctuary through the northern door of the icon screen onto the Soleas, pause before the Beautiful Gate for the proper entrance prayers and blessings, and re-enter the Sanctuary through the Beautiful Gate. The liturgical tradition prescribes three principal entrances:

KALYMMAFCHION (καλυμμαύχιον, τό) Slav. kamilavka: The familiar black cylindrical ‘stove pipe’ head covering worn by Orthodox clergy. In Greek use, those of the secular clergy have a small brim on top. Monks, whether priests or not, wear a monastc cowl or veil (Greek koukoulli, or Latin, cucullus) over the top of the hat. When worn by celibate Archimandrites and Bishops this is called an EPANOKALYMMAFCHION (over-kalymmafchion). In Slavic use, the cowl is permanently attached and the whole is called a klobuk, but the Greek cowl can be removed separately, and the rules for when to wear what are quite complicated. (Adapted from AE and FL.)

units.english_cohort_translation: **KALYMMAFCHION** (*Καλυμμαύχιον, τό*; Slav. *Kamilavka*): The cylindrical black clerical head covering worn by Eastern Christian clergy. In Greek liturgical use, the kamilavka of the secular (married) clergy features a small raised flat rim or peak at the crown, whereas that of monastics remains flat and smooth. Monks and celibate clergy (hieromonks, archimandrites, and bishops) wear the sacred monastic veil or cowl (Greek *koukoulion* / *ἐπανωκαλύμμαυχον*; Slav. *klobuk* / *namitka*) draped over the kamilavka. In the Slavic tradition, the veil is permanently fastened to the stiff cylindrical hat to form the composite vestment known as the *klobuk*, whereas in Greek tradition the epanokalymmafchion remains detachable.

units.slavonic_incipit: A hymn form that consists most
units.slavonic_diplomatic: A hymn form that consists most often of eight or nine odes, and more rarely, of four, three or two odes. This hymn form pertains to the sacred event or the saint(s) being commemorated and is sung at the service of Matins. Each ode consists of several stanzas or troparia. Each of the nine odes is patterned after a CANTICLE from the Holy Scriptures (i.e. a biblical canticle) which relates to an Old Testament event which prefigures a New Testament event. Complete Canons, as a rule, have nine odes; the Second Ode, however, is most frequently omitted because of its severe divine condemnation of mankind. The special service known as the Great Canon is sung on the evening of Wednesday of the fifth week of Great Lent.
units.english_cohort_translation: A monumental hymnographic poetic form comprising most frequently eight or nine Odes (and more rarely, four, three, or two Odes). The Canon commemorates the sacred mystery, feast, or saint of the day and forms the liturgical center of Matins (*Orthros*). Each Ode consists of an opening model hymn (**Heirmos**) followed by a prescribed series of poetic strophes (**Troparia**). Each of the nine Odes corresponds to and is typologically patterned after one of the nine Biblical Canticles of Holy Scripture, establishing an Old Testament event as the prophetic archetype of a New Testament revelation in Christ. Complete Canons encompass nine Odes; however, the Second Ode (patterned upon the severe song of condemnation in Deuteronomy 32) is sung exclusively during the weekdays of Great Lent. The Great Penitential Canon of Saint Andrew of Crete is chanted in sections during the first week of Great Lent and in its entirety on Wednesday evening of the Fifth Week.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: KATASARKION, (Κατασάρκιον, τό): A thin white linen cloth placed on the bare surface of the Holy Altar Table as a ‘skin’ during the Consecration Service of a church. It is permanently held in place by a cord around the base of the table.
units.english_cohort_translation: **KATASARKION** (*Κατασάρκιον, τό*; Slav. *Srachitsa*): Lit. "upon the flesh"; the white linen tunic or seamless undercloth fitted tightly over the bare stone surface of the Holy Table as a protective inner shroud during the rite of Consecration of a church. It represents the winding sheet of Christ in the tomb and is bound permanently to the four columns of the altar table with a consecrated cord (*spargana*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: KATAVASIA, KATAVASIE (Καταβασία, ἡ), pl. Καταβασίαι, αἱ): The title for a classification of hymns which conclude each ODE of a CANON. In Greek, the title suggests the act of descending since these hymns were sung when the chanters descended (Greek καταβαίνω) from their stalls (στασίδια) and gathered together to sing them. On Sundays and major Feasts there is a katavasia after every ode. “Katavasie” refers also to the entire CANON with its 9 Odes which is chanted mostly before the Morning Gospel in the ORTHROS. Katavasie are often ‘seasonal’ and anticipate the next Great Feast. Thus the katavasie of Christmas are sung from the 21 November up to and including 25 December. The Katavasie most frequently chanted are those of the Canon to the Mother of God in Mode IV, “I shall open my mouth”(«᾿Ανοίξω τὸ στόμα μου».
units.english_cohort_translation: **KATAVASIA, pl. KATAVASIE** (*Καταβασία, ἡ· pl. Καταβασίαι, αἱ*; Slav. *Katavasiya*): A liturgical classification of festive model hymns chanted at the conclusion of each Ode of the Canon at Matins (*Orthros*). In Greek ecclesiastical usage, the term derives from the verb *katabaino* (*καταβαίνω*, "to descend"), designating the ancient monastic practice whereby the chanters descended from their raised choir stalls (*stacidia*) into the center of the nave to unite in chanting these climactic heirmoi together. On Sundays and major festal celebrations, a Katavasia is chanted after every individual Ode. The term "Katavasiai" likewise denotes the complete set of festal heirmoi assigned across the nine Odes of Matins. Katavasiai are seasonal and anticipate upcoming Great Feasts: thus the Katavasiai of the Nativity of Christ (**"Christ is born, glorify Him!"** / *Χριστὸς γεννᾶται· δοξάσατε*) are chanted from November 21 through December 25. The most frequently chanted ordinary Katavasiai are those of the Canon to the Most Holy Theotokos in Tone 4, **“I shall open my mouth”** (*᾿Ανοίξω τὸ στόμα μου*). On ordinary non-festal days, the Katavasia is chanted only after the Third, Sixth, Eighth, and Ninth Odes.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: KATHISMA (Κάθισμα, τό) pl. KATHISMATA (Καθίσματα, τά); Slav. Sedalni: The word has several possible meanings. First, a Kathisma is one of the twenty sections into which the Septuagint (LXX) Old Testament Greek Psalter is divided for liturgical use in the Orthodox Church. Each Kathisma is divided into three sections (Στάσεις) composed of a variable number of Psalms, e.g., Kathisma #1 = Psalms 1-8; Kathisma #2 = Psalms 9-17; etc.
units.english_cohort_translation: - First, a Kathisma is one of the twenty major divisions or sections into which the Septuagint (LXX) Old Testament Psalter is partitioned for liturgical recitation throughout the weekly cycle in the Byzantine and Slavic traditions. Each Kathisma is subdivided into three states or antiphons (*Staseis* / *Στάσεις*), each comprising a variable group of psalms (e.g., Kathisma 1 = Psalms 1–8; Kathisma 2 = Psalms 9–17, etc.), concluded by the Doxology ("Glory... both now... Alleluia").[^627]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Kathismata are also a group of hymns (τροπάρια). These short hymns are sung after the reading of each Kathisma of the Psalter at Matins. The term Kathisma derives from the Greek word seat and refers to the fact that the clergy and the congregation may sit when the kathismata are chanted. (modified from APL and AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: - Second, Kathismata denote a class of liturgical troparia (**Sessional Hymns**, Slav. *Sedalni*). These short poetic hymns are chanted following the reading of each Kathisma of the Psalter, after the Polyeleos, and after the Third Ode of the Canon at Matins. The designation derives from the Greek verb *kathezomai* (*καθέζομαι*, "to sit"), indicating the rubrical dispensation allowing the clergy and faithful to sit during their recitation, in contrast to the standing posture required during solemn psalms and prayers.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Finally, our last definition of a kathisma is that of a single Monastic Cell as follows:
units.english_cohort_translation: - Third, in monastic administration, a Kathisma denotes a small solitary monastic dwelling or hermitage. On the Holy Mountain of Athos, each subordinate monastic settlement (*skete*, *cell*, *kalyve*, *hesychasterion*, or *kathisma*) exists under the jurisdiction of one of the twenty sovereign ruling monasteries. The Kathisma constitutes one of the smallest establishments, designed as a simple habitation for a single solitary hesychast monk.

units.slavonic_incipit: On Mount Athos, the Autonomous Monastic
units.slavonic_diplomatic: On Mount Athos, the Autonomous Monastic State of the Holy Mountain, a monastic republic in northern Greece, each of the monastic establishments (sketae, kellia, kalyvae, hesychasteria or kathismata), large or small, exists under the jurisdiction of one of twenty Sovereign Monasteries. One of the smallest types of these monastic establishments is called a Kathisma, a simple abode for one solitary monk.
units.english_cohort_translation: **KATHISMA HYMN**: Also designated **SESSIONAL HYMN** (lit. 'sitting hymn'; Slav. *sedalen*): A hymn chanted as an invitation to seated reflection and rest following lengthy periods of standing, such as the chanting of the Psalter, the singing of the Polyeleos, or the completion of the Third Ode of the Canon at Matins.

units.english_cohort_translation: **KATZION** (*Κάτζιον, τό*): A small hand-held censer fitted with a short handle and small jingling bells, utilized in monastic rubrics and at specific rites (such as the Lenten Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts or monastic commemorations) for swift censing of icons and brotherhood.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: KE NYN (Καὶ νῦν). Lit. ‘And Now’: An abbreviation for the text “And Now and Ever and unto the ages of ages,” («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων»). This abbreviation is used frequently in the TYPIKON being connected to the abbreviation DOXA.... The abbreviation is found in all Orthodox services.
units.english_cohort_translation: **KE NYN** (*Καὶ νῦν*): Lit. "And now"; the standard rubrical abbreviation for the concluding phrase of the liturgical doxology: **“Both now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** (*Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν*). This cue is employed ubiquitously in the **Typikon** and liturgical books, routinely following the abbreviation **Doxa** (*Δόξα* / "Glory...").

units.english_cohort_translation: **KINONIKON** (*Κοινωνικόν, τό*; Slav. *Prychasten*): The Communion Hymn; a liturgical verse, customarily excerpted from the Septuagint Psalter or appointed festal scriptures, chanted melismatically and ornately by the choir while the sacred ministers receive Holy Communion within the Sanctuary, immediately preceding the distribution of Holy Communion to the faithful. The ordinary Sunday Kinonikon is Psalm 148:1 [LXX 148:1 / MT 148:1]: **“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the highest. Alleluia!”** (*Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν· αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις. ᾿Αλληλούϊα*).

units.slavonic_incipit: Traditionally, in cathedrals, monasteries and larger
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Traditionally, in cathedrals, monasteries and larger churches such as chapels belonging to seminaries and major parishes there would have been a kliros on both the north and south sides of the soleas at the eastern end of the church. The result is two choirs which may sing antiphonally. This was the practice in the Byzantine Imperial Cathedral of Hagia Sophia, in Constantinople, whose historical liturgical practice became the standard for all churches following the Byzantine liturgical tradition.
units.english_cohort_translation: In traditional cathedral and monastic architecture, two choirs (*kliri*) are situated on the north (left) and south (right) flanks of the Soleas before the icon screen, enabling the antiphonary execution of hymns between the right and left choirs. This antiphonal choir arrangement was perfected in the Great Imperial Church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, establishing the benchmark for all monuments within the Byzantine liturgical sphere.

units.slavonic_incipit: This arrangement presupposes a number of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: This arrangement presupposes a number of singers on each side, adding up to a reasonably large total, and two highly-trained chanters skilled in leading the services. Unfortunately, highly-trained chanters are exceedingly rare today, and most churches have only one kliros, usually on the right of the SOLEA. Nevertheless some patriarchal cathedrals, larger monastic communities, seminaries, and churches with sufficient resources and singers, may continue to have two kliri.
units.english_cohort_translation: This classical structure presupposes two complete choirs led by two master chanters (*protopsaltes* and *lampadarios*). In contemporary parish practice, where resources are limited, a single kliros is often maintained on the right side of the Soleas, or singing is supported from a choir loft situated at the western end of the nave above the narthex.[^629]

units.english_cohort_translation: **KONTAKION, pl. KONTAKIA** (*Κοντάκιον, τό· pl. Κοντάκια, τά*; Slav. *Kondak*): The Kontakion was the preeminent poetical and hymnographic genre of early Byzantine hymnology, achieving its classic zenith in the inspired verse of Saint Romanos the Melodist (6th century), many of whose masterpieces remain central to the liturgical life of the Church. Thematically, the classical Kontakion presented an expansive narrative and dramatic homily upon the great feast of the day, notably the Nativity of Christ. Structurally, an ancient Kontakion consisted of 18 to 30 or more stanzas, each designated an **Ikos** (*Οἶκος*), composed in identical meter and rhythm and sung to the same melody. The initial letters of these stanzas formed an acrostic, spelling out the title of the feast, the poet’s name, or the Greek alphabet. These stanzas were preceded by a short independent introductory stanza called the **proimion** (*προοίμιον*) or **kukulion** (*κουκούλιον*), which established the musical Mode and the concluding refrain (**efymnion** / *ἐφύμνιον*) repeated at the end of every subsequent Ikos.

Structurally, an ancient Kontakion consisted of 18 to 30 or more stanzas, each designated an **Ikos** (*Οἶκος*), composed in identical meter and rhythm and sung to the same melody. units.english_cohort_translation: In contemporary Byzantine and Slavic practice, the ancient extended Kontakion has been largely replaced in the daily office by the Canon; today, only the introductory prelude (now bearing the name Kontakion) and a single Ikos are chanted at Matins between the Sixth and Seventh Odes of the Canon. Furthermore, this short Kontakion is chanted at the Divine Liturgy immediately preceding the Trisagion Hymn. The ordinary daily Kontakion chanted at the Divine Liturgy is the beloved Theotokion: **“The Protection of Christians”** (*Προστασία τῶν Χριστιανῶν*), honoring the Mother of God as an unashamed intercessor before the Creator.[^630]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Originally the Kontakion was a 'verse sermon' consisting of an Introductory preamble or Proimion (Προοίμιον) followed by a series of longer stanzas, the Iki (Οἶκοι), all ending with the same phrase similar to a refrain. Kontakia were gradually displaced by a subsequent poetical form, the CANON (κανών). In the present office only the Proimion or preamble, now called the Kontakion, and the first Ikos survive. In current Greek use they are normally read at Matins (῎Ορθρος), except on great Feasts, and the final phrase is repeated, a survival of the ancient practice. The Kontakion is also read at the Hours and sung at the Liturgy, though in Greek use those at the Liturgy are 'seasonal', like the KATAVASIES. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: Originally, the Kontakion was a poetic "verse sermon" consisting of an introductory preamble or Proimion (*Προοίμιον*) followed by a series of longer stanzas, the Ikoi (*Οἶκοι*), all terminating with an identical recurring phrase or refrain (*ephymnion*). Kontakia were gradually supplanted in the liturgical offices by a subsequent poetic hymnographic cycle, the **Canon** (*Κανών*). In the present ecclesiastical office, only the Proimion (now itself customarily designated simply as the Kontakion) and the first Ikos survive in liturgical recitation. In contemporary Byzantine practice, they are regularly read at Matins (*Orthros*), except on great feasts, and the final phrase is repeated by the choir—a living survival of the ancient practice. The Kontakion is likewise read at the Little Hours and chanted at the Divine Liturgy, where in standard usage the proper kontakia are seasonal, coordinating with the prescribed Katavasiai.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: No evidence is available to determine the date at which the Kontakion was received into the Byzantine liturgy. No reference to it is to be found in Byzantine documents or writings during the time it was in use. Even the name Kontakion only occurs for the first time in the ninth century; the monk who composed a hymn of that kind called it a Hymn (ὕμνος), Psalm (ψαλμός), Poem (ποίημα or ἔπος), Song (ᾠδή or ᾆσμα), Praise or Laud (αἶνος), Prayer (προσευχή) or Petition (δέησις).
units.english_cohort_translation: No direct documentary evidence survives to establish the exact date at which the Kontakion was formally incorporated into the Byzantine liturgical system. No reference to this poetic genre is to be found in imperial Byzantine documents or writings during the initial era of its flourishing. Even the technical name *Kontakion* appears for the first time only in ninth-century sources; the monastic hymnographers who originally composed works of this genre designated such a composition variously as a Hymn (*ὕμνος*), Psalm (*ψαλμός*), Poem (*ποίημα* or *ἔπος*), Canticle or Song (*ᾠδή* or *ᾆσμα*), Praise or Laud (*αἶνος*), Prayer (*προσευχή*), or Supplication (*δέησις*).

Even the name Kontakion only occurs for the first time in the ninth century; the monk who composed a hymn of that kind called it a Hymn (ὕμνος), Psalm (ψαλμός), Poem (ποίημα or ἔπος), Song (ᾠδή or ᾆσμα), Praise or Laud (αἶνος), Prayer (προσευχή) or Petition (δέησις).

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: No direct documentary evidence survives to establish the exact date at which the Kontakion was formally incorporated into the Byzantine liturgical system. No reference to this poetic genre is to be found in imperial Byzantine documents or writings during the initial era of its flourishing. Even the technical name *Kontakion* appears for the first time only in ninth-century sources; the monastic hymnographers who originally composed works of this genre designated such a composition variously as a Hymn (*ὕμνος*), Psalm (*ψαλμός*), Poem (*ποίημα* or *ἔπος*), Canticle or Song (*ᾠδή* or *ᾆσμα*), Praise or Laud (*αἶνος*), Prayer (*προσευχή*), or Supplication (*δέησις*).

units.english_cohort_translation: A complete historical Kontakion comprised from eighteen to thirty, or even more, structurally and metrically identical stanzas. A single stanza is designated a Troparion (*Τροπάριον*), varying in length from three to thirteen poetic lines. All subsequent Troparia in the work are composed upon the exact metric and rhythmic model of an initial stanza, the **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*). A Kontakion is either constructed upon the pattern of an Heirmos composed expressly for that poem, or adopts the meter of a pre-existing Heirmos previously composed for another Kontakion. units.slavonic_diplomatic: stage, often consists of two or three stanzas. Proimion and Kontakion are linked together by the refrain, the Ephymnion (ἐφύμνιον) with which all the stanzas end, and by the musical mode (ἦχος). The occurrence of the refrain at the end of each stanza indicates that the Kontakia were sung by a soloist, the choir singing the refrain. The stanzas of the Kontakion are connected either alphabetically or by a different acrostic, in the following way: The first letters of each stanzas sequentially are either the letters of the Greek alphabet in its usual order, or form a short sentence containing the name of the hymn-writer and the title of the poem. The acrostic is indicated in the title of the Kontakion. From the title we may learn, therefore, (1) the day of the feast on which the Kontakion is sung, (2) the feast for which it is composed, (3) the acrostic, (4) the musical mode of the melody. Taking for example the Kontakion 'Joseph the Chaste' by Romanos which the Orthodox church sings on Great Monday of Holy Week. This title, in Greek, reads as follows:
units.english_cohort_translation: stage often consists of two or three stanzas. The Proimion and the subsequent stanzas are linked together by the refrain, the Ephymnion (*᾿Εφύμνιον*), with which all stanzas conclude, and by the shared musical Tone (*Ἦχος*). The placement of this common refrain at the conclusion of each stanza demonstrates that the ancient Kontakia were chanted by a solo cantor, while the assembled choir and congregation joined in singing the refrain. The successive stanzas of the Kontakion are bound together either alphabetically or through an acrostic: the initial letters of each stanza sequentially form either the complete Greek alphabet in regular order, or an inscribed sentence containing the name of the hymnographer and the title of the composition. This acrostic is formally announced in the rubrical title of the Kontakion. From this liturgical heading we ascertain: (1) the day and feast upon which the Kontakion is chanted; (2) the sacred subject or person commemorated; (3) the exact acrostic schema; and (4) the musical Tone of the melody. For example, in the renowned Kontakion **"Joseph the All-Chaste"** composed by Saint Romanos the Melodist, chanted on Great and Holy Monday of Passion Week, the Greek heading reads as follows:

units.english_cohort_translation: From this title we learn that the Kontakion chanted on Great and Holy Monday was composed in honor of the Patriarch Joseph; that each successive stanza begins with a letter of the Greek alphabet, followed by an acrostic spelling out the words *᾿Αλφάβητον ῾Ρωμανοῦ* ("Alphabet of Romanos"); that the melody is set in Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal); and that it is modeled upon the pre-existing melodic model stanza beginning with the incipit **"Thy Son, O all-blameless Virgin"** (*῾Ο υἱός σου, παρθένε πανάμωμε*). This complete Kontakion therefore comprises forty stanzas, each beginning with one of the following letters:

units.slavonic_incipit: In another case, in the poem
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In another case, in the poem of an anonymous hymn-writer in memory of St. John Chrysostom, the principle of doubling letters is carried even farther. The direction from the title: φέρον ἀκροστιχίδα τήνδε· εἰς τὸν χρυσόστομον is executed as follows: εις τον χχρρυυσσοοοσσττομον. At the time when the Kontakia were written the Greek language had already lost the difference between long and short vowels, the basis of the quantitative metre of classical poetry; what had become equal to o, h, ei, and oi were pronounced as a short i, ai as e. A new system of versification had developed based on the principle that all the stanzas had to have the same number of syllables as the Irmos on which they were modelled and that the stress accents had to have the same place in all the stanzas as in the verses of the Irmos.... The composition of a Kontakion, or, at a later date, of a Kanon, was a task which a poet could not achieve who was not also a skilled musician. Music and poetry had to make a single entity. To adapt the Troparia to the melody of the Irmos it was not sufficient to make each line, corresponding to a line of the model strophe, of equal length, i.e. with the same number of syllables, but the stress accents must also fall on the same syllable as in the Irmos, in order to make the accentuated notes of the melody coincide with the accentuated syllables of the text of the stanzas.
units.english_cohort_translation: In another instance, in an anonymous hymnographer's poem composed in memory of Saint John Chrysostom, this principle of letter doubling is expanded even further. The prescription in the title: *«φέρον ἀκροστιχίδα τήνδε· εἰς τὸν χρυσόστομον»* ("bearing this acrostic: Unto Chrysostom") is executed through extensive gemination: *εις τον χχρρυυσσοοοσσττομον*. At the period when the classic Kontakia were composed, the Greek language had already surrendered the classical distinction between long and short vowels, which constituted the foundation of the quantitative meter of ancient classical poetry. The vowels and diphthongs *η*, *ει*, and *οι* had become phonetically equivalent to *ι* (iota), and *αι* equivalent to *ε* (epsilon). Consequently, a new tonic-rhythmic system of versification arose, founded upon the strict rule that all stanzas must possess the exact same number of syllables as the model **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*) upon which they were modeled, and that the word stress accents must occupy identical positions across all stanzas as in the corresponding verses of the Heirmos. The composition of a Kontakion—or, in later centuries, of a **Canon** (*Κανών*)—was a sophisticated undertaking that could be accomplished only by a poet who was simultaneously a master composer and musician. Melody and verse formed a single entity. In adapting the Troparia to the melody of the Heirmos, it was not merely necessary to equate the syllable count of each line with the model strophe; the dynamic melodic stress accents had to coincide precisely with the accented syllables of the hymnographic text.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Kontakion makes its appearance suddenly, without antecedents. Byzantine hagiography attributes its introduction into Eastern liturgy to Romanos, who is praised by Germanos, the author of a hymn in honor of the saint who gives the Greek hymn and its description and explanation. The association of the name of Romanos with the rise of the Kontakion makes it possible to fix the date of its reception into Byzantine liturgy within the first decades of the sixth century. Romanos was a Jew by birth. He was born at Emesa on the Orontes River, became deacon at Berytus in northern Phoenicia, and went to Constantinople in the days of Anastasius I (491-518) to join the clergy of the Theotokos Church. units.english_cohort_translation: The Kontakion appeared in Byzantine worship with striking suddenness, without direct literary antecedents in classical Greek forms. Byzantine hagiographical tradition attributes its introduction into Eastern Christian worship to Saint Romanos the Melodist, celebrated by Saint Germanos, who composed a hymn in his honor providing an account of his miraculous divine inspiration. The historical association of Saint Romanos with the rise of the Kontakion allows us to date its formal entry into the Constantinopolitan liturgical tradition to the early decades of the sixth century. Saint Romanos was of Jewish lineage, born in Emesa upon the Orontes River (modern Homs, Syria). He was ordained deacon at Berytus (Beirut) in Phoenicia, and subsequently journeyed to Constantinople during the reign of Emperor Anastasios I (491–518), joining the clergy of the Church of the Most Holy Theotokos in the Kyros district. There, according to sacred tradition, the Mother of God appeared to him on the Feast of the Nativity of Christ, bestowing upon him the miraculous charism of hymnography, whereupon he composed more than one thousand Kontakia. units.english_text: The Kontakion appeared in Byzantine worship with striking suddenness, without direct literary antecedents in classical Greek forms. Byzantine hagiographical tradition attributes its introduction into Eastern Christian worship to Saint Romanos the Melodist, celebrated by Saint Germanos, who composed a hymn in his honor providing an account of his miraculous divine inspiration. The historical association of Saint Romanos with the rise of the Kontakion allows us to date its formal entry into the Constantinopolitan liturgical tradition to the early decades of the sixth century. Saint Romanos was of Jewish lineage, born in Emesa upon the Orontes River (modern Homs, Syria). He was ordained deacon at Berytus (Beirut) in Phoenicia, and subsequently journeyed to Constantinople during the reign of Emperor Anastasios I (491–518), joining the clergy of the Church of the Most Holy Theotokos in the Kyros district. There, according to sacred tradition, the Mother of God appeared to him on the Feast of the Nativity of Christ, bestowing upon him the miraculous charism of hymnography, whereupon he composed more than one thousand Kontakia. In August 535, a catastrophic earthquake devastated a substantial portion of Constantinople, which was subsequently commemorated each[^633]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: year on the day it had happened by hymns and prayers. Romanos, who in his Kontakia frequently alludes to contemporary events, mentions the earthquake in a 'Psalm', which was sung on Wednesday of the third week of Lent. Since the Kontakion was obviously written under the immediate impression of the disaster, and no event later than the disaster is mentioned in a poem by Romanus, it may be assumed that he died shortly after 535. Antecedents of the Kontakion existed in Syriac ecclesiastical poetry, and it may also be assumed that Romanus, being of Syrian origin, was well acquainted with them. It was his great achievement to have adapted them to the spirit of Byzantine hymnography, and to have introduced the new form of ecclesiastical poetry into the liturgy of Constantinople. Here follows a comparison of the main forms of Syriac poetry the Memra, Madrasha, and Sogitha. The memra, the poetical homily, must be regarded as the most important for the development of the Kontakion. Like the Memra, the Kontakion had its place in the Morning Office after the reading of the Gospel and paraphrased the text of the Scriptures. There is, however, a noticeable difference between Memra and Kontakion. The Memra invariably has the character of a sermon, while the Kontakion in the most perfect hymns of Romanos loses this homiletic character and, by assimilating elements from Madrasha and Sogitha, develops into a poetical description of the object of the feast on which it is sung. (This foregoing description is from A History of Byzantine Music and Hymnography by E. Wellesz).
units.english_cohort_translation: year on the anniversary of the catastrophe with solemn hymns and supplications. Saint Romanos, who frequently incorporated references to contemporary historical events into his compositions, commemorated this earthquake in a hymn (styled a "Psalm") chanted on Wednesday of the third week of the Great Fast. Because this Kontakion was composed under the vivid and immediate impression of the disaster, and because no historical event occurring after 535 is mentioned anywhere in the corpus of Saint Romanos, it is reasonably concluded that he reposed shortly after that date. Notable antecedents to the literary form of the Kontakion existed in Syriac Christian poetry, with which Saint Romanos, being of Syrian provenance, was intimately familiar. His supreme achievement lay in translating and adapting these Semitic poetic structures into the spirit, elegance, and melody of Byzantine hymnography, thereby establishing an entirely new genre in the liturgical life of Constantinople. Scholars identify three primary genres of classical Syriac poetry: the *Memra*, the *Madrasha*, and the *Sogitha*. The *Memra*, or metrical homily, served as the principal structural prototype for the Kontakion: like the *Memra*, the Kontakion occupied a fixed station in the Morning Office (Matins) immediately following the reading of the Holy Gospel, providing an extensive poetic amplification and paraphrase of the sacred scriptural narrative. Yet an essential distinction remains: while the Syriac *Memra* remained strictly an homiletic discourse in verse, the Kontakion in the masterworks of Saint Romanos transcends mere moral exhortation and, by absorbing the lyricism of the *Madrasha* and the dramatic dialogue of the *Sogitha*, blossoms into a sublime theological contemplation and celebration of the sacred mystery of the feast. (Adapted from *A History of Byzantine Music and Hymnography* by Egon Wellesz).

units.slavonic_incipit: Originally, the Kontakion was a hymn
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Originally, the Kontakion was a hymn of many stanzas (18-24) whose lengthy text indeed required the use of a scroll. St. Romanos the Melodist (+556) is the most famous composer of such lengthy, free-style hymns. The hymns in their original, lengthy form have fallen into disuse in Orthodox worship. What now remains in the liturgical books as Kontakia are merely the short, preliminary stanzas of the earlier and longer hymns. The Kontakion is sung after Ode 6 (together with the Ikos, (or first strophe of the more ancient, lengthy kontakion) of the Canon at Matins, during the Hours, and after the Troparia at the Divine Liturgy. The Kontakion is not sung at Vespers. (Modified from APL)
units.english_cohort_translation: Originally, the Kontakion was an extended liturgical poem comprising eighteen to twenty-four stanzas, whose substantial length necessitated the use of a continuous parchment scroll. Saint Romanos the Melodist (+c. 556) stands as the pre-eminent master of these monumental compositions. Over time, these extended hymnographic cycles fell out of active liturgical performance in the Byzantine Rite. Today, what survives in the printed liturgical books under the designation of **Kontakion** represents only the brief introductory strophe (the ancient Proimion) accompanied by the initial **Ikos** (*Οἶκος*). In the current liturgical ordo, the Kontakion is chanted following Ode 6 of the Canon at Matins (jointly with the Ikos), at the Little Hours, and following the Dismissal Troparia at the Divine Liturgy. The Kontakion is never chanted at Vespers.[^634]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: KUVUKLION (κουβούκλιον, τό): A structure, usually of wood, representing the tomb of Christ or Sepulchre. During the Holy and Great Friday evening service, it stands on the SOLEAS and contains a cloth icon (EPITAFIOS) of the entombed Christ.
units.english_cohort_translation: **KUVUKLION** (*Κουβούκλιον, τό*): A ceremonial canopy structure, typically carved of wood, representing the Holy Sepulchre and Tomb of Christ. During the solemn Vespers and Matins services of Great and Holy Friday and Holy Saturday, it is erected upon the Soleas (or before the Tetrapod) to enshrine the sacred cloth icon of the entombed Savior, the **Plashchanytsia** (*Epitaphios* / *᾿Επιτάφιος*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: LAMB (ἀμνός, ὁ) Slav. Agnec: Is the raised stamped section of the sacramental bread loaf (PROSPHORA) indicated by the stamp ΙΣ ΧΣ ΝΙ KA, which abbreviate the Greek words Jesus Christ Conquers. This section is removed from the Prosphora during the PROSKOMIDI for later consecration in the Divine Liturgy. The New Testament refers to Christ as the "Lamb of God" (John 1:29 and 1:36). The Prophet Isaiah also refers to the coming Messiah as "the Lamb." (Isaiah 53)
units.english_cohort_translation: **LAMB** (*᾿Αμνός, ὁ*; Slav. *Agnets* / *Агнецъ*): The square Eucharistic host stamped and extracted from the principal liturgical loaf (**Prosphora** / *Προσφορά*), bearing the sacred cruciform inscription **IC XC NIKA** (Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Νικᾷ, "Jesus Christ Conquers"). This consecrated portion is excised with the holy Lance during the Office of Preparation (**Proskomide** / *Προσκομιδή*) for subsequent Eucharistic consecration at the Divine Liturgy. The Holy Scriptures designate Christ as the "Lamb of God" (John 1:29, 1:36), fulfilling the prophetic vision of Isaiah concerning the suffering Servant: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before its shearer, so He opens not His mouth" (Isaiah 53:7 [LXX 53:7]).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: LAMBADARIOS (Λαμπαδάριος, ὁ): The head chanter and soloist who stands at the ANALOGION in the KLIROS on the north side of the SOLEA before the ICONOSTASIS. The title also implies that he was the first to light his candle from that of the PATRIARCH ON PASCHA which was then transmitted to the candles of all the people .
units.english_cohort_translation: **LAMBADARIOS** (*Λαμπαδάριος, ὁ*): The leader and master chanter directing the left choir at the Analogion upon the northern side of the Kliros, before the Iconostasis. Historically, the title signifies the sacred dignitary privileged to receive the Paschal Flame directly from the hand of the Patriarch on Holy Pascha to distribute the light to the clergy and faithful.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *LITI (λιτή, ἡ) Slav. Litija: (1) A word implying a fervent, prolonged prayer. It generally designates a procession to the NARTHEX of the CHURCH, while petitions, hymns, and the blessing of loaves take place—a typical feature of the latter part of Great Vespers on the eve of great feasts. During the procession special stichira at the Liti are sung, which pertain to the occasion being celebrated. (From APL) Also, a brief form of the Memorial Service, which consists of the TRISAGION and TROPARIA for the departed (from PSALM, Inc.)
units.english_cohort_translation: **LITI** (*Λιτή, ἡ*; Slav. *Litiya* / *Литія*): (1) Liturgically, an earnest, prolonged entreaty and supplication. It denotes the solemn liturgical procession of the sacred ministers and choir into the Narthex of the church during Great Vespers on the eve of great feasts, accompanied by the chanting of festive idiomela stichera, lengthy petitions for ecclesiastical and civil well-being, and the solemn blessing of five loaves, wheat, wine, and oil (Artoklasia). During this procession, proper **Stichera at the Liti** are chanted according to the feast. (2) Also designates a brief memorial service for the departed, consisting of the Trisagion Prayers, the funeral Dismissal Troparia, and a memorial litany.

units.slavonic_incipit: LITURGICAL COLORS: In the Orthodox Byzantine
units.slavonic_diplomatic: LITURGICAL COLORS: In the Orthodox Byzantine Rite, which is used by all the member churches of the Eastern Orthodox Church and by the Greek-Catholic Churches (Eastern Catholic Churches of Byzantine Rite), there is no universal system of colors being used. In the Typikon of today's Greek Orthodox Church little is said about liturgical colors except for specifying “light” or “dark” vestments. In the Greek tradition, maroon or burgundy are common for solemn feast days, and a wide variety of colors are used at other times, the most common of which are gold and white.
units.english_cohort_translation: **LITURGICAL COLORS**: Across the Byzantine liturgical tradition, shared by Eastern Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic Churches, no rigid, uniform color canon exists comparable to the post-Tridentine Western rubrical system. In the authoritative Greek Typikon of George Violakis, rubrical directions regarding vesture focus primarily upon specifying "bright" (*λευκά* / light) or "dark" (*σκοτεινά*) vestments. In modern Greek practice, deep red, maroon, or burgundy vestments are customary for solemn feast days, while a broad spectrum of colors is employed on other occasions, with gold and white prevailing as standard festive tones.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: example, are associated with the Paschal period (although in some churches the tradition for Paschas is to use red), as the brightest and most radiant celebration of the vanquishing of death. It is a visual reminder that, “He that overcomes, the same shall be clothed in white raiment” (Rev. 3:5). Green, the color of life and spring, is used at Pentecost to symbolize the beginning of the life of the Church. It is also used on feasts of certain saints, particular monk saints, who dwelt in the wilderness. Red is used at the Nativity, on the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and for Martyrs. Blue is the traditional color of the Mother of God, as she is the Queen of Heaven. Deep purple is used during Lent as a reminder of the purple robe which the soldiers put on Christ to mock Him before His Passion. Outside of festal periods gold is used to remind us of the heavenly Jerusalem: “and the city was pure gold” (Rev. 21:18). The use of vestments, then, not only adds to the visual splendor of the church, but this use has a far greater significance in transforming the celebrants, even young acolytes, into representatives of the Kingdom of heaven, reflecting that otherworldliness which is the essence of Orthodoxy. (From a talk given at the St. Herman Winter Pilgrimage, Redding, California, 1983).
units.english_cohort_translation: example, are associated with the Paschal season (although in certain local traditions red vestments are donned at Pascha), symbolizing the radiant joy of Christ's resurrection and the destruction of death, echoing the apocalyptic vision: "He that overcomes, the same shall be clothed in white raiment" (Rev. 3:5). Green, signifying life, spiritual rebirth, and renewal, is appointed for Pentecost and the feast of the Holy Trinity, symbolizing the descent of the Holy Spirit, as well as for the feasts of venerable monastic saints who dwelt in the wilderness. Red vestments are worn at the Nativity of Christ, the feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and on the commemorations of holy martyrs who shed their blood for Christ. Blue is traditionally appointed for feasts of the Most Holy Theotokos, honoring Her as the Queen of Heaven. Deep purple or dark crimson is worn during the Great Fast as a solemn remembrance of the passion of Christ and the purple robe with which the Roman soldiers mockingly clothed Him before His Crucifixion. Outside of specific festal seasons, gold vestments serve as the universal standard, evoking the heavenly Jerusalem: "and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass" (Rev. 21:18). Liturgical vesture not only elevates the visual beauty of divine worship, but transforms the ministers—from the presiding hierarch to the youngest acolyte—into living icons of the heavenly court.

units.slavonic_incipit: Originally, in the Orthodox Church, six
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Originally, in the Orthodox Church, six liturgical colors were used: white, green, purple, red, blue, and gold. Later, black vestments also came into use. In some places, scarlet orange or rust color is used. Some have assigned meanings to the different colors: white for the pure light of God's energy; green, the color of life, for the Holy Spirit and the wood of the cross; purple for the suffering of Christ; deep red for the blood on the Cross or blood of the martyrs; blue for the Mother of God; gold for the richness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and bright red for the fiery flame of the Spiritual Host. While in the East, white is the color of death and morning, in the West black is the color used. In Russia, red is the color of beauty, brightness and joy. None of this is written in the Typikon, and different colors obviously have different meanings for different traditions. It is, therefore, more appropriate to describe various customs than it is to say what colors are 'proper' or 'improper.'
units.english_cohort_translation: Historically, six principal liturgical colors developed in Byzantine practice: white, green, purple, red, blue, and gold. In later centuries, black vestments were introduced, particularly for weekday services in Great Lent. In various regional customs, amber, saffron, or rust-colored vestments are also utilized. Liturgical commentators have attributed rich theological symbolism to these colors: white represents the uncreated light of the Divine Energies; green represents the life-creating power of the Holy Spirit and the life-giving Cross; purple signifies the suffering and sovereignty of Christ; deep red recalls the Precious Blood shed upon the Cross and the witness of the martyrs; blue honors the virginity and heavenly glory of the Mother of God; and gold represents the splendor of the Kingdom of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit. While in ancient Eastern tradition white was the mourning color of Christian burial—signifying the hope of resurrection—black became widespread in the West and eventually entered Slavic funeral usage. In traditional Ruthenian and Slavic lands, red (*krasny*) is the color of festal majesty, spiritual beauty, and joy. None of these specific color systems is mandated in the statutory text of the Typikon, and diverse local traditions preserve distinctive usages.[^637]

LITURGICAL YEAR (λειτουργικὸν ἔτος, τό): The liturgical year, also known by some as the Christian year or church year, consists of the cycle of liturgical seasons in the Eastern Orthodox Churches which determines when Feasts, Memorials, Commemorations, etc., are to be observed and which portions of Scripture are to be read. This cycle is reckoned as beginning on September 1, the date of Indiction, and ending August 31. Also, various and distinct liturgical colors may be used in connection with the different seasons of the liturgical year as mentioned under LITURGICAL COLORS.

units.english_cohort_translation: **LITURGICAL YEAR** (*Λειτουργικὸν ἔτος, τό*): The annual cycle of ecclesiastical seasons, festal periods, fasts, and commemorations in the Eastern Church governing the celebration of feasts, memorials, daily scriptural lections, and proper hymnography. In the Byzantine Rite, the liturgical year commences on September 1, designated the Feast of the Indiction and the beginning of the Ecclesiastical New Year, and concludes on August 31. Distinct liturgical colors and propers correspond to each liturgical cycle throughout the church year.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The dates of the festivals or feasts vary somewhat between the Eastern Orthodox churches and the western Church (Roman Catholic, Anglican, and Protestant) though the sequence and logic is the same. In both East and West, the dates of many festivals vary between years, in most cases because of the variation in the always shifting date of Pascha (Easter). In the Greek Orthodox Church those feasts which occur on the same date each year are known as IMMOVABLE FEASTS, while those that depend on the shifting date of Pascha (Easter) are called MOVEABLE FEASTS.
units.english_cohort_translation: The liturgical calendars of the Christian East and West share a common historical foundation and structural logic, though divergent calendar reckonings (Julian and Gregorian) and computational methods for calculating the date of Pascha create variations in festal dates. Feasts that fall upon a fixed calendar date every year (such as the Nativity of Christ on December 25 or the Dormition on August 15) are designated **Immovable Feasts** (*᾿Ακίνητοι ἑορταί*), whereas feasts whose annual celebration depends upon the moveable date of Holy Pascha (such as the Ascension, Pentecost, and all services of the Triodion and Pentecostarion) are designated **Moveable Feasts** (*Κινηταὶ ἑορταί*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: LITURGY (Λειτουργία, ἡ): Today, a liturgy comprises a solemn religious ceremony, following a carefully prescribed formal ritual. The word is a composite Greek word which originally meant a public duty, that is a service to the state undertaken by a citizen. The word comes from the Greek 'laos', 'people', or 'public' and 'ergon' or 'work'. The word, therefore, is best understood as “the work or duty of the people.” In the Greek (Eastern) Orthodox church, this word is solely applied to the celebration of the Holy Eucharist. The Orthodox Church celebrates several versions of the liturgy:
units.english_cohort_translation: **LITURGY** (*Λειτουργία, ἡ*): In general Christian usage, liturgy signifies the public, official prayer and sacramental worship of the Church. The word derives from the classical Greek composite *leitourgia* (*λειτουργία*, from *laos* / *leos*, "people", and *ergon*, "work"), originally denoting a public civic duty or service rendered by an individual citizen for the welfare of the commonwealth. In Christian theology and Byzantine liturgical terminology, the term is consecrated pre-eminently to designate the celebration of the Holy Eucharist—the Divine Liturgy. The Byzantine Rite celebrates several distinct Eucharistic liturgies:

units.english_cohort_translation: 4) **The Divine Liturgy of Saint James the Brother of the Lord**: The venerable Jerusalem Liturgy, historically attributed to Saint James the Just, the first Bishop of Jerusalem (not to be confused with Saint James the Apostle, brother of Saint John the Theologian). units.slavonic_incipit: The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, served on Wednesdays and Fridays during the Great Fast (Great Lent) and on the first three days of Holy Week is essentially the office of Vespers with an appended communion service, as the Holy Gifts were already consecrated and reserved for later use on the previous Sunday. It is traditionally attributed to St. Gregory the Dialogist.
units.english_cohort_translation: **The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts**: Celebrated on Wednesdays and Fridays of the Great Fast, on Thursday of the Great Canon, and on the first three days of Great and Holy Week (Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday). This rite is structurally an Office of Solemn Vespers conjoined to a communion rite, wherein the faithful receive the Holy Mysteries previously consecrated at the Divine Liturgy on the preceding Sunday and reserved upon the Holy Table. Sacerdotal tradition attributes the compilation and ordering of this service to Saint Gregory the Dialogist (Pope of Rome).

units.slavonic_incipit: Lent is generally a period called
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Lent is generally a period called “aliturgical,” which means that the celebration of the Divine Liturgy and the festive manner of its celebration in honor of the Resurrection is limited to Sundays. During the week the celebration of the Liturgy of the Presanctified is prescribed to allow more frequent communion of the faithful.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Great Fast is fundamentally an "aliturgical" season on weekdays, meaning that the full celebration of the Eucharistic sacrifice with its festal, resurrectal character is precluded on ordinary Lenten days and reserved for Saturdays and Sundays. The celebration of the Presanctified Liturgy was instituted to strengthen the faithful through frequent reception of Holy Communion during their ascetic struggle without interrupting the penitential character of the fast.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: LONCHI (Λόγχη, ἡ): A small knife or lance with a triangular-shaped, double edged tip at one end and a cross on the handle at the other end, used by the priest to cut out the particles of the altar bread (PROSFORA) used in the service of the Preparation of the Holy Gifts (see PROSKOMIDI). The Lonchi used here commemorates the piercing by a soldier of the side of Christ hanging on the cross.
units.english_cohort_translation: **LONCHI** (*Λόγχη, ἡ*; Slav. *Kopíye* / *Копіе* / Lance or Spear): A sacred liturgical implement consisting of a small, double-edged steel blade mounted upon a wooden or metal handle terminating in a cross. The priest employs the holy Lance during the Office of Preparation (**Proskomide**) to excise the **Lamb** (*᾿Αμνός*) and particles from the loaves of **Prosphora** (*Προσφορά*). The piercing action of the Lance mystically commemorates the Roman soldier piercing the side of Christ hanging upon the Cross, from which flowed blood and water (John 19:34).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MAKARISMOS, MAKARISMI (Μακαρισμός, ὁ· pl. Μακαρισμοί, οἱ). The eight blessings or beatitudes given by Christ at his Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5: 3-12). Also, a salutation addressed to an Orthodox Patriarch (“Your Beatitude”). The Makarizmi are also chanted in various services, e.g. in the Crucifixion Service on Holy Thursday evening. See BEATITUDES.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MAKARISMOS, MAKARISMOI** (*Μακαρισμός, ὁ· pl. Μακαρισμοί, οἱ*; Slav. *Blazhenni* / *Блаженни*): The Beatitudes; the eight evangelical blessings pronounced by Christ in His Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5:3–12). In the Byzantine Rite, the Beatitudes constitute the standard Third Antiphon at the Divine Liturgy, interspersed with Troparia from the Oktoechos or the feast. The term also designates the formal patriarchal address "Your Beatitude" (*Μακαριώτατε*). Special hymnographic Beatitudes are likewise appointed for specific solemn offices, such as the Twelve Passion Gospels on the evening of Great and Holy Thursday. See **BEATITUDES**.

Special hymnographic Beatitudes are likewise appointed for specific solemn offices, such as the Twelve Passion Gospels on the evening of Great and Holy Thursday. See **BEATITUDES**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MANDYAS (Μανδύας, ὁ): This garment is the monastic mantle or cloak of a hierarch and the non-eucharistic and processional dress of the Bishop. Purple in color it often has embroidered medallions of the evangelists and is closed at the front bottom. (See also under VESTMENTS: NON-LITURGICAL ATTIRE OF THE CLERGY)
units.english_cohort_translation: **MANDYAS** (*Μανδύας, ὁ*; Slav. *Mantiya* / *Мантія*): The monastic mantle or episcopal cloak, worn by bishops as their solemn non-eucharistic and processional vesture. Crafted of rich purple or crimson fabric, the episcopal mandyas features long flowing trains, red and white horizontal stripes representing the streams of divine teaching (*potamoi* / *струи*), and four embroidered square tablets or medallions at the neck and hem depicting the Four Holy Evangelists (or seraphim). It fastens at the neck and lower front. (See also under **VESTMENTS: NON-LITURGICAL ATTIRE OF THE CLERGY**).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MASTER ICONS (Δεσποτικαὶ εἰκόναι, αἱ): The term describes the following 4 icons on the Altar Screen (IKONOSTASION): 1) Christ, 2) the Theotokos, 3) St. John the Baptist and 4) the Icon of the Church.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MASTER ICONS** (*Δεσποτικαὶ εἰκόνες, αἱ*): The principal tier of four foundational icons enshrined upon the lower tier of the Iconostasis (**Ikonostasion**), flanking the Holy Doors: (1) Christ the Teacher; (2) the Most Holy Theotokos; (3) Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist (or the patronal icon); and (4) the Icon of the Patron Saint or Mystery of the Temple.[^640]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MATINS (ὄρθρος, ὁ). Slav. Utrenya: Matins is a western term which, in Greek Orthodox Churches, is known by the Greek term ORTHROS meaning "early dawn" or "daybreak." A part of the daily cycle of services, it is the last of the four night offices, which include Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office and Matins. In traditional monasteries it is celebrated daily so as to end at sunrise.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MATINS** (*ὄρθρος, ὁ*; Slav. *Utrenya* / *Утреня*): Matins is a Western term which, in Greek tradition, is designated by the Greek term **Orthros** (*Ὄρθρος*), signifying "early dawn" or "daybreak." As an integral part of the daily cycle of services, it constitutes the final office among the four nocturnal offices, which encompass Vespers, Compline, the Midnight Office, and Matins. In traditional monasteries it is celebrated daily in the early morning so as to conclude at sunrise.

units.slavonic_incipit: Matins is the longest and most
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Matins is the longest and most complex of the daily cycle of services. It is normally celebrated in the early morning, sometimes preceded by the Midnight Office, and usually followed by the First Hour. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as part of an All-Night Vigil on the evening before, combined with Vespers and the First Hour. In the Greek parish tradition, Matins is normally served just before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy on Sunday morning. In the Slavic tradition, an All-Night Vigil is served every Sunday (commencing on Saturday evening).
units.english_cohort_translation: Matins is the longest and most complex service of the daily cycle. It is normally celebrated in the early morning, on occasion preceded by the Midnight Office, and regularly followed immediately by the First Hour. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as the principal component of an All-Night Vigil on the preceding evening, conjoined with Great Vespers and the First Hour. In the Greek parish tradition, Matins is normally celebrated in the morning immediately preceding the Divine Liturgy. In the Slavic tradition, an All-Night Vigil is celebrated on every Saturday evening preceding Sunday.

units.slavonic_incipit: The fixed portion of the service
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The fixed portion of the service is composed primarily of psalms and litanies. The variable parts of Matins are composed primarily of HYMNS and CANONS from the PARAKLITIKI (OKTOICHOS), a book containing a cycle of hymns for each of eight modes for each day of the week, covering eight weeks), and from the MINEA, i.e., 12 books containing hymns for each of the 12 months of the year. During Great Lent, some of the portions from the Oktoichos and the Minea are replaced by hymns from the book called the TRIODION and during the Paschal Season with material from the book called the PENTIKOSTARION. On Sundays there are also Gospel readings and hymns from the eleven-part cycle of Resurrectional Gospels.
units.english_cohort_translation: The fixed psalmody of the service comprises primarily the Six Psalms, fixed morning psalms, and litanies. The variable hymnography of Matins is drawn principally from the canons and hymns of the **Paraklitiki** (**Oktoechos** / *᾿Οκτώηχος*), the liturgical volume containing the hymnographic cycle for each of the eight Tones across each day of the week, cycling over eight weeks, and from the **Menaion** (*Μηναῖον*, pl. **Menaia** / *Μηναῖα*), the twelve monthly volumes comprising the propers for each calendar day of the ecclesiastical year. During the Great Fast (Lent), portions of the Oktoechos and Menaion are superseded by the proper hymnography of the **Triodion** (*Τριῴδιον*), and during the Paschal Season by the joyful hymnography of the **Pentecostarion** (*Πεντηκοστάριον*). On Sundays, Matins also features Gospel lections and proper hymns from the eleven-part cycle of Resurrectional Gospels (*῾Εωθινὰ Εὐαγγέλια*).

During the Great Fast (Lent), portions of the Oktoechos and Menaion are superseded by the proper hymnography of the **Triodion** (*Τριῴδιον*), and during the Paschal Season by the joyful hymnography of the **Pentecostarion** (*Πεντηκοστάριον*). On Sundays, Matins also features Gospel lections and proper hymns from the eleven-part cycle of Resurrectional Gospels (*῾Εωθινὰ Εὐαγγέλια*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MEGA SYNODIKON (Μέγα Συνοδικὸν, τό): A Synodikon is defined as a written and eventually read proclamation in churches summarizing the decisions of a synod of bishops. With the appelation of "Mega" or "Great" it usually refers to the liturgical text used in the Eastern Orthodox Church on the Feast of Orthodoxy and composed c. 843 by Patriarch Methodios I. (Livingstone, E. A.)
units.english_cohort_translation: **MEGA SYNODIKON** (*Μέγα Συνοδικόν, τό*): A Synodikon is defined as a formal conciliar decree and synodal proclamation promulgated in churches summarizing the dogmatic definitions and canonical decisions of a council of bishops. With the qualifying epithet *Mega* ("Great"), it designates pre-eminently the solemn liturgical text proclaimed in the Eastern Church on the Sunday of Orthodoxy (the First Sunday of the Great Fast), originally compiled in 843 under Patriarch Methodios I upon the definitive triumph over Iconoclasm.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *MEGALYNARION (Μεγαλυνάριον, τό) Slav. Velichanie: A hymn praising or magnifying the Theotokos, sung after "Se Ymnumen" (Σὲ ὑμνοῦμεν) in the Divine Liturgy. The Megalynarion is often the initial hymn or irmos (εἱρμός) of the Ninth Ode or canticle of the Canon that is chanted in the Orthros of the day, e.g., the Fotizu, Fotizu, the initial hymn of the Ninth Ode of the Easter Canon. At other times, the Megalynarion is an independent hymn, such as "Epi Si Cheri" («᾿Επὶ σοὶ χαίρει»), sung in St. Basil's Divine Liturgy. The Megalynarion most commonly sung in the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom is Axion Estin («῎Αξιόν ἐστίν»).
units.english_cohort_translation: **MEGALYNARION** (*Μεγαλυνάριον, τό*; Slav. *Velichanie* / *Величаніе*): A hymn of praise and magnification in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos or a sacred feast, chanted following the epiklesis and the hymn **"We praise Thee, we bless Thee"** (*Σὲ ὑμνοῦμεν*) during the Anaphora of the Divine Liturgy. The Megalynarion is frequently the model strophe or **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*) of the Ninth Ode of the Canon appointed at Matins for the feast, such as **"Shine, shine, O New Jerusalem"** (*Φωτίζου, φωτίζου*) from the Ninth Ode of the Paschal Canon. On other occasions, the Megalynarion is an independent festive composition, such as **"All of creation rejoices in thee"** (*«᾿Επὶ σοὶ χαίρει»*) chanted at the Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great. The Megalynarion standardly chanted at the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom is **"It is truly meet"** (*«῎Αξιόν ἐστιν»*).[^642]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *MEGALYNARION AT THE DIPTYCHA (Μεγαλυνάριον εἰς τὰ Δίπτυχα): A Megalynarion dedicated to a specific saint or sacred object, sung in addition to the Megalynarion of the Divine Liturgy. It is sung by the choir immediately before its response "Ke panton ke pason" («Καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»). For the order, see the Ieratikon, ed. Apostoliki Diakonia (Athens, 1977 and 1987), p. 182. The Egkolpion tu Anagnostu (Manual of the Church Reader), ed. Apostoliki Diakonia (Athens, ca. 1970), p. 83, proposes a less common yet recent practice: that the Megalynarion at the Diptycha be sung immediately before the priest's petition "Remember also, Lord, those whom each of us calls to mind and all Your people." («Καὶ ὧν ἕκαστος κατὰ διάνοιαν ἔχει καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν.») Violakis' Typikon refers to only two such Megalynaria: for St. Basil, 1 January (pp. 137-138, ¶ 3); and for the Zoodochos Pigi, Friday following Easter Sunday (pp. 374-375, ¶ 8). The Egkolpion tu Anagnostu, on the other hand, contains several of them, possibly written after the publication of the Typikon (1888).
units.english_cohort_translation: **MEGALYNARION AT THE DIPTYCHA** (*Μεγαλυνάριον εἰς τὰ Δίπτυχα*): A proper Megalynarion dedicated to a specific saint or sacred commemoration, chanted in addition to the customary Megalynarion of the Divine Liturgy. It is sung by the choir immediately preceding its liturgical response **"And each and all"** (*«Καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»*). For the proper rubrical order, see the *Ieratikon* (ed. Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, 1977 and 1987, p. 182). The *Engolpion tu Anagnostu* (*Manual of the Church Reader*, ed. Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, c. 1970, p. 83) records a modern variant custom wherein the Megalynarion at the Diptycha is sung immediately preceding the priest's intercessory petition: **"Remember also, Lord, those whom each of us calls to mind and all Your people"** (*«Καὶ ὧν ἕκαστος κατὰ διάνοιαν ἔχει καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»*). The Typikon of George Violakis references only two such Diptych Megalynaria: for Saint Basil the Great on January 1 (pp. 137–138, § 3), and for the Life-Giving Spring (**Zoodochos Pege** / *Ζωοδόχος Πηγή*) on Bright Friday following Pascha (pp. 374–375, § 8). The *Engolpion tu Anagnostu*, by contrast, provides several additional compositions, composed after the publication of the 1888 Typikon.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MEGAS SYNAXARISTIS (Μέγας Συναξαριστής, ὁ): An extensive history of the lives of the saints in 12 volumes, organized into collections arranged by the month in which the saint is celebrated. A brief summary of these biographies is presented in a service book of the church called the SYNAXARION. Similar brief summaries are also included in the 12 books of the MINEA.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MEGAS SYNAXARISTIS** (*Μέγας Συναξαριστής, ὁ*): The Great Synaxaristes; a monumental twelve-volume compilation of the lives of the holy saints, arranged sequentially according to their calendar commemorations across each month of the ecclesiastical year. A concise abridgment of these hagiographical biographies is contained in the liturgical book entitled the **Synaxarion** (*Συναξάριον*), and corresponding summaries are likewise printed within the twelve volumes of the **Menaia**.

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: **MEGAS SYNAXARISTIS** (*Μέγας Συναξαριστής, ὁ*): The Great Synaxaristes; a monumental twelve-volume compilation of the lives of the holy saints, arranged sequentially according to their calendar commemorations across each month of the ecclesiastical year. A concise abridgment of these hagiographical biographies is contained in the liturgical book entitled the **Synaxarion** (*Συναξάριον*), and corresponding summaries are likewise printed within the twelve volumes of the **Menaia**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: METANIA (μετάνοια, ἡ): The act of repentance. The term also can mean a low bow in which the right hand touches the ground. Slav. poklon. Moreover it also may mean a full PROSTRATION done in penitence or obeisance.
units.english_cohort_translation: **METANIA** (*μετάνοια, ἡ*; Slav. *poklon* / *поклонъ*): An external bodily act of penitence and reverence, signifying spiritual repentance. The term designates either a waist bow (lesser metania) wherein the fingers of the right hand touch the ground, or a full prostration (great metania) cast upon the pavement in humble adoration and penitence before the Holy Mysteries or holy icons.

units.english_cohort_translation: **METHEORTA** (*μεθέορτα, τά*), **METHEORTIA** (*μεθεόρτια, τά*; Slav. *Poprazdnstvo* / *Попразднство*): The Greek neuter plural denoting the festal period of the **Afterfeast** (lit. units.english_cohort_translation: **METHEORTON** (*μεθέορτον*): The grammatical adjective designating a hymn as belonging to the festal period of a feast's Afterfeast (*Metheorta* or *Metheortia*), as in a Metheorton Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Metheorton Apolytikion'), Metheorton Kontakion, or Metheorton Canon. See also **AFTERFEAST** (lit. 'post-feast').

units.slavonic_diplomatic: From the Greek word for 'month'. The Minea are books containing the services for each day of the month of the calendar year. There are thus twelve volumes of the Mineon. For places without a full set of Minea there exists in both Greek and Slav. a volume containing general offices for each category of saint called the General Menaion. The contents of the Greek and Slavonic General Menaia are not identical, the Slavonic containing more offices, as well as texts for a full Vigil for each category of saint, and also for the Lord and the Mother of God. (modified from AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **MINEON, pl. MINEA** (*Μηναῖον, τό· Μηναῖα, τά*; Slav. *Mineya* / *Минея*): The **Menaion**, derived from the Greek noun for "month" (*μήν*). The Menaia comprise the liturgical volumes containing the variable offices for each calendar day of the twelve months of the liturgical year. For smaller parishes lacking the complete twelve-volume set of the Menaia, there exists in both Greek and Slavonic tradition a single-volume compendium containing common offices for each class of saint, designated the **General Menaion** (*᾿Ανθολόγιον* / Slav. *Obshtaya Mineya* / *Общая Минея*). The Greek and Slavonic General Menaia diverge in content: the Slavonic edition provides expanded propers, including complete All-Night Vigil texts for each order of saint, as well as common propers for feasts of the Lord and the Mother of God.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: MITRA (μίτρα, ἡ) Slav. Venec: The Byzantine Miter or Crown (functionally similar to the Western Mitre) is the ornate head covering worn by a Bishop. It typically is decorated with icons of Christ and the Evangelists as well as precious stones and bears a cross on top. It symbolizes the glory of the Lord and the highest ecclesiastical authority which has been conferred upon the Bishop at his ordination.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MITRA** (*μίτρα, ἡ*; Slav. *Venets* / *Вѣнецъ* or *Mitra* / *Митра*): The Byzantine Miter or Crown; an ornate, domed liturgical head covering worn by bishops (and by archimandrites or mitred archpriests by special award). It is richly embellished with embroidered or enameled icons of Christ and the Four Evangelists and decorated with precious jewels and pearls, surmounted by the Holy Cross. It symbolizes the Crown of Thorns, the imperial majesty of the King of Kings, and the episcopal authority conferred upon the hierarch at his consecration.[^645]

units.english_cohort_translation: **MODE** (*ἦχος, ὁ*; Slav. *Glas*, pl. *glasy* / *Гласъ*): The musical and liturgical **Tone**.
