A mode is likewise governed by its distinct melodic range (*ἔκτασις*), opening intonation formula (*ἀπήχημα*), foundational base tone or ison (*βάσις, ἶσον*), dominant tones (*δεσπόζοντες φθόγγοι*), modal and cadential signature marks (*μαρτυρίαι*), and modal modulation signs (*φθοραί*). The liturgical melodies within each mode are composed in three distinct melodic genres or styles:

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (1.) Irmologic (εἱρμολογικόν): The melodies are syllabic in character; that is, nearly each syllable of the text is sung to a different interval, lasting one and sometimes two beats. They are chanted in a rapid tempo, allegretto to vivace, often in cut-time. A good example of the Irmologic style is that used for the eight Resurrection Dismissal Hymns (APOLYTIKIA) sung at the SMALL ENTRANCE in the DIVINE LITURGY.
units.english_cohort_translation: 1. **Heirmologic** (*εἱρμολογικόν* / lit. 'irmologic'): The melodies are strictly syllabic in character, wherein each syllable of the sacred text corresponds to a single musical interval (or at most two beats). They are chanted in a brisk, rapid tempo (*allegretto* to *vivace*). A prime exemplar of the Heirmologic style is the musical setting appointed for the eight Resurrection Dismissal Troparia (lit. 'Apolytikia') chanted at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (2.) Sticheraric (στιχηραρικόν): the melodies are more ornate than in the Irmologic style; each syllable is given the average of two intervals and one to three beats. The tempo ranges generally from allegretto to andante. The sticheraric style is found in hymn types such as the Kekragaria in Vespers, Pasapnoaria in Orthros, and some of the Megalynaria in the Divine Liturgy.
units.english_cohort_translation: 2. **Sticheraric** (*στιχηραρικόν*): The melodies are moderately ornate and neumatic compared to the Heirmologic genre, with each syllable sustained across two to three beats. The tempo ranges generally from *allegretto* to *andante*. The Sticheraric style is employed for the Lucernarium stichera (**"Lord, I have cried"** / *Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*), the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Pasapnoaria*) at Matins, festal stichera, and select festal Megalynaria at the Divine Liturgy.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (3.) Papadic (παπαδικόν): The melodies are highly ornate, elaborate and extended—that is, melismatic. The tempo tends to be slow, although some ornate passages or melodies may be sung at a faster tempo. The Cherubic hymns and Communion hymns are prime examples of this style. The style or "kind" within each mode affects and alters to some extent all the musical elements mentioned in the first paragraph above.
units.english_cohort_translation: 3. **Papadic** (*παπαδικόν*): The melodies are highly melismatic, expansive, and elaborate. The tempo is stately and slow, though certain ornate passages are executed more rapidly. The Cherubic Hymn (*Χερουβικόν*) and the Communion Hymns (*Κοινωνικά*) serve as classic models of the Papadic genre. The particular melodic style chosen alters and expands the modal characteristics outlined above.

units.slavonic_incipit: The system of classifying Byzantine music
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The system of classifying Byzantine music and hymnology into eight tonal categories, known as Modes came to be applied to eight weekly cycles of hymns. As early as the 6th c., these hymns were compiled into a book known as the Octoichos, which was supposedly systematized and edited in the 8th century by St. John the Damascene.
units.english_cohort_translation: This eightfold modal classification system in Byzantine chant and hymnology gave rise to the weekly cycle of the Eight Tones. As early as the sixth century, these liturgical hymns were compiled into the hymnographic collection known as the **Oktoechos** (*᾿Οκτώηχος*), which was systematically edited and perfected in the eighth century by our venerable Father, Saint John of Damascus.[^646]

units.english_cohort_translation: In Byzantine liturgical music, eight canonical Tones are recognized: Tone 1 (Mode I), Tone 2 (Mode II), Tone 3 (Mode III), Tone 4 (Mode IV), Tone 5 (Mode I Plagal), Tone 6 (Mode II Plagal), Tone 7 (Varys / Grave Tone), and Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal). All hymnography of the Byzantine liturgical tradition is set within one of these eight Tones. The Eight Tones constitute the foundational architectural framework around which the Church organizes the daily offices and their hymnographic cycles throughout the ecclesiastical year. This structural logic is codified within the principal liturgical book of the daily cycle, the **Paraklitiki** (**Megali Oktoichos** / *Μεγάλη ᾿Οκτώηχος*).

units.english_cohort_translation: The Paraklitiki contains the appointed services and propers for every day of the week across the year. It is divided into eight modal sections or tone periods (*περίοδοι τῶν ἤχων*), each comprising the complete services of a full week from Sunday through Saturday. Each of the eight modal sections is sung in one of the eight Tones, advancing sequentially from Tone 1 through Tone 8. When the entire eight-week sequence has concluded, the cycle recommences with Tone 1, repeating continuously throughout the church year.

units.slavonic_incipit: The PARAKLITIKI contains the appointed services
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The PARAKLITIKI contains the appointed services and the hymnology for every day of the year. It is divided into eight sections or modal periods (περίοδοι τῶν ἤχων), each containing the services of one week, subdivided into its individual days from Sunday to Saturday. Each of the eight sections, or modal periods, is sung in one of the eight modes, moving progressively from Mode I to Mode IV Plagal. When the whole sequence of the eight modes has been gone through, a new one begins with Mode I, repeating itself as a cycle throughout the church year. This cycle of modes is initiated on each Sunday of Pascha (Easter) with Mode I, as is evident by the predominant use of Mode I in the Eni (Αἶνοι) or Hymns of Praise of the Easter Service sung in Mode I, before the Doxology in the Orthros. Through similar borrowings from the Paraklitiki in their services, the days in the week following Easter fall into the following modal pattern: Easter Monday—Mode II; Easter Tuesday—Mode III; Easter Wednesday—Mode IV; Easter Thursday—Mode I Plagal; Easter Friday—Mode II Plagal; Mode Varys (the Grave Mode) is omitted; Easter Saturday—Mode IV Plagal. The Second Sunday of Easter (Sunday of Thomas) returns to Mode I. From this point on, the modal pattern becomes weekly, the mode changing at the Vespers Service the night before each successive Sunday. Thus, the Third Sunday of Easter (Sunday of the Myrrh Bearers) moves to Mode II, and so on in the Sundays that follow, until Mode IV Plagal is completed. When Mode I is resumed, a new modal sequence begins, repeating itself cyclically until the Fifth Sunday of Lent of the following year. Palm Sunday,
units.english_cohort_translation: On the Second Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of Saint Thomas), the weekly cycle returns to Tone 1. From that day forward, the modal pattern shifts weekly, changing at Great Vespers on Saturday evening before each Sunday. Thus, the Third Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearing Women) is appointed in Tone 2, and so forth in unbroken progression through the subsequent Sundays until Tone 8 is completed. Upon reaching Tone 1 again, a new modal cycle begins, repeating cyclically until the Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast of the following year. Palm Sunday,[^647]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *MOVABLE FEAST (κινητὴ ἑορτή, ἡ): A feast that is not fixed to any particular calendar date of the LITURGICAL YEAR. Movable feasts occur within the periods of the TRIODION and PENTIKOSTARION, which constitute the whole framework of movable feasts. This framework begins with the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and ends with the Sunday of All Saints. Each movable feast has a fixed relationship to the Sunday of Pascha (Easter), which in the Gregorian Calendar may occur as early as April 4 and as late as May 8. The day on which a particular movable feast may be celebrated depends, therefore, on the date on which the Sunday of Pascha (Easter) falls each year. (For the earliest and latest possible dates of all the movable feasts, see p. 284 of Bogdanos' The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order. For the dates of both the movable and imovable feasts falling on Sundays in a particular year, see Schedule of Sunday Modes and Movable Feasts (A.D. 1992-2099), in Appendix D of the above Bogdanos book.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MOVEABLE FEAST** (*κινητὴ ἑορτή, ἡ*): A liturgical feast whose celebration is not tied to a fixed calendar date of the civil or ecclesiastical year. Moveable feasts are governed by the liturgical cycles of the **Triodion** and **Pentecostarion**, which together establish the liturgical framework of the Paschal cycle. This framework commences on the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and concludes on the Sunday of All Saints (the First Sunday after Pentecost). Every moveable feast stands in a fixed temporal relationship to the Sunday of Holy Pascha, which may occur between March 22 and April 25 on the Julian Reckoning (corresponding to April 4 and May 8 on the revised calendar). The precise calendar date for any moveable feast depends directly upon the date of Pascha in that particular year. (For the earliest and latest possible calendar limits of all moveable feasts, see scholarly liturgical tables and typikon guides).
units.slavonic_text: *MOVABLE FEAST (κινητὴ ἑορτή, ἡ): A feast that is not fixed to any particular calendar date of the LITURGICAL YEAR. Movable feasts occur within the periods of the TRIODION and PENTIKOSTARION, which constitute the whole framework of movable feasts. This framework begins with the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and ends with the Sunday of All Saints. Each movable feast has a fixed relationship to the Sunday of Pascha (Easter), which in the Gregorian Calendar may occur as early as April 4 and as late as May 8. The day on which a particular movable feast may be celebrated depends, therefore, on the date on which the Sunday of Pascha (Easter) falls each year. (For the earliest and latest possible dates of all the movable feasts, see p. 284 of Bogdanos' The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order. For the dates of both the movable and imovable feasts falling on Sundays in a particular year, see Schedule of Sunday Modes and Movable Feasts (A.D. 1992-2099), in Appendix D of the above Bogdanos book.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *MYROVLITIS (μυροβλήτης, ὁ): Myrrh-exuding. An epithet for a saint whose tomb has miraculously exuded a fragrant liquid: e.g., St. Demetrios, 26 October.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MYROVLITIS** (*μυροβλήτης, ὁ*): Myrrh-exuding or Myrrh-streaming; an honorary title bestowed upon a holy saint whose relics or tomb miraculously stream sweet-smelling, healing myrrh (*myron*), such as Saint Demetrios the Great Martyr of Thessaloniki (commemorated October 26).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *MYRRH BEARERS (μυροφόροι, αἱ): The women who brought perfumes and sweet spices to Christ's tomb to anoint His body. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome, the mother of John the Evangelist.
units.english_cohort_translation: **MYRRH-BEARERS** (*μυροφόροι, αἱ*): The holy women who brought aromatic spices, fragrant ointments, and perfumes to the tomb of Christ early on the first day of the week to anoint His sacred Body. Foremost among them were Saint Mary Magdalene, Mary the wife of Cleopas (mother of James), Salome the mother of the Sons of Zebedee, Joanna, and the sisters Martha and Mary of Bethany.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Another profound mystery is the nature and the function of the sacraments in their binding of man to God. For instance, man cannot understand how two humble, earthbound elements, bread and wine, are transubstantiated by the Holy Spirit into Christ's very body and blood. Pointing to the bread and the wine at the Last Supper, Christ said "this is my body...this is my blood," thus Himself instituting for posterity the Sacrament of Holy Communion. Today, by taking Holy Communion, the believer becomes one with God, partaking of His divine essence. The Orthodox Church celebrates seven Sacraments: Baptism, Chrismation, Communion (the Eucharist), Ordination (holy orders), Confession (Penance), Holy Unction, and Marriage. These sacraments sanctify and consecrate man in his faith and unite him with God, from birth to the end of his days on this earth.
units.english_cohort_translation: A third profound mystery is the divine action of the Holy Mysteries in uniting man unto God. In the Holy Eucharist, humble earthly gifts of bread and wine are transformed by the Holy Spirit into the true Body and the true Blood of Christ. Pronouncing over the bread and the chalice at the Mystical Supper: **"This is My Body... This is My Blood"**, Christ Himself instituted the Sacrament of Holy Communion for all generations. By receiving the Holy Mysteries, the Christian is united unto Christ, becoming a partaker of the Divine Nature through grace. The Church recognizes seven principal Holy Mysteries: Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist (Holy Communion), Holy Orders (Priesthood), Repentance (Confession), Holy Unction (Anointing of the Sick), and Holy Matrimony (Crowning). Through these Holy Mysteries, man is consecrated in faith and united unto God from birth until the conclusion of his earthly life.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: NAOS (ναός, ὁ): The church building or temple. The term has also been used to describe the largest section of the Greek Orthodox Church of today, the NAVE. See also EKKLISIA.
units.english_cohort_translation: **NAOS** (*ναός, ὁ*): The holy temple or church building. In architectural terminology, it specifically designates the central space of the temple, the **Nave**, reserved for the assembly of the faithful. See also **EKKLISIA**.

units.english_cohort_translation: **NARTHEX** (*νάρθηξ, ὁ*; Slav. *Pritvor* / *Притворъ*): The entrance vestibule of the church building. units.slavonic_incipit: the dead as they light candles
units.slavonic_diplomatic: the dead as they light candles and reverence icons. In early Christianity, the Narthex provided the Church many a service. On Sundays, it was filled with catechumens (candidates for baptism) and penitents who would follow the Liturgy; the poor and the lame also might be present asking for alms. Church history also recounts many priests and hierarchs who would stand in the Narthex and block the entrance of the impious who had strayed from the Orthodox way.
units.english_cohort_translation: the departed, light tapers, and reverence holy icons. In early Christian centuries, the Narthex fulfilled essential liturgical functions: on Sundays and feast days it was occupied by catechumens preparing for Holy Baptism and by penitents performing public penance, who followed the sacred services from this outer station. The poor and infirm gathered in the narthex to receive alms from the faithful. Ecclesiastical history records instances where holy hierarchs and pastors stood in the narthex to bar the entrance of heretics and unrepentant sinners from entering the church proper.

units.slavonic_incipit: During the years of Turkish occupation
units.slavonic_diplomatic: During the years of Turkish occupation in Greece and the years of Communist rule throughout Eastern Europe, the Narthex was often used for another purpose. Christian children would gather at nightfall to learn of the faith from the priest and, in some cases, to even learn to read and write. These secret schools, for years, took place in the sanctity of the Narthex. Today, as we offer material gifts for the work of the Church, light candles, and reverence icons, catechumens are no longer found in their traditional place. We may however find catechetical resources for those wish to learn more about their faith (i.e. books, tapes, icons, prayer ropes, prosforo seals, all in a kiosk). The poor and the lame who, following services, would, with out-stretched hand, ask for alms no longer are present. Instead, a container or tray is provided for the collection of donations that are then offered to an outreach ministry.
units.english_cohort_translation: During centuries of Ottoman subjection in Greece and under atheist Communist regimes throughout Eastern Europe, the Narthex served an additional sacred purpose: faithful children gathered there at night to receive secret instruction in the Christian faith and the native language from faithful clergy. In contemporary church life, while catechumens and public penitents no longer occupy separate stations in the narthex, it remains a space for prayerful preparation, purchasing candles, acquiring sacred books, prayer ropes, prosphora seals, and making charitable offerings for church benevolence.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: NAVE (ναός, ὁ): The architecture of the Orthodox Church of today is made up of three parts: the SANCTUARY, the NAVE and the NARTHEX (Vestibule). The Sanctuary of the Orthodox Church corresponds to the Holy of Holies of Solomon's Temple. The Holy of Holies was not used for daily worship and only the high priest could enter and then only once a year. The worship was held in the main part of the temple.
units.english_cohort_translation: **NAVE** (*ναός, ὁ*): The central hall of the church building situated between the Narthex (vestibule) and the Sanctuary. In Eastern Christian theology, the tripartite structure of the church building (Sanctuary, Nave, and Narthex) mirrors the tripartite structure of the ancient Tabernacle and Solomon's Temple (Holy of Holies, Holy Place, and Outer Court). While the Holy of Holies was entered exclusively by the High Priest once a year on the Day of Atonement, the Christian Sanctuary enshrines the Holy Table where the Eucharistic Sacrifice is continually offered, while the faithful assemble within the Nave to participate in the sacred mysteries.

units.slavonic_incipit: Sometimes spelled Omophorion Slav. Omofor, omoforij,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Sometimes spelled Omophorion Slav. Omofor, omoforij, nadramenia: A form of STOLE worn over the shoulders of a bishop. In the Orthodox tradition, the Omoforion is the distinguishing vestment of a bishop and the symbol of his spiritual and ecclesiastical authority. Originally of wool, today it is a band of brocade decorated with crosses and worn about the neck and shoulders. By symbolizing the lost sheep that is found and carried on the Good Shepherd's shoulders, it signifies the bishop's pastoral role as the icon of Christ.
units.english_cohort_translation: The distinguishing liturgical vestment of a bishop, worn over the shoulders, and the supreme emblem of his spiritual and pastoral authority. Originally fashioned from unbleached white sheep's wool, in modern usage it is tailored from rich liturgical brocade embroidered with crosses, worn encircling the neck and draped across the shoulders. Symbolizing the lost sheep that the Good Shepherd sought out and carried home upon His sacred shoulders, it signifies the bishop's pastoral vocation as a living icon of Christ.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Omoforion has two forms: the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Omoforion has two forms: the ancient great Omoforion, which passes around the neck, is folded in the front, and hangs down past the knees in both the front and the back; and the small Omoforion which is much simpler, passing around the neck and hanging down in the front similar to an EPITRACHILION (stole), only wider and shorter, coming down only a little past the waist. Because of the complexity of the great Omoforion, and because of the dignity of the episcopal office, whenever the bishop puts on this Omoforion or takes it off, he is assisted by two subdeacons.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Omophorion exists in two distinct forms: the ancient **Great Omophorion** (*μέγα ὠμοφόριον*), which passes around the neck, folds across the breast, and descends past the knees in both front and back; and the **Small Omophorion** (*μικρὸν ὠμοφόριον*), which is simpler in form, passing around the neck and descending in front similar to an **Epitrachilion** (stole), yet broader and shorter, reaching just past the waist. Owing to the intricate arrangement of the Great Omophorion and the liturgical dignity of the episcopal rank, whenever the bishop vests in this Omophorion or removes it, he is assisted by two subdeacons.[^651]

units.slavonic_incipit: Whenever he presides at any divine
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Whenever he presides at any divine service, the bishop will be vested in the Omoforion. If he is serving the Divine Liturgy he will wear both the great and the small Omoforion at different times over his liturgical vestments. At any service other than the Divine Liturgy he will usually wear the small Omoforion.

At any divine office other than the Divine Liturgy, he customarily wears the Small Omophorion.

units.slavonic_incipit: During the Divine Liturgy, the rubrics
units.slavonic_diplomatic: During the Divine Liturgy, the rubrics call for the bishop to put on and take off the Omoforion several times. When he is first vested, the subdeacons place the great Omoforion on him, but afterwards, when the rubric calls for him to wear the Omoforion, it is replaced, for the sake of convenience, with the small Omoforion. In some places, when several bishops celebrate together, it is now the custom for the chief celebrant to use the great Omoforion when called for, and the other bishops to wear the small Omoforion throughout.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the early church, the Omoforion
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the early church, the Omoforion was a broad band of white wool ornamented with crosses and draped loosely over the neck, shoulders, and breast. The modern Roman pallium developed from this early Omoforion; however, in the West it has changed over the centuries into a circular, thin woolen garment for the shoulders, with short, weighted pendants before and behind. Today, the papal pallium adopted by Pope Benedict XVI is closer to the original Omoforion.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the early Church, the Omophorion consisted of a broad band of white wool embroidered with crosses and draped loosely around the neck, over the shoulders, and across the breast. The modern Roman pallium developed from this primitive Omophorion; however, in the West it evolved over the centuries into a narrow circular woolen band resting upon the shoulders, with short, weighted pendants hanging before and behind. In contemporary times, the papal pallium adopted by Pope Benedict XVI returned closer to the original form of the ancient Omophorion.

units.slavonic_incipit: The only change in the Omoforion
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The only change in the Omoforion in the East has been the augmentation of its width, and the material from which it is made. We find distinct testimony to the existence of the Omoforion as a liturgical vestment of the bishop in Isidore of Pelusium about the year 400. It was made of wool and was already seen as symbolic of the duties of bishops as shepherds of their flocks. In the miniatures of an Alexandrian Chronicle of the World, written probably during the fifth century we already find pictorial representation of the Omoforion. In later times we meet the same representation on the renowned ivory tablet of Trier, depicting the solemn translation of relics. Among the pictures dating from the seventh and eighth centuries, in which we find the Omoforion, are the lately discovered frescoes in S. Maria, Antiqua in the Roman Forum. The representation in these frescoes is essentially the same as its present form.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the Christian East, the only structural alteration in the Omophorion has been an increase in its width and the adoption of embroidered silk and gold brocade in place of wool. Distinct historical testimony confirming the Omophorion as the liturgical vestment of the bishop is preserved in the epistles of Saint Isidore of Pelusium (c. 400). At that early date, it was already woven of wool and viewed as an explicit symbol of the pastoral duty of bishops shepherding their spiritual flocks. In the miniature illuminations of an Alexandrian World Chronicle, written probably during the fifth century, pictorial representations of the Omophorion already appear. In later centuries, the same depiction is found upon the celebrated ivory relief of Trier, depicting the solemn translation of holy relics. Among the sacred images dating from the seventh and eighth centuries in which the Omophorion appears are the frescoes uncovered in the church of Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum. The representation in these frescoes is essentially identical to its modern form.[^652]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Omoforion probably developed from the civil Omoforion, a shoulder garment or shawl in general use. Probably either the bishops introduced directly by a positive precept as a liturgical pontifical badge a humeral cloth resembling the ordinary Omoforion and called by that name, or the civil Omoforion was at first used by the bishops as a mere ornament without any special significance, but in the course of time gradually developed into a distinctively episcopal ornament, and finally assumed the character of an episcopal badge of office.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Omophorion probably evolved from the civil omophorion, a shoulder mantle or dignitary scarf in common civic use in late antiquity. Either the bishops introduced it directly by positive canonical enactment as a liturgical pontifical badge—a humeral cloth resembling the secular omophorion and bearing its name—or the civil omophorion was initially adopted by hierarchs as a simple dignitary ornament without special mystical signification, and in the course of time developed into an exclusively episcopal vestment, ultimately acquiring the canonical character of an episcopal badge of office.

units.english_cohort_translation: **OPISTHAMVONOS EFCHI** (*᾿Οπισθάμβωνος Εὐχή, ἡ*; Slav. *Zaamvonnaya Molitva* / *Заамвонная молитва*): The **Prayer behind the Ambo**; the solemn prayer recited by the priest near the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy. units.slavonic_diplomatic: "Lord, bless those who praise You and sanctify those who trust in You. Save Your people and bless Your inheritance. Protect the whole body of Your Church. Sanctify those who love the beauty of Your house. Glorify them in return by Your divine power, and do not forsake us who hope in You. Grant peace to Your world, to Your churches, to the clergy, to those in public service, to the armed forces, and to all Your people. For every good and perfect gift is from above, coming from You, the Father of lights. To You we give glory, thanksgiving, and worship, to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and forever and to the ages of ages. Amen."
units.english_cohort_translation: "Lord, bless those who praise Thee and sanctify those who trust in Thee. Save Thy people and bless Thine inheritance. Preserve the fullness of Thy Church; sanctify those who love the beauty of Thy house. Glorify them in return by Thy divine power, and forsake us not who place our hope in Thee. Grant peace unto Thy world, unto Thy churches, unto the priests, unto our civil authorities, unto the armed forces, and unto all Thy people. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from Thee, the Father of lights. And unto Thee we send up glory, thanksgiving, and worship, to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The sequence of hymns, prayers, and ritual actions in each service of the church as ordained by the Holy Synod of the Patriarchate of Constantinople and stipulated in the Typikon by George Violakis, published in 1888. Orders of service may be found also in the key service books of the church such as the Mineon, the Triodion, the Pentikostarion, the Paraklitiki, the Efchologion and the Ieratikon.
units.english_cohort_translation: The canonical sequence of hymns, prayers, and ceremonial actions prescribed for each divine office of the Church, as codified by the Holy Synod of the Patriarchate of Constantinople and set forth in the *Typikon* by George Violakis, published in 1888. Orders of service are likewise contained within the foundational liturgical books of the Church, including the **Menaion** (**Menaia**), the **Triodion**, the **Pentecostarion**, the **Paraklitiki**, the **Euchologion** (**Efchologion** / Slav. **Trebnik**), and the **Ieratikon** (Slav. **Sluzhebnik**). Since its publication, the Typikon has been modified through patriarchal decrees—a living and continuous pastoral practice of the Church.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: OROLOGION TO MEGA (῾Ωρολόγιον τὸ Μέγα) Slav. Chasoslov or Tchasoslov: The Great Book of Hours contains mainly the fixed texts for the services of the Daily Cycle, as well as the APOLYTIKIA and KONTAKIA of all the IMMOVABLE and MOVABLE FEASTS of the ecclesiastical year. It is one of the main service books of the Greek Orthodox Church. Alternate spelling: Horologion to Mega. As with the Efchologion to Mega there is also an abbreviated version.
units.english_cohort_translation: **OROLOGION TO MEGA** (*῾Ωρολόγιον τὸ Μέγα*; Slav. *Chasoslov* / *Часословъ* or *Velikiy Chasoslov* / *Великій Часословъ*): The **Great Book of Hours** (**Horologion**), containing the fixed texts for the offices of the Daily Cycle, as well as the **Dismissal Troparia** (lit. 'Apolytikia') and **Kontakia** for all immovable and moveable feasts of the ecclesiastical year. It is one of the principal liturgical books of the Eastern Church. Alternate spelling: **Horologion to Mega**. As with the *Euchologion to Mega*, an abbreviated edition is likewise published for reader and parish use.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: the word means the 'early Morning Prayer'. Orthros precedes the Divine Liturgy and is the longest and most complex service of the daily cycle of services. In monasteries, Orthros is normally celebrated in the early morning and is usually followed by the First HOUR. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as part of an All-Night Vigil beginning the evening before, and is combined with Vespers and First Hour. In Greek parishes on Sunday morning, Orthros is normally served just before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy. The service concludes with the Doxology and the DISMISSAL HYMN (APOLYTIKION) of the then occurring feast.
units.english_cohort_translation: the word signifies "early Morning Prayer" or "daybreak." Orthros precedes the Divine Liturgy and constitutes the longest and most complex office of the daily cycle of services. In monasteries, Orthros is celebrated in the early morning and is regularly followed immediately by the First Hour. On Great Feasts, it is celebrated as an integral part of an All-Night Vigil commencing on the preceding evening, conjoined with Great Vespers and the First Hour. In Eastern parish tradition on Sunday mornings, Orthros is standardly served immediately preceding the Divine Liturgy. The office concludes with the Great Doxology and the festal **Dismissal Troparion** (lit. 'Apolytikion') of the day.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: OSIOS, OSIA (Masc. Ὅσιος, ὁ; Fem. ὁσία, ἡ): A Righteous Saint. An epithet indicating that the named saint has led a saintly, monastic life, dying of natural causes. The epithet righteous martyr (ὁσιομάρτυς) usually refers to a martyred monk or nun.
units.english_cohort_translation: **OSIOS**, **OSIA** (Masc. *Ὅσιος, ὁ*; Fem. *ὁσία, ἡ*; Slav. *Prepodobnyy* / *Преподобный*, *Prepodobnaya* / *Преподобная*): A Venerable or Righteous Monastic Saint. A hagiographical title designating a holy saint who led an ascetical, monastic life, dying of natural causes. The conjoined title **Righteous Martyr** or **Venerable Martyr** (*ὁσιομάρτυς*; Slav. *prepodobnomuchenik*) refers to a martyred monk or nun.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *PARAKLITIKI or OKTOICHOS I MEGALI (Παρακλητική ἤ Ὀκτώηχος ἡ Μεγάλη) Slav. Oktoix, Paraklitik: Both titles, given in Greek, are names for the GREAT OKTOICHOS, one of the most important and commonly used liturgical books of the church. It contains the variable (substituted) sections of the services for all the immovable (fixed) dates of the year: 1) SMALL AND GREAT VESPERS, 2) the MESONYKTIKON (Midnight Service) for Sundays only, 3) the ORTHROS, and 4) the DIVINE LITURGY. For the chronological and modal structure as well as the liturgical use of the Paraklitiki, see the Cycle of Modes (under MODE).
units.english_cohort_translation: **PARAKLITIKI** or **OKTOICHOS I MEGALI** (*Παρακλητικὴ* ἢ *᾿Οκτώηχος ἡ Μεγάλη*; Slav. *Oktoikh* / *Октоихъ*, *Paraklitik* / *Параклитикъ*): Both Greek titles designate the **GREAT OKTOECHOS**, one of the most foundational and ubiquitous liturgical volumes of the Church. It contains the variable hymnographic parts of the services for all days of the year arranged across the Eight Tones (Modes): 1) Small and Great Vespers, 2) the **Mesonyktikon** (Midnight Office) for Sundays only, 3) **Orthros** (Matins), and 4) the Divine Liturgy. For the chronological and modal structure as well as the liturgical application of the Paraklitiki, see the *Cycle of Modes* (under **MODE** / **TONE**).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *PARAMONI (παραμονή, ἡ): The 'Eve' of an Orthodox feast begins the day before a major feast. The service of a feast's paramoni (eve) acts as a preamble to the feast itself, its hymns and prayers foretelling and anticipating the impending sacred event.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PARAMONI** (*παραμονή, ἡ*; Slav. *Navecherie* / *Навечеріе*, *Sochelnik* / *Сочельникъ*): The **Eve** or Vigil-Eve of a major feast, occurring on the day immediately preceding the feast. units.slavonic_diplomatic: PATEN (Δισκάριον, τό) Slav. Diskos: A small shallow dish with a permanent short stem or base which holds the bread prepared at the table of PROTHESIS in the rite of PROSKOMIDI or office of oblation. It stands for the cave in which Christ was born. In its circular shape it also symbolizes the heavens that hold God.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PATEN** (*Δισκάριον, τό*; Slav. *Diskos* / *Дискосъ*): The Diskos; a sacred shallow plate set upon a permanent base or foot, which holds the bread prepared at the Table of **Prothesis** during the rite of the **Proskomide** (Office of Oblation). It represents the cave of Bethlehem in which Christ was born and the tomb wherein He was laid. In its circular shape, it likewise symbolizes the heavens that encompass God.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *PLACING (κατάθεσις, ἡ): Specifically, the placing of a sacred object or relic into a shrine or place of worship: e.g., the Placing of the Robe of the Theotokos at the Church of Vlacherne in Constantinople, an event commemorated on 2 July.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PLACING** (*κατάθεσις, ἡ*; Slav. *Polozhenie* / *Положеніе*): Specifically, the liturgical feast commemorating the deposition or placing of a sacred relic or vestment into a shrine or place of worship; e.g., the Placing of the Precious Robe of the Theotokos at the Church of Blachernae in Constantinople, an event commemorated on July 2.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *PLIROTIKA (Πληρωτικά, τά): The series or litany of supplications and petitions following the Cherubic Hymn in the Divine Liturgy beginning with the word Plirosomen (Πληρώσωμεν...) "Let us complete...."
units.english_cohort_translation: **PLIROTIKA** (*Πληρωτικά, τά*; Slav. *Prositelnaya Ekteniya* / *Просительная ектенія*): The Litany of Supplication (Litany of Completion); the series of petitions chanted by the deacon following the Cherubic Hymn and the Great Entrance in the Divine Liturgy, commencing with the words **"Let us complete our prayer unto the Lord"** (*Πληρώσωμεν τὴν δέησιν ἡμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ*).

units.slavonic_incipit: The name Polyeleos is also given
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The name Polyeleos is also given to the great chandelier which hangs directly from the central dome of an Orthodox church. It symbolizes Christ, the 'all-merciful'. When this chandelier was furnished with oil lamps, it used 'many oil lamps' (Greek poly-eleos.) On the Holy Mountain of Athos, the monastic state in Greece, the Polyeleos is lighted and swung to spectacular effect in VESPERS at 'Lord, I have cried' and during the Polyeleos at great Vigils. It is also lighted at the Great Entrance on major Feasts, and also at funerals. Around the polyeleos there often hangs a great metal circle, decorated with icons, normally including the twelve Apostles, and surmounted by candles. This is known as a choros. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: The name Polyeleos is likewise given to the great chandelier suspended directly beneath the central dome of an Eastern church. It symbolizes Christ, the All-Merciful Light. When this chandelier was furnished with oil lamps, it was so designated because it employed "many oil lamps" (*poly-elaion* / *πολυέλαιον*). On the Holy Mountain of Athos, during solemn all-night vigils, the Polyeleos is illuminated and swung in a wide arc to spectacular effect at Vespers during the singing of **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*) and during the chanting of the Polyeleos at Matins. It is also illuminated at the Great Entrance on major feasts and at funeral services. Encircling the Polyeleos there often hangs a great brass or metal corona decorated with icons, normally depicting the Twelve Apostles, and surmounted by tapers. This circular chandelier is known as a **Choros** (*χορός*).

Around the polyeleos there often hangs a great metal circle, decorated with icons, normally including the twelve Apostles, and surmounted by candles. This is known as a choros. (AE)

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: The name Polyeleos is likewise given to the great chandelier suspended directly beneath the central dome of an Eastern church. It symbolizes Christ, the All-Merciful Light. When this chandelier was furnished with oil lamps, it was so designated because it employed "many oil lamps" (*poly-elaion* / *πολυέλαιον*). On the Holy Mountain of Athos, during solemn all-night vigils, the Polyeleos is illuminated and swung in a wide arc to spectacular effect at Vespers during the singing of **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*) and during the chanting of the Polyeleos at Matins. It is also illuminated at the Great Entrance on major feasts and at funeral services. Encircling the Polyeleos there often hangs a great brass or metal corona decorated with icons, normally depicting the Twelve Apostles, and surmounted by tapers. This circular chandelier is known as a **Choros** (*χορός*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PROFITOLOGION (Προφητολόγιον, τό) Slav. Paremijnik: Spelled by some as Prophetologion. This is a liturgical book that contains the Old Testament Lectionary readings assigned to Vespers and to other services during the Church year. Unfortunately, there has not been an edition of this book published in English. Old Testament readings are typically taken from the Mineon or other texts that contain these readings. There have also been texts containing the Lenten Lectionary which have been published in English. One classic text that contains the most commonly used portions of the entire Lectionary is the "Divine Prayers and Services of the Catholic Orthodox Church of Christ" by Fr. Seraphim Nassar. (From Orthodox Wiki)
units.english_cohort_translation: **PROFITOLOGION** (**PROPHETOLOGION** / *Προφητολόγιον, τό*; Slav. *Paremiynik* / *Паремійникъ*): The Old Testament Lectionary containing the scriptural readings (**Paroimiai** / *Παροιμίαι*, *Paremias*) assigned to Vespers, the Royal Hours, and other divine services throughout the ecclesiastical year. When a separate edition of this lectionary is unavailable, the appointed Old Testament readings are extracted from the **Menaia**, the **Triodion**, or the **Pentecostarion**. In English, classic collections containing these appointed lections include the *Divine Prayers and Services of the Catholic Orthodox Church of Christ* by Father Seraphim Nassar.

units.english_cohort_translation: **PROSFORA** (**PROSPHORA** / *Προσφορά, ἡ*; Slav. *Prosvira* / *Просвира*, *Proskura* / *Проскура*; lit. 'offering' or 'oblation'): A round loaf of leavened Eucharistic bread of pure wheat used in the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Upon its upper surface it bears a round relief seal, in the center of which is a square stamp inscribed with the sign of the Cross and the Greek letters **IC XC NIKA** (**ΙΣΧΣ ΝΙΚΑ**) at the four corners, representing *Jesus Christ Conquers* (**IC** being the abbreviation for Jesus, **XC** for Christ, and **NIKA** for Victor).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *PROTHEORIA (προθεωρία, ἡ): Lit. Pre-theory. In his Typikon, George Violakis devotes the introduction—which he calls the Protheoria—to defining the general principles that he uses to order the services of the church. In the main body of his Typikon, he applies these principles in a detailed fashion to the order of service of each specific feast day in the church calendar for both immovable and movable feasts.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PROTHEORIA** (*προθεωρία, ἡ*; lit. In the main body of his *Typikon*, he applies these principles systematically to the rubrical order of service for each specific feast day throughout the ecclesiastical year, encompassing both immovable and movable cycles.

units.slavonic_incipit: If one were to peer through
units.slavonic_diplomatic: If one were to peer through the central BEAUTIFUL GATE of the IKONOSTASION, one would likely see small alcoves, marble shelves or tables on either side of the back wall of the Sanctuary. This area on the left is known as the PROTHESIS while the area on the right is known as the DIAKONIKON. The unique purpose of each in the Sanctuary is realized by the various items that rest upon them and the various icons that are found on the wall immediately behind them.
units.english_cohort_translation: If one were to gaze through the central Holy Doors (the **Beautiful Gate** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη*) of the icon screen (**Iconostasis** / *Εἰκονοστάσιον*), one would observe small alcoves, marble shelves, or tables on either side of the eastern sanctuary wall. The alcove upon the left (north) is designated the **Prothesis**, while the corresponding area upon the right (south) is known as the **Diakonikon** (*Διακονικόν*). The distinct liturgical function of each within the Sanctuary is realized by the sacred vessels and implements that rest upon them and the sacred icons mounted upon the wall immediately behind them.

units.slavonic_incipit: Located in the SANCTUARY, the Prothesis
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Located in the SANCTUARY, the Prothesis is the place where the Eucharistic Gifts are prepared during the Morning MATINS Service (ORTHROS), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Additionally, the Prothesis is the place where the Eucharistic items i.e., the Holy Chalice, the Holy Paten, the communion cloths, the spoon used to distribute the Holy Gifts, etc., are stored. On the back wall of the Prothesis is traditionally found the icon of the Nativity.
units.english_cohort_translation: Situated in the Sanctuary, the Prothesis is the appointed place where the Eucharistic Gifts of bread and wine are prepared during the morning office of **Orthros** (Matins), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. In addition, the Prothesis serves as the repository where the sacred Eucharistic vessels and implements—namely, the Holy Chalice (*Ποτήριον*), the Holy Paten (*Δισκάριον*), the Asterisk (*᾿Αστερίσκος*), the liturgical spear (*Λόγχη*), the communion cloths, the communion spoon (*Λαβίς*), and the veils—are preserved. Upon the wall behind the Table of Prothesis is traditionally depicted the icon of the Nativity of Christ or the Extreme Humility (*Ἄκρα Ταπείνωσις*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PROTOPSALTIS (πρωτοψάλτης, ὁ): The First or Head Chanter of those who traditionally serve on the right or south side of the SOLEAS. Conversely, the chanter who serves on the left or north side of the soleas is known as the LAMBADARIOS.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PROTOPSALTIS** (*πρωτοψάλτης, ὁ*; Slav. *Pervopenets* / *Первопѣвецъ*): The First or Head Chanter who directs the right (southern) choir upon the **Soleas** (*Σολέα*). Conversely, the chanter who directs the left (northern) choir upon the soleas is designated the **Lambadarios** (*Λαμπαδάριος*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PROTOTHRONE or PROTOTHRONOS (πρωτόθρονος, ὁ): Lit. ‘First Throne’. In Eastern Orthodoxy the First Throne is considered to be the title of the throne occupied by the Archbishop and Patriarch of Constantinople and New Rome at the Ecumenical Patriarchate, formerly in the capitol of the Byzantine Empire and presently located at the Church of St. George in the Fener area of the Turkish city of Istanbul.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PROTOTHRONE** or **PROTOTHRONOS** (*πρωτόθρονος, ὁ*; lit. "First-Throne"): In Orthodox ecclesiology, the title of primacy accorded to the historic episcopal cathedra occupied by the Archbishop and Patriarch of Constantinople and New Rome at the Ecumenical Patriarchate, formerly in the imperial capital of the Byzantine Empire and currently located at the Patriarchal Church of Saint George in the Phanar (Fener) district of Istanbul.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PSALM (ψαλμός, ὁ): Lit. A Psalm. According to ancient practice, monastics would recite all 150 Psalms on a recurring basis. Originally, the hermits in the desert would recite the entire Psalter every day. With the spread of coenobitic (communal) monasticism, the practice began of chanting the Canonical Hours in common, and the Psalter thus became the foundation of the Daily Office, augmented by numerous hymns, prayers and scriptural readings. The custom of reciting all 150 Psalms each week during the course of the servies developed over time.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PSALM** (*ψαλμός, ὁ*; Slav. *Psalom* / *Псаломъ*; lit. "a psalm, song of praise"): According to ancient monastic discipline, monks recited all 150 Psalms of the Psalter on a continual, recurring cycle. In early Christian antiquity, desert hermits recited the entire Psalter daily. With the historical emergence and spread of cenobitic (communal) monasticism, the practice was instituted of chanting the Canonical Hours in common, and the Psalter thus became the foundational bedrock of the Daily Office, augmented by liturgical hymnography, prayers, and scriptural lessons. The universal monastic custom of chanting through all 150 Psalms every week during the course of the divine offices was established in due course.

Amen” («Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι· καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν,»)—at which time all stand in honor of the Holy Trinity.

    The Septuagint - Greek (LXX) is the version of the Old Testament used by the Orthodox Church. The LXX Psalter differs in several respects from the Masoretic Text (MT), which forms the basis for the King James Version and most modern English translations of the Bible.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PSALM 50 (Ψαλμὸς Ν΄, ὁ): This Psalm is frequently abbreviated as «ὁ Ν΄» in the Typikon. It begins with the line “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your great mercy, and according to the multitude of Your compassions blot out my transgression”; in Greek, «Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου, καὶ κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν σου ἐξάλειψον τὸ ἀνόμημά μου...» The complete text may be found in the Psalter (Ψαλτήριον).
units.english_cohort_translation: **PSALM 50** (*Ψαλμὸς Ν΄, ὁ*; Slav. *Psalom 50* / *Псаломъ 50*): This psalm is frequently abbreviated as *«ὁ Ν΄»* in the rubrics of the *Typikon*. It is the preeminent penitential psalm of King David, opening with the incipit: **"Have mercy on me, O God, according to Thy great mercy, and according to the multitude of Thy compassions blot out my transgression"** (*«Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου, καὶ κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν σου ἐξάλειψον τὸ ἀνόμημά μου...»*). units.slavonic_diplomatic: PSALM 119 (Ψαλμὸς ΡΙΘ΄): This psalm, which is the beginning Psalm in the 18th Kathisma (Δέκατον Ὄγδοον Κάθισμα, τό) of the Old Testament Psalter, has, in its beginning verse the Greek words Pros Kyrion (Πρὸς Κύριον). The Pros Kyrion (Τὰ Πρὸς Κύριον) is a common abbreviation used in the Violakis Typikon, and includes Psalms 119 through 133 inclusive.
units.english_cohort_translation: **PSALM 119** (*Ψαλμὸς ΡΙΘ΄*): This psalm, which begins the **Eighteenth Kathisma** (*Δέκατον Ὄγδοον Κάθισμα, τό*) of the Septuagint Psalter, opens with the Greek incipit *Pros Kyrion* (*Πρὸς Κύριον*, "Unto the Lord"). The title **Ta Pros Kyrion** (*Τὰ Πρὸς Κύριον*) is the standard rubric abbreviation in the Violakis *Typikon* designating the entire Eighteenth Kathisma, which encompasses Psalms 119 through 133 inclusive (the fifteen Songs of Ascents / Gradual Psalms).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: PULPIT (Ἄμβων, ὁ) Slav. Amvon, “an elevated place, a podium”. See also AMVON. The pulpit is a raised platform or elaborate podium in front of the icon screen (IKONOSTASION) at the left (north) side of the SOLEAS. Decorated with representations of the four Evangelists, it is the place from which the deacon or priest reads the Gospel or delivers his sermon. (From FL)
units.english_cohort_translation: **PULPIT** or **AMBO** (*Ἄμβων, ὁ*; Slav. *Amvon* / *Амвонъ*; lit. "an elevated place, podium"): See also **AMVON**. The pulpit is an elevated platform or elaborate architectural podium situated forward of the icon screen (**Iconostasis**) upon the north (left) side of the **Soleas** (*Σολέα*). Embellished with iconographic representations of the Four Evangelists, it is the designated station from which the deacon or priest proclaims the Holy Gospel or delivers the homily.

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: REFECTORY (Τράπεζα, ἡ): The dining room in a monastery. In Eastern Orthodox monasteries, the Refectory (Greek: Trapeza) is considered to be a sacred place and, in some cases, is even constructed as a full church with ALTAR and ICONOSTASIS. There is always at least one Icon with an oil lamp (lambada) kept burning in front of it. Some services are specifically intended to be performed in the Trapeza e.g., the Ceremony of Forgiveness celebrated at the beginning of Great Compline in some monasteries.

units.slavonic_incipit: In Eastern Orthodox monasteries, the Refectory
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In Eastern Orthodox monasteries, the Refectory (Greek: Trapeza) is considered to be a sacred place and, in some cases, is even constructed as a full church with ALTAR and ICONOSTASIS. There is always at least one Icon with an oil lamp (lambada) kept burning in front of it. units.english_cohort_translation: **REFECTORY** (*Τράπεζα, ἡ*; Slav. *Trapeza* / *Трапеза*): The communal dining hall of a monastery. In Byzantine and Eastern monasticism, the Refectory is revered as a sacred liturgical extension of the church; in many monastic establishments, it is architecturally fashioned with an altar and icon screen. An icon of Christ or the Mother of God, before which a vigil lamp (*lambada*) burns perpetually, is always present. Specific liturgical offices are appointed to be celebrated in the Trapeza, such as the Rite of Mutual Forgiveness at the opening of Great Compline in monastic communities.[^666]

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: REFECTORY (Τράπεζα, ἡ): The dining room in a monastery. In Eastern Orthodox monasteries, the Refectory (Greek: Trapeza) is considered to be a sacred place and, in some cases, is even constructed as a full church with ALTAR and ICONOSTASIS. There is always at least one Icon with an oil lamp (lambada) kept burning in front of it. Some services are specifically intended to be performed in the Trapeza e.g., the Ceremony of Forgiveness celebrated at the beginning of Great Compline in some monasteries.

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: **REFECTORY** (*Τράπεζα, ἡ*; Slav. *Trapeza* / *Трапеза*): The communal dining hall of a monastery. units.slavonic_diplomatic: RELICS (λείψανα, τά): The remains of the body of a Saint or even of a Saint’s possessions such as their clothes or vestments. These relics are honored and venerated by all Orthodox. When a consecration of a new church takes place, the consecrating bishop permanently places such relics in the Holy Altar Table following the ancient tradition in the church where the Eucharist was performed upon the tombs of Martyrs.
units.english_cohort_translation: **RELICS** (*λείψανα, τά*; Slav. *Moshchi* / *Мощи*): The physical bodily remains of a canonized Saint, or sacred personal possessions such as garments or vestments hallowed by a saint's life. Holy relics are venerated with religious devotion throughout the Church. When a new church is consecrated, the consecrating bishop permanently encloses and seals holy relics within the Holy Altar Table (**Holy Table** / *Ἁγία Τράπεζα*), perpetuating the primitive Christian tradition wherein the Holy Eucharist was celebrated upon the tombs of the holy Martyrs.

Lit. ‘I fan.’ In today's church, this action of fanning is described in the rite of consecration when the priest fans, or waves the AERA over the Gifts just before the prayer “So that they may be to those who partake of them for vigilance of soul, forgiveness of sins, communion of Your Holy Spirit, fulfillment of the kingdom of heaven, confidence before You, and not in judgment or condemnation...” («Ὥστε γενέσθαι τοῖς μεταλαμβάνουσιν εἰς νῆψιν ψυχῆς, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ Ἁγίου σου Πνεύματος, εἰς βασιλείας οὐρανῶν πλήρωμα, εἰς παῤῥησίαν τὴν πρὸς σέ, μὴ εἰς κρῖμα ἢ εἰς κατάκριμα...»). See also AERA or AIR. For an alternate descripition, see EXAPTERYGA.

In liturgical practice, this motion of fanning is witnessed in the Eucharistic Anaphora when the priest fans or gently waves the **Aer** (*ἀήρ*) over the Holy Gifts prior to the consecratory epiclesis, reciting the prayer: *"So that they may be to those who partake of them for vigilance of soul, forgiveness of sins, communion of Thy Holy Spirit, fulfillment of the kingdom of heaven, confidence before Thee, and not in judgment or condemnation..."* (*«Ὥστε γενέσθαι τοῖς μεταλαμβάνουσιν εἰς νῆψιν ψυχῆς, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ Ἁγίου σου Πνεύματος, εἰς βασιλείας οὐρανῶν πλήρωμα, εἰς παῤῥησίαν τὴν πρὸς σέ, μὴ εἰς κρῖμα ἢ εἰς κατάκριμα...»*). See also **AER** and **EXAPTERYGA**.

units.english_cohort_translation: **ROYAL DOOR** (*Βασιλικὴ Θύρα, ἡ*; Slav. *Tsarskie Vrata* / *Царскія врата*): While occasionally confused with the central Holy Doors of the icon screen (**Beautiful Gate** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη*), this term properly denotes the central portal leading from the narthex into the western end of the nave, through which Byzantine emperors solemnly entered the cathedral of Hagia Sophia.

units.english_cohort_translation: **SACRISTAN** (*ἱεροφύλαξ, ὁ*; Slav. *Riznichiy* / *Ризничій*): The church officer in charge of the sacristy (**Skevophylakion**) where sacred vessels, vestments, and liturgical treasures are preserved. units.english_cohort_translation: **SAKKOS** (*σάκκος, ὁ*; pl. *σάκκοι, οἱ*; Slav. *Sakkos* / *Саккосъ*; from Hebrew *saq*, sackcloth): The episcopal vestment (corresponding in form to the Western dalmatic) originally signifying a garment of humble sackcloth or tunic of mockery worn by Christ during His Passion. In modern liturgical usage, the Sakkos is a magnificent tunic tailored from rich brocade, modeled upon the imperial tunic bestowed by Byzantine emperors upon the Ecumenical Patriarch. Formerly reserved as an exclusive Patriarchal vestment, it is now worn by all bishops as the primary hierarchical vestment replacing the priestly **Phelonion** (**Felonion** / *φαιλόνιον*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: the rising sun which is considered to be a symbol or icon of the spiritual Son of God, Who will likewise rise from the East and illumine the world. However, because of local architectural circumstances, some churches may not be situated with the sanctuary exactly facing the east. In the center of the Sanctuary stands the ALTAR TABLE, at which the sacrament of the HOLY EUCHARIST takes place. The table of the PROTHESIS is situated on the north side of the Sanctuary while the area of the DIAKONIKON is situated on the south side.
units.english_cohort_translation: the rising sun, which is revered as a cosmic icon of the spiritual Sun of Righteousness, Jesus Christ the Son of God, Who will dawn from the East and illumine the cosmos. In the center of the Sanctuary stands the **Holy Table** (**Altar Table** / *῾Αγία Τράπεζα*), upon which the Eucharistic Sacrifice of the Divine Liturgy is celebrated. The table of the **Prothesis** is situated upon the northern side of the Sanctuary, while the **Diakonikon** is situated upon the southern side.

units.slavonic_incipit: The sanctuary of the Orthodox Church
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The sanctuary of the Orthodox Church is a holy place, a place where man, by the Grace of God, joins the angels in offering thanksgiving and all glory to our Heavenly Father. Even with its divine character, it remains a very functional place in the church. In other words, the Sanctuary like the NARTHEX and the NAVE is structured in such a manner to best facilitate the needs of those who utilize this sacred space, in this case, the clergy who officiate at Divine Services.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Sanctuary of the Church is the Holy of Holies, the earthly reflection of the heavenly court wherein the sacred ministers, by the grace of God, unite with the angelic hosts in offering thanksgiving, adoration, and ceaseless praise unto our Heavenly Father. While possessing an exalted mystical dignity, it serves as the functional presbytery designed to facilitate the ceremonial actions of the clergy who officiate at the divine offices.

Even with its divine character, it remains a very functional place in the church. In other words, the Sanctuary like the NARTHEX and the NAVE is structured in such a manner to best facilitate the needs of those who utilize this sacred space, in this case, the clergy who officiate at Divine Services.

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: The Sanctuary of the Church is the Holy of Holies, the earthly reflection of the heavenly court wherein the sacred ministers, by the grace of God, unite with the angelic hosts in offering thanksgiving, adoration, and ceaseless praise unto our Heavenly Father. While possessing an exalted mystical dignity, it serves as the functional presbytery designed to facilitate the ceremonial actions of the clergy who officiate at the divine offices.

units.slavonic_incipit: No one should enter the sanctuary
units.slavonic_diplomatic: No one should enter the sanctuary unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for a specific task. Clergy alone are intended to enter into the altar, and then only after they have spiritually prepared to serve among the angels and glorify God as they are ever present in the Sanctuary or Holy of Holies. As clergy, as laity, as catechumens, and as penitents, we find our respective places within the structure of the Church. As we each participate in the services from our specific place we are distinguished according to our roles within the priesthood of all believers. It is in these places that we both realize our stewardship to Christ, and “glorify God in every place of His dominion.” (Modified from the Church of the Holy Cross, Belmont, CA: http://www.goholycross.org.
units.english_cohort_translation: No person may enter the sacred precincts of the Sanctuary unworthily or without the explicit blessing of the presiding priest. Clergy alone are appointed to minister within the altar, entering only after devout spiritual preparation to serve among the angels in the presence of God. Within the ecclesial body, clergy, laity, catechumens, and penitents occupy their designated stations, participating in the divine praises according to their ordained charisms within the royal priesthood of all believers. In these sacred spaces we fulfill our stewardship unto Christ, and "glorify God in every place of His dominion" (Ps. 102:22 LXX).

units.slavonic_incipit: SCALE: Generally, in music, a scale
units.slavonic_diplomatic: SCALE: Generally, in music, a scale is a sequence of musical tones in ascending or descending order. Scales are ordered by the pitch of the tone which is the position of a tone in the scale with the sound being determined precisely by the frequency of vibration of the source of the tone. Such ordering of tones provides a measure of musical distance. The distance between two successive notes in a scale is called an interval or scale step.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SCALE** (*κλῖμαξ, ἡ*; *μουσικὴ κλῖμαξ, ἡ*): In music theory and acoustics, a scale is a structured sequence of musical tones arranged in ascending or descending pitch order. Scales are determined by the fundamental frequencies of their constituent pitches, providing a calibrated measure of musical intervals. The interval between two successive pitches is designated a scale step.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the science of acoustics, tones
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the science of acoustics, tones are measured by the frequency of their vibration numbers. Such frequencies are measured in cycles per second (CPS) or, in German, Hertz.
units.english_cohort_translation: In acoustics, musical pitches are measured by vibrational frequency, expressed in cycles per second (cps) or Hertz (Hz). In liturgical chant, musical tone is distinguished from noise by regular, periodic acoustic vibrations producing a distinct pitch, accompanied by dynamic amplitude (volume) and timbral timbre (vocal or instrumental color).

units.slavonic_incipit: In music, a tone is distinguished
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In music, a tone is distinguished from noise by having a definite frequency or pitch, caused by the regularity of the vibrations which produce it. Further, in addition to frequency, any tone will also possess the physical attributes of intensity (loudness), and quality (timbre or color); the latter helps identify the source of the tone (such as the voice or an instrument.)
units.english_cohort_translation: Diverse modal scales have developed across sacred musical cultures. In the sixth century B.C., Pythagoras formulated the mathematical ratios of the fundamental intervals: the octave (2:1), fourth (4:3), and fifth (3:2). In Christian antiquity, the ancient Greek tonal system was adapted into the eight ecclesiastical modes—the Byzantine **Oktoechos** (*᾿Οκτώηχος*, Tones 1 through 8) and Western church modes.

In Christian antiquity, the ancient Greek tonal system was adapted into the eight ecclesiastical modes—the Byzantine **Oktoechos** (*᾿Οκτώηχος*, Tones 1 through 8) and Western church modes.

units.slavonic_incipit: A great variety of scales have
units.slavonic_diplomatic: A great variety of scales have been used in the past and in different cultures; no single interval relationship is common to all of them. In the 6th cent. B.C., Pythagoras defined the mathematical relationship of the perfect intervals (the octave, fourth, and fifth) and of the intervals between them (an interval being the difference in pitch between two successive tones). Later, the Ancient Greek modal system was adapted and modified in the Middle Ages by the Eastern and Western Christian Churches.
units.english_cohort_translation: In Western ecclesiastical practice, the modal framework was gradually transformed by polyphony into the diatonic major and minor scales. The diatonic major scale comprises five whole tones (t) and two semitones (s) in the pattern: t–t–s–t–t–t–s (exemplified by the white keys of the keyboard from C to C′), which served as the foundation of classical Western musical architecture.[^670]

units.slavonic_incipit: cal tonality; tonality, in music, is
units.slavonic_diplomatic: cal tonality; tonality, in music, is the quality by which all tones of a composition are heard in relation to a central tone called the keynote or tonic. The diatonic minor scale is based on t-s-t-t-s-t-t. This arrangement produces the lower third, sixth, and seventh degrees that are characteristic of the minor mode; the higher seventh degree, a semitone rather than a whole tone below the main note, or “tonic,” is often borrowed from the major mode for use at cadences. Until the end of the 19th century, the use and influence of the diatonic scale in Western music was therefore predominant.
units.english_cohort_translation: cal tonality; tonality, in music, is the quality by which all tones of a composition are heard in relation to a central tone designated the keynote or tonic. The diatonic minor scale is based upon the interval sequence: tone–semitone–tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone (t–s–t–t–s–t–t). This arrangement produces the lower third, sixth, and seventh degrees characteristic of the minor mode; the higher seventh degree, situated a semitone rather than a whole tone below the primary note or "tonic," is frequently borrowed from the major mode for use at cadential resolutions. Until the close of the nineteenth century, the use and influence of the diatonic scale in Western music remained predominant.

units.slavonic_incipit: Related to musical scales is the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Related to musical scales is the concept of key. In music, the term “key” is used to indicate the scale from which the tonal material of a given composition is derived. To say, for example, that a composition is in the key of C major means that it uses as its basic tonal material the intervals of that scale.
units.english_cohort_translation: Related to musical scales is the fundamental concept of key. In musical theory, the term "key" is employed to designate the scale from which the tonal material of a given composition is derived. To state, for example, that a composition is set in the key of C major signifies that it utilizes as its primary tonal material the intervals proper to that scale.

units.slavonic_incipit: The idea of a key developed,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The idea of a key developed, whereby a home tone, or tonic, is the principal focus of a composition, and the various other tones assume importance according to their relationship to the tonic. The increasing complexity of instruments demanded more refined tuning system methods for assigning pitches to the twelve Western pitch names that constitute the octave. The term usually refers to this procedure in the tuning of keyboard instruments.
units.english_cohort_translation: The conception of key developed wherein a home tone, or tonic, serves as the principal focus of a musical composition, while the remaining tones assume structural importance according to their harmonic relationship to the tonic. The increasing complexity of musical instruments necessitated more refined tuning systems for assigning specific pitches to the twelve Western pitch classes that constitute the octave. In standard usage, this procedure designates the method employed in the tuning of keyboard instruments.

units.slavonic_incipit: By J. S. Bach's time, equal
units.slavonic_diplomatic: By J. S. Bach's time, equal temperament in music, the altering of certain intervals from their acoustically correct values to provide a system of tuning whereby music can move from key to key without unacceptably impure sonorities, had become established. The resulting scale, called chromatic, consisted of 12 notes divided by semitone intervals (the white and black notes of the keyboard). Although the diatonic scale is basically heptatonic (seven-noted), music, that is, in a usually major or minor tonality employs the remaining five tones of the chromatic scale as auxiliary or ornamental tones. Music that employs them freely is said to be highly chromatic, while music that employs them sparingly is said to be diatonic.
units.english_cohort_translation: By the era of J. S. Bach, equal temperament—the calibrated adjustment of specific intervals from their mathematically pure acoustical ratios in order to establish a tuning system wherein music may modulate freely from key to key without unacceptable dissonance—had become firmly established. The resulting chromatic scale comprises twelve semitone intervals within the octave (represented by the white and black keys of the keyboard). Although the diatonic scale is fundamentally heptatonic (seven-toned), compositions set in standard major or minor tonality employ the remaining five tones of the chromatic scale as auxiliary or ornamental pitches. Music that employs them freely is characterized as highly chromatic, whereas music that employs them sparingly is designated diatonic.

units.slavonic_incipit: concomitant minor scales remained the basic
units.slavonic_diplomatic: concomitant minor scales remained the basic organizing structure of Western music until the system was challenged by the dodecaphonic (twelve-tone scale) composers, in particular Arnold Schoenberg 1874–1951, an Austrian composer born in Vienna. He revolutionized modern music by abandoning all tonality and developing a twelve-tone, “serial” technique of composition. Schoenberg worked into the mid-20th cent. In his compositions, he esablished the principle of atonality, which is the systematic avoidance of harmonic or melodic reference to tonal centers. The term is used to designate a method of composition in which the composer has deliberately rejected the principle of tonality.
units.english_cohort_translation: concomitant minor scales, remained the primary organizing framework of Western music until the tonal system was challenged by dodecaphonic (twelve-tone) composers, notably Arnold Schoenberg (1874–1951), an Austrian composer born in Vienna. He revolutionized modern music by abandoning traditional functional tonality and formulating a twelve-tone "serial" technique of composition. Schoenberg composed actively into the mid-twentieth century. In his compositions, he established the principle of atonality, defined as the systematic avoidance of harmonic or melodic reference to tonal centers. The term designates a compositional method in which the composer deliberately rejects functional tonality.

units.slavonic_incipit: The whole-tone scale, which divides the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The whole-tone scale, which divides the octave into six equal whole tones (C, D, E, F sharp, G sharp, and A sharp, on the piano), gives a feeling of vagueness that made it adaptable to impressionism; its possibilities were thoroughly explored in the works of Debussy. The pentatonic scale (the black keys of the piano illustrate one form) has long been thought of as having an Asian character because of the prevalence of pentatonic scales in Chinese, Japanese, and Javanese music. The most complex scales known belong to Arabian music, used in the classical musical tradition of the Islamic peoples of Arabia, the Fertile Crescent, and North Africa.
units.english_cohort_translation: The whole-tone scale, which divides the octave into six equal whole tones (represented by C, D, E, F-sharp, G-sharp, and A-sharp on the keyboard), imparts an ambient quality that rendered it adaptable to Impressionism; its harmonic possibilities were explored extensively in the works of Claude Debussy. The pentatonic scale (exemplified by the five black keys of the keyboard) has traditionally been associated with Eastern musical cultures owing to its prevalence in Chinese, Japanese, and Javanese traditions. The most intricate scales known belong to Arabian music, cultivated in the classical musical traditions of the Islamic peoples of Arabia, the Fertile Crescent, and North Africa.

units.slavonic_incipit: The musical scales of Byzantine sacred
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The musical scales of Byzantine sacred music (Byzantine Chant) are modal in character. They belong to eight modes: I, II, III, IV, I Plagal, II Plagal, III Plagal (Varys), and IV Plagal.
units.english_cohort_translation: The musical scales of Byzantine sacred hymnography (Byzantine Chant) are fundamentally modal in character. They comprise eight ecclesiastical modes: Tone 1, Tone 2, Tone 3, Tone 4, Tone 5 (Tone 1 Plagal), Tone 6 (Tone 2 Plagal), Tone 7 (Grave Mode / Tone 3 Plagal / *Varys*), and Tone 8 (Tone 4 Plagal).

units.english_cohort_translation: Although derived historically from the Ancient Greek modal system, both Byzantine and Western church modes in the Middle Ages diverged from their classical predecessors in nomenclature as well as in intervallic structure. Having exerted a formative influence upon Western plainchant (Gregorian Chant), Byzantine modal scales were structurally analogous to those of the medieval West and, like them, essentially diatonic. Under the influence of prolonged exposure to Near Eastern musical traditions during the four centuries of Ottoman rule following the fall of the Byzantine[^672]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: tine empire (1453-1821), the scales of Byzantine sacred music became increasingly chromatic. Thus, whereas the 14th-century scale of Mode II Plagal was diatonic—E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E′—by the end of the 18th century, this scale became fully chromatic—E, F, G#, A, B, C, D (#), E′—with a different melodic range (ἔκτασις) and dominant tones (δεσπόζοντες φθόγγοι). See MODE. Because of these pervasive changes, the period from the 16th century to the present day has been more accurately called Post-Byzantine.
units.english_cohort_translation: Empire (1453–1821), the scales of Byzantine ecclesiastical chant became increasingly chromatic. Thus, whereas the fourteenth-century scale of Tone 6 (Tone 2 Plagal) was purely diatonic—E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E′—by the close of the eighteenth century this mode had become fully chromatic—E, F, G-sharp, A, B, C, D (D-sharp), E′—with an altered melodic range (*ekstasis* / *ἔκτασις*) and distinctive dominant reciting tones (*despozontes phthongoi* / *δεσπόζοντες φθόγγοι*). See **MODE**. By reason of these structural developments, the era extending from the sixteenth century to the present is designated the *Post-Byzantine* period.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (1) The Diatonic Genus, in its middle octave, begins on C and ends on C′, with the pitches E and B slightly flatter—microtonally—than the E and B of the Western tempered scale. To this genus belong the scales of the following modes: First, First Plagal, Fourth Plagal (with an occasional minor seventh—C, D, E, F, G, A, B (B-flat), C′, and Fourth (the papadic Fourth Mode has a minor seventh and occasionally a minor third—G, A, B (B-flat), C, C, E, F-natural, G′.
units.english_cohort_translation: (1) The **Diatonic Genus** (*Διατονικὸν γένος*), in its central octave, spans from C to C′, with the pitches E and B pitched microtonally flatter than the corresponding E and B of the Western tempered scale. To this genus belong the scales of Tone 1, Tone 5 (Tone 1 Plagal), Tone 8 (Tone 4 Plagal, with an occasional minor seventh: C, D, E, F, G, A, B-flat, C′), and Tone 4 (the papadic melodies of Tone 4 employ a minor seventh and occasionally a minor third: G, A, B-flat, C, D, E, F-natural, G′).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (3) The Hard Chromatic Genus is well represented by the scale of two disjunct (unconnected to each other), identical tetrachords: d, e, f, g and a, b, c, d. Their second pitches (E and B) are flatter than the e-flat and b-flat of Western music, while their third pitches f and c are sharper than the F-sharp and C-sharp in Western music. To the Hard Chromatic Genus belong the scales of the papadic and sticheraric Second Plagal Mode and the heirmologic Second Mode.

To the Hard Chromatic Genus belong the scales of papadic and sticheraric Tone 6 (Tone 2 Plagal) and the heirmologic melodies of Tone 2.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: (4) The Soft Chromatic Genus is well represented by a scale of two disjunct (unconnected to each other), identical tetrachords: the first being C, D, E, F, and the second being G, A, B, C. Their second pitches (D and A) are intervalically larger than the D-flat and A-flat yet smaller than the D-natural and A-natural of Western music by a third of a tone (i.e. a microtone). They are therefore notated as D-crossed flat (𝄫) and A-crossed flat (𝄫).
units.english_cohort_translation: (4) The **Soft Chromatic Genus** (*Μαλακὸν Χρωματικὸν γένος*) is characterized by a scale of two disjunct, identical tetrachords: the first comprising C–D–E–F and the second G–A–B–C. Their second degrees (D and A) are intervalically broader than D-flat and A-flat, yet narrower than D-natural and A-natural by approximately one-third of a tone (a microtone). In Byzantine musical notation, they are designated by crossed-flat accidentals (D-crossed flat and A-crossed flat).

units.slavonic_incipit: Unless he can read Post-Byzantine neumes—a
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Unless he can read Post-Byzantine neumes—a rather infrequent skill—the present-day church musician learns his chant transcribed into Western stave notation with the aid of a tempered keyboard instrument (e.g. piano or organ). Consequently, scales conceived initially as microtonal are now rendered in tempered approximations. In Post-Byzantine Chant, most of the time, the intervalic distance between the initial microtonal scale and its tempered rendition is not perceptible enough to alter the ethos or character of the initial microtonal melody and its scale.
units.english_cohort_translation: Unless proficient in reading Post-Byzantine neumatic notation, contemporary church musicians typically learn ecclesiastical chant transcribed into Western staff notation with the assistance of a keyboard instrument. Consequently, scales conceived originally as microtonal are executed in tempered approximations. In liturgical practice, the intervalic variance between the authentic microtonal scale and its tempered rendering does not substantially alter the sacred *ethos* or spiritual character of the chant.
