units.slavonic_incipit: Byzantine Chant to transcribe into a
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Byzantine Chant to transcribe into a Western tempered scale, demands a more calculated adjustment. The D-crossed flat and the A-crossed flat, though lower, are intervalically closer to the D-natural and the A-natural of the Western tempered scale. At the same time, the D-crossed flat and the A-crossed flat, though higher, are intervalically more distant than the D-flat and A-flat of the Western tempered scale. It is, therefore, more accurate to sing these pitches as D-natural and A-natural. The choice is often decided by the movement of the melody: If the D-crossed flat and the A-crossed flat are followed by a descending note, they are sung as a D-flat and A-flat. If followed by an ascending note, these pitches are sung as D-natural and A-natural.
units.english_cohort_translation: Byzantine chant to transcribe into Western tempered notation, requires deliberate adjustment. The D-crossed flat and A-crossed flat, although lowered, are intervalically nearer to D-natural and A-natural in the tempered scale, while remaining more distant from D-flat and A-flat. Accordingly, it is more faithful to sing these pitches as D-natural and A-natural in tempered execution. The practical performance is determined by melodic contour: if the altered pitch is followed by a descending figure, it is sung as D-flat or A-flat; if followed by an ascending figure, it is sung as D-natural or A-natural.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: SEXTON (νεωκόρος, ὁ) Slav. Pricetnik: An employee or officer of the church, who is in charge of the care of the church building and various sacred objects such as the relics, vessels, vestments, etc., belonging to the church. The Sexton may assist the officiating clergyman, and perform other duties pertaining to the church, such as ringing the bells, lighting or extinguishing candles etc.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SEXTON** (*νεωκόρος, ὁ*; Slav. *Prichetnik* / *причетникъ*, *Ponomar* / *пономарь*): An officer or caretaker charged with the physical maintenance of the church edifice, sacred vessels, holy relics, and liturgical vestments. The sexton assists the officiating clergy and performs auxiliary duties, including the sounding of bells, the lighting and extinguishing of candles, and the preparation of the censer.[^675]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: SKEVOPHYLAKION (Σκευοφυλάκιον, τό): The Treasury. Today, this area is known as the DIAKONIKON, or SACRISTY. It is an area or utility room on the south side of the sanctuary where liturgical vestments, sacred vessels, holy relics, and crosses are kept and where the clergy may vest for services (a vestry). In the early church, the Skevophylakion was a separate structure near the eastern end of the main church building.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SKEVOPHYLAKION** (*Σκευοφυλάκιον, τό*; Slav. *Sosudokhranilishche* / *Сосудохранилище*; lit. "vessel-treasury"): The sacred treasury and sacristy. In contemporary ecclesiastical architecture, this area functions as the **Diakonikon** (*Διακονικόν*) or vestry, situated on the southern side of the Sanctuary, where liturgical vestments, sacred vessels, holy relics, and crosses are preserved and where the clergy vest prior to divine services. In early Christian antiquity, the Skevophylakion was erected as a distinct, freestanding structure near the eastern facade of the church basilica. From this repository, the Book of the Gospels and the Eucharistic Offerings were solemnly carried into the church in procession, a liturgical movement commemorated in the Small and Great Entrances of the Divine Liturgy.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Patriarchal Treasury of today contains
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Patriarchal Treasury of today contains a reduced number of embroidered vestments, primarily of the last three centuries, used by Patriarchs, Synodical clergymen, priests and deacons. Nothing has survived from the Byzantine age. The devastating fires and other calamities, as well as the offering of generous gifts to Orthodox rulers and church dignitaries, particularly of Russia, both before and after the Ottoman Conquest, have depleted the Patriarchal Treasury. units.english_cohort_translation: The liturgical embroidery ateliers of Constantinople, and subsequently of Trebizond and Smyrna, attained renown for their exquisite gold and silver metallic needlework executed upon precious brocades and silks from Bursa (Brusa). These workshops produced gold-embroidered hierarchical and ministerial vestments of extraordinary artistic merit. Among the celebrated embroideresses whose signatures survive upon extant works are Despoineta, Mariora, Euphrosyne Agatha, Sophia, Theodosia, and Daphnitsa. Following the eighteenth century, comparable embroidery ateliers were established in Russia and Vienna.

units.english_cohort_translation: *Patriarchal Sakkoi*: The **Sakkos** (*σάκκος, ὁ*), a tunic featuring wide half-sleeves, originated as an imperial garment bestowed exceptionally by Byzantine emperors upon the Ecumenical Patriarch and selected autocephalous hierarchs. Following the Fall of Constantinople, the *sakkos* was adopted universally by all bishops, replacing the ancient *polystavrion phelonion* (*πολυσταύριον φαιλόνιον*, a Phelonion adorned with multiple crosses).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The embroidery ateliers of Constantinople and later of Trebizond and Smyrna, are famous for their fine gold and silver wire needlework on precious woven fabrics and silks from Brusa and their production of gold-embroidered hierarchical and liturgical vestments that are true works of art. Some of these outstanding works have survived and so have the names of the best known embroideresses: Despoineta, Mariora, Euphrosyne Agatha, Sorhia, Theodosia and Daphnitsa. After the 18th century, in addition to the celebrated ateliers for the production of hieratic vestments in Constantinople and Asia Minor, similar ateliers were also active in Russia and Vienna.
units.english_cohort_translation: Within the Patriarchal Treasury are preserved renowned historical *sakkoi*, designated respectively as the *Sakkos of Tiberias*, the *Sakkos of the Tree of Jesse*, the *Sakkos of the Enamels*, the two *Sakkoi of the Eagle*, and the *Sakkos of the Evangelist Matthew*, which are utilized by the Ecumenical Patriarch on solemn feasts.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *Patriarchal sakkoi*: The SAKKOS (short tunic with wide half-sleeves) of the prelates was originally an imperial garment. It was only in exceptional cases that Emperors allowed Patriarchs and hierarchs to wear it. After the Conquest it became the practice for all prelates to wear the sakkos, which replaced the polystavrion phelonion (chasuble ornamented with crosses). In the Patriarchal Treasury are kept the famous sakkoi known as “of Tiberias”, “of the Tree of Jesse”, “of the enamels”, “of the eagle” (two sakkoi), “of the Evangelist Matthew” etc., which are now used by the present Ecumenical Patriarch Demetrios. The “sakkos of Tiberias”: This precious sakkos is embroidered with two scenes from the Appearance of Christ, after His Resurrection, to the Disciples fishing in the Sea of Tiberias. The event is described in the Gospel according to St. John (21:1-14) and in the 10th Eastern hymn which begins with the words “Sea of Tiberias...” The scene on the back of the sakkos, embroidered with gold and silver threads against the whitish background of the pure silk material, shows Christ on

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Under the scene an inscription informs us: “Repaired in the patriarchy of Dionysius of Adrianople. 1888.” The “sakkos of Tiberias”, distinguished for the originality of its subject, is considered a master piece of Constantinopolitan embroidery. The sakkos belonged to Dionysios Calliades Metropolitan of Ephesus, who died in 1821.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The “sakkos of the Tree of Jesse”: The embroidery on the sumptuous crimson-coloured fabric shows “the Tree of Jesse” on the back and “the Glorious Second Coming of Christ” on the front. Gold threads are used for the tree of the first representation and the background of the second, whereas the dresses of the figures are highlighted in vivid colours. Gold-embroidered lilies adorn the borders of the vestment. The first scene conforms to the Byzantine iconographic tradition. The root of the tree is Jesse, the founder of the House of David, Christ's ancestor.
units.english_cohort_translation: The *Sakkos of the Tree of Jesse*: Embroidered upon rich crimson silk, this vestment portrays the *Tree of Jesse* upon the back and the *Glorious Second Coming of Christ* upon the front. The genealogical tree and the heavenly background are worked in gold thread, while the figures are highlighted in colorful silks, bordered by gold-embroidered lilies. The genealogical scene follows traditional Byzantine iconography, depicting the righteous Jesse as the ancestral root of the House of David and of Christ.

units.slavonic_incipit: John the Baptist, is portrayed raising
units.slavonic_diplomatic: John the Baptist, is portrayed raising the right hand in benediction. A great number of saints can be seen below, between clouds. This explains why some earlier researchers had called this vestment “sakkos of the All-Saints”.
units.english_cohort_translation: John the Baptist, is portrayed raising His right hand in benediction. Beneath the clouds appears the assembly of the righteous, which led earlier scholars to designate this vestment the *Sakkos of All Saints*. In addition to the primary scenes, the vestment is adorned with six medallions depicting the Passion of Christ: the Raising of Lazarus, the Entry into Jerusalem, the Mystical Supper, Ecce Homo, the Crucifixion, and the Lamentation at the Tomb. These secondary scenes reflect Western stylistic influence. The vestment was presented by Patriarch Kallinikos of Alexandria (1858–1861).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: This sakkos (dalmatic) is sewn in the traditional Byzantine manner, with wide sleeves formed from two straight pieces of cloth stitched to the body of the robe at the shoulders and fastened with round buttons down the sides (Johnstone 1967, figs. 1, 7, 11). The material is a luxurious double damask woven in gold and silver thread in a pattern of medallions framing busts of Christ as the Great High Priest, alternating on the horizontal rows with seraphs in smaller circlets. The intermediary spaces are ornamented with crosses fleury. Christ is depicted wearing a sakkos decorated with crosses in medallions and an OMOPHORION with large crosses, over a long-sleeved inner garment. He has a cruciate halo around which is woven (in reverse) the inscription: ‘Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest’. The monograms around the cross, ‘Jesus Christ Conquers’, are also woven back to front. units.slavonic_diplomatic: date 1614: this is a terminus ante quem, being the date when it was sewn to other pieces of cloth to make a Felonion. On the basis of the evolution of Ottoman decorative motifs, most Ottoman fabrics are dated to the mid-sixteenth century or later (Mackie 1980, p. 352). The absence from this sakkos of any typically Ottoman ornamentation suggests a date in the first half of the sixteenth century. A document date 1548 attests that Ottoman merchants in Leontopolis (Lwow) were selling textiles ‘with crosses’ (Rogers - Tazcan - Delibas 1986, p. 29), which means that these had already been available on the domestic market for some time. An early dating is supported by the pattern of repeated medallions, already considered archaic in the fifteenth century (Geijer 1979, pp. 143, 146-8). This archaism may be interpreted either as an adherence to painted prototypes of this iconographic theme (Papamastorakis 1993-4) or as the survival of Late Byzantine models in a period not very far removed from the Fall of Constantinople.
units.english_cohort_translation: date 1614, establishing a firm *terminus ante quem* when the fabric was remounted as a priestly Phelonion (*φαιλόνιον*). On stylistic grounds regarding the development of Ottoman textile design, such fabrics date from the mid-sixteenth century onward (Mackie 1980, p. 352). The absence of characteristic Ottoman floral motifs suggests an origin in the first half of the sixteenth century. A commercial archival register of 1548 records that Ottoman merchants in Leontopolis (Lviv) offered for sale textiles decorated with Christian crosses (Rogers, Tezjan, and Delibas 1986, p. 29), demonstrating the established circulation of such fabrics in Ukrainian and Central European trade. This early dating is corroborated by the medallion layout, an iconographic scheme regarded as archaic by the fifteenth century (Geijer 1979, pp. 143–148).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Tradition assigns this vestment to St Nephon, an Athonite monk who served as Patriarch three times (1486-9, 1497-8, 1502). After a brief sojourn in Wallachia, he returned to his own Monastery of Dionysiou where he remained until his death in 1508 (Actes de Dionysiou 1968, p. 18. Nasturel 1986, p. 142-4). There is nothing in the style or technique to refute this tradition, which would make the Dionysiou sakkos the oldest dated textile from the Bursa looms, and certainly the oldest in the series with Christian inscriptions. (Index of exhibits of the Monastery of Dionysiou, 16th century.)
units.english_cohort_translation: Athonite tradition attributes the Dionysiou vestment to Saint Niphon II, an Athonite hesychast who served as Ecumenical Patriarch on three occasions (1486–1489, 1497–1498, and 1502). Following a pastoral mission in Wallachia, he retired to Dionysiou Monastery, where he reposed in 1508 (*Actes de Dionysiou*, 1968, p. 18; Nasturel 1986, pp. 142–144). Textile analysis substantiates this dating, establishing the Dionysiou *sakkos* as the earliest dated figured textile from the Bursa looms bearing Christian epigraphy.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *SMALL ENTRANCE (Μικρὰ Εἴσοδος, ἡ): A procession in which the clergy, preceded by Acolytes, take the Holy Gospel from the ALTAR, exit the SANCTUARY through the north door, and move to the center of the SOLEAS, where they stop, facing the Altar. The clergyman carrying the Holy Gospel raises it and chants loudly: Σοφία. Ὀρθοί (Wisdom. Let us stand!) The clergy chant the ISODIKON (Entrance Hymn) before re-entering the Sanctuary through the BEAUTIFUL GATE. When a bishop is officiating in the Divine Liturgy, the ritual of the Small Entrance varies to some degree (see Appendix A in The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SMALL ENTRANCE** (*Μικρὰ Εἴσοδος, ἡ*; Slav. *Malyi Vkhod* / *Малый входъ*): A solemn liturgical procession during the Divine Liturgy wherein the celebrants, preceded by candle-bearers and acolytes, take the Book of the Holy Gospels from the Holy Table, exit the Sanctuary through the northern diaconal door, and advance to the center of the Soleas facing east toward the Altar. The deacon (or priest) elevates the Holy Gospel and proclaims aloud: **"Wisdom. Let us stand!"** (*«Σοφία. Ὀρθοί»*). The clergy chant the Entrance Hymn (**Isodikon** / *Εἰσοδικόν* / Slav. *Vkhodnoye*) before re-entering the Sanctuary through the Holy Doors (**Beautiful Gate** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη*). When a bishop presides at the Divine Liturgy, the Small Entrance is celebrated with distinct pontifical rubrics.[^680]

units.english_cohort_translation: **SOLEAS** (*σωλέας, ὁ*; Slav. *soleya* / *солея*): In contemporary liturgical architecture, this term designates the entire raised area immediately fronting the **Iconostasis** (*εἰκονοστάσιον, τό*). The soleas is elevated one or more steps above the floor level of the **Nave** (*ναός, ὁ*). In early Byzantine churches, the outer perimeter of the soleas was demarcated by a low chancel screen or balustrade known as the **Templon** (*τέμπλον, τό*).

units.slavonic_incipit: The SANCTUARY is usually one to
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The SANCTUARY is usually one to three steps higher than the floor of the NAVE. The ICONOSTASION is not located directly on the edge of the Sanctuary, but is usually set a few feet back from the edge of the top step. This forms a walkway in front of the iconostasis for the clergy, called a SOLEAS. In the very center of the soleas immediately before the BEAUTIFUL GATE and on the same level as the Sanctuary, is a small extension (or thrust), often rounded, called the AMBON, on which the Priest or Deacon may stand to read the gospel during the services.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **Sanctuary** (*βῆμα, τό* / *ἱερατεῖον, τό*) is elevated one to three steps above the floor of the Nave. The Iconostasis is not positioned flush at the edge of the Sanctuary platform, but is recessed several feet behind the uppermost step. This arrangement creates a continuous walkway in front of the screen reserved for the liturgical movements of the clergy, designated the soleas. In the exact center of the soleas, immediately before the **Beautiful Gate** (**Holy Doors** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη* / *Ἅγιαι Θύραι*) and upon the same level as the Sanctuary floor, extends a semicircular projection designated the **Ambon** (*ἄμβων, ὁ*), upon which the priest or deacon stands to proclaim the Holy Gospel, recite litanies, and deliver homilies during the divine services. In larger cathedral churches, the soleas is expanded to accommodate episcopal ceremonies, solemn entrances, and liturgical processions.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: STAFF (Ποιμαντορικὴ Ῥάβδος, ἡ): The Pastoral Staff (Western Crozier) of a Greek Orthodox Hierarch is fashioned at the top to resemble the heads of two serpents, recalling Christ’s words: “Be you wise as serpents.” (Matt. 10:16). As a serpent each year forces its way through thorny plants to shed its old skin, so also must the Bishop lead others and follow along the thorny path which leads to the renewal of our souls. The use of the staff indicates that the Bishop is the shepherd of Christ’s flock.

Exemplified by the successive strophes (troparia or oikoi) of a **Kontakion** (*κοντάκιον*) or the odes of a **Canon** (*κανών*). See **STROPHE**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In Byzantine hymnology, as in most poetry, a stanza (strofi) is a section of a large poetic work, dealing with the same theme or topic, copying the versification of the larger work, and fitting into its overall structure or form. See, for example, the stanzas (or troparia) in the Byzantine poetic forms of the KONTAKION or the CANON. See also STROFI (STROPHE).
units.english_cohort_translation: **STASIDIA** (*στασίδια, τά*, sing. *στασίδιον, τό*; Slav. *stasidii* / *стасидії*): Monastic choir stalls affixed to the perimeter walls of church naves and chancels. Characterized by high panelled backs, folding hinged seats, and elevated armrests designed to support chanters and monastics during prolonged standing offices. The undersurface of the folding seat is fitted with a small supportive ledge (misericord) that affords physical support while maintaining an upright posture. See **KATHISMATA**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: STASIDIA (στασίδια, τά): The choir stalls or seats used in Orthodox monasteries and churches. They are characterized by having high backs and elevated arm rests to help support the weight of the user/chanter when standing. They also may have a hinged seat which has a small shelf-like projection on the under surface called a misericord also provided to help support the weight of the user. See also KATHISMATA.
units.english_cohort_translation: **STASIS** (*στάσις, ἡ*; Slav. *stattya* / *статія*; lit. "standing"): In liturgical usage, a stationary structural section of a service; specifically, the three subdivisions comprising each **Kathisma** of the Psalter, each stasis concluding with the doxological triad: "Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God."

units.slavonic_diplomatic: STAVROTHEOTOKION (Σταυροθεοτοκίον, τό): A hymn to the Theotokos that refers to her standing by the Cross of Christ. These are typically found in the PARAKLITIKI in the hymnography for Wednesdays and Fridays.
units.english_cohort_translation: **STAVROTHEOTOKION** (*σταυροθεοτοκίον, τό*; Slav. *krestobohorodichnyj* / *крестобогородиченъ*): A hymn addressed to the Most Holy Theotokos contemplating her standing beside the Cross of her Son and God during His Holy Passion. These hymns are chanted in the weekly cycles of Wednesday and Friday within the **Octoechos** (**Parakletike** / *Παρακλητική*).

units.slavonic_incipit: tunic was the first article of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: tunic was the first article of clothing that one would wear in the morning. Working-class people wore knee-length tunics, while older people and people with less active occupations wore ankle-length tunics. The tunic was originally sleeveless, as Greeks and Romans thought sleeves were barbaric as barbarians, who generally lived in colder climates, wore them. Tunics did not acquire sleeves until the third century when a Roman Emperor is described as coming back from a military campaign wearing a tunic with sleeves.
units.english_cohort_translation: tunic constituted the foundational article of attire donned at the beginning of the day. Working-class laborers wore knee-length tunics, whereas venerable elders and citizens of sedentary rank wore ankle-length tunics. The classical Greco-Roman tunic was originally sleeveless, as sleeves were regarded as barbarian apparel typical of northern climates. Tunics did not incorporate sleeves until the third century, when imperial portraits depict Roman emperors returning from eastern campaigns clad in sleeved tunics (*tunica manicata*).

units.slavonic_incipit: In the first century, most people
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the first century, most people wore another garment called the himation over their tunics. The himation was a rectangular garment that was wrapped around the body. The designs on the himation, as well as its color and quality, varied depending on the wearer’s sex, occupation, and social status. Because of the relatively precarious way it was worn and the way it hindered movement, people had to remove it when they were engaged in certain physical activities. For example, when blind Bartimaeus ran to Jesus in Mark 10:46-52, he threw off his himation. Matthew 9:20-22 tells about a woman who was healed when she touched the hem of His himation. In Revelation 3:5, 3:18, and 4:4 people are given white himatia. Perhaps the writer of Revelation wanted us to think of people who had received a white tunic at their baptism now receiving an elegant and triumphant white himation to wear over it. (Note that most Bible translations are not consistent with the names of articles of clothing.) The himation never became a church vestment, probably because as servants, the clergy would have to remove it anyway. Scripture tells us that Jesus wore a himation over a tunic to the crucifixion. The soldiers tore the himation into four pieces, but because the tunic was woven in one piece, they cast lots for it. Jesus’ tunic would have been sleeveless and ankle-length. Ancient writings from that period refer to seamless tunics, but the technology for weaving them that way was lost in the fall of the Roman Empire, so the way in which this was done is not known. In the first four centuries of the Church, people were baptized in the nude. For propriety, they were baptized in three groups: men, women, and children; and female deacons baptized the women.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the apostolic era, citizens donned an outer mantle known as the **himation** (*ἱμάτιον, τό*) over the inner tunic. The himation was a rectangular woven cloak draped loosely across the shoulders and wrapped about the body. Its textile weave, coloration, and decorative fringes varied according to the wearer's sex, vocation, and social standing. Because of its loose draping, the mantle impeded vigorous physical movement and was routinely removed during physical exertion. For instance, when blind Bartimaeus sprang up to approach Jesus in Mark 10:46–52, he cast aside his himation. The Gospel of Matthew (9:20–22) records that the woman afflicted with an issue of blood received healing when she touched the hem of His himation. In the Book of Revelation (3:5; 3:18; 4:4), the righteous are clothed in white himatia, evoking the luminous heavenly attire bestowed upon those who had received the white tunic at Holy Baptism. The himation never entered ecclesiastical vesture, as its loose folds rendered it impractical for the active manual duties of the liturgical ministers. The Holy Gospels record that Jesus was led to His Crucifixion clad in a himation over an inner tunic. The Roman soldiers partitioned His himation into four parts, but because His tunic was woven in one continuous piece from top to bottom, they cast lots for it (John 19:23–24). The seamless tunic of Christ was sleeveless and reached to the ankles. While patristic authors reference seamless weaving techniques, the classical methods for producing seamless garments were largely lost following the fall of the Western Roman Empire. During the first four centuries of the Church, catechumens were baptized unclothed; for modesty, baptisms were conducted in separate groups of men, women, and children, female deaconesses assisting at the baptism of women.[^683]

units.slavonic_incipit: When they emerged from the water,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: When they emerged from the water, they were immediately clothed in a white tunic (In Latin, a tunica alba, or alb). For this reason, the sticharion or alb is a reminder of baptism and a symbol of the resurrection on the Last Day.
units.english_cohort_translation: Upon emerging from the baptismal waters, the newly illuminated were immediately clothed in a pure white tunic (in Latin, *tunica alba*, whence *alb*). For this reason, the sticharion represents the robe of incorruption and recalls both the cleansing of Holy Baptism and the glorious resurrection of the body on the Last Day.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Sticharion worn by the Reader/Chanter
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Sticharion worn by the Reader/Chanter is his basic ecclesiastical garment. There is a also a much shorter garment called the Reader’s Felonion which barely covers the shoulders and is only used when he is first tonsured by the Bishop as a Reader. It symbolizes his dedication to the service of God. The Sticharion for Readers, Sub-Deacons and Deacons has wide sleeves while for Priests and Bishops it has narrower sleeves. It is called the robe of salvation and the garment of joy, symbolizing a pure and peaceful conscience, a spotless life, and the spiritual joy in the Lord which flows in him who wears it. (Modified from http://www.stots.edu/article.php?id=25, the web page of St. Tikhon Monastery in South Canaan Pennsylvania.)
units.english_cohort_translation: The sticharion worn by the Reader and Chanter constitutes his primary liturgical vestment. At his tonsure, the bishop vests him briefly in the Reader's small phelonion (*μικρὸν φαιλόνιον* / *kravatsion* / *кукуліонъ*), which drapes over the shoulders and symbolizes his dedication to the divine service of God. The sticharion fashioned for readers, subdeacons, and deacons features wide, loose sleeves, whereas the priestly and episcopal under-sticharion features tapered sleeves fastened at the wrists by cuffs (**epimanikia** / *ἐπιμανίκια*). Ecclesiastically designated the robe of salvation and the garment of joy, it symbolizes a clean and peaceful conscience, a blameless life, and the spiritual joy in the Lord which flows in him who wears it.

units.slavonic_incipit: According to AE the Sticharion is
units.slavonic_diplomatic: According to AE the Sticharion is a tunic-like vestment, resembling the Western dalmatic when worn by servers, readers, sub-deacons and deacons. When it is worn by bishops and priests it more closely resembles the alb; although it is not necessarily white.
units.english_cohort_translation: In architectural and liturgical manuals, the diaconal sticharion is described as a tunic-like vestment resembling the Western dalmatic when worn by servers, readers, subdeacons, and deacons. When worn by bishops and priests beneath the chasuble or phelonion, it corresponds to the alb, though it is not restricted to white fabric.

units.slavonic_incipit: When worn as the outer garment
units.slavonic_diplomatic: When worn as the outer garment by deacons, subdeacons, altar servers, and sometimes by readers, the sticharion is a long robe with wide, loose sleeves. It is fastened at the neck, and is often open down the sides but held shut with buttons or ties. In appearance it is similar to the dalmatic and tunicle of the Western Church. It usually has a cross embroidered on or applied to the centre of the back, between the shoulder blades.
units.english_cohort_translation: When donned by deacons, subdeacons, and altar servers, the outer sticharion presents a flowing robe with wide sleeves, fastened at the collar and along the sides. In design, it corresponds to the dalmatic and tunicle of the Western Church. An embroidered cross is customarily appliquéd to the back between the shoulder blades.[^684]

units.slavonic_incipit: During the Order of PROTHESIS or
units.slavonic_diplomatic: During the Order of PROTHESIS or Preparation, the Priest takes his Sticharion, blesses the cross on the back and says, “Blessed is our God, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen. My soul rejoices in the Lord; for He has clothed me with the garment of salvation and He has covered me with the robe of righteousness, He adorns me with a crown as a bridegroom, and adorns me with jewels as a bride. (Isaiah 61:10); now and always and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («᾿Αγγαλιάσεται ἡ ψυχή μου ἐπὶ τῷ Κυρίῳ· ἐνέδυσε γάρ με ἱμάτιον σωτηρίου, καὶ χιτῶνα εὐφροσύνης περιέβαλέ με· ὡς νυμφίῳ περιέθηκέ μοι μίτραν, καὶ ὡς νύμφην κατεκόσμησέ με κόσμῳ· (Ἰσαία 61·10) Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: During the Order of **Prothesis** (Preparation of the Holy Gifts), the priest takes his sticharion, blesses the cross upon the back, and recites the vesting prayer: **"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Latin vestment equivalent to the sticharion is the alb. It too is a long white garment worn by the bishop or priest under the CHASUBLE which itself is equivalent to the Eastern Orthodox FELONION. The alb may be plain or decorated with embroidery or lacework, but in Latin usage is almost always white. (From Orthodox Wiki)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: STICHIRON, pl. STICHIRA (στιχηρόν, τό· στιχηρά, τά) Slav. Stixirons, Stixira: A hymn that is preceded by a line or VERSE (in Greek, a STICHOS), from the Psalms. Stichira are always done at VESPERS and the PRAISES (ENI) at Matins. At the APOSTICHA at VESPERS the first Stichiron is sung without a psalm verse. The Aposticha at Vespers on Sundays form an alphabetical acrostic, three letters each week, but the first Stichiron of each Mode does not form part of the acrostic series. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **STICHIRON**, pl. **STICHIRA** (*στιχηρόν, τό*, pl. *στιχηρά, τά*; Slav. *stikhira*, pl. *stikhiry* / *стихира*, *стихиры*): A liturgical hymn chanted in alternate succession with a psalm verse (**Stichos** / *στίχος*). Stichira are sung at **Vespers** (at **"Lord, I have cried"** [*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*]) and at **Matins** (**Orthros**) at the **Praises** (*Ainoi* / *Αἶνοι*). At the **Aposticha** (*ἀπόστιχα*) of Vespers, the first stichiron is chanted without a preceding psalm verse. The Sunday evening Aposticha form an alphabetical acrostic across the weeks, though the initial stichiron of each Tone does not form part of the acrostic series.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Festal stichira, accompanying both the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Festal stichira, accompanying both the fixed Psalms at the beginning and end of Vespers and the psalmody of the Eni (Praises or Lauds) in the Morning Office (ORTHROS), exist for all special days of the year, the Sundays and weekdays of Lent, and for the recurrent cycle of eight weeks in the order of the MODES beginning with Pascha (Easter).
units.english_cohort_translation: Festal stichira accompany the fixed psalmody of Vespers and the Praises of Matins throughout all liturgical seasons of the year, including the Sundays and weekdays of the Great Fast and the recurring eight-week cycle of the **Tones** (Tone 1 to Tone 8) commencing at Holy Pascha.[^685]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *STROFI, spelled STROPHE in English. (στροφή, ἡ): Lit. a turn, bend or twist. In Classical Greek and Latin lyric poetry, a STANZA. It was said to have derived its name from the performance of the lyric of a chorus, in which a strophe or STANZA was sung as the chorus proceeded in its dance in one direction, followed by a second stanza, the antistrophe, corresponding exactly in metre with the strophe, sung when the chorus turned and reversed its dance in the opposite direction. In modern poetry, the strophe becomes synonomous with the stanza.
units.english_cohort_translation: **STROPHE** (*στροφή, ἡ*; Greek *strofe*; lit. "a turning"): In classical Greco-Roman lyric poetry, a metric stanza. Historically derived from the movements of the dramatic chorus, which chanted a strophe while circling the orchestra in one direction, followed by an antistrophe (*ἀντιστροφή*) of identical metric measure as the chorus reversed its circular movement. In ecclesiastical hymnography, strophe is synonymous with the metric stanza or troparion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: SYNAPTI (Συναπτή, ἡ): The word derives from the Greek synaptin (συνάπτειν)— to join together. This is the grouping together of a set of petitions each of which asks for a specific blessing from God. See also LITANY.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SYNAPTE** (*συναπτή, ἡ*; Slav. *synaptiya* / *ектенія*): Derived from the Greek *synaptein* (*συνάπτειν*, "to join together"); a continuous series of liturgical petitions joined together into a single litany, each petition soliciting a specific spiritual or material blessing from God, followed by the people's response: **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Κύριε, ἐλέησον*). See **LITANY** and **EKTENIA**.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: SYNAXARION (Συναξάριον, τό): The name of a liturgical book in the Greek Orthodox Church. The book contains a collection of short biographies of the Saints for each day in the MINEON. These are read after the KONTAKION in the ORTHROS or morning prayer (MATINS).
units.english_cohort_translation: **SYNAXARION** (*Συναξάριον, τό*; Slav. *Sinaksar* / *Прологъ*): A liturgical book containing historical notices and brief biographies of the saints commemorated on each calendar day throughout the twelve monthly volumes of the **Menaion** (*Μηναῖον*). The synaxarion entry is read at Matins (**Orthros**) immediately following the Kontakion and Oikos after the Sixth Ode of the Canon.

units.slavonic_incipit: The exact meaning of the term
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The exact meaning of the term Synaxarion has been different at various times. Its first use was for the index to the Biblical and other lessons to be read in church. In this sense it corresponds to the Latin Capitulare and Comes. Later, the Synaxarion was filled up with the whole text of the Gospel and Apostolos pericopes to be read.
units.english_cohort_translation: The liturgical application of the term *Synaxarion* shifted through different historical epochs. Originally, it designated the systematic index or calendar of biblical pericopes appointed for reading in church, corresponding to the Latin *Capitulare* and *Comes*. Subsequently, the synaxarion came to incorporate the complete pericopes of the Holy Gospel and the **Apostolos** (*᾿Απόστολος*).[^686]

units.slavonic_incipit: As far as the Divine Liturgy
units.slavonic_diplomatic: As far as the Divine Liturgy was concerned this was replaced by the Gospel and APOSTOLOS books. Synaxarion remained the title for the index to the other lessons. Without changing its name it was filled up with complete texts of these lessons in the same way. As the lessons in the Byzantine Divine Office are always lives of saints, the Synaxarion became the collection of histories of the lives of saints and accounts of events whose memory is meant to be eternally remembered. There are a number of extant medieval Synaxaria manuscripts. The biographies contained in these manuscripts were composed or collected by various authors, one of the most eminent being Symeon Metaphrastes (12th cent). The Synaxarion is not now used as a separate book, as its information has been incorporated in brief sections in the 12 volumes of the MINEON.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the Divine Liturgy, these readings were eventually excerpted into distinct liturgical volumes: the Book of the Holy Gospels (**Evangelion** / *Εὐαγγέλιον*) and the Book of the Epistles (**Apostolos** / *᾿Απόστολος*). The designation *Synaxarion* was retained for the lectionary index of the Divine Office, which in turn was augmented with the complete hagiographical narratives of the saints. The synaxarion evolved into a comprehensive martyrology and compendium of the sacred events commemorated by the Church. Numerous medieval synaxaria survive in manuscript witness, composed and edited by Byzantine hagiographers, preeminent among whom was Symeon Metaphrastes (tenth to twelfth centuries). In modern liturgical usage, the synaxarion no longer forms a standalone volume, its texts having been distributed across the twelve monthly volumes of the **Menaion** (*Μηναῖον*).

The designation *Synaxarion* was retained for the lectionary index of the Divine Office, which in turn was augmented with the complete hagiographical narratives of the saints. The synaxarion evolved into a comprehensive martyrology and compendium of the sacred events commemorated by the Church. Numerous medieval synaxaria survive in manuscript witness, composed and edited by Byzantine hagiographers, preeminent among whom was Symeon Metaphrastes (tenth to twelfth centuries). In modern liturgical usage, the synaxarion no longer forms a standalone volume, its texts having been distributed across the twelve monthly volumes of the **Menaion** (*Μηναῖον*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *SYNAXIS (σύναξις, ἡ): A public gathering of the faithful or re-union of the faithful to honor a sacred personage that has played an important role in the event commemorated the previous day: e.g., the Synaxis of the John the Forerunner, 7 January, follows the Epiphany (Baptism) of Our Lord; the Synaxis of the Theotokos, 26 December, follows the Nativity of Our Lord, 25 December. It is exactly equivalent to the Latin collecta (from colligere), and similar to the word synagogue (synagoge), the place of reunion.
units.english_cohort_translation: **SYNAXIS** (*σύναξις, ἡ*; Slav. *Sobor* / *Соборъ*; lit. "gathering" or "assembly"): A liturgical assembly of the faithful convoked on the day following a Great Feast of the Lord or of the Theotokos to honor a sacred personage centrally instrumental in the salvific event celebrated on the previous day. For example, the Synaxis of Saint John the Baptist and Forerunner (January 7) follows the Theophany of Our Lord (January 6); the Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos (December 26) follows the Holy Nativity of Our Lord (December 25); and the Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel (March 26) follows the Annunciation (March 25). The term corresponds in concept to the Latin *collecta* (from *colligere*, "to gather together") and relates etymologically to *synagoge* (place of reunion).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: SYNTHRONON (σύνθρονον, τό): This is the primary THRONE of the Ecumenical Patriarch. It is a raised throne found within the Holy Sanctuary behind the IKONOSTASION and the HOLY TABLE. It is an elevated marble throne surrounded by eleven smaller wooden thrones in an arc on the eastern wall of the SANCTUARY. In the Patriarchal Church, only the Patriarch may sit on it. The other smaller thrones on either side are for the remaining members of the Patriarchal Synod of Bishops. Since some of the marble on the Synthronon dates back to the early fifth century, it may well have been graced by the presence of St. John Chrysostom. The use of a synthronon is an ancient liturgical practice of the Christian Church. It represents the unity of the faithful around the local bishop, who serves as the key celebrant of the Eucharistic gathering. It is also symbolic of the pastoral collegiality of the body of bishops, chaired by the president of the local synod. The episcopal throne therefore symbolizes the teaching au-
units.english_cohort_translation: **SYNTHRONON** (*σύνθρονον, τό*; Slav. *Gorneye mesto* / *Горнє мѣсто* / *сопрестоліе*): The semicircular tiered bench and cathedra situated in the central apse of the Sanctuary behind the Holy Table (**Altar** / *῾Αγία Τράπεζα*). In the Patriarchal Church of Saint George at the Phanar, it comprises an elevated marble cathedra flanked by eleven wooden thrones arranged in an arc along the eastern wall for the members of the Holy Synod of Bishops. In patriarchal celebrations, only the Ecumenical Patriarch ascends the central cathedra, while the concelebrating synodal hierarchs occupy the flanking stalls. Since portions of the marble masonry date to the early fifth century, patriarchal tradition associates its historical provenance with Saint John Chrysostom. The synthronon represents the ecclesial unity of the local church assembled around the bishop as chief celebrant of the Holy Eucharist, and manifests the apostolic collegiality of the episcopal synod. The episcopal cathedra signifies the pastoral and teaching au-[^687]

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: TEMPLON (τέμπλον, τό, pl. τέμπλα, τά): Lit. temple. In today’s churches, the templon is called the IKONOSTASIS. The Byzantine templon was an architectural feature first appearing in Christian churches about the fifth century AD and is still found in some form in all Eastern Orthodox churches today. The templon evolved gradually into the modern IKONOSTASIS. The templon separated the laity in the nave or NAOS from the priests preparing the sacraments at the altar in the SANCTUARY or BEMA. It was usually waist high and composed of carved wood or marble colonnades supporting a horizontal beam on top called an architrave or epistyle. Three doors lead into the sanctuary: a large central one referred to as the BEAUTIFUL GATE through which only the clergy may pass and two smaller doors located at the north and south ends of the templon which may be on the same plane or at right angles to the central gate. The templon did not originally obscure the laity’s view, but as time passed, icons were hung from the beams, curtains were placed in between the colonnetes, and the templon became more and more opaque. units.slavonic_diplomatic: The templon separated the laity in the nave or NAOS from the priests preparing the sacraments at the altar in the SANCTUARY or BEMA. It was usually waist high and composed of carved wood or marble colonnades supporting a horizontal beam on top called an architrave or epistyle. Three doors lead into the sanctuary: a large central one referred to as the BEAUTIFUL GATE through which only the clergy may pass and two smaller doors located at the north and south ends of the templon which may be on the same plane or at right angles to the central gate. The templon did not originally obscure the laity’s view, but as time passed, icons were hung from the beams, curtains were placed in between the colonnetes, and the templon became more and more opaque. It may be covered with icons and can be very elaborate. In the liturgical theology of the Eastern Orthodox Church, it is understood that the Beautiful Gate symbolizes the womb of the Virgin Mary. In some churches, there is a curtain that is drawn closed at certain times during the services especially during the preparation of communion during the Divine Liturgy. The smaller flanking doors at either end of the templon have been called ANGEL DOORS because the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are usually depicted on them; alternatively, they have also been called deacon’s doors because the deacons enter and leave the Sanctuary through them.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TEMPLON** (*τέμπλον, τό*, pl. *τέμπλα, τά*; Slav. *templon* / *темплонъ*; lit. "temple" or "shrine"): The low marble or carved wood chancel barrier that separated the Nave (**Naos** / *ναός, ὁ*) from the Sanctuary (**Bema** / *βῆμα, τό*) in early Christian and Byzantine basilicas, evolving into the multi-tiered **Iconostasis** (*εἰκονοστάσιον, τό*). First appearing in the fifth century, the classical templon was waist-high, consisting of parapet slabs (*thorakia*), colonnettes, and a continuous horizontal architrave (*epistyle* / *ἐπιστύλιον*). Three portals pierced the barrier: a central opening designated the **Beautiful Gate** (**Holy Doors** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη* / *Ἅγιαι Θύραι*) reserved for the celebrants, and two flanking portals on the north and south. Originally the templon left the sanctuary visually open to the faithful; over successive centuries, icons were suspended from the architrave, curtains were hung between the colonnettes, and the structure developed into the solid iconostasis. Liturgically, the central Holy Doors symbolize the virginal womb of the Most Holy Theotokos and the gate of heavenly paradise. In many traditions, a liturgical curtain is drawn during specific intervals of the Divine Liturgy. The lateral doors are customarily designated the **Angel Doors** because the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are depicted upon them, or the Diaconal Doors because the deacons enter and exit the Sanctuary through them.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: IERATIKON (῾Ιερατικόν) of the Greek Orthodox Church as an item located in the DIAKONIKON (SACRISTY). The thalassidion is a sink that drains into a hallowed place in the ground where liquids such as the water used to wash holy things may be poured. The thalassidion is the place where the clergy may wash their hands before serving the Divine Liturgy. However, in Orthodoxy the consecrated elements are never poured into the thalassidion, but must always be consumed by a deacon or priest. The prayer by the celebrants associated with the washing of their hands is “I will wash my hands in innocence and walk around Your altar, O Lord, to hear the voice of praise and declare all Your wonderful works. O Lord, I have loved the beauty of Your house, and the place where Your glory abides. Destroy not my spirit along with the wicked, nor take my life with bloodthirsty men who have crimes on their hands, whose right hand is filled with bribes. As for me, I have walked in innocence; redeem me, Lord, and have mercy on me. My foot is set on a straight path.
units.english_cohort_translation: **Ieratikon** (**Sluzhebnik** / *῾Ιερατικόν* / *Служебникъ*) as a mandatory installation within the **Diakonikon** (Sacristy / *διακονικόν, τό*). The thalassidion is a consecrated sink draining directly into clean earth beneath the church foundations, into which holy water, water utilized for washing sacred vessels or liturgical linens, and the water of Holy Baptism are reverently poured. The thalassidion is likewise the basin at which the celebrants wash their hands prior to vesting and celebrating the Divine Liturgy. Under strict canonical regulation, the consecrated Eucharistic Gifts are never poured into the thalassidion, but must be consumed entirely by the priest or deacon at the Prothesis table following the Divine Liturgy. While washing his hands, the celebrant recites the Lavabo prayer from the Septuagint Psalter: **"I will wash my hands in innocency, and will compass Thine altar, O Lord; that I may hear the voice of Thy praise, and tell of all Thy marvelous works. O Lord, I have loved the beauty of Thy house, and the place where Thy glory dwells. Destroy not my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is filled with gifts. But as for me, I have walked in mine innocence; redeem me, O Lord, and have mercy upon me. My foot stands in uprightness; in the congregations will I bless Thee, O Lord"** (Psalm 25:6–12 [MT 26:6–12]; *«Νίψομαι ἐν ἀθῴοις τὰς χεῖράς μου, καὶ κυκλώσω τὸ θυσιαστήριόν Σου, Κύριε, τοῦ ἀκοῦσαί με φωνῆς αἰνέσεώς Σου, καὶ διηγήσασθαι πάντα τὰ θαυμάσιά Σου. Κύριε, ἠγάπησα εὐπρέπειαν οἴκου Σου, καὶ τόπον σκηνώματος δόξης Σου. Μὴ συναπολέσῃς μετὰ ἀσεβῶν τὴν ψυχήν μου, καὶ μετὰ ἀνδρῶν αἱμάτων τὴν ζωήν μου, ὧν ἐν χερσὶν αἱ ἀνομίαι· ἡ δεξιὰ αὐτῶν ἐπλήσθη δώρων. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἐν ἀκακίᾳ μου ἐπορεύθην· λύτρωσαί με, Κύριε, καὶ ἐλέησόν με. Ὁ ποῦς μου ἔστη ἐν εὐθύτητι· ἐν ἐκκλησίαις εὐλογήσω σε, Κύριε»* [Ψαλμὸς 25:6–12 / MT 26:6–12]).

units.english_cohort_translation: In early basilicas, the thalassidion was situated directly beneath the Holy Table; in contemporary practice, it is located within the diakonikon. Ancient monastic custom appointed that the habit of a newly tonsured monastic be placed upon the thalassidion prior to the rite; following its relocation to the diakonikon, the monastic habit is placed directly upon the Holy Table. When a monk or nun receives the tonsure, the shorn hair is reverently deposited into the thalassidion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Note that In some ancient churches, the thalassidion was placed under the Holy Table (altar); today, however, it is almost always located in the diakonikon. At one time, before a monk or nun was tonsured, their religious habit would be placed on the thalassidion; now, since the separation of the thalassidion from the Holy Table, the habit is placed on the Holy Table. When a monk or nun is tonsured, if the hair must be disposed of, it is put into the thalassidion.

units.english_cohort_translation: **THEOTOKARION**, pl. **THEOTOKARIA** (*Θεοτοκάριον, τό*, pl. *Θεοτοκάρια, τά*; Slav. *Bohorodychnyk* / *Богородичникъ*): A liturgical hymnographic collection containing canons and suites of troparia composed in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos, organized according to the eight Tones and appointed for devotion throughout the ecclesiastical year (such as the *Theotokarion* compiled by Saint Nicodemus the Hagiorite).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: THEOTOKION (Θεοτοκίον, τό) pl. THEOTOKIA (Θεοτοκία, τά) Slav. bohorodichnyj: A hymn (TROPARION) or a group of hymns composed in honor of the Theotokos, the Mother of God, Lit. ‘God bearer’. The Theotokion usually concludes a larger body of hymnography, e.g.: troparia at the end of Vespers, stichira for “Lord, I cry out” (Κύριε ἐκέκραξα,) aposticha, etc. Many series of hymns end with a hymn to the Theotokos; this Theotokion often follows the short doxology, “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, Both now and for ever and to the ages of ages. Amen” (Δόξα Πατρί, καὶ Υἱῷ, καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι. Καὶ νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.) and is normally sung in the same Mode as the preceding DOXASTIKON. At Saturday evening vespers, however, the Theotokion at the Entrance is nearly always that of the Mode of the week, regardless of the Mode of the Doxastikon. It is also sung again at Vespers on the following Friday. In Russian usage this Theotokion is called the Dogmatic, whereas in Greek the Dogmaticon (Δογματικόν) is used for the corresponding Theotokion at Small Vespers. (AE)
units.english_cohort_translation: **THEOTOKION**, pl. **THEOTOKIA** (*Θεοτοκίον, τό*, pl. *Θεοτοκία, τά*; Slav. *bohorodychnyj* / *богородиченъ*): A hymn (troparion) composed in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Mother of God (lit. "Birth-giver of God"). The Theotokion customarily concludes a larger liturgical cycle of hymnography, such as the troparia at the conclusion of Vespers, the stichira at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*), or the Aposticha. A series of stichira or troparia concludes with a Theotokion following the Little Doxology: **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen"** (*Δόξα Πατρί, καὶ Υἱῷ, καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι· καὶ νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν*). The Theotokion is chanted in the same Tone as the preceding Doxastikon. At Saturday Great Vespers, however, the Theotokion of the Entrance is the solemn **Dogmatikon** (*Δογματικόν* / Slav. *Dogmatik* / *Догматикъ*) of the Tone of the week, regardless of the Tone of the Doxastikon. The same Theotokion is repeated at Vespers on the following Friday. In Slavic usage, this entrance Theotokion is designated the Dogmatikon, whereas in Byzantine practice the term *Dogmaticon* is likewise applied to the corresponding Theotokion at Small Vespers.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: THEOTOKOS (Θεοτόκος, ἡ): Theotokos is a Greek word meaning “God-bearer.” It is a title assigned to the Virgin Mary by the early Christian Church at the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus in 431 A.D. The theological significance at the time was to emphasize that Mary's son, Jesus Christ, was fully God as well as fully human, and that Jesus' two natures (divine and human) were united in the consubstantial and undivided Holy Trinity.
units.english_cohort_translation: **THEOTOKOS** (*Θεοτόκος, ἡ*; Slav. *Bohorodytsya* / *Богородиця*; lit. "Birth-giver of God"): The supreme dogmatic title of the Virgin Mary, solemnly affirmed by the Universal Church at the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in 431 A.D. The Council defined that Mary's Son, Jesus Christ, is simultaneously true God and true Man, and that His divine and human natures are united hypostatically in the one Divine Person of the Son, the Second Person of the Holy Trinity.

units.slavonic_incipit: Church developed, the bishop's throne was
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Church developed, the bishop's throne was erected in its present location on the Soleas on the southern wall of the church. The hierarchical integrity of the SYNTHRONON behind the altar table in the SANCTUARY has not been compromised by the erection of another throne outside of the sanctuary on the soleas; it remains the bishop's seat as well during divine services. Perhaps the most authentic Patriarchal throne in today's Church is that found in the Patriarchal Cathedral of St. George in Constantinople (present day Istanbul, Turkey). On this throne there are 3 inscriptions: 1. Beneath the eaves of the throne gables there is a statement that the Throne was a gift of the Patriarch Jeremiah in 1577 to the then Patriarchal Church of Panagia Pammakaristos. 2. Another inscription at the base of the throne says it was the craftsmanship of the Athenian artist Lavrentios. 3. On one of the gables over its eaves the inscription says it was damaged between 1652-1654 during the tenure of Patriarch Paisios I (1652-1653) and (1654-1655). This throne was renovated under Patriarch Iakovos (1679-1682). The above damage caused the loss of gems and the icons of Christ the Pantokrator or all ruler and the Descent into Hades and burial of Christ which was described by Malaxios in 1577. Its exact location on the throne then is unknown. The current icon is a replacement commissioned by Patriarch Paisios I.
units.english_cohort_translation: Church developed, the bishop's throne was erected in its present location upon the soleas against the southern wall of the church. The hierarchical integrity of the **Synthronon** (*σύνθρονον*) behind the Holy Table in the Sanctuary has not been compromised by the erection of another throne outside the Sanctuary upon the soleas; it remains the bishop's seat during divine services. Perhaps the most authentic Patriarchal throne in the Church today is that preserved in the Patriarchal Church of Saint George at the Phanar in Constantinople (modern Istanbul). Upon this throne are inscribed three historical epigraphs: 1. Beneath the eaves of the throne gables, an inscription records that the throne was the gift of Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremiah II (Tranos) in 1577 to the former Patriarchal Church of the Panagia Pammakaristos. 2. An inscription at the base of the throne records that it was the craftsmanship of the Athenian master artist Lavrentios. 3. Upon one of the gables above the eaves, an inscription records that the throne was damaged between 1652 and 1654 during the patriarchate of Paisios I (1652–1653, 1654–1655). The throne was subsequently restored under Patriarch Iakovos (1679–1682). This damage caused the loss of precious gems and the original icons of Christ the Pantocrator (*Παντοκράτωρ*, Ruler of All) and the Descent into Hades with the Entombment of Christ, described by Malaxios in 1577; their original placement upon the throne is no longer known. The current icon is a replacement commissioned by Patriarch Paisios I.

units.slavonic_incipit: In addition to the SYNTHRONON and
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In addition to the SYNTHRONON and the throne erected on the soleas described above, there is a third kind of throne seen in the Patriarchal Cathedral of St. George. This is the so-called PARATHRONE. It is located between the larger and more ornate throne of the Patriarch and the KLIROS. Since the Patriarchate is also considered to be a monastic establishment, the parathrone is used by the abbot of the monastery or the MEGAS PROTO-SYNGELLOS when he officiates in the absence of the Patriarch.
units.english_cohort_translation: In addition to the Synthronon and the throne erected upon the soleas, a third type of throne is situated within the Patriarchal Church of Saint George: the **Parathrone** (*παραθρόνιον, τό*). It is positioned between the larger, ornate Patriarchal Throne and the Kliros. Because the Patriarchate is likewise constituted as a stauropegial monastic community, the parathrone is occupied by the hegumen or by the Grand Protosyngellos (**Megas Protosyngellos** / *Μέγας Πρωτοσύγκελλος*) when he presides in the absence of the Patriarch.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: TIMIOTERA (Τιμιωτέρα, ἡ): The 6 verses of the 9th Biblical Ode or Ode of the Theotokos beginning with “Magnify, O my soul, the Lord” («Μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν Κύριον»), each verse followed by the refrain “More honorable than the Cherubim” («Τὴν Τιμιωτέραν τῶν Χερουβείμ...»): The Timiotera is chanted at Matins (Ὄρθρος) after the 8th Ode of the KATAVASIE, which come before the EXAPOSTILARION.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TIMIOTERA** (*Τιμιωτέρα, ἡ*; Slav. *Chestneyshuyu* / *Честнѣйшую*; lit. "More honorable"): The six strophes of the Ninth Biblical Canticle or Song of the Most Holy Theotokos (Magnificat, Luke 1:46–55), beginning: **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** (*«Μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν Κύριον»*), each verse accompanied by the venerable refrain: **"More honorable than the Cherubim, and more glorious beyond compare than the Seraphim, who without corruption gavest birth to God the Word, the very Theotokos, thee do we magnify"** (*«Τὴν τιμιωτέραν τῶν Χερουβείμ, καὶ ἐνδοξοτέραν ἀσυγκρίτως τῶν Σεραφείμ, τὴν ἀδιαφθόρως Θεὸν Λόγον τεκοῦσαν, τὴν ὄντως Θεοτόκον, σὲ μεγαλύνομεν»*). The Timiotera is chanted at Matins (**Orthros**) following the Eighth Ode of the Katavasiai and preceding the Exapostilarion.

units.slavonic_incipit: TONSURE: In the Orthodox Church, a
units.slavonic_diplomatic: TONSURE: In the Orthodox Church, a tonsure means the cutting off of four locks of hair from the scalp of the one being tonsured; this is done in a cruciform pattern as follows: at the front of the head as the tonsuring celebrant bishop, priest or abbot says “In the Name of the Father” («Εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρός,»); at the back of the head as the celebrant says “and of the Son” («καὶ τῷ Υἱῷ»); and on either side of the head as he says the words “and of the Holy Spirit” («Καὶ τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος»). The service of tonsure represents an offering of one's self to God and is a part of several of the sacraments.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TONSURE** (*κουρά, ἡ*; Slav. *postryzheniye* / *постриженіе*): In the Eastern Church, tonsure signifies the ceremonial cutting of four locks of hair from the head of the candidate in the form of a cross: at the crown of the head as the celebrant bishop, priest, or hegumen proclaims: **"In the Name of the Father"** (*«Εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Πατρός»*); at the back of the head: **"and of the Son"** (*«καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ»*); and upon either side of the head: **"and of the Holy Spirit"** (*«καὶ τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος»*). The rite of tonsure represents a dedication and sacrificial offering of oneself to God and forms an integral component of several sacred mysteries and rites.

units.slavonic_incipit: Today, there are three types of
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Today, there are three types of tonsure: baptismal, monastic, and clerical. In all cases, the hair is allowed to grow back; the tonsure, therefore, is not adopted as a permanent hairstyle. The hair which has been cut is burned in the censer.
units.english_cohort_translation: In contemporary practice, three distinct types of tonsure are celebrated: baptismal, monastic, and clerical. In all cases, the shorn hair is permitted to grow naturally, the tonsure not being retained as a permanent tonsured hairstyle; the severed hair is reverently consumed by fire within the censer.

units.slavonic_incipit: Tonsure is also done prior to
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Tonsure is also done prior to the ordination of a layman to the rank of reader. This has led to the commonly used statement that one is “tonsured a reader,” although in sequence the rite of tonsure occurs prior to the actual ordination by the laying on of hands by the celebrant.
units.english_cohort_translation: Tonsure is also administered prior to the chirothesia of a layman to the minor order of Reader (**Anagnostes** / *ἀναγνώστης*). This liturgical sequence has given rise to the common expression that a candidate is "tonsured a reader," although canonically the rite of tonsure immediately precedes the ordination proper effected by the imposition of hands (*chirothesia* / *χειροθεσία*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *TRANSLATION (ἀνακομιδή, ἡ) of the remains of a saint or a relic: The transference from one place (shrine) to another: e.g., 27 January, Translation of the Remains of St. John Chrysostom. Chrysostom's remains were taken from Kukuso, a desert village in Asia where he had been exiled, to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople in 438.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TRANSLATION (OF RELICS)** (*ἀνακομιδὴ λειψάνων, ἡ*; Slav. *pereneseniye moshchey* / *перенесеніе мощей*): The solemn transfer of the relics of a holy saint or martyr from one shrine or tomb to another. For example, on January 27, the Church celebrates the Translation of the Relics of Saint John Chrysostom, which were translated in 438 A.D. from Cucusus (*Κουκουσός*), an isolated village in Armenia where he had reposed in exile, to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.

units.slavonic_incipit: the hymnographer and Kesarios, the brother
units.slavonic_diplomatic: the hymnographer and Kesarios, the brother of St. Gregory the Great, St. John the Evangelist did not experience natural death but was bodily taken up to heaven—a belief that gained currency in the early Middle Ages. The Church has never accepted this notion as official dogma, yet it celebrates St. John's demise not as a Kimisis (dormition, sleep, repose) but as a metastasis (translation to heaven), perhaps in special honor of the Evangelist as Christ's “beloved disciple” and as a visionary of the apocalyptic realm.
units.english_cohort_translation: the Hymnographer and Caesarius (the brother of Saint Gregory the Theologian), Saint John the Evangelist did not undergo natural physical corruption, but was bodily taken up into heaven—a pious tradition that gained widespread currency in the early medieval era. While the Church has never formulated this pious belief as a binding dogma of faith, it commemorates the departure of Saint John not as a Dormition (*koimesis* / *κοίμησις* / sleep, repose), but as a *metastasis* (*μετάστασις* / translation), honoring the Evangelist as Christ's "beloved disciple" and as the visionary seer of the Apocalypse.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: TRIADIKA (Τριαδικά, τά): A series of four hymns composed in honor of the Holy Trinity and found in the Service of the MESONYKTIKON of Sunday in the GREAT OROLOGION. These are sung near the end of this service and prior to the beginning of the service of ORTHROS (MATINS or Morning Prayer). These are sometimes referred to as the Triadic Magnificats (Triadika Megalynaria).
units.english_cohort_translation: **TRIADIKA** (*τριαδικά, τά*; Slav. *troichni* / *троичны*): A suite of four hymns composed in honor of the Holy Trinity, appointed in the Sunday **Midnight Office** (**Mesonyktikon** / *Μεσονυκτικόν*) within the **Great Horologion** (*Ὡρολόγιον τὸ Μέγα*). They are chanted toward the conclusion of this office prior to the commencement of Matins (**Orthros**). They are likewise designated the Triadic Magnifications (*Τριαδικὰ Μεγαλυνάρια*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *TRIODION (Τριῴδιον, τό) Slav. Postnaya Triod: The word has two meanings: (1) The period beginning on the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and ending on Holy Saturday; or (2) the service book that contains the services of all the MOVABLE FEASTS beginning on the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and ending on Holy Saturday.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TRIODION** (*Τριῴδιον, τό*; Slav. *Postnaya Triod* / *Постная Тріодь*; lit. "Three Odes"): The term bears two liturgical significations: (1) The liturgical season commencing upon the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and concluding upon Holy Saturday; and (2) the liturgical service book containing the hymnography, scriptural readings, and proper rubrics for all movable feasts and fasts from the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee through Holy Saturday.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Trisagios Hymn. On 14 September (Elevation of the Holy Cross) and the Third Sunday in Lent (Adoration of the Holy Cross), Ton Stavron Su is sung instead of the Trisagios Hymn. According to some sources, this hymn dates from the middle of the 4th century. The Trisagios Hymn continues to be sung, in Greek, in certain ceremonies of the Roman Church, such as the Improperia of Good Friday.
units.english_cohort_translation: Trisagion Hymn. On September 14 (Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross) and the Third Sunday of the Great Fast (Veneration of the Precious Cross), **"To Thy Cross we bow down in worship, O Master, and Thy holy Resurrection we glorify"** (*«Τὸν Σταυρόν Σου προσκυνοῦμεν, Δέσποτα, καὶ τὴν ἁγίαν Σου Ἀνάστασιν δοξάζομεν»*) is chanted in place of the Trisagion Hymn. According to liturgical witnesses, this hymn dates to the middle of the fifth century. The Trisagion continues to be chanted in Greek in certain Western rites, notably during the *Improperia* (Reproaches) of Good Friday (*Agios o Theos, Sanctus Deus*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *TRISAGION TU VIMATOS (Τρισάγιον τοῦ Βήματος): The thrice-holy hymn as sung when a bishop officiates in the Divine Liturgy. For a detailed outline of this hierarchal format, see Appendix A. of The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by T. Bogdanos. According to the order of service of a hierarchal Divine Liturgy, the elaborate separate phrases of the hymn are sung by the clergy or chanters from the Sanctuary—hence the term tu Vimatos (of the Vima [Sanctuary]). In Greek Orthodox Churches in the United States, these separate phrases of the hymn are often sung by the choir.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TRISAGION TOU VIMATOS** (*Τρισάγιον τοῦ Βήματος*): The Thrice-Holy Hymn as chanted when a bishop presides at the Divine Liturgy. In the hierarchal order of the Divine Liturgy, the elaborate antiphonal phrases of the hymn are chanted alternately by the clergy from within the Sanctuary (*Bema* / *Βῆμα*)—whence the designation *tou Vimatos* (of the Sanctuary)—and answered by the chanters or choir upon the soleas.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: TROPARION (Τροπάριον, τό) pl. TROPARIA (Τροπάρια, τά): One of the oldest titles used in the Greek Orthodox Church for a specific piece of hymnography in the form of a free poetic composition, as opposed to a quoted Scriptural text. As a generic title, Troparion can be applied to virtually any composed hymn although today it is used to more specifically indicate the following three types of hymns: (1) Dismissal troparia (APOLYTIKIA, Slav. otpustitel'ny) i. e., troparia of the Resurrection, of the Feast or of the Day — hymns that keynote the main theme of the occasion being celebrated on a given day. These are sung before the dismissal at Vespers and then repeated throughout the services of the day — at Matins, Compline, Hours, and at the Divine Liturgy after the Small Entrance; (2) Troparia Evlogitaria — a series of several hymns, each preceded by the refrain “Blessed art Thou, O Lord,” sung at Resurrectional Matins after the 17th Kathisma of the Psalter and at the Matins of Holy Saturday; and (3) Troparia of a KANON — brief verses that follow the IRMOS in each ODE of the kanon. units.english_cohort_translation: **TROPARION**, pl. **TROPARIA** (*τροπάριον, τό*, pl. *τροπάρια, τά*; Slav. *tropar*, pl. *tropari* / *тропарь*, *тропари*): One of the most ancient designations in Eastern hymnography for an ecclesiastical poetic strophe composed in free meter, as distinguished from a quoted scriptural text. While as a generic term *Troparion* may designate virtually any ecclesiastical hymn, in liturgical taxonomy it specifically denotes three principal categories: (1) Dismissal Troparia (*ἀπολυτίκια*, lit. "apolytikia"; Slav. *otpustytelni* / *отпустительны*), namely troparia of the Resurrection, of the Feast, or of the Saint of the day, summarizing the central theological theme of the commemoration. These are chanted prior to the dismissal at Vespers and repeated throughout the offices of the day—at Matins, Compline, the Hours, and at the Divine Liturgy following the Small Entrance; (2) Troparia Evlogitaria (*Εὐλογητάρια* / Slav. *Neporochny*), a suite of resurrectional strophes, each preceded by the scriptural refrain: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes"** (*«Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά σου»* / Psalm 118:12 [MT 119:12]), chanted at Sunday Matins following the seventeenth Kathisma of the Psalter and at the Matins of Holy Saturday; and (3) Troparia of a Canon (*κανών*), the concise strophes following the **Heirmos** (*εἱρμός*) in each Ode of the canon. units.slavonic_diplomatic: Saturday with the verses of Psalm 118 [119] are also called troparia. Troparion implies that the composed hymn has been written in a particular style and manner (Gr. tropos—τρόπος). A Troparion is also a succinct summary of a sacred event or saintly person being celebrated in the services. It also serves as a response and refrain to the PSALM verses sung by the chanter. The name Troparion was, therefore, given to short prayers which, in the earliest stage of hymnography, were written in poetic prose and inserted after each verse of a psalm.
units.english_cohort_translation: Saturday with the verses of Psalm 118 [MT 119] are likewise designated troparia. The term *Troparion* indicates that the hymn is composed in a defined rhythmic style or melodic pattern (Greek *tropos* / *τρόπος*, mode, manner, or turn). A Troparion provides a concise theological distillation of the sacred event or holy saint celebrated in the services. In early hymnography, it served as an antiphonal response and refrain to the psalm verses chanted by the cantor. The name Troparion was thus originally applied to short prayers composed in rhythmic prose and inserted after each verse of a psalm.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: In the fifth century, when the Troparia were composed in strophic form and became longer, these poetical prayers were sung only after the last three to six verses of a psalm. Hymns of this kind were known to have formed part of Matins and Vespers in churches and monasteries of the fifth century. In this period the liturgy consisted of Psalms, of the nine Odes or Canticles, of certain formulae dating back to the earliest times of Christianity, and of the Troparia, added by contemporary hymnodists.
units.english_cohort_translation: In the fifth century, when troparia expanded into strophic forms of greater length, these poetic prayers were chanted only after the final three to six verses of a psalm. Hymns of this character formed part of Matins and Vespers in ecclesiastical and monastic centers of the fifth century. In this era, the divine office consisted of the Psalter, the nine Biblical Odes or Canticles, established liturgical formulas deriving from apostolic antiquity, and troparia composed by contemporary hymnographers. This practice, however, did not obtain in strictly secluded desert monastic communities: anchorites and hermits of the strict desert tradition, according to surviving accounts, rejected all forms of florid melodic chanting.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: TROPEOFOROS (Τροπαιοφόρος, ὁ): Trophy bearer *TU NAU (τοῦ ναοῦ): ‘of the church.’ This is the title for the Apolytikion of the saint or sacred event to which a particular church has been dedicated and after which it is named. The full term in Greek is Ἀπολυτίκιον τοῦ ναοῦ (Dismissal Hymn of the Church). The Hymn of the Church is usually sung as one of sometimes several apolytikia before the Kontakion in the Divine Liturgy. For the specific Hymns of the churches in the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, see Appendix B. of The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by T. Bogdanos.
units.english_cohort_translation: **TOU NAOU** (*τοῦ ναοῦ*; lit. "of the temple" or "of the church"): The designation for the Dismissal Troparion (*ἀπολυτίκιον*, lit. "apolytikion") honoring the patron saint or sacred mystery to which a church edifice is dedicated and after which it is named. The complete Greek term is *Ἀπολυτίκιον τοῦ ναοῦ* (Dismissal Troparion of the Temple). The Dismissal Troparion of the Temple is chanted among the Dismissal Troparia following the Small Entrance at the Divine Liturgy prior to the Kontakion.

For the specific Hymns of the churches in the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, see Appendix B. of The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by T. Bogdanos.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Liturgy daily although it is rare for any Priest to serve daily. Also, an emergency beyond his control may have prevented him from preparing according to the Rule for Holy Communion, or he may have suffered an injury which would not permit him to enter the Sanctuary, etc.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Typika office, which in ancient monastic practice was chanted prior to the **Beatitudes** (*Μακαρισμοί, οἱ*) at the commencement of the Divine Liturgy, consists principally of Psalm 102 [MT 103]: **"Bless the Lord, O my soul"** (*«Εὐλόγει, ἡ ψυχή μου, τὸν Κύριον»*) and Psalm 145 [MT 146]: **"Praise the Lord, O my soul"** (*«Αἴνει, ἡ ψυχή μου, τὸν Κύριον»*). The service incorporates the fundamental psalmody and prayers of the Liturgy of the Catechumens. Under ordinary rubrics, the Typika is read following the Third and Sixth Hours (in the temporal position where the Divine Liturgy would otherwise be celebrated). During the Great Fast, the Ninth Hour precedes the Typika and the structural order is adapted.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Typika which was at one time chanted before the BEATITUDES (Μακαρισμοί, οἱ) at the beginning of the Divine Liturgy consists mainly of Psalm 102 (PB) “Bless, my soul, the Lord” («Εὐλόγει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν Κύριον») and Psalm 145 (PME) “Praise, my soul, the Lord”
units.english_cohort_translation: During the reading of the Typika, proper troparia may be intercalated between the verses of the Beatitudes, as during the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. During the Great Fast, however, this hymnographic interpolation is omitted; instead, the Beatitudes are chanted by the choir with the penitential refrain intercalated between each verse: **"Remember us, O Lord, when Thou comest into Thy kingdom"** (*«Μνήσθητι ἡμῶν, Κύριε, ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ Σου»* / Luke 23:42).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: During the reading of the Typika, TROPARIA may be inserted be- tween the verses of the BEATITUDES, as when the Divine Liturgy is cel- ebrated. However, during Great Lent this is not done; instead, the Beati- tudes are chanted by the choir and between each verse they chant “Re- member us, O Lord, when You come into Your kingdom.” («Μνήσθητι ἡμῶν, Κύριε, ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ Βασιλείᾳ Σου....»)
units.english_cohort_translation: In the parochial celebration of the Divine Liturgy, the traditional Typika psalms have largely been superseded by the three Antiphons: the First Antiphon refrain: **"Through the intercessions of the Theotokos, O Savior, save us"** (*«Ταῖς πρεσβείαις τῆς Θεοτόκου, Σῶτερ, σῶσον ἡμᾶς»*), and the Second Antiphon: **"Save us, O Son of God... who sing to Thee: Alleluia"** (*«Σῶσον ἡμᾶς, Υἱὲ Θεοῦ... ψάλλοντάς Σοι· Ἀλληλούϊα»*). The Beatitudes have likewise been superseded by the Third Antiphon, consisting of the Dismissal Troparion chanted with the Entrance Verse.

units.english_cohort_translation: (*τάξις, ἡ*, class or order) of every divine service throughout the ecclesiastical calendar. The normative Typikon governing contemporary Byzantine practice is George Violakis's *Typikon of the Great Church of Christ* (*Τυπικὸν τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ Μεγάλης Ἐκκλησίας*, Constantinople, 1888). This monumental work serves as the foundation for modern annual liturgical manuals, such as the *Diptycha* (*Δίπτυχα*) issued by the Apostoliki Diakonia of the Church of Greece, the *Taxis ton Ieron Akolouthion* (*Τάξις τῶν Ἱερῶν Ἀκολουθιῶν*) of George G. Bekatoros (Athens), and the *Liturgical Guide Book* of Frank Desby (Columbus, Ohio). The rubrical dispositions of the Violakis Typikon have from time to time received authoritative modifications by the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople.

units.english_cohort_translation: **VERSE** (*στίχος, ὁ*; Slav. *stikh* / *стихъ*): A line of poetic or scriptural text. In Byzantine hymnography, a *stichos* is typically a psalm verse chanted in recitative (*chyma* / *χύμα*) prior to a hymn chanted with an expansive melodic rhythm. Exemplified by the evening stichira of **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*) at Vespers, and the stichira of the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Αἶνοι*) at Matins (**Orthros**).

units.english_cohort_translation: **VESPERS** (*Ἑσπερινός, ὁ*; Slav. *Vechirnya* / *Вечерня*; from *hespera* / *ἑσπέρα*, evening): The foundational opening service of the liturgical day, celebrated at eventide. In the ecclesiastical calendar, the liturgical day begins at sunset of the preceding civil day (Genesis 1:5: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day") and concludes at sunset of the calendar day itself.
