units.slavonic_diplomatic: Reader (Ἀναγνώστης, ὁ): The essential role of the READER is to recite the Readings and Psalms from the Old Testament and the Epistle lessons from the New Testament during church services. He also recites some non-sacramental prayers (e.g., the Trisagion) and chants the psalm verses for certain ANTIPHONS. There is a special service for the tonsuring of a reader, although in contemporary practice a lay- man may simply receive the priest's blessing to read on a particular occasion.
units.english_cohort_translation: **Reader** (**Anagnostes** / *ἀναγνώστης, ὁ*; Slav. *Chtets* / *чтецъ*): The essential liturgical duty of the reader is to recite the lections and psalms from the Old Testament (Paremias) and the Epistle (Apostolos) lessons from the New Testament during divine services. He likewise recites non-sacramental prayers (such as the Trisagion Prayers) and chants the psalm verses for appointed antiphons. The candidate is set apart through a dedicated liturgical rite of tonsure and chirothesia, though in contemporary circumstances a layman may receive an ad-hoc blessing from the priest to read on a given occasion.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Readers are permitted to wear a CASSOCK according to the cus- tom of his particular church, although most do so only while attend- ing services. Readers do not wear a clerical shirt, as they are not considered clergy and may not perform any of the duties reserved for clergy. After being tonsured, the reader is vested in a short FELONION, which he wears while reading the Epistle for the first time. This vestment is then removed and never worn again. It is replaced with a STICHARION, which the reader wears thereafter when he reads the
units.english_cohort_translation: Readers are permitted to wear the inner cassock (*anteri* / *ἀντερί*) according to local parish tradition, customarily donned while assisting at services. At his ordination, the newly tonsured reader is vested in the Reader's short phelonion (*μικρὸν φαιλόνιον* / *kravatsion* / *кукуліонъ* / Slav. *malyi felon*), in which he recites the Epistle lection for the first time. This vestment is immediately removed and is not donned again; it is replaced by the Reader's **Sticharion** (*στιχάριον*), which the reader wears thereafter whenever reciting the Epistle. This practice is not universally observed, however, and many bishops permit a reader to perform his duties vested solely in the cassock.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Deacon (of any rank: Subdeacon, Deacon, Protodeacon, or Archdea- con). In some traditions, a Deacon may be given a double orarion as an award of distinction; in Byzantine Greek practice, however, all grades of the diaconate (sub-deacons, proto-deacons, arch-deacons) wear the double orarion. The orarion is a long, narrow ribbon like band of bro- cade which is usually worn over the left shoulder, wrapped around the chest to the waist in back and brought back over the left shoulder to the front. At other times it is crossed upon the breast and back. The Sub- Deacon wears his Stole always crossed, for convenience in the fulfillment of his duties. The Deacon, however, binds his Stole about him in the form of a cross shortly before the Holy Gifts are consecrated, thus typifying the wings of the Angels who serve about the Altar, as the Deacons them- selves, as servants and messangers, typify the Cherubim and Seraphim.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **Orarion** (**Stole** / *ὠράριον, τό*; Slav. *orar* / *орарь*) is the distinctive vestment worn by the deacon (across all ranks: subdeacon, deacon, protodeacon, or archdeacon). In certain Slavic traditions, a deacon may be awarded the double orarion as an ecclesiastical distinction; in Byzantine Greek praxis, however, all grades of the diaconate wear the double orarion. The orarion is a long, narrow band of brocade draped over the left shoulder, wrapped about the chest to the waist in back, and brought over the left shoulder to the front. The Subdeacon wears his stole crossed permanently across the chest and back for ease of manual service. The Deacon, however, binds his orarion crosswise about his body shortly before the consecration of the Holy Gifts in the Anaphora, typifying the wings of the Seraphim who minister before the heavenly Altar (Isaiah 6:2–3), as the deacons themselves, as sacred ministers, typify the Cherubim and Seraphim. The angelic Trisagion hymn—**"Holy, Holy, Holy"** (*«Ἅγιος, Ἅγιος, Ἅγιος»*)—is frequently embroidered upon the orarion. The stole is bound crosswise about the Subdeacon at his ordination, symbolizing that through purity of heart and bodily continence he dons the vesture of chastity.

units.slavonic_incipit: Stole. The Stole is bound about
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Stole. The Stole is bound about the Sub-Deacon in the form of a cross at his ordination, as a symbol that, through the meekness and continence of his members and the purity of his heart, he is to put upon himself the robe of purity.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Deacon likewise wears the **Cuffs** (**Epimanikia** / *ἐπιμανίκια, τά*; Slav. *poruchi* / *поручи*), which are fastened with laces about the wrists beneath the sleeves of the sticharion (in contrast to priests and bishops, who wear them over the sleeves of the inner sticharion). They admonish the deacon not to place trust in his own human strength, but in the right hand of the Lord, Almighty and merciful God, and in His divine strength and assistance.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: When vesting with the Sticharion, the Priest holds it in his left hand and first blesses the cross on the back saying: “Blessed is our God, al- ways: now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.») He then continues: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον.») He then prays: “My soul rejoices in the Lord. He has clothed me in the garment of salvation and has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bride- groom decks himself with a garland and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels (Isaiah 61:10); now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.”
units.english_cohort_translation: When vesting in the Sticharion, the priest takes it in his left hand, bows toward the East, and blesses the cross upon the back, proclaiming: **"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*). He continues: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον»*). He then recites the vesting prayer: **"My soul shall rejoice in the Lord, for He hath clothed me with the garment of salvation, and with the tunic of gladness hath He encompassed me; as a bridegroom He hath set a crown upon me, and as a bride hath He adorned me with ornament; always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Ἀγαλλιάσεται ἡ ψυχή μου ἐπὶ τῷ Κυρίῳ· ἐνέδυσε γάρ με ἱμάτιον σωτηρίου, καὶ χιτῶνα εὐφροσύνης περιέβαλέ με· ὡς νυμφίῳ περιέθηκέ μοι μίτραν, καὶ ὡς νύμφην κατεκόσμησέ με κόσμῳ [Isaiah 61:10]. Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.slavonic_incipit: CASSOCK, passes round the neck and,
units.slavonic_diplomatic: CASSOCK, passes round the neck and, hanging straight down, it is per- manently joined in front for its entire length. It signifies the conse- crating grace of the Priesthood. The Priest, like the Deacon, can celebrate no office without his Stole. In it, without the FELONION, he celebrates the less solemn Offices: Small Vespers, ordinary Compline, Praises or Lauds (Slav. Polunochniza), and the Hours (if the Gospel is not appointed to be read in them.) In various Prayer-services in private dwellings, such as those at the birth of a child or the blessing of homes the Priest will also wear the Stole.
units.english_cohort_translation: (2) The **Epitrachelion** (**Priestly Stole** / *ἐπιτραχήλιον, τό*; Slav. *epitrakhil* / *єпитрахиль*; from *epi*, upon, and *trachelos*, neck): The epitrachelion consists of a broad band of brocade worn about the neck and hanging straight down in front, permanently joined along its entire length. It signifies the outpouring of sacerdotal consecrating grace upon the priesthood (Psalm 132:2 [MT 133:2]). The priest, like the deacon, cannot celebrate any divine office without his stole. Vested in the Epitrachelion alone, without the **Phelonion** (*φαιλόνιον*), he celebrates the less solemn offices: Small Vespers, ordinary Compline, the Midnight Office (Greek *Mesonyktikon* / Slav. *Polunoshchnitsa*), and the Hours (when no Gospel is appointed to be read). At diverse prayer services (*treby*) in private dwellings, such as the prayer at the birth of a child or the blessing of homes, the priest likewise wears the Epitrachelion.[^700]

Amen.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ ἐκχέων τὴν χάριν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἱερεῖς αὐτοῦ· ὡς μύρον ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ πώγωνα, τὸν πώγωνα τοῦ Ἀαρών, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ τὴν ᾤαν τοῦ ἐνδύματος αὐτοῦ (Ψαλμὸς 132 (133)·2)· Πάντοτε νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The ZONI (Ζώνη, ἡ) Slav. Poyas) is a cloth belt with which the Priest girds himself about his Epitrachilion and Sticharion to keep them in place for convenience in serving. It is symbolic of the gift of strength with which God aids him in his service, and exhorts him to blamelessness of life. It also denotes the priest’s readiness to serve the Lord and that he is bound to Christ. In putting on this belt he prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Blessed is God Who girds me with strength, and has made my way blameless (Psalm 17(18):32); now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ περιζωννύων με δύναμιν· καὶ ἔθετο ἄμωμον τὴν ὁδόν μου. (Ψαλμὸς 17 (18)·32) Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: The **ZONE** (**Girdle** or **Belt** / *ζώνη, ἡ*; Slav. *poyas* / *поясъ*): A textile belt wherewith the priest girds himself over his Epitrachelion and Sticharion to secure them in place for convenience during divine service. It symbolizes the gift of spiritual strength wherewith God assists him in his sacerdotal ministry, and admonishes him unto purity and blamelessness of life. It likewise denotes the priest's readiness to serve the Lord and that he is bound unto Christ. In putting on this girdle, he blesses the cross embroidered upon it and prays: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Blessed is God Who girds me with strength, and hath made my way blameless"** (Psalm 17:33 [MT 18:32]); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. When vesting with the cuffs, the priest’s prayers are: first for the right hand “Your right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; Your right hand, O Lord, has vanquished the enemy, and in the multitude of Your glory have You crushed the adversaries (Exodus 15:6). Always, now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen.” («Ἡ δεξιά σου, Κύριε, δεδόξασται ἐν ἰσχύϊ· ἡ δεξιά σου χείρ, Κύριε, ἔθραυσεν
units.english_cohort_translation: The **EPIMANIKIA** (**Liturgical Cuffs** / *ἐπιμανίκια, τά*, sing. *ἐπιμανίκιον, τό*; also termed *ἐπιμάνικα* or *ὑπομάνικα*; Slav. *poruchi* / *поручи*): These are the ceremonial cuffs that are likewise worn by the deacon; however, whereas the deacon laces them about his wrists beneath the wide sleeves of the outer sticharion, the priest wears them laced securely over the tapered sleeves of the priestly sticharion. When vesting with the cuffs, the priest recites the appointed prayers: first, for the right cuff, he prays: **"Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, hath shattered the enemy, and in the multitude of Thy glory Thou hast crushed the adversaries"** (Exodus 15:6–7); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Ἡ δεξιά Σου, Κύριε, δεδόξασται ἐν ἰσχύϊ· ἡ δεξιά Σου χείρ, Κύριε, ἔθραυσεν*[^701]

units.slavonic_incipit: ἐχθρούς· καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῆς δόξης
units.slavonic_diplomatic: ἐχθρούς· καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῆς δόξης σου συνέτριψας τοὺς ὑπεναντίους. (Ἐξόδου 15·6) Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.») And then for the left hand, he prays: “Your hands have made me and fashioned me; give me understanding that I may learn Your commandments. (Ps. 118:73). Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Αἱ χεῖρές σου ἐποίησάν με καὶ ἔπλασάν με· συνέτισόν με καὶ μαθήσομαι τὰς ἐντολάς σου· (Ψαλμὸς 118·73) Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.») The cuffs symbolize the bonds endured by Christ at His passion and serve as a reminder that a minister of the Church must rely not on his own strength, but on the help of God.
units.english_cohort_translation: *ἐχθρούς· καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῆς δόξης Σου συνέτριψας τοὺς ὑπεναντίους. Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*). And then for the left cuff, he prays: **"Thy hands have made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, and I shall learn Thy commandments"** (Psalm 118:73 [MT 119:73]); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. units.slavonic_diplomatic: The EPIGONATION (Ἐπιγονάτιον, τό or Ὑπογονάτιον, τό), Slav. Palitsa) is a stiffened diamond shaped piece of brocade, which is suspended from the ZONI as an award of distinction for a priest. Its origin is traced to the practice of Byzantine Emperors awarding ceremonial swords to their military commanders in recognition of their valor in defending the empire. Such swords were often used with an elaborate thigh-shield which was suspended from the belt under the sword and protected the leg from bruising caused by the constant bumping of the sword against the thigh. The Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. It has also been explained as being symbolic of the towel with which the Lord girded himself to wash the disciples’ feet. In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored to wear the Epigonation or Palitsa may also be honored to wear the Thigh-shield (Slav. Nabedrennik). The Nabedrennik is also a stiffened brocaded fabric, rectangular in shape and worn over the right hip, suspended by a strap drawn over the left shoulder and attached to the two upper corners. It is not worn in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slav use, the Palitsa is worn over the right hip; however, if the Priest has also been awarded the use of a Nabedrennik, the Palitsa is worn over the left hip.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **EPIGONATION** (*ἐπιγονάτιον, τό*, or *ὑπογονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *palitsa* / *палица*; from *epi*, upon, and *gonu*, knee): A stiffened, lozenge- or diamond-shaped piece of brocade suspended by a ribbon from the belt (Zone) over the right hip as an ecclesiastical award of distinction for a deserving priest (protoiereus, archpriest, or economos). Its historical origin is traced to the Byzantine imperial practice whereby emperors awarded ceremonial swords to military commanders in recognition of valor in defense of the empire. Such swords were accompanied by an elaborate thigh-shield suspended beneath the hilt to shield the warrior's leg from bruising caused by the motion of the scabbard. Spiritually, the Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:17). It is likewise interpreted mystically as symbolizing the linen towel wherewith the Lord girded Himself to wash the feet of the disciples at the Mystical Supper (John 13:4–5). In Slavic traditions, a priest awarded the Epigonation (*palitsa*) may previously have received the rectangular thigh-shield (Slav. *nabedrennik* / *набедренникъ*). The *nabedrennik* is likewise a stiffened brocade vestment, rectangular in shape, worn suspended over the right hip by a strap passed over the left shoulder. The *nabedrennik* is not utilized in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slavic usage, if a priest possesses only the *palitsa*, it is worn upon the right hip; if he has also been awarded the *nabedrennik*, the *palitsa* is transferred to the left hip, while the *nabedrennik* occupies the right hip.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The FELONION (Φελόνιον, τό) is the distinguishing vestment of the Priest. It is a long, sleveless conical vestment similar to a cape, shortened in front to facilitate the movement of his hands and with an opening for his head. The Felonion is worn over all the other vestments.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **PHELONION** (**Felonion** / *φελόνιον* or *φαιλόνιον, τό*; Slav. *felon* / *фелонь* or *riza* / *риза*): The distinctive outer vestment of the priest. It is a long, sleeveless conical vestment resembling a cape, shortened in the front to facilitate the unhindered movement of his hands, with an opening for the head. The Phelonion is donned over all the other sacerdotal vestments.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: It is symbolic of the robe Christ wore during His Passion. It is also a reminder that the Priest is “clothed with righteousness (Psalm 131:9) and thus protected from all iniquities. It was for a few centuries also worn by bishops until it was replaced by the SAKKOS. The Felonion is similar to the Western Chasuble.
units.english_cohort_translation: It symbolizes the seamless robe and the purple mantle wherewith Christ was clothed during His Passion. It stands as a reminder that the priest is clothed with righteousness (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]) and thereby shielded from all iniquities. For many centuries, the phelonion (specifically the polystavrion) was likewise worn by bishops until it was replaced among hierarchs by the **Sakkos** (*σάκκος*). The Eastern phelonion corresponds historically and functionally to the Western chasuble.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: When vesting with the Felonion, the priest reverences the Cross on the back of the Felonion as he prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. May Your priests Lord, be clothed in righteousness, and Your faithful ones rejoice (Psalm 131 (132):9); now and ever and unto all ages of ages. Amen.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἱερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται (Ψαλμὸς 131 (132)·9). Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: When vesting with the Phelonion, the priest reverences the cross upon the back of the vestment as he prays: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thy priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and Thy holy ones shall rejoice with joy"** (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἱερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται· Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Bishop (Ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ) The BISHOP wears all the vestments of a Priest, save the FELONION.
units.english_cohort_translation: **BISHOP** (**Hierarch** / *Ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ*; Slav. *Yepyskop* / *Єпископъ* or *Archierey* / *Архіерей*): The bishop wears all the sacerdotal vestments of a priest, with the exception of the Phelonion, which is replaced by the Sakkos, and is adorned with additional pontifical insignia.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: As the bishop vests with the STOLE (EPITRACHILION) the 1st Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Blessed is God Who pours out His grace upon His priests like the oil of myrrh upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, upon the beard of Aaron, which runs down to the fringe of his raiment.” (Psalm 132:2) («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ ἐκχέων τὴν χάριν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἱερεῖς αὐτοῦ, ὡς μύρον ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ πώγωνα, τὸν πώγωνα τοῦ Ἀαρών, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ τὴν ᾤαν τοῦ ἐνδύματος αὐτοῦ.») (Ψαλμὸς 132·2) He then completes the prayer with “Always, now and ever, and to the ages of ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε, νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ τίς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The 1st Deacon then prays for the Left Cuff “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. units.slavonic_diplomatic: The SAKKOS (Σάκκος, ὁ), meaning a “sackcloth garment” or “garment of humility”: Liturgically, except for the FELONION, the Bishop wears all the vestments of a priest. Originally the bishop also wore the FELONION but it was later replaced by the Sakkos, a garment like a short tunic with half-sleeves, fashioned in all likelihood after the vestment of a Byzantine emperor; as such it is a sign of special distinction and honor. Symbolically it serves as a reminder that the Bishop must rise to holiness of life. As the Bishop is vested with the Sakkos, the 1st Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Your Priests shall be clothed with righteousness, and Your righteous shall rejoice.” (Psalm 132:9). («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται.») (Ψαλμὸς 132·9). The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying: “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: The **SAKKOS** (*σάκκος, ὁ*; Slav. *sakkos* / *саккосъ*; lit. "sackcloth" or garment of penitential humility): In divine services, with the sole exception of the Phelonion, the bishop wears all the vestments of a priest. Originally, bishops likewise wore the phelonion (embellished as the polystavrion), but it was subsequently replaced by the Sakkos, a tunic-like garment with short half-sleeves, modeled after the imperial dalmatic of Byzantine emperors; as such, it constitutes a mark of high ecclesiastical honor and episcopal dignity. Symbolically, while recalling the mockery of the purple robe placed upon the Savior, it admonishes the bishop to ascend unto eminent holiness of life. As the Bishop vests with the Sakkos, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thy high priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and Thy holy ones shall rejoice with joy"** (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]) (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).[^705]

Originally, bishops likewise wore the phelonion (embellished as the polystavrion), but it was subsequently replaced by the Sakkos, a tunic-like garment with short half-sleeves, modeled after the imperial dalmatic of Byzantine emperors; as such, it constitutes a mark of high ecclesiastical honor and episcopal dignity. Symbolically, while recalling the mockery of the purple robe placed upon the Savior, it admonishes the bishop to ascend unto eminent holiness of life. As the Bishop vests with the Sakkos, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thy high priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and Thy holy ones shall rejoice with joy"** (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]) (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).[^705]

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source: The SAKKOS (Σάκκος, ὁ), meaning a “sackcloth garment” or “garment of humility”: Liturgically, except for the FELONION, the Bishop wears all the vestments of a priest. Originally the bishop also wore the FELONION but it was later replaced by the Sakkos, a garment like a short tunic with half-sleeves, fashioned in all likelihood after the vestment of a Byzantine emperor; as such it is a sign of special distinction and honor. Symbolically it serves as a reminder that the Bishop must rise to holiness of life. As the Bishop is vested with the Sakkos, the 1st Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Your Priests shall be clothed with righteousness, and Your righteous shall rejoice.” (Psalm 132:9). («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται.») (Ψαλμὸς 132·9). The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying: “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The EPIGONATION (Ἐπιγονάτιον, τό or Ὑπογονάτιον, τό), Slav. Palitsa is a stiffened diamond shaped piece of brocade, which is suspended from the ZONI by all Bishops. It is an award of distinction for a priest. Its origin is traced to the practice of Byzantine Emperors awarding ceremonial swords to their military commanders in recognition of their valor in defending the empire. Such swords were often used with an elaborate thigh-shield which was suspended from the belt under the sword and protected the leg from bruising caused by the constant bumping of the sword against the thigh. The Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. It has also been explained as being symbolic of the towel with which the Lord girded himself to wash the disciples’ feet. In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored to wear the Epigonation or Palitsa may also be honored to wear the Thigh-shield (Slav. Nabedrennik). It is also a stiffened brocaded fabric, rectangular in shape and worn over the right hip, suspended by a strap drawn over the left shoulder and attached to the two upper corners. It is not worn in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slav use, the Palitsa is worn over the right hip; however, if the Priest has also been awarded a Nabedrennik, the Palitsa is worn over the left hip.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **EPIGONATION** (*ἐπιγονάτιον, τό*, or *ὑπογονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *palitsa* / *палица*): A stiffened diamond-shaped piece of brocade suspended from the Zone (Belt) over the right hip, worn universally by all bishops as a mandatory pontifical vestment, whereas for priests it is granted only as an ecclesiastical award of distinction. Its origin is traced to the custom of Byzantine emperors presenting ceremonial swords to military generals for valor in defending the empire. These swords were accompanied by a padded thigh-shield suspended beneath the weapon to protect the thigh against friction while marching. Mystically, the Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:17). It is likewise explained as symbolizing the towel wherewith the Lord girded Himself to wash the feet of the disciples (John 13:4–5). In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored with the Epigonation (*palitsa*) may also have been awarded the rectangular thigh-shield (Slav. *nabedrennik* / *набедренникъ*), which is worn over the right hip suspended from a strap over the left shoulder. The *nabedrennik* is not utilized in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slavic usage, if a priest possesses only the *palitsa*, it is worn upon the right hip; if he has also been awarded the *nabedrennik*, the *palitsa* is transferred to the left hip, while the *nabedrennik* is worn upon the right.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: As the Bishop vests with the Epigonation, the 1st Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Gird your sword upon your thigh, mighty One, in your splendor and beauty. Stretch out your bowstrings, go forth and rule in the cause of truth, gentleness and justice, and may your right hand lead you to wondrous deeds.” (Psalm 44 (45): 3-4); («Περίζωσαι τὴν ῥομφαίαν σου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν σου, Δυνατέ, τῇ ὡραιότητί σου καὶ τῷ κάλλει σου· καὶ ἔντεινε, καὶ κατευοδοῦ, καὶ βασίλευε ἕνεκεν ἀληθείας, καὶ πραότητος, καὶ δικαιοσύνης· καὶ ὁδηγήσει σε θαυμαστῶς ἡ δεξιά σου.») (Ψαλμὸς 44 (45) 3·4. The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying: “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)

Gird Thy sword upon Thy thigh, O Mighty One, in Thy splendor and in Thy beauty! String Thy bow, go forth, prosper, and reign, for the sake of truth, meekness, and righteousness; and Thy right hand shall lead Thee marvelously"** (Psalm 44:4–5 [MT 45:3–4]) (*«Περίζωσαι τὴν ῥομφαίαν σου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν σου, Δυνατέ, τῇ ὡραιότητί σου καὶ τῷ κάλλει σου· καὶ ἔντεινε, καὶ κατευοδοῦ, καὶ βασίλευε ἕνεκεν ἀληθείας, καὶ πραότητος, καὶ δικαιοσύνης· καὶ ὁδηγήσει σε θαυμαστῶς ἡ δεξιά σου»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.slavonic_incipit: worn when the Bishop is vested
units.slavonic_diplomatic: worn when the Bishop is vested for the liturgy up to the the time of the reading of the Gospel. Thereafter he is revested with the short version. The word Omoforion meaning “shoulder covering” originally referred to a piece of sheepskin worn over the shoulders by the aged and infirmed for warmth. Later it was made out of the same material as the rest of the vestments, but its origin still recalls the parable of the lost sheep which the good shepherd found and laid on his shoulders. So too, the bishop is entrusted to safely guide his flock and be mindful of the conversion of the erring.
units.english_cohort_translation: worn when the bishop is vested for the Divine Liturgy from the beginning until the reading of the Holy Gospel. Thereafter, he is revested with the Small Omophorion, which is worn draped about the neck with both ends hanging down over the chest. The word *Omophorion*, signifying a "shoulder-covering," originally denoted a strip of woolen sheepskin worn over the shoulders by the aged and infirm for warmth. In later centuries, it was fashioned from the same rich fabric as the sacerdotal vestments; its spiritual origin, however, perpetually evokes the parable of the lost sheep which the Good Shepherd found and laid upon His own shoulders (Luke 15:4–6). Thus the bishop is reminded that he is entrusted to shepherd his flock safely and to seek untiringly the conversion and restoration of the erring. The Omophorion is the principal symbol of the bishop's apostolic, spiritual, and canonical jurisdiction; clergy and ecclesiastical communities subject to a hierarch's jurisdiction are said to be "under his Omophorion."

slavonic_provenance.verbatim_source:
worn when the Bishop is vested for the liturgy up to the the time of the reading of the Gospel. Thereafter he is revested with the short version. The word Omoforion meaning “shoulder covering” originally referred to a piece of sheepskin worn over the shoulders by the aged and infirmed for warmth. Later it was made out of the same material as the rest of the vestments, but its origin still recalls the parable of the lost sheep which the good shepherd found and laid on his shoulders. So too, the bishop is entrusted to safely guide his flock and be mindful of the conversion of the erring. The Omoforion is the symbol of the Bishop’s spiritual and ecclesiastical authority and clergy and ecclesiastical institutions subject to a bishop’s authority are said to be “under his Omoforion.”

    The equivalent vestment for the Omoforion in the usage of Western (Roman) Christianity is the archiepiscopal pallium or pal, the use of which is subject to different rubrics and restrictions, while all Orthodox bishops wear the Omoforion.

units.slavonic_incipit: As the Bishop is vested with
units.slavonic_diplomatic: As the Bishop is vested with the Omoforion, the 1st Deacon initially prays: “Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. When You did take upon Your shoulders human nature which had gone astray, O Christ, You did bear it to heaven, to God Your Father.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων, Χριστέ, τὴν πλανηθεῖσαν ἄρας φύσιν, ἀναληφθεὶς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ προσήγαγες.») The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: As the Bishop vests with the Omophorion, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. When Thou didst take upon Thy shoulders our human nature which had gone astray, O Christ, Thou didst ascend and offer it unto God Thy Father"** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων, Χριστέ, τὴν πλανηθεῖσαν ἄρας φύσιν, ἀναληφθεὶς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ προσήγαγες»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Engolpion (In Greek, something ‘worn on the chest’) is worn by both priests and bishops as a reminder that they should not merely carry Christ in their hearts, but also confess Him in the face of all men. Engolpion formerly also included pectoral crosses; however, today, the word Engolpion is used for a medallion with an icon in the center, worn as a vestment by Orthodox and Eastern Catholic bishops. Some Engolpia are hollow, for use as a reliquary. All bishops wear a particular kind of Engolpion called the Panagia (see below).
units.english_cohort_translation: The **ENGOLPION** (*ἐγκόλπιον, τό*; from *en*, in/upon, and *kolpos*, chest or bosom; Slav. *nagrudnik* / *нагрудникъ*): The sacred badge worn upon the breast by both archpriests (formerly) and bishops, admonishing them that they must not only carry Christ within their hearts, but boldly confess Him before all mankind. Historically, the term *engolpion* included pectoral crosses and reliquary medallions; in modern usage, however, the designation applies primarily to an oval or circular medallion bearing an icon in enamel or relief, worn suspended by a chain over the chest by Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic hierarchs. Certain engolpia are hollowed to serve as reliquaries (*enkolpia-reliquaries*). All bishops wear a specific form of engolpion depicting the Mother of God, designated the **Panagia** (*Παναγία*).

units.slavonic_incipit: When the Bishop is vested with
units.slavonic_diplomatic: When the Bishop is vested with the First Medallion (Ἐγκόλπιον α΄) or the Panagia (Παναγία, ἡ) or All-holy one—a small, circular Holy Image (Icon) of our Savior and the Birth-giver of God which hangs by a gold chain from the neck over the chest by a Bishop and reminds the Bishop that he must always bear in his heart the Lord and His holy Mother (the Theotokos or Panagia), the Intercessor before God; and, to that end, the Bishop’s heart must be pure and his spirit upright. When a bishop vests with the engolpion, the 2nd Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν.») The 1st Deacon then prays “Lord, have mercy” («Κύριε, ἐλέησον.») and continues “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. (Psalm 50:10) («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου.») The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)
units.english_cohort_translation: When the Bishop vests with the **First Medallion** (**First Engolpion** / *Ἐγκόλπιον α΄*) or the **Panagia** (*Παναγία, ἡ*; lit. "All-Holy Lady")—a circular icon of our Savior and the Most Holy Theotokos hanging from a golden chain over the breast—it reminds the hierarch that he must perpetually bear in his heart the Lord and His all-pure Mother, the supreme Intercessor before God; and to this end, his heart must remain undefiled and his spirit upright. When the bishop vests with this first engolpion, the Second Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν»*). The First Deacon then responds: **"Lord, have mercy."** (*«Κύριε, ἐλέησον»*), and continues: **"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me"** (Psalm 50:12 [MT 51:10]) (*«Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The MITER (Μίτρα, ἡ), spelled by some as Mitre, is a richly embroidered crown or diadem representing the crown of thorns worn by Christ at His passion and serving as an emblem of the power bestowed upon the Bishop as minister of the Church. It is worn by all those in episcopal office and is modeled after the crown worn by Byzantine emperors.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **MITER** (*μίτρα*), also spelled *mitre*, is a richly embroidered and adorned domed crown or diadem representing the crown of thorns worn by Christ during His holy Passion, and serving as an insignia of the pastoral authority bestowed upon the bishop as an apostle and shepherd of the Church. It is worn by all hierarchs in episcopal orders and is patterned architecturally upon the imperial crown (*kamelaukion*) of the Byzantine emperors.

units.slavonic_incipit: It is highly unlikely that it
units.slavonic_diplomatic: It is highly unlikely that it was modeled after the Old Testament miter since it was not adopted by bishops of the Church until the 15th century. While in the Greek Orthodox Church the Miter is only worn by a hierarch, in more recent centuries the Russian Orthodox Church has allowed the Miter to be given to some archimandrites and archpriests as an honorary distinction.
units.english_cohort_translation: It is historically improbable that the Christian episcopal miter was derived from the Old Testament high-priestly headdress (*miznephet*), since crown-like miters were not adopted by Eastern bishops until after the fall of Constantinople in the fifteenth century. While in Byzantine Greek usage the miter is reserved exclusively to hierarchs (bishops, metropolitans, and patriarchs), in Slavic praxis the privilege of wearing a miter has in recent centuries been granted to certain distinguished archimandrites and protopresbyters as an ecclesiastical decoration.

units.slavonic_incipit: or cities to which they minister
units.slavonic_diplomatic: or cities to which they minister and as a sign that it behooves them to feed the flock of Christ. The staff is of metal and at the top is made to resemble the heads of two serpents thus recalling the Savior’s words: “Be you wise as serpents.” As a serpent each year forces its way through thorny plants to shed its old skin, so also must the Bishop lead others and follow himself along the thorny path which leads to the renewal of one’s soul.
units.english_cohort_translation: or eparchies committed to their charge, and as an emblem of their sacred duty to pasture the flock of Christ. The pastoral staff is fashioned of metal or carved wood, and its summit is shaped to resemble two entwined serpents facing an orb and cross, recalling the Savior's admonition: **"Be ye wise as serpents and simple as doves"** (Matthew 10:16). Just as a serpent each year sheds its old skin by pressing through narrow and thorny places, even so must the bishop guide others and walk himself along the narrow and arduous path of ascetic virtue leading unto the renewal of the soul.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Eagle or AETOS (Ἀετός, ὁ) Slav. Orlets is a small round or oval rug, with the representation of a one-headed eagle soaring over a city. A Bishop stands on this rug during divine service, and to him alone is its use accorded. He is led upon a large “Eagle” at his consecration, as the Service of Consecration sets forth. The view of the city suggests the Bishop’s rule over the city while the Eagle denotes the loftiness and purity of his teaching. Thus, the Eagle-rug spread for a Bishop to stand upon signifies that he, by his life and doctrine, must resemble the eagle, which with its excellent vision soars above all lower things, and aspires unto heaven.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **EAGLE** (**Aetos** / *ἀετός, ὁ*; Slav. *orlets* / *орлецъ*): A small circular or oval liturgical rug depicting an eagle with outspread wings soaring over a fortified city. The bishop stands upon this rug during divine services, and its use is reserved strictly and exclusively unto him. A larger Eagle-rug is placed beneath the bishop-elect during the rite of episcopal consecration, as prescribed in the Pontifical Archieratikon. The representation of the city denotes the bishop's pastoral oversight and canonical governance over his diocese, while the soaring eagle signifies the celestial loftiness and purity of orthodox theological doctrine. Thus the eagle-rug spread beneath the bishop symbolizes that in his life, virtue, and sacred teaching, he must emulate the eagle, which with keen vision soars above all earthly and corruptible things, fixing its gaze upon heavenly realities.[^710]

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The MANDYAS (Μανδύας, ὁ) or mantle of the Bishop is also a monastic garment, which, like a cloak, covers the whole body with the exception of the head. All monks, when present at divine services, must be robed in their mantles. The Mantle is not technically speaking a liturgical vestment but in Vespers and Matins (Orthros) it is worn when a bishop first arrives for the service and is presiding from the episcopal throne; it is later removed with assistance by the priests or deacons before he is vested for the liturgy. In Greek Orthodox practice, the bishop descends from the Throne after the chanting of the KATAVASIE, enters the sanctuary through the BEAUTIFUL GATE where, after reverencing the book of the gospels lying on the altar table, he proceeds to the DIAKONIKON where the mantle is removed, and if he is to be the celebrant of the liturgy, he begins vesting with full episcopal vestments for the liturgy. In Slav. practice, after the bishop descends from the Throne as described above, he proceeds to the center of the soleas where the mantle is removed and, if he is to be the celebrant, he is publicly vested for the liturgy with the assistance of the deacon or priest.

units.slavonic_incipit: One peculiarity of a Bishop’s mantle
units.slavonic_diplomatic: One peculiarity of a Bishop’s mantle is that it is not black, like the monastic mantle, but usually of purple, or some other color. Upon it are sewn the so-called “Tables of the Law” (Slav. Skrizhali), and, in particular, the “Fountains” (Slav. Istotchniki). The Tables (square patches at the neck and feet) typify the Old and the New Covenants, from which the ministers of God should draw their doctrine. The Fountains are ribbons, usually red and white in hue, sewn horizontally round the Mantle which represent the streams of teaching which flow from the mouth of the Bishop. Small bells are attached to the Mantle of a Bishop, and to his Dalmatic, as they were on the upper robe of the High Priest of the Jews.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: 2. The ANTIRI (Ἀντίρι, τό), or Inner Cassock more often simply called the Rason (Slav. Zostiko or Podrjaznik) is also usually black, gathered at the waist with a narrow cloth belt and with a high collar buttoned in the front. Unlike the Roman Cassock, the Antiri does not have buttons down the front. It is usually worn under the liturgical vestments of all clergy. The Antiri symbolizes the death of the clergyman to this world, his burial and subsequent dedication to God and His heavenly kingdom. It should be noted that the wearing of the inner and outer cassock is common to bishops, priests, deacons, monks and nuns and that permission to wear a cassock is sometimes given by a bishop to seminarians, monastic novices, sub-deacons and readers. As for liturgical vestment colors, when the Typikon says anything about them, it only specifies ‘light’ or ‘dark’ vestments, so local tradition is the only standard.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Kalymafchion (Καλυμαύχιον, τό) (alternate spellings may be: kamilavka, kalimaft or kameloukion): The so-called ‘Stove-Pipe’ hat is a hat of stiff fabric which, in the Greek style, is cylindrical with a flattened conical brim at the top. In the Slavic style it is flared and flat at the top, while in the Serbian style it is cylindrical and flat at the top.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **KALYMAFCHION** (*Καλυμαύχιον, τό*; also termed *kamilavka*, *kalimafi*, or *kamelaukion*; Slav. *kamilavka* / *камилавка*): The cylindrical clerical head-covering fashioned of stiffened fabric. In Byzantine Greek usage, it is cylindrical with a flattened conical brim projecting around the top rim. In Slavic usage, it is flared outward toward the top and flat without a brim, while in Serbian usage it is cylindrical and flat at the top.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Epanokalymafchon (Ἐπανοκαλύμαυχον, τό): A black veil worn by bishops and archimandrite monks. The veil is attached to the top of the traditional black ‘stove-pipe’ hat or KALIMAFCHION. The latter without a veil may be worn by other clergy.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **EPANOKALYMAFCHON** (*Ἐπανοκαλύμαυχον, τό*; Slav. *klobuk* / *клобукъ*): A black veil worn by bishops and archimandrite monks. The veil is attached to the top of the cylindrical black kamilavka (*kalymafchion*). The latter worn without a veil may be worn by married priests and other secular clergy.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Pectoral Cross (Σταυρός, ὁ): In Greek Orthodoxy today, the Pectoral Cross is awarded only when a priest is elevated to the rank of Ikonomos; unlike the Slavic tradition, there is no distinction made between the various kinds of crosses.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **PECTORAL CROSS** (*Σταυρός, ὁ*; Slav. *nagrudny krest* / *нагрудный крестъ*): In modern Byzantine Greek usage, the pectoral cross is awarded only when a priest is elevated to the dignity of *Economos* (*Ikonomos*) or Protopresbyter; unlike the Slavic tradition, which establishes an ascending hierarchy of silver, gold, and jeweled pectoral crosses, Greek praxis does not distinguish separate classes of sacerdotal crosses.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: VESTRY (Σκευοφυλάκιον, τὸ or Ἱεροφυλάκιον, τό): The titles in Greek mean an area where the Vestments or Holy things may be kept protected. In the earliest history of the church, the SKEVOFILAKION was a separate building adjacent to the SANCTUARY in which these items were stored when not in use. When they were needed for the Liturgy, they were carried into the Church in procession. The Great Entrance of the Divine Liturgy of today recalls this procession.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **VESTRY** (*Σκευοφυλάκιον, τό* or *Ἱεροφυλάκιον, τό*; sacristy / Slav. *sosudokhranilishche* / *сосудохранилище*): These Greek designations signify the sacred depository where the sacred vestments, holy vessels, and liturgical implements are securely preserved. In early Christian antiquity, the *Skevophylakion* was a separate architectural annex erected adjacent to the sanctuary wherein these holy items were kept when not in use. When required for the Divine Liturgy, they were solemnly carried into the temple in public procession. The Great Entrance of the Divine Liturgy today mystically recalls that ancient transfer.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: VIGIL (Ἀγρυπνία, ἡ) Slav. Vsenoshnoe Bdenie: Watchfulness or vigilance; from the verb Ἀγρυπνῶ meaning to be ‘wakeful,’ ‘watchful’ or ‘awake,’ or ‘to be intent upon something.’ Hence, Ἀγρυπνία may be interpreted as ‘without sleep’ or ‘sleeplessness’ (Latin, invigilare). In Byzantine Orthodox practice, the All-Night Vigil follows Great Vespers including Liti and Artoklasia, Orthros, the First Hour, Third Hour, and Sixth Hour, and culminating with the Divine Liturgy. If the Divine Liturgy is celebrated immediately after any of the above offices, the First through the Sixth Hours may be omitted. The All-Night Vigil, because of its length, is not usually celebrated in the parishes; however, on major feast days, it is sometimes done. In monasteries, the service is commonly celebrated on Great Feasts and the patronal feast of the monastic community.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **VIGIL** (*Ἀγρυπνία, ἡ*; Slav. *Vsenoshchnoe Bdenie* / *Всенощное бдѣніе* / All-Night Vigil): Watchfulness, alertness, or vigilance; derived from the Greek verb *ἀγρυπνέω* (*agrypneo*), signifying to remain wakeful, watchful, or intently attentive upon a sacred duty. Hence, *agrypnia* denotes literally "without sleep" or "sleepless devotion" (Latin *invigilare*). In Byzantine practice, the All-Night Vigil comprises Great Vespers with the Liti and Artoklasia, Matins (*Orthros*), the First Hour, Third Hour, and Sixth Hour, culminating in the Divine Liturgy. If the Divine Liturgy is celebrated immediately following these offices, the First through the Sixth Hours may be omitted or recited separately. The All-Night Vigil, on account of its great length, is not customarily celebrated in ordinary parochial churches, though it is sometimes observed on major solemnities. In monasteries, it is regularly celebrated on Great Feasts of the Lord and the Mother of God, and on the patronal feast of the monastic community.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: the sanctuary and is the third section in the Orthodox house of worship. As the NARTHEX was historically the place of the penitent and the catechumens and the NAVE was the place of the faithful, the SANCTUARY is the place of the clergy. Although the penitent and the catechumens today find themselves integrated with the faithful in the nave, the sanctuary continues to be the place of the presbyters of the CHURCH.
units.english_cohort_translation: the Holy Table, the Prothesis (*table of oblation*), and the Synthronon, forming the third and innermost precinct in the traditional Byzantine temple. Just as the Narthex was historically the station of the penitents and the catechumens, and the Nave was the congregation hall of the baptized faithful, so the Sanctuary is the sacred precinct of the ordained clergy. Although penitents and catechumens in modern times stand integrated with the faithful within the nave, the sanctuary continues to be reserved unto the sacred ministers of the Church.

units.slavonic_incipit: The Vima is separated from the
units.slavonic_diplomatic: The Vima is separated from the NAVE by the IKONOSTASION or icon screen. Up until the 14th century a simple, waist-high railing, the TEMPLON, separated these places. Although it divides space in the house of worship, it serves a greater purpose of uniting humanity with the Divine. The people of God are united with the saints, the Theotokos, and the angels to offer up all glory to Christ.
units.english_cohort_translation: The Vima is separated from the Nave by the **Iconostasion** (*Eikonostasion* / icon screen). Up until the fourteenth century, a low waist-high marble chancel railing, designated the **Templon** (*τέμπλον*), separated these areas. Although the iconostasis physically partitions the sacred space within the temple, its mystical purpose is to unite humanity with the Divine: through the holy icons of Christ, the Mother of God, the angelic orders, and the saints, the earthly congregation joins in offering perpetual adoration unto the Holy Trinity.

Although it divides space in the house of worship, it serves a greater purpose of uniting humanity with the Divine. The people of God are united with the saints, the Theotokos, and the angels to offer up all glory to Christ.

cohort_provenance.verbatim_source: The Vima is separated from the Nave by the **Iconostasion** (*Eikonostasion* / icon screen). Up until the fourteenth century, a low waist-high marble chancel railing, designated the **Templon** (*τέμπλον*), separated these areas. Although the iconostasis physically partitions the sacred space within the temple, its mystical purpose is to unite humanity with the Divine: through the holy icons of Christ, the Mother of God, the angelic orders, and the saints, the earthly congregation joins in offering perpetual adoration unto the Holy Trinity.

units.slavonic_diplomatic: Regardless of the direction the local church faces, the sacred space remains an awesome place. No one should enter the Vima unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for a specific task. Clergy alone are meant to enter into the altar, and then only after the clergy have spiritually prepared to glorify God and serve among the angels who are ever present in this the ‘Holy of Holies’. As clergy, as laity, as catechumens, and as the penitent, we find our respective places within the structure of the Church. As we celebrate the Divine Liturgy from our place we are distinguished according to our roles within the priesthood of all believers and It is in these places that we both realize our stewardship to Christ, and “glorify God in every place of His dominion.” The raised platform in a synagogue, also known as a Vima, was the place from which the Pentateuch and the Prophets were read.
units.english_cohort_translation: Regardless of the physical orientation of a local church building, the sanctuary remains an awe-inspiring, holy place. None may enter the Vima unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for an assigned ministry. Sacred clergy and blessed servers alone may enter within the sanctuary, and only after preparing themselves with prayer to stand before the Holy Table and minister alongside the unseen angelic hosts who perpetually surround the Holy of Holies. While all the baptized participate in the royal priesthood of believers according to their respective orders, the sacred ministers execute their stewardship before Christ that all may "glorify God in every place of His dominion" (Psalm 102:22 [MT 103:22]).

units.slavonic_incipit: Today, the Ypakoi is the title
units.slavonic_diplomatic: Today, the Ypakoi is the title of a hymn sung during Resurrectional Matins. It varies according to the Mode of the week from the Oktoichos and comes after the Resurrectional hymns which are sung together with the refrain from Ps. 119: “Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your statutes” («Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά Σου.») The Ypakoi of Pascha is the one most commonly known.
units.english_cohort_translation: In contemporary liturgical usage, the **Ypakoe** is the title of the proper Resurrectional troparion chanted during Sunday Matins (*Orthros*). It changes according to the appointed Tone of the week from the Octoechos, occurring immediately after the Evlogitaria (*Resurrectional Troparia with the refrain from Psalm 118:12 [MT 119:12]*: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes"** / *«Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά Σου»*). units.english_cohort_translation: In the Greek language, *ypakoe* signifies "obedient hearing" or attentive listening (from *hypo*, under, and *akouo*, to hear). The designation indicates a musical and theological response, taking the form of a proper Troparion. Historically and rubrically, the Ypakoe is appointed: (1) at Sunday Compline; (2) at the Sunday Midnight Office; (3) at Sunday Matins before the Antiphons of the Tones and the Matins Gospel; and (4) after the Third Ode of the Matins Canon, taking the place of the Kathisma Hymn (*modified from APL*).

units.slavonic_incipit: In Greek the word ypakoi means
units.slavonic_diplomatic: In Greek the word ypakoi means “obedient hearing” The term suggests a response, which takes the form of a TROPARION. The Ypakoi is performed: (1) at Sunday Compline; (2) at the Sunday Midnight Service; (3) at Sunday Matins before the gradual antiphons and the reading of the Gospel; and (4) sometimes after the 3rd Ode of the Canon, in place of the KATHISMA HYMN. (modified from APL.)
units.english_cohort_translation: Furthermore, the Ypakoe serves as a short poetic strophe that replaces the third Kathisma hymn at Sunday Matins and upon certain Great Feasts of the Lord. In common parish praxis it is read rather than chanted. In Byzantine Greek usage it is also read during the Sunday Hours in place of the Kontakion. In strict Athonite monastic practice, it is chanted at the Divine Liturgy after the Dismissal Troparia (lit. "Apolytikia", *ἀπολυτίκια*) and before the Kontakia (*AE*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: ZONI (ζώνη, ἡ) Slav. Poyas: The belt or girdle surrounding the STICHARION and passing over the EPITRACHELION to hold it in place. The zoni is similar to the cincture in the Latin Church. The zoni stands for God's power with which the Priest has girded himself. (modified from the Byzantines.net: http://www.byzantines.net/moreinfo/vestments.htm.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **ZONE** (*Ζώνη, ἡ*; belt, girdle / Slav. *Poyas* / *поясъ*): The liturgical belt surrounding the Sticharion and securing the Epitrachelion in place. The Zone corresponds historically and functionally to the cincture of the Western Church. Symbolically, the Zone denotes the divine power and fortitude wherewith the sacred priest is girded for holy service (*modified from Byzantines.net*).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: *ZOODOCHOS PIGI (Ζωοδόχος Πηγή, ἡ) Lit. “life-containing fountain or spring.” This is the name given to a miraculous spring in the church dedicated to the Theotokos. The spring was erected in Eptapyrgos, near Constantinople, in the middle of the 5th century, during the reign of the emperor Leo the Great (called Makelis). The Orthodox Church commemorates the consecration of this sacred edifice every year on the First Friday of Easter.
units.english_cohort_translation: The **ZOODOCHOS PEGE** (*Ζωοδόχος Πηγή, ἡ*; Life-Giving Spring): Literally, "Life-Receiving or Life-Giving Spring." This is the feast and title bestowed upon the miraculous shrine and spring dedicated to the Most Holy Theotokos situated at Baloukli (*Eptapyrgos*) outside the walls of Constantinople. The sanctuary was originally founded in the mid-fifth century during the reign of Emperor Leo I the Great (*Makelles*). The Orthodox Church commemorates the consecration of this sacred shrine annually on Bright Friday (the Friday of Renewal Week following Pascha).

units.slavonic_diplomatic: 42. The Typikon of the St. Savvas (Sabbas) (439-532) Monastery, situated in the desert of Judea, was derived from the Typikon of Jerusalem consisting of rules and regulations handed down to St. Savvas by St. Efthimios (Euthymius) the Great (377-473) and by St. Theoktistos (+467), derived, in turn, from rules started and compiled originally by St. Chariton the Confessor (+350). The St. Savvas Typikon, destroyed during the destruction and desecration of the monasteries of Palestine, was assembled and reconstituted by St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem (550-638) and further reconstituted by St. John Damascene (+749). All of this information originates in Melkite Arabic sources. See the Melkite cybertyptypikon athttp://www.typicon.com/.
units.english_cohort_translation: 42. The Typikon of the Laura of St. Savvas (Sabbas) the Sanctified (439–532), situated in the wilderness of Judea, was derived from the ancient Typikon of Jerusalem consisting of liturgical ordinances handed down unto St. Savvas by St. Euthymius the Great (377–473) and St. Theoktistos († 467), which derived in turn from the ascetic rules established by St. Chariton the Confessor († 350). The monastic Typikon of St. Savvas, damaged and scattered during ancient devastations of the Palestinian monasteries, was collected and reconstituted by St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem (550–638), and subsequently reedited by St. John of Damascus († 749). These historical notices are preserved in ancient Melkite Christian Arabic sources (*see the Melkite Typikon portal at <http://www.typicon.com/>*).
